Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Oṃ bhūri svāhā!
When joined with the trident mudrā, this destroys all fevers.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
Oṃ nu re svāhā!
This knowledge-mantra named Tārāvatī is praised for all ritual actions.
When joined with the mudrā of the power-staff, it destroys obstacles.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
It is as follows: Oṃ vilokini svāhā!
This vidyā, named Lokavatī, brings all treasuries under one's control.
When joined with the vajra-mudrā, she bestows all happiness.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
It is as follows: Oṃ! O you who are universal, born from the universe, possessing universal forms! Kaha kaha! Enter, enter! Recollect the pledge!
"Ruru tiṣṭha svāhā!
This knowledge-mantra (vidyā) of great power has been revealed by the Leaders of the World;
when combined with the fang-seal (daṃṣṭramudrā), it enters into all beings as a weapon."
She is auspicious, the bestower of boons to all beings, and is proclaimed as Viśvā.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms!
It is as follows: Oṃ śvetaśrī vapuḥ svāhā!
When applied with the peacock-throne mudrā, this [mantra] accomplishes all activities.
Renowned as Mahāśvetā, she possesses inconceivable and wondrous form;
she brings about good fortune in the world and subjugates both men and women.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous.
Namely: Oṃ khikhi-rikhiri bhaṅguri, paralyze all enemies, strike them down, delude them, bring them under control, svāhā!
This vidyā is proclaimed as the Mahāvidyā Yoginī.
When joined with the seal of the mouth, it pacifies malevolent beings.
Homage to all Buddhas, who move with unimpeded gait.
It is as follows: Oṃ Śrīḥ!
This vidyā, Mahālakṣmī, was taught by the Lords of the World.
When joined with the *sampuṭa* mudrā, she bestows great sovereignty.
Homage to all Buddhas, who grant fearlessness to all sentient beings.
It is as follows: Oṃ! Ajite!
O you who have the form of a youth! Come, come hither!
Accomplish my purpose! Svāhā!
The maiden known as Ajitā, born from nectar,
when joined with the full mudrā, is the warder-off of all enemies.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
It is as follows: Oṃ jaye svāhā!
Svāhā to Vijayā!
Svāhā to Ajitā! Svāhā to Aparājitā!
Renowned as the Four Sisters, they are attendants of the Bodhisattva;
they wander throughout the entire earth, acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
Their brother, renowned as Stamburu, is their attendant.
Mounted upon a boat, they dwell within the waters;
when invoked with the fist-seal, they fulfill all hopes. (Mmk 2.17)
Homage to all Buddhas, the sovereign lords of the world.
It is as follows: Oṃ!

O Youth, Great Youth, play, play! O Six-faced One, authorized by the Bodhisattva, with a peacock-throne and hands raised by the Saṅgha, red-limbed, fond of red perfumes and ointments, kha kha, devour, devour, devour, huṃ! Dance, dance!
O you whose form is worshipped with red flowers, remember the pledge!
Wander, wander! Cause to wander, cause to wander, cause to wander!
Quickly, quickly! Do not delay! Accomplish all my tasks, accomplish them! O you who assume manifold forms, stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ! You who are authorized by all the Buddhas, svāhā!
When these words were spoken by the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, the Guide,
the entire earth shook in six ways in every direction.
For the benefit of all sentient beings and for the subduing of wicked beings,
the formidable son of Maheśvara has come here for the sake of those to be trained.
Skanda and Aṅgāraka were clearly marked by their planetary signs;
then Mañjubhāṣiṇī spoke with a mind permeated by compassion.
This Great Being is a Bodhisattva who acts for the benefit of the ignorant; since he is declared to be engaged in the conduct of a sentient being, he wanders everywhere throughout the world.
When joined with the staff of the power of the mudrā, that [mantra] of the Great-Souled One causes even those beginning with Brahmā to revolve; how much more so, then, the fruit for human beings?
This mantra of Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī has been proclaimed as a summary of the entire protective rite for children to be performed at dawn. Mmk_2.23 //
The Bodhisattva has come here with the desire to favor sentient beings;
the three-syllable heart-essence of this mantra has been proclaimed.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, one who is intent on attracting enjoyments should employ the mudrā of the power-staff; when properly applied, it accomplishes all ritual actions.
Oṃ hūṃ jaḥ.
This mantra, in brief, shall produce human results.
Homage to all Buddhas whose forms are universally radiant.
Oṃ vikṛtagraha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
And when its subsidiary heart-mantra is joined with the power of the mudrā,
it causes all beings— including the grahas and the mātṛs— to turn toward [the practitioner].
When applied to all the sealed mudrās, it becomes effective;
it terrifies malevolent spirits and liberates those possessed by evil influences. (Mmk 2.27)
This is the youth named Kārttikeyamañjuśrī, the attendant of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; he performs all rites by mere recitation,
and he terrifies and summons all spirits.
He brings under control,
withers, and destroys.
Or rather, it accomplishes everything for the vidyādhara according to his desire.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, Brahmā, Subrahmā, O you of Brahmic splendor, bring peace! Svāhā!
This mantra, the Great Brahma, was spoken by the Bodhisattva;
at that very moment, all beings attained peace and became cool.

The mudrā joined with five crests (pañcaśikhā) will swiftly bring about well-being; it is used in all rites of sorcery (ābhicāruka), or if it is not recited [in that context]. This ritual manual (kalpa) for it has been taught in brief, in summary.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ! You whose vehicle is the garuḍa, wielder of the discus, four-armed one, huṃ huṃ! Remember the pledge!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
Commanded by Mañjughoṣa, he who swiftly accomplishes the purpose and brings auspiciousness causes the spirits of embodied beings to flee, appearing in the form of Viṣṇu.

When joined with the three-crested mudrā, it is firm and swiftly accomplishes one's aims. Whatever extensive ritual manuals (kalpa) have been taught in the Vaiṣṇava tantras were spoken by Mañjughoṣa as skillful means for the sake of training sentient beings.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ, Great Maheśvara, Lord of Beings, Bull-bannered One, wearer of the crown of long, matted locks, whose form is greyed with white ashes, hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
This mantra has been proclaimed by me out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings;
when joined with the trident mudrā, it is the destroyer of all malevolent spirits.
Regarding that ancient eon which I previously described,
the beings dwelling upon the surface of the earth will say, "It was thus," for the various extensive qualities proclaimed by me in the Śaiva Tantra [shall endure].
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
It is as follows: Oṃ! O Śakuna, Great Śakuna, you whose wings are spread like a lotus, destroyer of all serpents, kha kha khāhi khāhi! Remember the pledge!
Huṃ! Stay!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
This mantra is of great power, renowned as Vainateya;
it is the supreme tamer of the difficult-to-subdue and the destroyer of the poison of serpents. (Mmk 2.34)
When joined with the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), it destroys most terrible misfortune;
there is no doubt that it neutralizes both stationary and mobile poisons. Mmk_2.35 //
To discipline beings through skillful means, that king of birds of great splendor roamed about in the form of a garuḍa at the command of the Bodhisattva.
All the extensive ritual manuals (kalpa) that have been taught in the Gāruḍa Tantra have been proclaimed by me alone for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
The Garuḍa Bodhisattva, having come here for the sake of Vainateya,
moved about in the form of a bird to destroy the poison of the serpents.
As many worldly mantras as there are, they have all been proclaimed in this ritual manual;
for the sake of training sentient beings, I move among them in such various ways.
However, those mantras of the Tathāgatas belonging to the Vajra and Jewel families have already been spoken previously in this extensive ritual manual.
Just as a nurse diligently caresses children in many ways,
so do I move among those of childish intellect in the form of mantras.
That which was taught by the Ten-Powered Ones in the past and is now spoken by me—
the entire meaning of mantra and tantra— has also been declared by the youth of great splendor.
Those which were sung by the supreme Jinas and sung by the sons of the Ten-Powered One,
those were sung by Mañjusvara, [the masters] of inconceivable and wondrous form.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having surveyed the entire Śuddhāvāsa abode and that great circle of the assembly, entered the samādhi called "The Exhortation of All Samayas.
Established in this samādhi, all sentient beings became established in the mental conduct that accomplishes the welfare of all beings without exception.

As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered [that samādhi], the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities became a maṇḍala adorned with a manifold array of various jewels and gems, a display of the inconceivable and marvelous miraculous transformations of a bodhisattva, which cannot be drawn as a maṇḍala even by bodhisattvas who have entered the conduct of all pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas,
nor even by those lords established on the ten stages.

How much more so for ordinary beings who, having seen Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta established in the state of the accomplishment of the divine, noble, and samaya-mandala, [would not be moved]— [seeing him] all the Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, all the noble Śrāvakas,
and all the Bodhisattvas?
Established on the ten stages,
having attained the consecration of the crown prince, and being noble ones who have entered the path— all beings, both with outflows and without outflows—
through the empowerment of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, [perceived] that inconceivable, special samādhi which arises from the mind and is the natural outflow of the conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
They perceived themselves as having entered the maṇḍala;
it is not possible even for ordinary beings to take that as an object of mind with their thoughts,
let alone to draw it or have it drawn.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
having entered into the samaya of that great assembly circle, addressed the beings:
Listen, worthy ones!
This commitment of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas is not to be transgressed;
how much less so for other beings, whether noble or ignoble?
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas:

"O Son of the Conqueror, you have explained the supramundane ritual procedure arising from the mind; now I shall explain the mundane procedure for those Tathāgatas who have entered final nirvāṇa, by entering which sentient beings may attain all mundane and supramundane accomplishments."
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Speak, speak, O Son of the Conqueror, whenever you deem it the right time!
For the peerless Lord of the World, the Lion of the Śākyas, has entered final nirvāṇa."
Just as Buddhahood [is the goal] for sentient beings, so is your mandala upon the earth.
For in this world, mere sight [of the practitioner] brings success to the mantras;
however, [success is lost] through ignorance, lack of ritual procedure, or by one who is lying down or in a state of mental derangement.
The mantras would not attain accomplishment even for the great-souled Brahmā himself,
if one is unpracticed in this tantra and has not seen the samaya proclaimed therein.
Mantras do not attain success even with repeated effort if they are devoid of the application of the samaya, even for Śakra himself despite his exertion.

Mantras do not attain success even on this human earth; how much less so for one who knows the reality of the *samaya*, the scriptures, and the principles, yet fails in the practices, rituals, and means of accomplishment?
For both noble and worldly mantras are accomplished merely by being recited.
Having entered the maṇḍala of Mañjughoṣa, one performs all rites;
for him, the accomplishment of mantras is certain within the very teaching of the Youthful One.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, spoke to that Mahāsattva in the midst [of the assembly]:
"O, O Mahābodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, speak briefly of the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala."
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Guhyakas, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke this ritual procedure for the maṇḍala for the benefit of all sentient beings:
"First, during the fortnight of the new moon, in the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha, in the bright fortnight,

on an auspicious day observed by pure planets, conjoined with a favorable constellation, on the first day of the waxing moon or the full moon— or at other times, excluding the months of the rainy season."
In the forenoon, the Maṇḍalācārya should take his stand upon the ground, having approached a great city where he himself resides, or having resorted to a river flowing to the ocean,

or near the shore of the sea; in the northeastern direction of the great city, neither too far nor too near, the Maṇḍalācārya should construct a secluded hut for seven days or for just a fortnight for the sake of sentient beings.
One should dwell there. In that place, one should prepare a very clean area of ground, square on all sides, measuring sixteen cubits or twelve cubits,
free from stones, gravel, ash, charcoal, husks, potsherds, and bones, and made very clean and well-prepared.

One should sprinkle that area of ground with water consisting of the five products of a cow mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron— or with water alone— over which the wrathful king Yamāntaka has been empowered eight thousand times and which is joined with the great mudrā of the Five Crests; one should cast it everywhere in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, across, and in the intermediate points.
Then, one should prepare that area of ground, square on all sides and measuring sixteen cubits, twelve cubits, or eight cubits;
among these, the sixteen-cubit is the superior (*jyeṣṭha*), the twelve-cubit is the middling (*madhya*), and the eight-cubit is the inferior (*kanyasa*).

This threefold mandala has been proclaimed by the All-Seeing Ones. For one desiring sovereignty, the superior is used; the middling increases enjoyment; and the inferior, which is merely for the observance of the pledge (*samaya*), accomplishes all rites.
Auspicious!
Then one should draw whichever mandala is desired by the mind.
There, one should dig that spot of earth to a depth of two cubits.
If various things such as stones, charcoal, ashes, bones, hair, or other kinds of living creatures are seen there,
one should dig in another spot of earth;
it should be free from harm and free from danger.

If he has not already done so, he should carefully examine mountain peaks, riverbanks, the shores of the ocean, the sands of great rivers, and heaps of sand, and having made that area of earth very clean and free of living beings, he should write there; furthermore, that spot should be filled with water free of living beings mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with pure clay from a riverbank, or with anthill-clay where no living beings are found.
Having filled it and smoothed it out so that it is level on all sides, one should have the threefold mandala constructed as desired.
One should drive four stakes of *khadira* wood into the four directions,
having consecrated them seven times with the King of Wrath mantra itself.
Having prepared a five-colored thread that has been consecrated seven times with the *krodha-hṛdaya* mantra, one should encircle that entire mandala on all sides in a square shape.
Likewise, one should cause it to be made square in the central area and similarly within.

Standing in the central place, the mandala master should recite the root mantras eight thousand times; having bound the great mudrā of the five crests (*pañcaśikhā*), he should perform protection for his companions and protection for himself by means of the root mantra.
And it should be performed as follows:

while reciting [the mantra], having circumambulated the entire mandala which has been cleared of all impurities, one should sit facing east upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, keeping in mind all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and surround that mandala on all sides with a square-shaped enclosure.
Having made her stay outside for one night, he should cause her to be banished.

In that regard, the mandala master— having completed the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*), being skilled in the independent mantras, devoted to the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings through skillful means,

having fasted for one night, and accompanied by good companions— should, by means of the ritual action seen in the procedural treatises, consecrate that powder with the six-syllable mantra and the heart-mantra; the powder should be five-colored, fine, radiant, well-prepared, and thoroughly processed.

One should place [the image] in the center of the mandala. Outside, one should prepare the site of the earth adorned with raised banners, flags, and archways at the four crossroads, with clusters of fruit-laden plantain trunks suspended from them, and made to resound with the sounds of beaten bherī drums, mṛdaṅga drums, conchs, and lutes.
He should recite from books placed in the four directions Mahāyāna sūtras that are conducive to the fourfold assembly and consist of the hearing of the dharma of excellent sounds;
namely, he should recite the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā* in the southern direction,
and the *Āryacandrapradīpasamādhi* in the western direction.

One should request a Dharma-preacher, a person who has studied the four sūtras— the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha* in the northern direction and the *Āryasuvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra* in the eastern direction— in the absence of a physical book.

Then, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, the Maṇḍala Master should rise and scatter white fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron all over that maṇḍala while reciting the root mantra; having scattered them, he should go outside.

After seven days, he should admit two or three highly skilled painters who have subsisted on sacrificial food (haviṣyāhāra), who have been established in the vow of fasting, who have generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and who are accustomed to the Upoṣadha fast.
Having bound the topknot with the root mantra itself,
one should then take a copper vessel adorned with five kinds of brilliant and beautiful fine powders made of gold, silver, and various jewels;
it should be caused to be written by beings of great fortune and by righteous great kings.
It is directed toward awakening, tending toward awakening, and certain [of it].
If such is the case merely by seeing the maṇḍala, how much more so when accomplishing the mantras?
For sentient beings of little merit, once the Bull of the Śākyas has passed into nirvāṇa. (Mmk 2.50)
"How could such enjoyments as these exist? This must surely be the work of destiny.
Thus did Mañjughoṣa, of great splendor, reflect upon seeing the poverty of the people.
One should proclaim the summary of the ritual manual and the maṇḍala in brief:
one should color it with fine powders of śāli rice, radiant with five colors— white, yellow, red, black, and green.
The Maṇḍala Master himself should take the powder previously set aside,
form the five-crested Mahāmudrā, and seal that powder while reciting the root mantra.
Meanwhile, another practitioner-master should have a fire-pit constructed outside the maṇḍala in the southeast direction, according to the ritual procedure.
Measuring two cubits in width and one cubit in depth, shaped like a lotus bud on all sides, with an outer perimeter also shaped like a lotus bud;

having kindled a fire there with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, one should summon [the deity] by forming the *mudrāmuṣṭi* and offering fuel-sticks of *śrīphala* wood— one *vitasti* in length, moist, and smeared with curd, honey, and ghee— while reciting either the root mantra or the six-syllable heart mantra.
And having summoned [the deity], one should again offer oblations one hundred and eight times with that very same previously mentioned single-syllable root-mantra-heart.
Then the mandala master, having bound the uṣṇīṣa and prepared his equipment, should himself or have highly skilled painters execute [the work].

Then the mandala master, keeping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind, should offer incense with the previously mentioned incense mantra; having joined his palms in *añjali* and bowed to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having paid homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, he should take the powder and draw [the design].
The painting should be filled in by artists.

According to this procedure, one should first paint the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni, endowed with the excellence of all attributes, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, teaching the Dharma. Once it has been painted, the assistant of the maṇḍala master, having performed the ritual for self-protection with the root mantra, should offer a bali-offering to all spirits and cast it out in the four directions, above, below, and outside the maṇḍala.

Then, having bathed and gone near the fire-pit, being pure and clothed in clean garments, and having performed the protective rites, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee mixed with saffron while reciting the root mantra.
Thereafter, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and performing the recitation, one should remain right there.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds eight times with the wrathful king Yamāntaka, one should place them in a pair of shallow earthen bowls (*śarāva*).

Upon seeing any kind of obstacle that has arisen—such as a storm of wind and rain with various distorted forms and terrible sounds—one should offer seven oblations of mustard seeds with clarified butter (*huta*).
Thereby, the obstacles will perish.
Or, if there are obstacles caused by humans, five oblations should be offered.
Men become paralyzed and powerless, or they die;
or else they are seized by non-human beings at that very instant—of this there is no doubt. Even Śakra would somehow die quickly.
How much more so will humans with evil minds,
or other obstacles, flee here and there, utterly destroyed by the fear of the wrathful Yamāntaka?
Then the assistant practitioner, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass in that very place, should remain performing the recitation of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.
Then, the Maṇḍala Master should depict two Pratyekabuddhas seated upon lotus thrones in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) on the right side of the image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni;
beneath them, two great Śrāvakas should be depicted listening to the Dharma.
To their right is the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white as an autumn reed, seated upon a lotus throne,
holding a lotus in his left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right hand.
To his right is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī, holding a lotus in her hand and [touching] the Blessed One with her right hand.
Bowing to Śākyamuni, seated upon a lotus throne, wearing a crown of matted hair, clothed in white silk garments, with a silken upper robe, and marked with three circles of black ash—
thus should Tārā and Bhrukuṭī be depicted, each well-established in their respective seats and postures.
And above them is the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā,
Tathāgatalocanā, and the Uṣṇīṣarāja, each performing their respective functions.
In this way, sixteen bodhisattvas are to be visualized, namely:
Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, and so forth.
Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha Maitreya,
and [the one] with a yak-tail whisk in his hand.
Gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One,
Vimalagati and Vimalaketu—
Sudhana, Candraprabha, Vimalakīrti,
The healer of all diseases, the sovereign king of all dharmas, the course of the world, and the one of great intelligence.
And Patidhara—
these sixteen great bodhisattvas, with serene forms and adorned with all ornaments, are to be painted;
[as is] the preeminent Vidyārāja.

The Vidyārājñī is the form-seal (rūpaka-mudrā) upon a lotus pedestal; she and the remaining [deities] should be drawn in their respective places according to tradition and scripture. Finally, in that place, one should establish a square-shaped area adorned with lotus flowers.
"By which [mantra] the deity of the vidyā has been remembered, may they abide in this place."

Thus, on the right side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there are two Pratyekabuddhas, namely Gandhamādana and Upāriṣṭa. In this manner, the mandala should be made facing east, with an entrance door on all sides.
Beside the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two other Pratyekabuddhas, namely Candana and Siddha, are to be depicted.
Below them, two great Śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and Mahākātyāyana, are to be depicted.
To their left, the noble Vajrapāṇi is to be depicted, with a complexion dark like a blue lotus, of serene form, and adorned with all ornaments.

With his right hand holding a chowrie and his left hand in the form of wrath, [he is accompanied by] Vajramuṣṭi, Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Subāhu, and Vajrasena, each with their respective dress, emblems, positions, and seats, together with all the vidyārājas and vidyārājñīs and their retinues; they should be depicted in their forms, mudrās, and so forth, according to tradition.
To the left of those as well, one should draw a square-shaped double-vajra mudrā; and having drawn it, one should say:
"Those groups of vidyās who are not remembered here in this place,"
The hosts of vidyās are remembered here by their respective positions;
may they remain here in this place.
Above them, the goddesses Pāramitās and Māmakī are to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments and possessing serene forms.
Above them as well, the eight Uṣṇīṣa Kings, surrounded by garlands of all-pervading flames, should be depicted;
their respective seals and the forms of great universal monarchs (cakravartin) should be drawn,
golden-hued, with serene faculties, and adorned with every ornament.
The Tathāgata likewise slightly [perceives] those born with the view of a reflected image,
namely: the universal monarch (cakravartin) and the uṣṇīṣa.
Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa.
Kamaloṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa.
Therefore, these Uṣṇīṣarājas should be painted to the left of the Pratyekabuddhas;
at the door, the Buddha and the Bodhisattva should be depicted, and to the right of the entrance, one named Lokātikrāntagāmin, wearing a crown of matted hair, with a serene form,
holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left, facing toward the door.
With a face slightly frowning, at the entrance on the left, the great bodhisattva named Ajitañjaya should be depicted.
Of serene form, wearing a crown of matted locks (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), with a staff and water-pot resting in his left hands,
holding a rosary in his right hand and making the gesture of granting boons (*varapradāna*), he should be painted facing the door with a slightly frowning countenance.
Beneath the lion throne is the Wheel of Dharma, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides;
beneath that as well is a jeweled celestial palace,
wherein resides the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, in youthful form, with a complexion as fair as saffron.

With a serene form and a beautiful appearance, his face slightly smiling, his left hand holding a blue lotus, and his right hand bestowing boons while grasping a *śrīphala* fruit; adorned with all the ornaments of a youth and graced by five locks of hair (*pañcacīra*); wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a silken upper garment, and clothed in silk raiment; possessing a universal radiance, surrounded on all sides by a garland of flames, he is seated upon a lotus throne.
The wrathful king Yamāntaka, with his gaze fixed upon the entrance to the mandala, should be depicted facing the door of entry, beautiful to behold from all sides.

On its right side, beneath the lotus, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be depicted, possessing a greatly distorted form, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, awaiting his command, and with his gaze fixed upon the Great Bodhisattva;
he is to be painted everywhere [on that side].
On the left side, beneath the lotus, five Bodhisattvas in the form of sons of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be depicted.
Namely: Sunirmala (Extremely Pure), Sudānta (Well-Tamed), Suśānta (Perfectly Peaceful), Saṃśuddha (Completely Purified), and Tamodghātana (Dispeller of Darkness).
And it is called Samantāvaloka.

All of them are seated in the abodes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods; they have the appearance of stone surfaces blazing with many jewels, are strewn with various flowers emitting light on all sides, and are beautiful in form as if depicted in a painting.

Outside, on all sides, an inner mandala should be constructed in a square shape with four archways (toraṇas) facing the four directions, blazing with various five-colored hues and bound by well-proportioned lines. In the eastern direction, above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in the center of the lines, there should be a small-sized image of the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
Seated cross-legged.
To its right, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin mudrā should be drawn;
to its left, the Tejorāśi mudrā should be drawn;
and above Tathāgatalocanā, the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā should be drawn.

Above the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara, to the right of the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā, the Blessed One Amitābha should be depicted in the form of a Tathāgata, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varapradāna), seated upon a lotus throne, and surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.
To the right of that as well, the mudrās of the bowl and the robe should be made.
In this same sequence, lotus mudrās should be made at the entrance.
Or, according to the intention of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja, the Uṣṇīṣatejorāśi mudrā should be drawn, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.

To his left, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu should be depicted, seated upon a mountain of jewels, teaching the Dharma; he should be painted with a universal radiance emanating from all sides amidst variegated flames and rays of blue beryl, emerald, and ruby.

To his left as well, the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, should be depicted. To his left as well, the Dharmacakra mudrā, possessing flames on all sides, should be depicted.
To his left as well, the khakharaka, the water-pot, the rosary, the water-pot, and the Bhadrapīṭha mudrā should be depicted.
In due order, at the location of the door, a vajra-needle with flames on both sides should be drawn all around.

Below the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, either the great mudrā named Pañcaśikhā or the utpala mudrā should be drawn. These two, possessing flames all around, should be drawn joined to one another in the form of a complete mandala.
From the door, one should enter facing west, and [the practitioner] should be made to face east.
In all cases, there is an outer mandala, radiant with five-colored pigments, variegated and beautiful to behold.
It should be divided into four corners and shaped with four archways (*toraṇa*), to be drawn outside the inner maṇḍala which measures two cubits on each side.

In the eastern direction is Mahābrahmā, four-faced, dressed in white garments, wearing a white upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); he is golden-hued, wears a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), and holds a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
With his left hand resting upon her.
To his right, the son of the gods Ābhāsvara is to be depicted, golden in color, with a form absorbed in meditative concentration (dhyāna).

He is dressed in silk garments, with a silken upper cloth; his face is very serene, he wears a crown of matted hair, a white sacred thread, and is seated in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), granting boons with his right hand.

To his right, the god Akaniṣṭha is to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, of serene form, his mind absorbed in meditation; he is clothed in silk garments, wears a silken upper robe, and sits in the paryanka posture to the right, granting boons with his right hand and wearing a white sacred thread.
In this same successive order:
Santuṣita, Sunirmita, and Paranirmita.
The sons of the gods, beginning with Suyāma and Śakra, are to be depicted in successive order, adorned according to their respective attire.
Below Śakra, the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods—namely the Sadāmattas, Mālādhāris, Karoṭapāṇis, and Vīṇādvitīyakas—are to be depicted.
Furthermore, the terrestrial sons of the gods (bhauma-devaputras) are to be painted in their proper order and according to their respective attire.

In the same way, in the southern direction, the deities Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Parīttābha, Puṇyaprasava, and so forth, should be depicted as sons of the gods, arrayed according to their respective attire and positions.
In this manner, they should be depicted in rows of two below them in the western and northern directions.
Outside the second maṇḍala is the third maṇḍala;
there, the four Great Kings are to be depicted in succession in the four cardinal directions.
As he enters from the northern direction, there is Dhanada on the right,

appearing in the form of a yakṣa, adorned with all ornaments, standing near a treasure, and wearing a slightly bent crown. To his right, the two yakṣa generals Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra are to be depicted.

In this manner, Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī, should be depicted in due order. The youth Priyaṅkara, seated upon her lap and gazing at the maṇḍala, should be depicted. Pañcika, Piṅgala, and Bhīṣaṇa should also be depicted.
And near them, the seals (mudrās) of the yakṣas should be drawn.
In this same sequence, Varuṇa, with a noose in his hand, should be drawn in the western direction;
and the two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, as well as the eight great nāga kings beginning with Takṣaka and Vāsuki, should be drawn.

In this manner, those residing in two rows should be depicted in successive order: yakṣas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and ṛṣis; siddhas, pretas, piśācas, garuḍas, kinnaras, humans, and non-humans; as well as medicinal herbs, various kinds of precious gems, mountains, rivers, and islands—all these principal beings should be drawn in succession. In the southern direction, Yama should be depicted together with his retinue.
The seven Mothers are in the southeastern direction.

Agni is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides; his hands are occupied with a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary; he wears a crown of matted hair, is clothed in white garments, has a silk upper robe, and a white sacred thread;
he is golden-colored, marked with three lines of ashes.
In this manner, they should be painted arranged in two rows according to their specific differences in weapons, attire, posture, complexion,
and essential nature. On the outer circle, entering from all sides, is Umāpati, who rides upon a bull and holds a trident in his hand.
And the goddess Umā, golden-hued and adorned with all ornaments;
and Kārttikeya, seated upon a peacock, with a spear raised in his hand, possessing the form of a youth, six-faced, with a body of reddish luster,
clothed in yellow garments, with a yellow upper garment, holding a bell in his left hand and a red banner, followed in succession by Bhṛṅgiriṭi.
One of extremely emaciated form; Mahāgaṇapati, Nandikeśvara, and Mahākāla; the Seven Mothers, to be depicted according to their respective ornaments, weapons, attire, and postures;
the eight Vasus;
and the seven Ṛṣis.
Viṣṇu has a discus in his hand, four arms, and holds a mace, a conch, and a sword; he is seated upon Garuḍa and adorned with all ornaments.
[There are also] the eight planets and the twenty-seven lunar mansions.
In those mandalas upon the earth where they move, the eight subordinate deities are to be drawn in successive order, as well as the fifteen lunar days (tithis) of both the bright and dark fortnights,
the twelve zodiac signs, the six seasons, the twelve months, and the year.

The four sisters, with their brother as the fifth, who dwell in the waters— these deities should be briefly established within the mudrās; they should be depicted in two rows in succession, based on the three mandalas, with the pitṛ-maṇḍala as their support,
and the shape should be square.
This arrangement applies to all three mandalas as well.
In brief, the Buddha, the Blessed One, must certainly be depicted at the head of all sentient beings.
In the Lotus family, the noble Avalokiteśvara must certainly be depicted to the right.
On the left, Vajrapāṇi must certainly be depicted in the Vajra family;
at the head of the Bodhisattvas, the noble Samantabhadra must certainly be depicted;
and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta must certainly be depicted.
This very [deity] is to be depicted among the mudrās according to their established arrangement.
Within this inner maṇḍala, in the middle maṇḍala as well, Brahmā Sahāmpati must certainly be depicted in the eastern direction;
likewise, Ābhāsvara in the southern direction.

The Akaniṣṭha gods and the formless (arūpin) gods are circular in shape and unmanifest; likewise the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In the northern direction, Śakra, king of the gods, along with Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, and the sons of the gods beginning with Parīttābha—each one of these kings of the gods must certainly be depicted;
this is how they are to be established among the seals (mudrās).
Likewise, in the third mandala, in the northern direction, Īśāna, the lord of spirits, must certainly be depicted together with Umā.

Near the second gate, Kārttikeya Mañjuśrī should be drawn, seated upon a peacock, holding a spear in his hand, his form radiant with a reddish glow, dressed in yellow lower garments and an upper robe, with a bell and a banner attached to his right hand; having the appearance of a youth, he gazes toward the mandala.
In the eastern direction, Vainateya in the form of a bird and the sage Mārkaṇḍeya must certainly be depicted;
these two should also be established among the mudrās.
To the southeast, the four maidens together with their brothers, the Kumāras, should be depicted situated upon a boat, wandering about the great ocean;
and Agni, the king of the gods, must certainly be drawn there.
Likewise, in the southern direction, the city of Laṅkā and Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [should be drawn].
Stationed there, resting upon a *picumanda* tree, the Bodhisattva in the form of a yakṣa named Jambhalajalendra must certainly be depicted.
In this manner, proceeding in due order, King Yama, possessed of great supernatural power over the hungry ghosts (preta), must certainly be depicted;
likewise, the Piśāca king named Vikarāla must certainly be depicted.
This is how they are to be established among the seals (mudrās).

In this manner, in the southwestern direction, the two chief nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, must certainly be depicted. In the western direction, the chief of planets, Āditya, and the excellent sage named Kapila Muni— the bull among the Nirgrantha Tīrthaṅkaras— should be shown in the form of a Nirgrantha, arranged in successive order.
This very [deity] is to be established among the mudrās;
and in the northwestern directions are Dhanada, the king of the yakṣas,
and Pañcaśikha, the king of the gandharvas.
Druma, the king of the kinnaras—
these must certainly be depicted;
they are to be drawn in their proper places, arranged in sequence according to the seals (mudrās).

The fourth maṇḍala is outside, consisting of five lines, adorned with mind-seals (mudrās) and garlands; it is square, shaped like four archways (toraṇas), and embellished by the Four Great Kings stationed in their respective order. As for the seals: in the front region, a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is to be drawn; to the right and to the left are a lotus, a vajra, an axe, a sword, a spear, a trident, a mace, a wheel, a svastika, a vase, a fish, a conch, an earring, a banner, and a flag.

One should surround the square perimeter with a garland of various types of weapon-mudrās, such as the noose, bell, double-headed staff, bow, iron arrow, and mallet; beyond this, in the four directions, the four great oceans are to be established.
In the northern direction, having made a square-shaped mandala, one should place a triangular-shaped mandala that is three-pointed, consisting of two vajras, and surrounded by flames on all sides.
In the southern direction, having made a bow-shaped mandala, one should place a bowl emitting flames on all sides.

In the western direction, having made a mandala in the shape of universal radiance, one should place a blue lotus complete with its stalk and leaves, emitting flames on all sides; and in the intermediate directions, there are four mudrās.
In the northwestern direction, having made a circular mandala, one should place a noose emitting flames on all sides; and in the southwestern direction...

Having made a long-shaped mandala in that direction, one should place a staff with flames on all sides; having made a triangular-shaped mandala in the south-western direction, one should place an axe with flames on all sides; and in the north-eastern direction, one should place a sword with flames on all sides.
"Having drawn [the lines] on all sides," means that at the time of the door-seals, three [seals]—above, below, and across—are to be drawn outside the maṇḍala using colored powders alone.
Namely: the vajra, the fan, and the sandals; these, blazing on all sides, are to be depicted.
This procedure for the mandala has been taught here in brief by the wise Mañjughoṣa, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings. Mmk_2.53 (=“52”)
Then, the mandala master should first of all accept as disciples those who have unimpaired faculties and beautiful limbs;
who are Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras; who have generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and follow the Mahāyāna; who are by nature devoid of longing for other vehicles;
who are great beings (mahāsattva), faithful, and possessed of virtuous qualities; who desire great sovereignty, loathe meager enjoyments, and are intent upon great wealth.

They were auspicious, disciplined, and virtuous— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who remained steadfast in their observances, established in the vows of the *upoṣadha* fast, free from hatred toward the great bodhisattvas, born into the lineage of great yakṣas, naturally practicing the Dharma, having fasted for a day and night, clad in clean garments, with fragrant hair, bathing three times a day, and observing silence.

On that day, those who possess the fragrance of camphor, saffron, and cloves from their mouths, who have constantly performed ritual ablutions (*upaspṛśita*), who sit upon bundles of *kuśa* grass, who have performed the rites of protection (*rakṣāvidhāna*), who are celibate (*brahmacārin*) and truthful—these should be stationed not too close to the maṇḍala.
They must be pure and very clean; there should be eight or more, down to at least one, and no others.

And those Kṣatriyas who were consecrated as great kings were not mutually connected [by kinship], nor were their sons—the princes and princesses—acquainted with the ways of the world. The Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who takes the form of a youth, was the cause; for he is the awakener of ignorant people and is devoted to the play of a youth.
Therefore, he appeared first of all. (Vaidya 33)
In this way, the youth should be led inside.
O Great King, for one who desires the increase of longevity, health, and sovereignty, and especially the increase of enjoyments, the accomplishment of mantras for children is established as certain.
Having performed this preliminary rite, accompanied by good companions and remaining vigilant, the Maṇḍala Master should then go out from behind the circle while burning camphor incense.

Having gone forth, one should bathe and perform ritual sipping with water that is appropriate for the season and has been consecrated eight hundred times with the root mantra while sealed with the five-crested great mudrā; then, being pure and dressed in clean garments, one should go to the fire-pit, sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing northeast, and offer eight thousand oblations mixed with camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.

Having summoned [the deities] and dismissed them again according to the previously mentioned rite, one should re-enter the maṇḍala. Having entered, one should present eight full vases— adorned with clean cloths and decorated with mango sprouts, their interiors filled with gold, silver, jewels, and grains of rice— one to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
The second is for all the Buddhas;
the third is for the entire Saṅgha of Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas;
the fourth is for all the Mahābodhisattvas.
The fifth belongs to the noble Mañjuśrī, the Great Bodhisattva;
the sixth belongs to all the gods.
The seventh and eighth are to be placed in the door-chambers of the second maṇḍala.
Clad in clean garments,
one portion is for all spirits;
the second portion, dedicated to all sentient beings, should be set aside as common property.

Then, burning incense according to the very procedure previously described and forming the great mudrā with five crests (mahāmudrā-pañcaśikhā), one should again perform the invocation of all the Buddhas and all the Pratyekabuddhas.
One should invoke the noble disciples, the great bodhisattvas, all spirits, and all sentient beings, as well as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
In this manner, one should present flowers, incense, perfumes, lamps, and food offerings according to the very ritual previously specified.
One should perform these for all [deities] in every respect, in proper succession.
By the mention of "lamps," one should offer lamps of ghee.

Having offered to all— both noble and non-noble— by means of receiving the consecrated food (nivedya), one should present to the Tathāgatas everything including rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with curd, special honeyed milk-porridge (madhupāyasa), cakes baked with ghee specially prepared, aśokavartī, sugar-candies, and other delicacies. One should also present to all the Pratyekabuddhas, Noble Śrāvakas, Great Bodhisattvas, and Noble Deities offerings such as clarified butter (havis), śrīveṣṭa, honey-heads (madhuśiras), and various milk-prepared foods.

In this manner, one should offer the aforementioned specific ingredients for the cakes (*laḍḍuka*), which serve as the materials for the sacrificial cakes (*pūpa*), along with all the hosts of gods and spirits and all sentient beings, empowered by mantras according to the ritual procedure. Likewise, one should offer fragrant flowers— such as *jāti*, *tagara*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *punnāga*, and so forth, as previously specified— to all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Noble Śrāvakas, and Great Bodhisattvas, whether they be noble or ordinary.

Specifically, the *jātī* flower is for the Tathāgata family, the lotus for the Padma family, and the blue water-lily for the Vajrapāṇi [Vajra] family; for other mantras, a different one is used, such as camphor incense for the Tathāgata family and sandalwood for the Padma family. Guggulu resin is likewise recommended for the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Vajrī himself.
One should offer incense to all mantras other than these; one should cause clarified butter lamps to be given to all noble mantras,
and one should cause fragrant oil to be given to the non-noble mantras,
according to the sequential procedure and for the reasons previously observed.
In the same way, it is taught that [fragrance] is always [superior] among all mantras.
Whatever has been proclaimed by Avalokita and whatever has been proclaimed by Vajrapāṇi,
regarding the accomplishment of the purpose of mantra practice in their respective tantras—
all those should be seen here in this ritual manual and always followed.
Thus [it is said].
Then, the mandala master, having performed the rites of invocation, worship, incense offering, and the presentation of food offerings according to the previously observed procedure,
the skillful assistant, acting with haste, should then offer the meatless *bali* for all spirits in every direction.

Resounding with the sounds of drums, conchs, and the joyful cries of the *nandī*, and adorned with incense, flowers, lamps, and garlands, one should circumambulate the outer maṇḍala in all directions—

north, south, east, west, the intermediate points, above, below, and across— and having offered all the sacrificial materials, one should perform eight thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

For one who offers oblations with the heart of the six-syllable root mantra, [there are] those great beings previously established for entry into the mandala, for whom the rites of protection have been performed, who have accepted the status of disciples under the mandala master, who have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), who observe the upoṣadha vows,

who have offered their own bodies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who share in the enjoyments of sentient beings for the sake of accomplishment, and who are skilled in ascending to the seat of unsurpassed awakening (anuttarabodhimaṇḍa).
For those who desire to attain the Buddha-knowledge of omniscience, they are liberated from all sins merely by seeing the maṇḍala;
even those people who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution are liberated at that very moment.

Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having covered the faces of those wishing to enter the maṇḍala with a cloth that is unwashed, extracted from the Tantra, free of hair, consecrated seven times with the root mantra, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood and saffron,
[should first cover] those from sixteen years of age down to three years of age, adorned with five locks of hair or adorned with a single lock.
One should cause a prince who is consecrated as a king, or a son of a Kṣatriya, or another person of great energy desiring a great kingdom, to enter— either adorned with a topknot or even headless.
Having wrapped the face of one situated in the second mandala and having formed the utpala mudrā,
one should recite the root mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once.
Having had fragrant flowers prepared and offered them,
one should have the flowers cast with clean hands mixed with sandalwood and saffron;
then, one should give him that mantra upon which his flower alights.
It is proclaimed as one's own mantra;

it is that very [mantra] which follows him through his succession of births, and it is that very [mantra] which acts as his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of fulfilling the knowledge of the Great Bodhisattvas as he proceeds toward the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It is that very [mantra] which is to be accomplished by him.
He also brings about association with individuals of great wealth, great sovereignty, and great renown.
In this very life, without deliberation, success is achieved in all rites.
Thus, for those desiring accomplishment, one should proceed in due order, beginning with one and continuing up to eight, but not others.

For the sake of others who wish to exhaust their sins, it may suffice as a mere ritual commitment (*samaya*). Thus, the mandala master, while bestowing the consecration, should first consecrate and purify with mantra a plot of ground in the northeastern direction outside the mandala, neither too far nor too near; then, regarding himself as one being consecrated to kingship, he should be one who has single-minded faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

One who is faithful, possesses great enthusiasm, is never separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), follows the Mahāyāna, is a benefactor of the Three Jewels, has unimpaired faculties, is not blameworthy in this very life, desires to accomplish the mantras, has a noble disposition, is intent on the practice of mantra, is curious by nature, seeks to know for the sake of inquiry, and whose mind is focused on the meaning of the mantras without conceptualization— such a person, beginning with one and up to as many as there may be, should be consecrated.
"Those to be served and those to be avoided," "the wise and those of unerring conduct"—
by these [criteria], the remainder are to be consecrated.
Nor for others.
Then, having gathered all the requisites as if for a royal consecration, or whatever else might satisfy the preceptor,
[the disciple] proceeds while a white parasol is held over his head and white yak-tail whisks are fanned [upon him], with canopies spread out and banners and flags raised high.
Being honored with great ceremony— being praised with the sounds of the word "Nandi," conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and shouts of victory,

as well as with auspicious verses and verses of benediction spoken by the Jina— he circumambulated that mandala, bowed to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and prostrated his head at the feet of the preceptor.

And it should be spoken thus: "In order to enter into the accomplishment of the mantra-practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, O Ācārya; in order to enter into the secret maṇḍala of liberation that transcends all worldly things; in order to attain Buddhahood through entering into the sovereignty over all dharmas—in short, it should be said: 'May I become a Buddha!'"
Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing the east, having caused [the disciple] to tie five tufts of hair (*pañcaśikhā*), one should cause him to recite the mantra.

Then, whichever mantra he prefers should be written with *gorocanā* on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*). Having written it, one should smear both hands with sandalwood and saffron, and likewise the hollowed-out pair of earthen bowls (*śarāvasampuṭa*). Then, that birch-bark leaf, placed inside the pair of earthen bowls, [should be offered] to the Bodhisattva...
It should be placed at the base of the feet.

Then, having sat down there, one should recite the root-mantras of the vidyā one hundred and eight times. Prior to that, however, he who is to be consecrated should be seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
The preceptor, taking the full water-jar—which was previously placed near the entrance and belongs to all sentient beings in common—should sprinkle him on the head while reciting the root-mantra.
The remaining [offerings] may be performed with water as one desires.
Then that vessel-cover should be given to him alone;
and he should be made to recite it by means of a lamp.
If she herself is the mantra, it will be accomplished through effort in due course.
Alternatively, another [practitioner] achieves success through the mere recitation of the mantra.
Furthermore, even if the mantra is given with syllables deficient or redundant, one achieves success at the very first practice; this is certain when free from doubt.
This very [mantra] previously written by the Teacher succeeds effortlessly when performed with the three means of accomplishment.

Thus, one should first bestow the Knowledge Empowerment (*vidyābhiṣeka*). For the second, the Mandala Empowerment, one should consecrate [the disciple] with that full vase which was offered to all the deities in the second mandala.
Or, by means of that very same procedure as previously described for the crown of the head, one is liberated from all transgressions.
One is authorized by all the Buddhas and becomes unimpeded in all worldly and supramundane samaya-mandalas and in the accomplishment of all mantras and mudrās.
Thus, [the master] should bestow the master’s initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka) by all the Bodhisattvas.

In the third mandala, one should consecrate [the candidate] on the head with a full vase offered to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, according to that same ritual procedure. It should be said: "You are authorized by all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power to write, recite, teach the mandala, explain the mantras, tantras, mudrās, and conduct, or to practice and instruct yourself in all worldly and transcendent mantras."
In this very life, and throughout successive lifetimes until the very last one, Buddhahood is to be attained with certainty.

Likewise, during the consecration of Jaya and Vijaya, according to the previously prescribed rite, he was consecrated with the full vase offered by the Blessed One Buddha and the full vase offered by the Bodhisattva;
and with that same full vase, he was consecrated in the very same manner.
And thus it should be said: "You have been authorized by all the Blessed Buddhas, by the Great Bodhisattvas, and by the Śrāvakas."
Invincible to all beings, unconquered by all embodied ones, may you be victorious over all mantras; accomplish whatever you desire.
Then, by the mandala master, the five empowerments should be bestowed upon each individual according to their desire; indeed, all [disciples] should receive exactly five.
Then, having led her into the mandala in due order and having offered her to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should circumambulate the mandala three times to the right and dismiss her.
On the day following that, she should be instructed in due order and appointed to the practice of mantras.

At that very moment, taking the full jar that had previously been offered by the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, one should have those who have entered the maṇḍala face the east and drink three handfuls of water from it.
And they should be told: "O, do not transgress this secret pledge (*samaya*) of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta."
"Do not produce much demerit.
Furthermore, no mantras should be rejected,
and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas must not be deceived.
The guru must be propitiated;
otherwise, there would be a transgression of the samaya,
and the mantras would not attain accomplishment.
"There would be great merit.
Thus they should be dismissed.
Then the Maṇḍala Master should again offer oblations of *śāli* rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using the eight-syllable heart mantra.

Then, having risen and entered the center of the maṇḍala, he should offer the *arghya* to all [the deities] with the previously mentioned flowers according to the previously stated ritual, while mentally visualizing them.

With the very same incense as mentioned before, he should [worship] all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas, and all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, yogins, siddhas, and ṛṣis.
Having incensed all sentient beings and scattered flowers over them, one should sprinkle them with water scented with sandalwood and saffron.
One should dismiss them according to the very procedure previously described.
"Liberation from all [fetters] occurs through the mind. Thus it is said.
Then the mandala master should cause the offerings, the sacrificial cakes (*bali*), and the ritual powders to be all washed away in a river,
or they should be given to suffering living beings.
Having made the area of ground well-swept, well-sprinkled, and beautifully adorned, it should be smeared with cow dung.
It should be washed away with water, or smeared with very clean clay, or covered with sand; once this has been done, one may go wherever one pleases.
Those who have entered the maṇḍala must subsist on a diet of milk-rice or sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Thus concludes the second chapter, the Instruction on the Ritual for the Maṇḍala, from the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, the Great Sovereign of Ritual Manuals (*Mahākalparājendra*), from the *Mañjuśrīkumārabhūtavikurvaṇa*, the Extensive Section on Bodhisattvas.
(Vaidya 37) Now begins the third chapter:
(The Chapter on the Ritual for the Mandala).
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having again gazed upon that palace of the Pure Abodes and having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assembled in the great circle of the assembly,

spoke the single-syllable mantra— the supreme secret, the destroyer of all poisons, the performer of all rites, the means for accomplishing one’s own mandala, and to be employed in all minor activities. And what is it?
Homage to all Buddhas!
It is as follows: *Jaḥ*.
This noble sage and the hosts of all spirits should apply this second mandala ritual for this very single-syllable mantra in brief.
Having purified an area of ground measuring eight cubits or four cubits, one should draw it oneself using powders of five colors;
it must not be drawn by others.
Whether in this place or that, there is no fault in doing so.
First, one should draw a square mandala, equal on all sides and adorned with three concentric circles, featuring the great five-crested mudrā.
One should also draw the blue-lotus mudrā, the fang mudrā, the vajra mudrā, and the staff mudrā of the Blessed Mañjuśrī.
These mudrās are to be drawn in the eastern sector of the inner mandala.

Then, at the base of the outer gate, one should have drawn figures in the form of a lotus, a vajra, a blue lotus, a banner, a flag, a parasol, an archway, a chariot, an elephant, a horse, a bull, a buffalo, a svastika, a peacock, a goat, a ram, and a young man;
they should be drawn in successive rows, resting upon the three circles, and should be executed in this manner.
Then, with the one-syllable mantra itself, the fire-ritual (agnikārya) should be performed in the southeastern direction.
One hundred and eight oblations of apāmārga wood, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, should be offered.
Thereafter, an arghya offering of flowers should be presented.
With the single-syllable mantra alone, one should offer the bali, the food offering, and the lamp as desired;
or one may offer incense, and perform the rites of invocation and dismissal.
Then, one who desires sovereignty should be led into the middle of the city and [the mantra] should be written there;
one who desires food near a *vaṭa* tree; and one who desires a son near a *putrañjīvaka* tree.
One who is childless and desires elephants or horses [should be placed] in an elephant stable or a horse stable;
one bitten by a snake [should be placed] in a great lake or a temple of the Nāgas;
and those suffering from quartan fever, constant fever, or any other fever [should be placed] at a solitary liṅga or in the southern direction of the village.
One seized by a *rākṣasa* should be treated in a cremation ground or an empty house; one seized by a *piśāca* near a *vibhītaka* tree or an *eraṇḍa* tree;
and those seized by the *mātṛs* at crossroads or near a house where there is a death or birth impurity.
If one is possessed by a *brahmarākṣasa*, [the patient] should be placed under a palm tree or a *śleṣmātaka* tree;
for one who has administered poison, water should be consecrated seven times with the single-syllable mantra itself and poured right there in the center of the mandala, and he shall be liberated.
In this manner, for a woman or a man seeking fame, it should be drawn at a crossroads or in a sacred precinct (*brahmasthala*).
For a woman whose children have died, it should be drawn at a fruit-bearing tree or a milky sap tree;
for a woman who is childless, it should be drawn in the midst of a field where rice grain is being cultivated.

In cases of various diseases caused by women or by malevolent spirits, when one is afflicted by a great illness on boats and the like, a rite for the destruction of *rakṣas* should be inscribed on a riverbank, a shore, or a mountain peak;
this applies in all respects to all diseases.
Even those [rites] performed by ḍākinīs [should be done] in a temple of Brahmā, an empty house, a secluded place, or a low-lying area.
Thus, for all rites, one should draw [the mandala] at midnight or at midday, or at any time.
Having offered water for honor (arghya) with flowers using that very same single-syllable mantra, and having dismissed [the deities], the mandala should be flooded with water.
Great protection is afforded to all who are ill.
One is liberated from all diseases and one's desired aims are accomplished;
a sonless man obtains a son, and the unfortunate becomes fortunate. (Mmk 3.1)
Upon merely seeing the maṇḍala, even a poor person—
whether woman or man, and whether faithful or following ritual practice— shall always obtain wealth in various forms according to their desire. Mmk 3.2.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Ritual for the Mandala, from the *Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-mūla-kalpa*, an extensive section of the *Bodhisattva-paṭala*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Homage to the Buddha, and to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Then Mañjuśrī, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities,
and having again looked upon that great assembly gathered in the maṇḍala, prostrated at the feet of Śākyamuni.
With a smiling countenance,
he addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would grant this extensive chapter on the rain-cloud of Dharma— the outflow of the performance of the rites for accomplishing the practice of mantras— which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings and produces desired fruits."

It is the source of unsurpassed merit, the producer of the seed of perfect enlightenment, the producer of the complete knowledge of the omniscient one; in brief, it fulfills all aspirations, is correctly joined with the fruits of all mantras, brings them to fruition, and unfailingly accomplishes the goal for the practitioner.
It fulfills all the practices of a bodhisattva; it is the donning of the great armor of a bodhisattva, which overcomes and turns back the entire host of Māras.
May the Blessed One, out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings, please speak of that.
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One Śākyamuni said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you have set out for the benefit of many people and out of compassion for the world, thinking it right to question the Tathāgata on this matter."
Listen to that well and thoroughly;

take it to heart, for I shall speak to you. I shall explain to you, in due order, the entry into the practice for the accomplishment of all sentient beings through the expansion of the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), as previously taught by all the Tathāgatas;
I too shall now speak of it.
First of all, in a clean area of earth free from dust, those beings who have entered the pledge (*samaya*) should take cotton and purify it.
Having purified it, the mandala master should consecrate it with this mantra one hundred and eight times:
"Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose movement and course possess unimpeded intelligence!"
Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, the King of Kings who purifies and pacifies suffering.
It is as follows: Oṃ, purify, purify! O destroyer of all obstacles, O Great Compassionate One, who assumes the form of a youth!
Manifest, manifest!
Remember the pledge! Stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Then [he should select] a maiden who has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, born of a brahmin family, a kṣatriya family, or a vaiśya family—

not from one of excessively dark complexion nor from a low-caste origin— whose limbs are unimpaired and beautiful in every part, approved by her mother and father, who observes the *upoṣadha* fast, has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), is compassionate, fair-complexioned, and free from any other [inferior] complexion.

In brief, on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, when observed by white and favorable planets, in a pure location free from smoke, odors, dust, and wind, one should bathe the previously designated maiden who possesses the most excellent marks of female characteristics;
having dressed her well in clean garments, she should be clothed in purity.

Having performed protection endowed with the Mahāmudrā by means of this very mantra, one should stir white sandalwood and saffron with water free of living organisms; then, while the girl drinks it, one should sprinkle her with that same mantra for purification.
Furthermore, one should scatter white sandalwood and saffron water in the four directions.
Thus, having combined white sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, one should first cause [the offering] to be given above, below, and in the intermediate directions;
or one may give it oneself, or have the practitioner-teacher (sādhakācārya) give it.
Thus, one should speak these words three times: "May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, preside over this cloth-thread.
Then those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great bodhisattvas will attend to it.
While burning incense at that time, various auspicious birds— peacocks, curlews, swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and others, whether moving on water, on land, or through the air—
should pass by or utter auspicious cries;
this should be recognized by the practitioner.
Fruitful is this action of mine; it has been empowered for me by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and by the great Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, that cloth and thread are well-lived for me in this birth; my accomplishment of the mantra is not in vain.
There may arise the sounds of drums, kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, lutes, flutes, small drums, and large drums—or, as Vaidya reads, the sound of the mouth.

Or they might speak thus out of delusion: "At that time, victory! Success! Accomplished! Given! Bestowed! Take! Prosperity! Fruitful! Like Śakra! Or others might utter such auspicious words, or there might be the sound of bells, or the sound of a drum of joy.
Then the vidyādhara should know:
"This is the empowerment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great bodhisattvas; it is not otherwise, for its accomplishment is never fruitless."
Then, at that time, as they utter cruel cries— words such as "Seize!", "Eat!", "Make him eat!", "Lost!", "Perished!", "Misfortune!",
"Far away!", "Very far!", and "It does not exist"— and as the sounds of monkeys, buffaloes, jackals, donkeys, cats, and other loathsome two-legged and four-legged animals should issue forth,
the practitioner should then know: "I shall have no success."
In this very life, he should be brought to an end;
or else, having performed the preliminary service again, one should begin once more,
repeating this up to seven times.
Even for one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, success is achieved upon the seventh application of the ritual action.
Then the practitioner, having performed the protection ritual for that maiden, should have her sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
Having established her facing either the east or the north, he himself should consume sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and he should feed that girl sacrificial food as well.
Upon that very bundle of *kuśa* grass previously prepared, he should have her spin the cotton according to this procedure.

Having gathered that well-spun white thread from a girl previously instructed, one should prepare a highly praised number of strands—starting from eight, five, three, or one, up to sixteen *mātrās*, *palas*, or *karṣas*.
For a medium [rite], there should be eight *gāthās*; for others, five or one, according to one's ability, in the case of minor rites to be accomplished.
The knower of mantras should perform [this] in all ritual actions.
From that time forward, whatever evil deed was previously committed perishes at that very moment, provided one does not doubt the meaning of this Sūtra. Mmk 4.1.
Having collected this sūtra, one should place it in a clean vessel;
indeed, one should not wrap it in thread and then fumigate it with camphor incense.
Or [an image] produced from non-living materials, such as saffron, sandalwood,
and the like, and honored with fragrant flowers such as jasmine and campaka.
Having established [the image] in a clean place, secured with protective rites and a covering,
the knower of mantras, skilled in all rituals, having performed his recitation, remains well-composed.
Then, having gone to a weaver and given him the desired price,
[one should obtain] one who is free from physical defects, not emaciated, and always devoted to pure dharma.
One who is not afflicted by disease, not aged, and free from cough and asthma;
one who is free from cough and asthma, not impotent, and born of a true womb.
Blameless and free from physical deformities, devoid of lameness or paralysis, endowed with all the auspicious marks, praiseworthy, and beautiful to behold. (Mmk 4.7)
One who desires accomplishment should request such a person— whose conduct is characterized by pure intellect and who follows worldly livelihood— for the weaving of an excellent cloth.
They are praised for their auspicious color; they are intelligent and well-trained, being the most excellent and supreme among those skilled in the art of weaving cloth.
One should perform the highest rites with the best [substances], the middling rites with middling means;
with others, one performs minor and inferior actions in every respect.
Then, having paid the craftsman his price according to what the craftsman says at the first utterance of his speech, that knower of mantras [should act]. Mmk 4.11.
Then one should quickly bestow the merit; this is called "heroic purchase.
And by the mere request of this [mantra], the reciter becomes a partaker of merit.
For this supreme, unsurpassed cloth-painting brings swift accomplishment;
it performs all rites, is worthy of worship, and bestows divine and human happiness. It is for the welfare of all beings and was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One. (Mmk 4.13)
Thus [it is said].
Then, the vidyādhara, having administered the *poṣadha* vows to the weaver, at an auspicious lunar mansion during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*),

on a bright day under the gaze of favorable planets— or at another time during the bright fortnight— at that most excellent season, the springtime when the mango trees were in full bloom and abounding with the finest flowers and clusters of blossoms;
at that very time, when the sun had risen in the forenoon, [he summoned] the weaver previously designated.

Having ensured that [the practitioner] eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), is clothed in clean garments, has his head bound with a turban, is well-bathed, and is well-anointed— his limbs smeared with either white sandalwood or saffron, his face scented with camphor, his mind joyful, and his hunger and thirst dispelled— one should everywhere wash the vessels and all implements such as ropes with clay and cow dung, and repeatedly wash the new ones with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having washed it with water free of living organisms,
one should sprinkle it with white sandalwood and saffron.
On a pure spot of earth, free from clamor, devoid of people, in a secluded seat that is serene, protected, and honored with flowers;

Then the practitioner, having consecrated white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times with the purification mantra itself, should scatter them in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, and in the intermediate directions. Then, having struck the weaver with the mustard seeds and having bound the great five-crested mudrā,
One should perform the binding of the topknot;
thus great protection is established.
If it is the supreme cloth-painting, one should have it woven by a weaver to these dimensions: four cubits in width and eight cubits in length.
The medium [size] is two cubits in width and five cubits in length;
the smallest is one Sugata-span in width and one thumb-cubit in length.
In this context, the span of the Blessed Buddha—measured by the hand of a man of middle stature—is proclaimed as "the Sugata-span."
By this measure, its authoritative validity is declared.
"Arise! The supreme accomplishment has been proclaimed by the leaders of the world;
for those desiring sovereignty, it is in the middle [period], while the other is for the sage who has attained invisibility. (Mmk 4.14)
For men who desire great enjoyments, as well as for gods, asuras, and bhogins, success is declared in the lowest [grade]; in the middling [grade], middling success is attained. (Mmk 4.15)
Minor rites are always accomplished on a small cloth;
indeed, all tasks and all substances are always accomplished [therein]. (Mmk 4.16)
The accomplishment taught for the three types of cloth is for men who seek the highest good;
if one deviates from the prescribed rules, it will not be achieved even for Śakra, the lord of Śacī.
In this way, all rites are accomplished quickly and without effort,
even for one who has been born three times, provided they are joined with the prescribed ritual procedure.
This path has been fully proclaimed by the Victors and the sons of the Supreme Victors,
for the welfare of all beings who are poor, protectorless, and suffering.
Indeed, the entire path to enlightenment has been shown by those who perceive reality;
this path, which is the cause of enlightenment, has been revealed through the way of mantra.
The mantras of all worldly maṇḍalas are accomplished without effort,
and even those supramundane maṇḍalas that have been described are accomplished.
Success shall always belong to those whose minds are set on the cause of enlightenment;
success is not said to belong to others who are always harmful to the world.
Success is always proclaimed for those beings who have set out for enlightenment,
and especially so here for the high-souled Mañjuśrī Kumāra.
In order to accomplish his task swiftly, he shall obtain everything here;
thereafter, the artisan should diligently weave the cloth in the proper sequence.
In sixteen days, or in five, eight, twelve, or four days,
or indeed in a single day and night, the weaving of the cloth is swiftly completed.
For those desiring the highest accomplishment, it is indeed better [to practice] day and night;
the artisan, endowed with purity and proper conduct, must remain constantly focused.
Having gone a distance of one *āvarta* from afar, one should void urine in a hut;
then, having bathed with one's clothes on and having put on other garments, [one should proceed].
Wearing white garments and adorned with garlands, having repeatedly performed ritual ablutions,
and having anointed his limbs with white sandalwood paste, he should rub the hands of the artisans.
One should weave it further with effort, always smooth and well-knit;
by means of such applications or others spoken by the Jina.
One who is reflective and diligent should complete the weaving of the cloth without exception; once the cloth is finished, it is said that the preliminary rites have been performed. (Mmk 4.30)
