When the time is measured and the ritual is not deficient, one should perform [the rite] on an auspicious day;
then, during the most beautiful bright fortnight, one should cause it to descend through the tantra.
Having taken the clearly manifested cloth, its fringes bound and beautifully adorned,
and having secured the cloth upon a bamboo staff, one should then depart.
Having provided for the welfare of the artisan with extensive distributions of gifts,
the mantra-practitioner, well-conducted and firm in his vows, may go wherever he desires.
Having worshipped it with fragrant flowers, one should place it in a clean location,
having performed protection and established a seal with this very mantra.
With that very same cotton, having first purified it in many ways,
one should perform the protection of both oneself and the cloth.
The great hero Mañjuśrī has been spoken of in the form of a mantra by many past [Buddhas], and by me as well, now and again.
He alone wanders as all mantras, taking the form of mantra;
he is of great heroism and great splendor, the accomplisher of the purpose of all mantras.
The beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, whose conduct and intentions are deluded, perform three kinds of diverse acts that serve as causes for protection.
But those who lack faith, who are the opposite [of the faithful], who follow false conduct, and who are full of greed,
do not indeed accomplish the mantras nor any of the ritual substances.
For this very reason, they wander in the dark prison of saṃsāra;
whereas he whose mind is always pure, who is faithful, and who is ever intent upon auspicious rites and wonders, [is liberated].
Always eager in the grasping and retaining of all mantras, those great-souled ones desire accomplishment; they possess great energy and great splendor.
For them, the mantras spoken by the Jina will ultimately succeed;
however, for beings who lack faith, the white dharma does not take root.
Just as a seed sown in saline soil produces no sprout,
so too has it been said by those who see all things that faith is always the root of the Dharma;
for those who are devoted to the purpose of the Dharma, the accomplishment of mantras is always proclaimed.
Thus it is said.
Then, for the purpose of accomplishment, artisans, or a well-trained painter, or one who is himself skilled, should be commissioned to paint [the image].
Taking a pigment that is entirely radiant, endowed with color, and free from clinging to the limbs, one should proceed according to the same ritual as before;

by means of a painter who possesses the required characteristics and follows the very same procedure as a weaver, the detailed description should be carried out extensively, just as the previous ritual for the weaver was.
That very cloth should be painted upon;
or it may be painted by oneself.
It should be perfumed with camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and other such substances.

Having recited that same mantra eight hundred times while burning incense, and having scattered over that cloth flowers such as *nāgakesara*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, *campaka*, *vāpīka*, *dhānuṣkārika*, and *mālatī*, he should paint the cloth while facing east, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, with a composed mind, his thoughts directed toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
holding a fine brush in his hand, and with a mind free from effort.
First of all, one should draw the Tathāgata Śākyamuni,
endowed with the excellence of all aspects, marked by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics,
seated upon a jewel-lotus, blazing with light on all sides, beautified for a fathom in every direction, and teaching the Dharma in person.

One should depict Nanda and Upananda, who have serene forms, are endowed with the excellence of all marks, and stand at the center of a lotus with a beryl stem; below, the two naga kings, white in color and adorned with all ornaments, having human heads and half-serpent bodies, should be drawn holding that lotus stalk while gazing at the Tathāgata and paying homage with their right hands.

And all around that lotus-shaft, it should be depicted as filled with lotus leaves, flowers, buds, blossoming aquatic plants, and creatures such as birds and fish, with every form beautifully arranged and exquisitely lovely;
from that very root-lotus stalk of the Blessed One, many lotus flowers have emerged, gradually increasing in height, with eight lotus flowers on the left side.
And upon those lotuses, the forms of eight great Bodhisattvas are to be depicted.

First, Ārya Mañjuśrī: slightly pale like the filaments of a lotus, or the color of saffron-gold; having the appearance of a youth, in the form of a young boy; with five locks of hair on his head; adorned with the ornaments of a youth; holding a blue lotus in his left hand.

With his right hand paying homage to the Tathāgata, possessing a beautiful form, his gaze fixed upon the Tathāgata, with a gentle appearance and a slightly smiling face, surrounded by a circle of blazing, awakened jewels; on another lotus, the noble Candraprabha Kumārabhūta should be depicted in the same manner;
and on the third, Sudhana.
In the fourth [bhūmi] is Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; in the fifth, Gaganagañja;
in the sixth, Kṣitigarbha.
In the seventh [birth] he was Anagha,
and in the eighth, Sulocana.

All these should be depicted in the form of young boys, adorned with the ornaments of youths. On the right side of the Blessed One are the eight great bodhisattvas, all adorned with every ornament; however, excluding Maitreya, the noble Maitreya is near the Blessed One, wearing the attire of a celibate student (brahmacārin), with his head bound by a crown of matted hair.
Golden-hued, wearing saffron-colored robes, with a red cloth as an upper garment, marked with the triple sectarian streak (*tripuṇḍra*), possessing a physical form,
with his left hand resting upon a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and holding a rosary in his right hand which rests upon his left shoulder over a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇasāracarma*),
he pays homage to the Tathāgata, his gaze fixed upon him, his mind and conduct absorbed in the object of meditation.

On the second lotus, Samantabhadra is to be depicted in this same manner: dark green in color like the priyaṅgu fruit, his body adorned with all ornaments, his left hand holding a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇiratna), and his right hand holding a śrīphala fruit while granting the boon of charity; he is of beautiful form.

In the third [panel], there is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), with the omniscient one (Amitābha) placed upon his head. He sits with the noble Amitābha resting against the edge of his matted locks; he is of beautiful form, holding a lotus with a fly-whisk in his hand, while his right hand is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). His mental activity is focused on the object of meditation, and his body is illuminated on all sides.

In the fourth [panel], there is the noble Vajrapāṇi, golden-colored, adorned with all ornaments, holding a vajra in his left hand; his right hand is raised in the boon-granting gesture while grasping a fruit; he is of beautiful form, gentle in appearance, and his body is draped with necklaces and half-necklaces.

Ārya Avalokiteśvara should likewise be depicted wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a crown shimmering and variegated with jewels, and clad in a lower garment of fine silk with a white silken upper robe; Samantabhadra, on the other hand, should have his body draped in the attire of a *tīrthika* with a lower garment and an upper shawl, their forms and appearances as previously described.
Likewise, in the fifth lotus is the noble Mahāmati; in the sixth is Śāntamati;
and in the seventh is Vairocanagarbha.
And the eighth is Apāyajaha. These are the Bodhisattvas who are to be depicted;

they have their hands placed upon fruits and books, are beautifully adorned with all ornaments, wear upper garments of silk cloth, are decorated with every kind of ornament, and are dressed in silken lower garments.
And above them, eight Pratyekabuddhas are to be depicted;

they wear the robes of monks, possess bodies endowed with the marks of a Great Man, are clad in saffron-colored garments, and sit cross-legged upon jeweled stones. They are serene in appearance, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, and strewn with fragrant flowers.

For example— one should paint a celestial palace (*vimāna-maṇḍala*) adorned with the king of mountains, appearing like a mountain covered with precious stones and fashioned from many jewels, which is being strewn on all sides with flowers such as *mālatī*, *vārṣikā*, *dhānuṣkārikā*, *puṇṇāga*, and *nāgakesara*; it should be depicted above the noble Mañjuśrī on the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
One should depict eight Blessed Buddhas situated therein, as follows:

[the Buddha] whose light radiates everywhere for a fathom’s width, shimmering with jewels such as the crest-jewel Ratnaśikhi, Vaidūrya-prabhā, Padmarāga, Indranīla, and Marakata, as well as Vaidūrya, Aśmagarbha, and other such extraordinary great maṇi-jewels, blazing forth on all sides.

One should depict the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, whose body has the color of the rising sun, wearing a yellow upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and a yellow lower garment (*nivāsita*), seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) and teaching the Dharma; his body is armored with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), his form is adorned with the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), he is serene in appearance, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, and is the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin.
Second, one should depict the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, golden in color, profusely strewn with flowers such as nāgakeśara and bakula;
he should be depicted gazing toward the Noble One, possessing universal radiance, and surrounded by a halo shimmering with the luster of jewels.
One should depict the third Tathāgata, Śālendrarāja,
with the luster of lotus filaments, teaching the Dharma.
One should paint the fourth Tathāgata, Sunetra,
just like this Duḥprasaha;
the sixth is the Victor Vairocana.
The seventh is Bhaiṣajyavaidūryarāja;
the eighth, one should paint the Tathāgata Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanarājendra.

All the forms of the Tathāgatas should be depicted as having a golden complexion and with hands in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*). Above the Tathāgatas, situated within the clouds at both corners of the cloth, two divine sons (*devaputra*) belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be painted, releasing a rain of flowers.
Standing in the atmosphere, they should be depicted paying homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.
And to the north of the Pratyekabuddhas, eight great Śrāvakas are to be depicted, seated in subordinate positions below the heads of the Bodhisattvas.
They are as follows: the Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, Nanda, Bhadrika, and Kaphiṇa.
The Pratyekabuddhas were as follows: Gandhamādana, Candana, Upariṣṭa, Śveta, Sitaketu, Nemi, and Sunemi.
All of them were exceedingly beautiful, dressed in peaceful attire, and possessed a most self-controlled appearance.
The great śrāvakas also, with palms joined in reverence, gazed upon the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Above them, two other sons of gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven stood nearby, holding long, beautiful, and auspicious silk canopies on all sides;
they held these above all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble śrāvakas, wearing divine garlands and garments.
Two sons of gods (devaputra) are to be depicted.

Above the head of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, one should paint a cluster of jeweled threads woven with pearl necklaces, gems, rubies, sapphires, and so forth; upon that, a canopy of silk (paṭṭavitāna) is well-arranged, adorned on all sides by hanging pearl necklaces.

And below the lotus seat of the Buddha, the Blessed One, near the feet of Noble Mañjuśrī and beside the Naga king Upananda, there is a great jewel mountain rising from a lotus lake, encircled by jeweled sprouts, caves, ravines, and coral creepers;
it is a tree of jewels frequented by great sages and perfected ones. Upon the lofty peak of that mountain is Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.
Of most terrible form, holding a noose in his hand and a staff grasped in his left, with a frowning face, he receives the command;

his gaze is fixed upon Noble Mañjuśrī; he has the belly of a wolf, hair standing erect, and resembles a black cloud of crushed collyrium; his tawny beard is long and formidable, his nails are long, and his eyes are red; his neck is adorned with snakes, he is clothed in a tiger skin, and he is the destroyer of all obstacles.
One should depict the Great King of Wrath Yamāntaka, who is exceedingly terrible, blazing all around.

Below that mountain, one should depict the practitioner seated upon a stone slab on the ground with his knees bent; his hands occupied with an incense burner, wearing the appropriate attire and bearing the characteristic marks, his gaze fixed upon Noble Mañjuśrī whose conduct he follows.
He should be depicted near Nandana, the king of the nāgas, and below the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
On the right side, one should depict the Great King of Mountains of Precious Jewels rising from a lotus lake, as described;
one should depict it free from the wrathful king Yamāntaka and strewn with divine flowers.
One should depict the noble Avalokiteśvara upon that mountain.
One should depict that mountain, which is as high as a peak and composed of rubies, with its summit shaped like a single sprout of lapis lazuli; and resting upon it,
one should paint the Noble Lady Āryāvalokiteśvara’s Compassion, the Noble Tārā, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a jeweled silk scarf as an upper garment and variegated silk robes,
her entire body embellished with feminine ornaments, and holding a blue lotus in her left hand.

[One should visualize] the Noble Avalokiteśvara, who is golden-colored, with a slender waist, neither too thin nor too young, nor too old; his consciousness absorbed in meditation, awaiting a command; his body slightly bent forward, his right hand in the *varada* (boon-granting) gesture; seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*); with his gaze turned slightly away [from the goddess];
and surrounded on all sides by a garland of flames, he is situated right there upon that peak of lapis lazuli gem, encircled by *punnāga* trees.

Upon the branches, one should paint the Blessed Lady Tārā, covered by fully blossomed flowers arranged all around; she should be depicted as looking toward the face of the goddess Tārā, who is herself adorned with that very [tree] whose branches are removed, entwined with sprouts and shoots, and radiant with various beautiful colors.
One should draw the auspicious goddess, the destroyer of all obstacles, the supreme dispeller of fear,
who grants boons, for the sake of protecting the practitioner.
The Goddess who assumes a female form, born of the Compassionate One who possesses the ten powers,
the bestower of boons for the welfare of all beings, should be depicted.
Here, the mother of the youth Mañjughoṣa, of great splendor,
[is present] for the sake of destroying all obstacles for the practitioner on every side.
For the protection of lords of men and for their ultimate welfare, one should place that Lord of Wrathful Kings, who stands upon the mountain peak, upon a cloth-painting. (Mmk 4.47)
It was taught by the sons of the Supreme Victors for the destruction of all obstacles;
it is most formidable, highly venerable, exceedingly fierce, and of great splendor.
It is intended solely for the subjugation of beings who are hostile toward the teaching;
furthermore, it serves to protect the practitioner and destroy all obstacles.
Terrible and wrathful by nature, he is the mantra-deity who, when invoked,
is most fearsome and of horrific form, the restrainer of all those devoid of compassion.
And he brings under his control those who are otherwise unsubdued, even those who act with sin and cruelty—
whether they move through the sky, upon the earth, or throughout the netherworld.
It destroys all those who are wicked and hostile toward the teaching of the Sage;
one should indeed paint the cloth as a square with four corners on all sides. Mmk_4.52 //
And at the bottom edge of the cloth, one should depict the abode of the vast ocean,
with the bodies of the nāgas coiled around it on every side.
Born with a body in human form, possessing white and auspicious limbs,
one should always place her with her head toward the north and join one's palms in reverence.
Seven-faced and of great heroism, renowned as the Great Lord and known by the name Ananta,
he gazes upon the Tathāgata, adorned with precious jewels.
One should draw the renowned great king of nāgas, who is exceedingly beautiful, of lovely form, adorned with jewel ornaments, and garlanded with flames.
One who is dedicated to the welfare of the entire world and has entered the teaching of the Sage should draw [the deity] situated upon a river for the destruction of all obstacles.
This supreme procedure for the cloth-painting, spoken by the Jina,
has been described both briefly and in detail, as previously taught by the Tathāgatas; indeed,
the merit of that wise person who paints it is infinite.
Whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed over ten million eons perishes at that very moment upon seeing the cloth-painting on the ground.

One should not withhold the painting even from those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, those of immoral conduct, those who are loathsome, those engaged in every kind of evil, those wandering in the darkness of saṃsāra, or those of the most degraded destinies and births.
The sight of this cloth, spoken by the Lord of Sages, is fruitful for them;
merely by seeing it, they are instantly liberated from that evil. (Mmk 4.61)
How much more so, then, will humans attain accomplishment, being of pure conduct, possessing perfectly purified conduct, and being ever-diligent in the attainment of mantra-siddhi? Mmk_4.62 //
Whatever merit is gained by all sentient beings through making offerings for ten million eons,
that same merit a practitioner of mantra obtains on this earth by painting the cloth mandala.
As many grains of sand as are said to be in the Ganges,
so many would be the Buddhas and the noble sons of the Pratyekajinas.
In this world, practitioners who possess the sword, having conquered [obstacles] in many ways,
shall obtain that fruit as mortals through the vision of the painted cloth.
Merely by reciting it, or by honoring it, or even by rejoicing in it,
the accomplishment of the mantra for that person is certain, as are all the rites prescribed therein.
Whatever worldly mantras have been spoken by the preeminent Jinas,
by their disciples, by those possessing the sword of wisdom, by the divine ones, and by the great-souled Bodhisattvas—
all those mantras are indeed accomplished in the presence of the foremost cloth-painting.
From the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the fourth [chapter],
the first detailed exposition on the ritual procedure for the cloth painting (*paṭavidhāna*), is completed.
The Fifth Chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that entire circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Mañjuśrī, there is yet another procedure for your medium-sized cloth painting (*paṭavidhāna*).
I shall speak of it;
listen, and attend to it well and thoroughly.

First of all, by means of the very same thread previously specified, according to the very same procedure previously described, and by artisans previously selected, one should have that central cloth made with the same measurements as before— using a very beautiful, white, well-woven, new cloth free from stains, animal hair, and refuse such as hair— exactly as it was done at first; however, excluding the actual proportions and forms, that cloth should subsequently be caused to be painted.

First of all, one should depict the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, which is beautiful in its entirety, appearing as if composed of radiant jewels, and adorned with white pearl necklaces; in its center, the Blessed One Śākyamuni should be painted, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, teaching the Dharma, endowed with all the supreme marks.

On the right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, with the luster of a lotus filament or the color of saffron and the sun; on the region of his left shoulder he holds a blue lotus, his hands are joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjalipuṭa*), and he gazes at the Blessed One Śākyamuni with a slightly smiling face. He has the form of a youth, his head is adorned with five locks of hair, he is decorated with the ornaments of a young child, and his head is bowed toward the circle of his right knee.
And on the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, is to be depicted exactly as previously described;

however, with a fly-whisk being waved beside the Blessed One, [the following should be depicted] at his side: the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmati, Śāntamati, Gaganagañja, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
These should be drawn in successive order;
just as the first one is, so too should all of them be painted adorned with every ornament.

And above them, eight Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are to be depicted standing, with their right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*), their bodies draped in yellow upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*), their left hands holding the corner of the robe, wearing well-fitted saffron lower garments with a slight reddish luster, possessing all-around radiance, and endowed with the excellence of all marks.
Namely: the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, Ratnaśikhin, Śikhin, Viśvabhuk, Krakucchandaka, Bakagrīvin, Kāśyapa, and Sunetra.
These Blessed Buddhas are to be depicted in this manner.

On the right side, near the Blessed One and Āryamañjuśrī, the great assembly maṇḍala should be depicted. The eight great śrāvakas and the eight pratyekabuddhas should be depicted exactly as they were previously described.
However, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra should be painted standing, fanning the Blessed One Śākyamuni with whisks.
In this manner, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm are to be depicted;
as well as Śakra, the lord of the gods, along with Yāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Śuddha, Vimala,
Sudṛśa, Atapa, Ābhāsvara, Brahmā Sahāmpati, Akaniṣṭha, and other such sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).

The deities of the desire realm (kāmāvacara) should be painted in successive order, situated near the noble Mañjuśrī and arranged within the surrounding circle of the assembly; they should be depicted wearing their own natural forms and attire.
Below the lion throne of the Blessed One, a great mountain rising from the great ocean should be painted all around, extending as far as the edge of the cloth.

In one corner of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his actual dress, appearance, and form, with his knees, elbows, and head bent down, and his hands occupied with an incense burner.

On that mountain of jewels, beneath Noble Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be painted as previously described. On the left side, beneath the Blessed One’s lion throne and near the feet of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the goddess Tārā should be painted seated upon that mountain of jewels.

They should be painted exactly as previously described. Furthermore, that cloth [painting] should be strewn all around with loose flowers—scattered everywhere with flowers such as the *campaka*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *saugandhika*, *mālatī*, *vārṣika*, *dhānuṣkārīka*, *puṃnāga*, and *kesara*. The cloth [should be] strewn all around with these flowers.

And at the upper corners of the edge of the cloth, on both sides, two sons of gods (devaputra) should be depicted, white in color, wearing various forms, standing in the intermediate space, hidden within clouds of water, emitting a great shower of flowers, and appearing as if they are flying upward.
This is declared to be the Madhyamaka, the manifestation of the cloth for the sake of the highest good;
for the middling accomplishment of men on this earth depends upon it.
Whatever evil has been committed previously while wandering in saṃsāra,
that perishes at that very moment from seeing the cloth-painting here.
Deluded beings, wandering through the wheel of rebirths, do not know [this], even though they behold the image of Mañjughoṣa in the center of the cloth. (Mmk 5.3)
Even if one should be a wrongdoer, or a perpetrator of the five acts of immediate retribution,
or even one of immoral conduct, the mantras spoken in various ways shall be effective for them.
Furthermore, one who has performed the recitation shall attain accomplishment even more swiftly:
the sick are freed from disease, the poor obtain wealth,
and the childless obtain a son upon the viewing of the middle-sized cloth painting.
Merely by seeing it at that time, one shall obtain vast and great merit;
that person will certainly become a partaker of the happiness of gods and humans,
and at the end of his life, Buddhahood will surely be his.
By writing, by reciting, by performing worship, by drawing [the mandala],
and likewise by seeing or touching it, one is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, through such prayer and entreaty for this one of great splendor who wanders [the earth], one obtains a fruitful birth; and likewise, rejoicing [in his deeds] brings swift results.
It is not possible, even in tens of millions of aeons, to describe by speech the merit that a living being would obtain from seeing this painted cloth, for it is truly fruitful.
From the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, this is the fifth chapter-section.
The second section on the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhānavisara*) is completed.
(Vaidya 50) The Sixth Chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Mañjuśrī, there is yet another secret procedure for the cloth-painting, the third one, known as the "Minor" (kanyasa).
By means of this, all sentient beings shall attain accomplishment without even effort.

Following the previously described rite, artisans should have the cloth painted as before, measuring one span of the Sugata in width, likewise equal and square in shape, with the previously specified features.

First of all, the noble Mañjuśrī should be depicted as previously described, seated upon a lion throne in the form of a young boy, teaching the Dharma, with beautiful forms and rays of light radiating in all directions.

On his left side, the noble Samantabhadra should be depicted as before, standing upon a jeweled stone, holding a *cāmara* in his hand and resting his left hand upon a *cintāmaṇi*, dark green in color like the *priyaṅgu* flower.
On the right side of the noble Mañjuśrī, the noble Avalokiteśvara should be depicted as before, standing upon a jeweled stone.
He should be depicted with his right hand occupied by a fly-whisk and his left lotus-hand resting [upon it], his form radiant on all sides.
Below the lion-throne, a golden-colored mountain should be painted extending as far as the edge of the cloth.
In the corner at the edge of the cloth, on the right side beneath the lion-throne of the noble Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be painted as before.
With a censer held in his hand, the practitioner, just as before,

should have the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra painted above the noble Mañjuśrī, measuring sixteen finger-breadths and nestled within a cave on a mountain of jewels. Ten mountains with precipitous slopes, resembling gabled pavilions, should be painted.
And one should paint that cloth [mandala] surrounded on all sides by mountain-like forms.

Above, situated at the corners of the cloth and clinging to the mountain slopes, two sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm— one named Śuddha and the other named Viśuddha— should be depicted as before, flying upward and scattering a profusion of flowers from celestial palaces.
And that cloth painting should be caused to be painted strewn with various flowers.
All this has been told regarding the threefold characteristics of the cloth;
indeed, by name this is the "inferior" cloth, which is superior for minor rites.
Whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed or caused to be committed,
one is liberated from it by the mere sight of the painting for thousands of millions of eons.
Indeed, upon merely seeing the cloth, one is liberated at that very moment.
A wise person who would honor thousands of millions of Buddhas does not equal even a sixteenth part of one who has seen the smallest cloth.
Whatever merit is gained by performing worship to all the Buddhas, the compassionate ones—that merit the wise person shall obtain from beholding the cloth painting (paṭa) for even a moment.
Furthermore, one should perform auspicious deeds in this world for the sake of enjoyments. Mmk_6.4 //
Whatever mantras there may be spoken by Brahmā, Indra, and the ṛṣis, as well as those proclaimed by Vainateya, Varuṇa, Āditya, and Kubera— Mmk_6.5.
All the mantras spoken by Dhanada and the others, by all the Rākṣasas, by the lords of the Dānavas and the great serpents, by Soma, Vāyu, Yama, and the rest, and by Hari, Hara, and so forth—
all these mantras brought here are accomplished before the cloth-painting.
One should always perform rites for pacification and likewise for nourishment here;
one should avoid fierce rites, for they are censured by the best of Jinas in this world.
The sixth detailed chapter from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka;
the third section on the ritual procedure for the small cloth-painting is hereby completed.
The Seventh Chapter. Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having risen from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times.

Having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Excellent, excellent! This Dharma discourse, which has been well-spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of those who practice the vows of all branches of knowledge, and out of compassion for the world."

The skillful means (*upāyakauśalyatā*) of the Bodhisattvas has been shown, which leads upward toward Nirvāṇa; the continuum (*santati*) of the Bodhisattvas is distinguished by its path and is certain to have Awakening as its ultimate goal. This shall be the means for accomplishing the practice of the purpose of all mantras, and it will serve to spread this secret of mantras among all people in the future age, when the Teacher of the World has passed away, when the sun of the Tathāgata has set, and when his lineage has been left behind.
In all buddha-fields, when the world-receptacle has become shrouded in darkness by all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, noble śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;
when the noble path has been severed;

when [the world] is bereft of all sciences, mantras, medicinal herbs, jewels, and gems, and abandoned by virtuous people; and when the realm of sentient beings is without light—[therein dwell] sentient beings.
There will be those who are indolent due to a loss of aspiration, lacking faith, fragmented, embraced by evil friends, deceitful, fraudulent, and of rogue-like conduct;
having heard this Dharma discourse, they will fall into terror.

Delighting in indolence and laziness, they will have no faith; seeking after sensual desires, they will not have conviction; delighting in false views, they will produce much demerit. Being opponents of the True Dharma, destined for the Avīci hell, they have gone from terrible to even more terrible states.

For the sake of those suffering beings—to bring under control those who are uncontrollable, to strike fear into those already subdued, and through the gathering power of skillful means—may the Blessed One speak the ritual procedure for the mantra-painting.
Do now whatever you deem to be the right time.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.

Mañjuśrī, there exists your own supreme and most secret expansion of the chapters on the ritual procedures for the cloth-paintings (*paṭavidhāna*) and the practice of the vidyā-vow; it is the meaning of the supreme heart-mantras, the most secret, and of great significance."
They are the treasury of all mantras;
these six supreme six-syllable heart-mantras attain accomplishment at that time through non-conceptualization.

For the sake of taming those beings, for their entry into the mantras of the equipment of skillful means, and for their certain attainment of perfect awakening, they were previously spoken by seventy-six billion Buddhas, and I too now [speak them].
Now I shall speak;
out of regard for future generations, listen well and attend thoroughly to it with your mind,
and I will speak to you.
And what is that?
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this mantra: Oṃ vākyārthe jaya | Oṃ vākyaśeṣe sva | Oṃ vākyeyanayaḥ |
Oṃ, obeisance to the one established in speech.
Oṃ, obeisance to the speech.
Oṃ, obeisance to that which is speech.

Thus, Mañjuśrī, these six-syllable mantras of yours possess great power; they are equal in strength, supreme essences, and most highly accomplished. Arisen like a Buddha for the benefit of all sentient beings, they have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas.
Bound by the pledge (*samaya*), thoroughly activated, effective for all rites, they point the way to enlightenment.

In the family of the Tathāgata, the most excellent mantras—associated with the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior—are exceedingly beautiful and bestow the ripening of karmic fruit; they will attain accomplishment during the time of the disappearance of the Teaching.
Those who practice them for the sake of protecting the eye of the True Dharma will, by the mere application of their value, accomplish great kingdoms, vast enjoyments, and sovereign power.

For them, at that time and at that moment, these will attain accomplishment most swiftly. Indeed, even for the sake of mere investigation, these supreme heart-mantras should be practiced; in brief, in whatever manner they are employed, in that very manner they will, in summary, attain accomplishment.
At that time, at that period, during the Great Terror— the age of the five corruptions— sentient beings will have little merit;

they will be of little renown, short-lived, possessing few enjoyments, and weak in vigor, such that they will not be able to undertake rites such as the extensive procedures for the cloth-painting (*paṭa*).
For their sake, I shall speak in an even more concise manner.

First of all, having purchased thread by means of sale— either a full *pala* or half a *pala*— one should have a cloth woven by a weaver, one cubit in length and half a cubit in width, complete with its fringe.
Alternatively, having taken a fresh piece of cloth free from hair, a new scrap of fabric, or a recently acquired cloth— measuring two, four, six, five, ten, or eight cubits, and being very white—
one should have it painted by a painter according to one's desire.
Using non-sticky pigments of sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and white [chalk], one should mix the sandalwood, saffron, and camphor together for the cloth.
Having stirred the cloth in a new vessel with water that is free of living organisms and free from impurities, one should soak it for three days, keeping it well-covered while on the road.
Having performed the protection ritual in a clean place and having become pure oneself, [one should proceed].

On the full moon day of the bright fortnight, facing east in front of the painted cloth and its container, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, these mantra-words should be recited one hundred and eight times:
*Tadyathā — oṃ he he bhagavan bahurūpadhara divyacakṣuṣe avalokaya avalokaya māṃ samayamanusmara kumārarūpadhāriṇe mahābodhisattva kiṃ cirāyasi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.*
Having performed the recitation with this mantra, one should sleep right there;
in a dream, it reveals whether success or failure will occur.
Then, having risen and seen a dream that is a sign of unimpeded success, one should have that cloth-painting executed;
provided that dreams indicating failure are not seen.
Having removed that cloth from its container, one should dry it in the sun.
Having dried it again, one should place it in another new vessel;
then, having secured it and performed the protective rite, one should set it aside.
Thereafter, having taken one of those supreme heart-mantras, one should proceed.
One should further recite the six syllables as many times as desired, up to one hundred thousand repetitions;
then that cloth-painting will quickly be accomplished.
First of all, having taken that cloth-painting on a day of miracles, or on another bright day joined with an auspicious constellation,
on an auspicious lunar date, or on a day of the waxing moon, when there are very beautiful omens and the night is considered auspicious,
at the time of midnight, a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* vows should paint that cloth in a clean place.
While burning camphor incense.

First of all, one should visualize the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a young boy, with hair tied in five tufts and adorned with the ornaments of a child; he is golden in color, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk and an upper robe of blue silk, teaching the Dharma, seated upon a lion throne with his right leg half-lotus-postured, resting on a jeweled footstool placed upon the lion seat.
One should depict [the deity] endowed with all ornaments, beautiful to behold, with a slightly smiling face, and with his gaze directed toward the practitioner.

On the right side, one should cause Noble Samantabhadra to be depicted, fanning with a white chowrie, dark green like the *priyaṅgu* flower, with a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) placed in his left hand, beautiful in all his limbs, adorned with all ornaments, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and seated upon a white lotus throne.

To the left side of Noble Mañjuśrī is Noble Avalokiteśvara, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, beautiful in all his limbs, and adorned with every ornament; he has a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), holds a white lotus in his left hand, and in his right hand holds a white fly-whisk (*cāmara*) being waved, fixed upon a golden handle; he is of gentle appearance and his gaze is directed toward Noble Mañjuśrī, just like Noble Samantabhadra.
Both of these should be depicted seated upon white lotus thrones, resting together upon the stalk of a single lotus.
There are three lotuses.
In the center, upon the pericarp of the root lotus, is the lion throne and jeweled seat of the noble Mañjuśrī.
On another lotus is the noble Samantabhadra,
and on the third lotus is the noble Avalokiteśvara.
And that lotus stalk is beautiful, shaped like an emerald lotus, with many lotus flowers in bud and provided with leaves.
The great lake of blooming and half-blooming flowers rises from the Anavatapta [Lake], its center supported by two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda.

That lotus stalk is white in color; those two Naga kings are adorned with seven hoods, their bodies beautified by all ornaments, possessing human upper bodies and forms marked by serpent coils, gazing at the noble Mañjuśrī while half-submerged within the water.
The two [deities] should be depicted with canopies adorned with precious jewels.

And all around the great lake, beneath it, on the right side at the corner of the edge of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his actual appearance: gazing at the foot-mandala of the noble Mañjuśrī, his hand occupied with an incense burner, his head bowed, and his body with elbows and knees bent.

Above the noble Mañjuśrī, from both corners of the painting, two very beautiful sons of gods (devaputra) should be depicted, bearing garlands and holding flower-garlands, flying upward while hidden within the clouds, emitting a great shower of flowers.
One should depict that cloth [painting] strewn all around with flowers such as *nāgakesara* and others;

or one may depict it as presided over by three forms as desired. Noble Mañjuśrī teaching the Dharma, Noble Samantabhadra, and Noble Avalokiteśvara—with their hands holding yak-tail whisks—should be caused to be painted.
Alternatively, three images must certainly be caused to be painted according to the practitioner's preference;
they may have whatever form is desired or be arranged in whatever configuration suits the practitioner, and should be painted exactly as it pleases him.
In the center is Ārya Mañjuśrī; at both ends are Ārya Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra, and others as desired must certainly be caused to be painted.

On whatever cloth fragment is available— whether measuring a span or a cubit— it should be caused to be painted by oneself or by another artist, whether that artist observes the *poṣadha* vows or does not, whether he is faithful or faithless, pure or impure, or possessed of moral virtue or of bad character.
The practitioner himself must necessarily have completed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), be endowed with faith, and have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
In this way, mantras are indeed accomplished; they are not for others who are evildoers.
Having become faithful, one should thus practice the mantra-deities.
The king of mantras is accomplished for that person who possesses faith, and not otherwise;
for faith is the supreme vehicle by which the Vināyakas proceed.
In a person who lacks faith, the pure dharma does not grow, just as a green sprout does not emerge from seeds scorched by fire. Mmk 7.3.
For a mortal established in faith, the deities are accomplished through his ritual action;
for one lacking faith, they are not accomplished.
All mantras,
especially those that are mundane deities as well as those that are supramundane.
Indeed, for one who possesses faith and is free from defilement, everything succeeds.
For those whose minds are fixed upon that, awakening and its swift accomplishment are certain;
for others, accomplishment is not spoken of, as they are excluded from this teaching.
The cloth [painting] is proclaimed as being of small, superior, or middling quality;
now, however, I shall explain the means of accomplishment for all ritual activities.

Thus concludes the fourth section on the procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), from the seventh chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
[End of] the eighth section.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, for the sake of those beings whom you have described, this detailed procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) has been explained;
they shall accomplish [their goals] by means of very little effort."
For their sake, I shall explain the analysis of the divisions of qualities and the classification of activities that are conducive to accomplishment.
Listen to this; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One:

"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-spoken by you is this description of the practice of mantra, which illuminates our own realization and brings about the manifestation of the perfection of its qualities.
May the Blessed One speak upon that."
Now, do as you deem the right time for our sake, out of compassion for us.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, smiled.
Then, from the gateway of the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s mouth, rays of light—blue, yellow, crystal-colored, and so forth—issued forth.
As soon as they had issued forth, those rays illuminated the entire circle of the assembly and the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
Having eclipsed the entire world-system and all the abodes of the Māras, as well as the radiance of all the stars, luminaries, mountains, and hosts of celestial bodies—
even those two, the moon and the sun, who possess great supernatural power and great majesty— were eclipsed by that light so that they no longer shone and became devoid of luster.

They did not shine and were seen to be eclipsed; having rendered the radiance of all jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and gems lusterless, they then vanished once more into the mouth of the Blessed One, Śākyamuni.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present and seated in that very assembly circle.

Rising from his seat with a sense of urgency, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
What, Blessed One, is the cause?"
What was the reason for manifesting a smile?
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"So it is, Vajrapāṇi; so it is.
It is just as you say."
The smile of the Tathāgatas does not occur without cause or condition;
there is a cause, there is a condition.

It is for one who [upholds] this sovereign king of sūtras, the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which relies upon the cloud of Dharma consisting of the application of the practice of vidyās, the performance of rites, and the means for accomplishing activities.

They will fully enter into it, follow it, uphold it, recite it, and have faith in it; having written it in a book, they will honor it with salutations, powders, ointments, incense, and garlands, with parasols, banners, and flags, or by various kinds of musical instruments and diverse types of percussion and cymbals.
Even those who obtain at least a mental continuity accompanied by rejoicing, or who experience horripilation, or who rejoice and approve upon hearing the power and efficacy of the *vidyā*,
or who undertake the practice—
they have all been prophesied by me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they shall all become [Buddhas].
The Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, smile for this very reason and not otherwise.

First of all, one who has seen the ritual conventions (*samaya*), completed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and received initiation, having taken hold of either the root-mantra, the heart-mantra, or the subsidiary-heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) from this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), or another mantra, or even a single-syllable mantra, or whichever other he desires, should go to a great forest and recite it three million times while subsisting on fruits and water or eating roots and leaves; thus he becomes one who has completed the preparatory rites.
Then, having ascended a mountain and installed the supreme cloth-painting facing westward,
one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing eastward and [offer] one hundred thousand white lotuses smeared with white saffron.

One should offer [these] beneath the cloth painting of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, along with all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas; one should also burn camphor incense according to one's means and perform worship for the sons of gods and the nāgas.
With flowers as they are obtained,

then at the time of midnight on the full moon of the bright fortnight, when the night is complete during a *prātihāraka*, one should prepare a fire-pit before the cloth painting in the shape of a lotus, kindle a fire with white sandalwood wood,
and combine saffron and camphor.
One should offer eight thousand oblations,
having performed the protection rites according to one's means.
Then, rays of light issue forth from the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and the cloth painting becomes a single mass of flame on all sides.

Thereupon, the practitioner, moving with great haste, should circumambulate the cloth three times to the right, prostrate before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas, and take hold of the cloth.
Then, having grasped the hem of the previously described practitioner’s cloth from the past, he flies up as soon as it is taken;
with a mere snap of the fingers, he transcends the world of Brahmā and arrives at the Kusumāvatī world-system.

Wherever that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, resides, stays, maintains himself, and teaches the Dharma, there one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī in person, hears the Dharma, and sees many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas whom one serves; for a thousand great eons, one enjoys the state of being free from old age and death.

The cloth painting remains right there, empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he perceives their empowerment, traverses hundreds of thousands of fields, or manifests hundreds of thousands of bodies; he becomes endowed with manifold miraculous powers, has the noble Mañjuśrī as his spiritual friend, and is destined for enlightenment as his ultimate goal.
Thus concludes the first [chapter] from the eighth section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment, from the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, the Ornament of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
(Vaidya 57) Now begins the ninth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed the assembly of gods seated within the entire circle of the retinue:

Listen, noble sirs, to this most secret heart-mantra, the supreme king of great vidyās spoken by all the Tathāgatas, which serves as the means for accomplishing the mantra-maṇḍala practice of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and provides protection for the practitioner;
by the recitation of which, all mantras are considered recited.
"O hosts of gods, this King of Vidyās is not to be transgressed;
even Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was summoned, brought under control, and made compliant by this King of Vidyās—
how much more so, then, other Bodhisattvas?"

It destroys all mundane and supramundane mantras; this great heroic power, possessing singular heroism, is declared to be the foremost of all mantras. It alone is declared to be the single syllable among all single-syllabled [mantras].
And what is that?
It is the single syllable that accomplishes all aims,
performs all tasks, cuts through all mantras [of adversaries], destroys the evil deeds of those who act wickedly, eradicates all sins, and fulfills all mantras.

For one who performs auspicious deeds, it stands above and beyond all worldly and supramundane mantras; it is the unimpeded heart of all Tathāgatas and the fulfiller of all hopes. And what is that? It is as follows: *kaḷlhīṃ*.
O worthy ones, this is the King of Vidyās named "The Single Syllable," which is supremely secret, efficacious for all rites, and not to be transgressed by any sentient beings.

He is unassailable by all beings, the auspiciousness of all Buddhas, the accomplisher of all mantras, the lord of all worlds, the sovereign of all masters of wealth, the embodiment of loving-kindness toward all who hate him, compassionate toward all living creatures, and the destroyer of all obstacles. In short, however he is employed, he acts accordingly; even if not yet accomplished, he performs his rites.
By reciting the mantra over whom one touches, that person becomes submissive. Having consecrated garments with the mantra, if one puts them on, one becomes fortunate.
Having consecrated a tooth-stick and chewing it, one removes toothache.
Having consecrated a white *karavīra* tooth-stick and chewing it, food is obtained without having to ask for it.

For eye pain, one should grind rock salt (*saindhava*), empower it seven times with the mantra, and fill the eye; this removes the eye pain. For earache, one should cook a small ball (*chatrikā*) made from the dung of an elephant that has just excreted and from *arjuna* tree sap, wrapped in *kedhuka* leaves, over a gentle fire. Once it is well-cooked and comfortably warm, one should strain it through rock salt powder and fill the ear with it after empowering it seven times.
It pacifies [the pain] at that very moment.

At the time of childbirth, for a woman suffering from difficult labor or overcome by the pains of a retained fetus, one should grind the root of *āṭaruṣaka* with water free of living organisms and smear it on the region of the navel; she will give birth with ease. Or, for a man with an embedded splinter, one should empower old ghee eight hundred times with the mantra and have him drink it, or smear that area; at that very moment, he becomes free of the splinter.

In cases of indigestion, colic, or diarrhea, one should empower either black salt (*sauvarcala*), rock salt (*saindhava*), or any other salt seven times with mantras and consume it; one is then liberated from that disease and becomes healthy on that very day.
In cases of both types of diarrhea or acute diarrhea, one is liberated from that affliction by drinking the juice of *mātuluṅga* fruit mixed with water free of living organisms.

For one desiring the birth of a child from a woman who is barren or incapable of bearing offspring, [the practitioner] should cook the root of *aśvagandhā* with cow’s ghee, grind it with cow’s milk, and having mixed it with cow’s milk, recite the mantra over it twenty-five times. At the time of her menses, after she has bathed, he should have her drink it; meanwhile, the householder should avoid the wives of others and refrain from sexual misconduct.
One should approach one's own wife. She shall give birth to a son for her husband, even if the time for delivery has exceeded three or five years,

or if she has been obstructed for many years, or if [the obstruction] is caused by another’s mantras, tantras, or medicinal herbs, or by a supreme seal (*paramudrā*), or by the malevolent acts of others, or by the suppression of the womb, or by the arising of disease.

Or whatever other disease there may be— whether caused by the influence of others, or by stationary or moving poisons, or artificial or natural poisons and the like, or produced by the application of roots, mantras, herbs, friends, or enemies— one should grind together twenty-seven times old ghee and the eye of a peacock feather.
Then, having ground it well and mixed it with sugar, one should consume a dose the size of a *harītakī*.
For seven days, one should have [the patient] drink boiled milk combined with sugar, having consecrated it repeatedly with mantras.
In the case of a headache, one should rub [the head] with a crow’s wing feather that has been consecrated seven times; [the patient] becomes healthy.

In cases of diseases such as menorrhagia and others, one should grind the root of *ālambuṣā* with milk, add the root of *nīlikā*, and after consecrating it eight hundred times with mantras, stir it with milk and have the patient drink it.

Likewise, for quartan, quotidian, tertian, quaternian, continuous, chronic, or irregular fevers and the like, one should have them eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee that has been consecrated eight hundred times;
thus they will become healthy.
Likewise, for those seized by *ḍākinī* spirits, one should empower one’s own face with the mantra one hundred and eight times and gaze upon them;
they will become healthy.

Similarly, for those seized by all non-human, wicked, and cruel entities such as *mātṛ*, *vāla*, *pūtana*, *vetāla*, and *kumāra* spirits, one should empower one’s own hand one hundred and eight times and touch the head of the possessed person.
He becomes established in his own nature.

With one recitation, there is protection for oneself; with two recitations, protection for one’s companions; with three recitations, protection for the house; with four recitations, protection for the village; with five recitations, there is protection for those who have gone out to the pastures during the watch of the night.
In this manner, up to ten recitations, protection for the entire army camp is accomplished.
All these and other minor rites are performed even when [the mantra] has not been mastered through formal consecration.
Now, if one wishes to accomplish minor rites (*kṣudrakarmāṇi*),
one should go to a solitary place in a secluded region— either at the source of a river flowing to the ocean, on the shore of the ocean, on the bank of the Ganges River,
or resorting to the bank of a great river— and having constructed a hut in a pure location, one should bathe three times a day and change one's clothes three times.

Remaining silent, subsisting on alms-food, barley-gruel, milk, or fruit, one should recite [the mantra] thirty lakhs for the sake of the signs of accomplishment; having seen those signs, one should then begin the sādhana.
In that very place and at that spot, having performed a great worship of the superior cloth-painting (paṭa) made of gold and silver...

One should offer one hundred thousand lamps for the cloth [painting], using lamps made of copper or clay, filled with either Turkish oil or cow’s ghee, with wicks fashioned from pieces of fresh cloth.
When all these lamps are lit simultaneously on every side, rays of light issue forth from the cloth.
Immediately upon the rays' emergence, the cloth becomes enveloped on all sides by a garland of flames;
above, in the sky, drums resound and the sound of "Well done! is heard.

Then, by the Vidyādhara, appearing in a form of great haste, the previously painted cloth that had emerged from the corner of the practitioner’s cloth should be taken after offering *argha* and circumambulating it, having paid homage to all the Buddhas.
As soon as it is grasped, he flies up together with all the beings who hold lamps, or they go toward a single supreme celestial palace (*vimāna*).

Surrounded on all sides by Vidyādharīs accompanied by divine musical instruments and endowed with sweet-sounding songs, singing, instrumental music, and dance, they consecrate that practitioner in the sovereignty of a Vidyādhara Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
Together with those who carry lamps, he sports like one who is ageless and immortal;
he remains for a great eon (mahākalpa),
resembling the rising sun, adorned with the beauty of divine limbs and arrayed in variegated garments.
These very ones are his servants;
he wanders together with them,
and all the kings of the vidyādharas attend upon him as his slaves.
One becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas;
long-lived and invincible,
one becomes most fortunate among all the Siddhas.
One gains mastery over the daughters of the *vidyādharas* and worships all substances as well as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thereafter, in a mere instant, one goes even to the world of Brahmā.
He does not even take Śakra into account, much less other vidyādharas;
and in the end, he attains the state of Buddhahood.
And for him, the practice of the noble Mañjuśrī becomes even more intensely refined.
Then, having gone to a solitary place, free from people and devoid of attachment or social ties, he should enter a great forest.

In a place where there is a lotus pond provided with a river, situated near a single mountain, one should ascend a mountain peak and take up either the single-syllable King of Vidyās spoken in the Mañjuśrī-kalpa, or another mantra spoken by a Tathāgata or other Bodhisattvas;
then, subsisting on lotus roots and fruits as desired, or consuming milk products, one should recite that vidyā three million six hundred thousand times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having installed the supreme cloth-painting according to that very same previously described procedure, one should kindle a fire with *khadira* wood and offer thirty-six thousand previously prepared lotuses that have been anointed with white sandalwood and saffron.

Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, rays of light issue forth from the cloth painting of the Blessed One Śākyamuni; having illuminated the practitioner, they vanish into his crown. As soon as he is touched by them, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges.
Having attained the stage of a bodhisattva, possessing a divine form, he wanders as he pleases;
he lives for thirty-six kalpas and traverses thirty-six buddha-fields.
He perceives their power;
he retains the teachings of thirty-six Buddhas;
and he becomes devoted to honoring and attending upon them.
And he becomes one who is destined for awakening; he is taken into the care of the noble Mañjuśrī as a spiritual friend, until reaching the culmination of awakening and the finality of nirvāṇa.

Thus concludes the second section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment, from the ninth chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 60) Now begins the tenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke once more on the supreme accomplishment of ritual action.

In this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), having taken up any one of the mantras, one should descend into the great river Gaṅgā and, staying upon a boat in the middle of the Gaṅgā, subsisting on a diet of milk-rice, recite [the mantra] three million times over as many days as desired.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, one beholds all the *nāgas*.
Thereafter, one should begin the practice (*sādhana*); right there in the middle of the boat, one should have a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) constructed in the shape of a lotus.

Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth with *nāgakeśara* flowers, one should establish the principal cloth facing west and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east. Having consecrated each individual *nāgakeśara* flower seven times with mantras,
one should offer them as oblations into a fire kindled with fuel of *khadira* wood.
Up to thirty thousand white sandalwood and saffron-scented *nāgakesara* flowers—no other *nāgas* are to be looked upon—and they may attempt to entice one with perfected substances;
these must not be accepted.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, he flies up together with the boat;
he becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas,
and all the kings of the Nāgas become his attendants.
They stand like servants;
he lives for thirty intermediate kalpas,
and he becomes one who moves according to his own will.
With unimpeded movement, he beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
he touches him on the crown of his head, and as soon as he is touched, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges and will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there is another method for accomplishing the supreme ritual application:
having descended into the great river Gaṅgā, one should construct a boat from a single piece of wood made of the *vilva* tree, ensuring it is well-examined and well-crafted.
Having boarded that vessel made of *vilva* wood, the practitioner, clearly manifesting himself as the sādhaka, should proceed upon that very boat.

One should cause [the water] to flow with great skill; one should cause the great river Gaṅgā to flow everywhere without abandoning it, whether crosswise or lengthwise. Having taken one or another of these mantras—the root mantra, the six-syllable, the eight-syllable, or the single-syllable mantra—[one should employ] the wrathful female messenger or male messenger.

Having taken another or some other mantra, one should install the senior cloth-painting right there facing west, while oneself faces east; first [one should remain thus], and afterwards it may be as one desires. Subsisting on milk, barley-gruel, or fruit, or subsisting on water, tubers, roots, and fruit, observing silence, bathing three times a day, changing clothes three times, practicing pure deeds, and possessing a perfectly pure intellect;
First, in front of the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra six million times according to the previously taught and observed procedure.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, a boat that travels upon the great ocean will appear.
Then the practitioner, having gathered the requisites previously prepared, should place them right there on the boat.
Thereafter, one traveling across the great ocean should neither fear nor turn back.
And they cannot be turned back, except by the power of the practitioner.
Then, in just a moment, he enters the great ocean even though it is situated at a distance of a thousand yojanas, let alone a short distance.
Having entered there into the abode of the rivers, he should begin the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhanakarma*).

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood in a previously prepared fire-pit or in an earthen vessel made by a potter, one should offer sixty lakhs of oblations of *nāgakeśara* filaments mixed with white sandalwood and camphor, in either very small or very large quantities.

And as they were making offerings, the Rākṣasas dwelling in the city of Laṅkā, assuming many forms, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! while the Nāga kings dwelling in Bhogavatī, the city of the Nāgas, also arose, assuming various forms—some more cruel and others more gentle.
Those Nāgas and Rākṣasas spoke thus: "May the Blessed One arise! May the Blessed One arise!"
"May he be our lord!
Thus do the asuras, yakṣas, gods, mahoragas, siddhas, and all human beings entice him;
one must not rise [from his seat].
And one must not be afraid.
Then, while reciting the mantra, the vidyādhara should threaten them with the index finger of his left hand;
thereupon they will flee, running away hither and thither, and shall perish.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, she takes that practitioner and in an instant goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

She also travels to and returns from other world-systems; he becomes a knower of the minds of Bodhisattvas, possesses the five superknowledges, and becomes one of great supernatural power and great majesty.
And he constantly beholds the noble Mañjuśrī.
All nāgas, all rākṣasas, all gods, all asuras, and all sentient beings become subject to him;
they carry out his commands, with the exception of all buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, noble śrāvakas, and those who have attained mantra-siddhi here.
They become friendly toward him and supportive of him, until he becomes invincible to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is another supreme means for the performance of ritual action:
one should have a large boat constructed from *bilva* wood,
or one should construct a large dwelling using a collection of logs from a single type of timber.
One should prepare a boat on an island situated in the middle of the Gaṅgā;

and upon that boat, one should station one hundred and twenty persons wearing white garments, who have performed the protective rites (*rakṣā*), whose hands are occupied with lamps, and who are mounted upon the boat, in front of the image established according to the previously described procedure for the Great Cloth Painting (*jyeṣṭhapaṭa*).

Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting, one should offer thirty-six thousand oblations into a fire of khadira wood, using powdered nāgakesara mixed with saffron, white sandalwood, and camphor.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, that boat travels to the world of Brahmā in a mere instant and returns;
it moves about as one desires.
One beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
upon merely seeing him, one attains the stages, possesses the five superknowledges, becomes long-lived, remains for a great eon, and becomes a universal monarch among the holders of great vidyās.
Furthermore, those who hold lamps for him become accomplished vidyādharas.
He roams with those companions as he pleases and becomes one who moves according to his own will;
he delights in making offerings to other Blessed Buddhas;
and in the end, his attainment of Buddhahood becomes certain.
Furthermore, it also becomes the supreme means for accomplishing ritual actions.
On a riverbank, on the shore of the ocean, or likewise on the Himalayan mountain,
or on this king of mountains, Vindhya, one should accomplish the supreme rite.
On Sahya and Malaya, on Arbuda and Gandhamādana,
and on this Trikūṭa, the king of mountains, one should accomplish the supreme rite.
In the great ocean, likewise on mountains rich with trees and abounding in flowers—
in these regions, the mantras spoken by the Jina indeed attain accomplishment.
In a secluded, pure, and remote place, free from the ways of village life,
as well as in mountain caves, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
In a delightful place for reclining and sitting at the edge [of a forest], as likewise praised by the Jinas,
and free from wicked beings, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
When the king is righteous, when the people in the land are devoted to purity and proper conduct,
when they are devoted to their mothers and fathers, and when the twice-born castes are not excluded,
then the deities attain success in that place, but not otherwise.
On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, on the most beautiful Yamunā, on the banks of the Sindhu and Narmadā, and on the pure shore of the Candrabhāgā. (Mmk 10.7)
The Kāverī, the Sarasvatī, and the Sitā, the great river of the gods—
these are declared by the sons of the One Possessing Ten Powers to be fields of accomplishment.
The fields of the mountains of the Northern Path were proclaimed by the Ten-Powered Ones,
as well as those in Kaśmīra, the land of China, Nepāla, and likewise in Kāviśa.
In Mahācīna, indeed, all the fields of accomplishment without exception are located;
as are the mountains and rivers situated in the northern direction.
Those lands which are declared to be meritorious, where people subsist on barley and wheat,
and where beings are compassionate— in those places, success will certainly be attained.
On the great mountain Śrīparvata, known as Dakṣiṇāpatha,
at the shrine of Śrīdhānyakaṭaka on earth, which contains the relics of the Jina.
Mantras are indeed quickly accomplished there in all matters and rites—
at the Vajrāsana, at the great caitya, and at the beautiful Dharmacakra.
The supreme sage has attained peace; even there, success is seen at the great shrine of Devāvatāra and at Saṅkāśya, the site of the great miracle.
In the great city named Kapila, in the excellent grove of Lumbinī,
the preeminent place praised by the most eminent of Jinas, the King of Mantras attains accomplishment there.
Likewise, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, always in the Sītavana grove on earth, in the city named Kusuma, and always in the delightful city of Kāśī; Mmk_10.16 //
In Madhura, Kanyakubja, and the city of Ujjayinī on earth;
likewise in Vaiśālī, at the Caitya, and in Mithilā, always upon the earth.
Whether they be the principal cities and towns or others inhabited by people,
accomplishment is ordained for them in those places that are praised as meritorious.
These and other regions indeed— villages, districts, market towns, cities,
excellent capitals, and sacred places situated along rivers.
There, following the practice of alms-gathering, one should be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings;
and one should always remain in speech, in the open air, or in an empty abode.
One should perform the preliminary service for all ritual acts of the mantras;
the practitioner of mantra should always recite the mantra everywhere in the Middle Country.
Constantly engaged in recitation and ever-disciplined through the practice of renunciation, the knower of mantras is virtuous,
well-conducted, truthful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

Faithful in the practice of mantras, the practitioner, having first undertaken the vow, should recite [the mantra] in a pure place and an auspicious field, free from barbarians and thieves. (Mmk 10.23)
In all places [such as] among reptiles and the like, it is considered avoided;
however, it is praised in a place endowed with fruits and flowers and possessing pure water.
All those who know the mantras should recite the mantra; it is not proclaimed in other places, but rather in a temple, a cremation ground, or a place characterized by solitude.
Likewise, at a solitary linga or in a remote place, the knower of mantras,
having performed self-protection and protection for his companions, should indeed perform the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
Endowed with mantra, the practitioner of mantra should always cultivate the supreme mantra in a great forest, amidst large trees rich in flowers and yielding fruit.
Furthermore, on a mountain peak, at a waterfall, in a pure and clean place by the water, or on the excellent bank of a great river— Mmk_10.28.
The knower of mantras should practice the mantra in these locations here:
in the eastern region, at Lauhitya, at the great river, and at auspicious rivers. (Mmk 10.29)
Likewise, in the land of Kāmarūpa, in the most excellent city of Vardhamāna,
where that most meritorious and foremost of rivers, the Nimnāgā, flows.
In that place, one who is pure and constantly reciting [the mantra] should resort to a beautiful cow;
for that reason, one should indeed perform the preliminary service for all ritual acts.
Likewise, at Gaṅgādvāra and constantly at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
one who is pure and observant of vows should indeed recite the mantra during its application.
These are the great cremation grounds; there the reciter should always perform his recitation, as well as by rivers with pure water that are free from worms.
Therefore, the reciter, being composed, should recite the mantra there;
for no merit whatsoever is seen in worldly activity in that place.
However, under the pretext of receiving mantra-instruction, one should indeed reside there for a short time;
or else, one should depart from there at the proper time, like [one leaving] during a lunar eclipse.
Having reached the proper time, he should dwell there for some time, and not otherwise;
or else, the knower of mantras who is capable should depart from there quickly.
One should always dwell upon the ground at caityas where the Sugatas have resided,
as well as at all the world's shrines and those fallen into wrong views.
One who knows the mantras should always avoid other places of pilgrimage;
the knower of mantras should not dwell there, for such places give rise to the path of false causes.
The surface of the earth is pervaded by the supreme Victors, by those who possess the individual rhinoceros-like wisdom,
by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and by the Śrāvakas, the sons of the supreme Victors. (Mmk 10.39)
The knower of mantras, reciting the mantra, should frequent all those places;
first, with such diligence, he should always practice in that location.
One who knows the mantras should recite the mantra again and again according to the prescribed rite;
for through recitation and burnt offerings, he destroys all the sins of embodied beings without exception.
Therefore, with every effort and with a well-composed mind, one should recite the mantra. Thus it is said. (Mmk 10.41)
These locations have been prescribed for all rites and for the practice of the supreme ritual means.

In the absence of these, however, one who is liberated through faith should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) in any clean place whatsoever, and carry out the supreme ritual means appropriate for the accomplishment.
First, having installed the principal cloth-painting facing west and having positioned oneself facing east,

one should take earth from the top of an anthill or earth from the bank of the Ganges river, and mixing it with ushira, white sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and other substances, one should fashion the form of a peacock.

Having placed that [image] before the cloth painting, and having fashioned a circle out of kuśa grass with uncut tips grown in a pure location, one should hold it with the right hand while holding a peacock with the left hand before the cloth painting. On a night during the full moon of the bright fortnight,
having performed a great worship of the cloth painting and burning camphor incense, one should recite the mantra until dawn.
Then, at the time of sunrise, that peacock made of clay becomes the Great Peacock King;
the wheel becomes ablaze,
and he himself possesses a divine body, adorned with celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments, resembling the risen sun and capable of assuming any form at will.

Having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, circumambulated the cloth-painting, and taken hold of the cloth-painting, he sits upon that peacock-throne; in a moment, he transcends the world of Brahmā.
Surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Vidyādharas, he becomes a Vidyādhara-Cakravartin.
He lives for sixty intermediate kalpas of a Manvantara.
He moves with his gait according to his desire;
his movement is unimpeded, and he becomes endowed with divine prosperity.
He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face-to-face, he beholds him face-to-face.
He alone becomes his virtuous friend,
and in the end, he attains Buddhahood.
Likewise, [one should fashion] clay models of staffs, water-pots, sacred threads, realgar, yellow orpiment, swords, iron arrows, slings, axes, and various other types of weapons;
as well as two-legged and four-legged beings, and specific types of bird-vehicles such as lions, tigers, and bears;
and seats, vehicles, couches, white parasols, crowns, and various ornaments, all made from anthill earth or river mud and saturated with fragrant scents.
All varieties of precious gems and all varieties of requisites for renunciants— such as rosaries, sandals, wooden clogs, bowls, robes, girdles, needles, knives, and so forth;
whether made of flower-metal or whatever other implements and utensils there may be, whether made of flower-metal, or of anthill clay, or of clay from a riverbank—
all of these should be washed or sprinkled with the five products of the cow and consecrated one hundred and eight times.
Having performed the purification with either the *saṃśodhana* mantra, the single-syllable (*ekākṣara*) mantra, or any other mantra taught in this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*),
excluding the mantra used for the actual practice (*anusādhana*), he— having protected himself as desired and according to his preference,
having provided protection for his assistants, and being one who knows the secret mantras and tantras— should face westward in the previously specified locations.
Having established [the image] for oneself as before and having performed a great worship of the cloth-painting (*paṭa*),
while burning camphor incense for the eldest [deity], one should take up any one of those previously specified weapons, implements, and all the special [objects]—
which were previously described as artificial— and recite the mantra throughout that night on the previous full moon.
Until the time of sunrise.
In the meantime, a cloth [painting] encircled by great radiance is seen.
If a particular vehicle has been taken up by the practitioner, then having mounted it, he goes wherever he desires.
If it is a particular ornament or a particular weapon, having taken that, he becomes a venerable universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
