Possessing a divine form, he travels at will, resembling the rising sun, garlanded with great radiance, his body illuminated like lightning— the lord of all *vidyādharas*, long-lived, remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *vidyādharas*,
moving through the sky with divine great jewels and *maṇi*-gems; whatever vehicle was previously envisioned by him when he first attained accomplishment, that very one becomes his.
He becomes possessed of great power;

that very [being] becomes his mount, and he alone becomes his companion. Having set aside the accomplishment of other mantras, he applies himself to the accomplishment of his own mantra—being of a friendly nature, desiring his welfare, and constantly following him—with whatever specific weapons, ornaments, and jewels he may have.
Beings such as those who provide seats, beds, and vehicles will always follow him for the sake of his great protection, defense, and guardianship.
He becomes possessed of great majesty, great heroism, and a great body.
He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face.
He gives his approval and,
with his head stroked [by the teacher], he obtains the state of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
until he reaches the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍala), he will certainly attain the ten powers (daśabala).
He becomes worthy of worship;

he is invincible by all sentient beings and unassailable by all spirits; he is one who does not sever the lineage of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭīvaṃśa*); he attains the stages (*bhūmi*) and follows the certainty of the bodhisattvas regarding the ten powers. In brief, all these supreme activities are performed by one who delights in supreme worship before the supreme cloth painting situated in a supreme place.
One should perform only the supreme deeds:

for the sake of fulfilling the lineage of the Ten Powers, [one should practice] for the sake of attaining the state of a Vidyādhara, traveling through the sky, entering the state of a Bodhisattva, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the attainment of the [Bodhisattva] stages, traversing world-systems with this very body, and [meeting] the noble Mañjuśrī.
For the sake of direct vision; for the sake of hearing the teaching of the Dharma whose vision is never fruitless; for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddhas;

for the sake of attaining the sequential progression toward the knowledge of the Omniscient One; for the sake of entering into that which is emitted from the clouds of Dharma; for the sake of pacifying through the bearing of a rain of nectar that does not dry up the afflictions; for the sake of carrying out the activity of favoring the world; and for the sake of protecting the eye of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.

To make the words of the Tathāgata fruitful, to manifest the ritual procedures for the accomplishment of mantra practice, and to reveal the majesty of the Dharma of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, this extensive King of Rituals (Kalparāja) must be accomplished.

This King of Cloth-paintings (Paṭarāja), joined with the recitation of mantras, should be accomplished according to the path of ritual in all mundane and supramundane mantra-rituals and all tantras— whether in brief or through the rites spoken in other rituals— even while standing near the foremost cloth-painting.
As for what I have stated—that the accomplishment of those mantras is swift—it will certainly be accomplished.

Thus concludes the tenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the procedure for the supreme cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 66) Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, there exists within your tradition a medium-sized cloth-painting ritual (*paṭavidhāna*), a concise procedure for the means of accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) suitable for intermediate rites; I shall explain it.
Listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly.
"I shall speak.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, the Teacher who has compassion for the world and who delights in the welfare of all beings, speak it now, if you deem it the right time."

"Out of compassion for us and having regard for future generations," when Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him: "Listen, Mañjuśrī! First of all, hear the procedure for ethical discipline, vows, purity, conduct, observances, recitation, fire-offerings, and meditation, in which all the practices, accomplishments, and rites of mantra are established and become fruitful."
They become fruitful;
quickly all rites for the practice and accomplishment of mantras become non-vain and fruitful;
and quickly all applications of mantras attain success.
And what is that?
I shall speak; listen, O youth.
First of all, one should initially undertake the undertaking of the vows, conduct, and observances of the vidyā. First, one should enter the pledge (samaya) taught by the maṇḍala master.

Having found a clear and intelligent person who has received the master’s initiation, who is skilled and knowledgeable in the teaching, as prescribed in your King of Rituals (Kalparāja), [one should proceed].
It is evident that one who is righteous, truthful, highly energetic, grateful, firm in friendship, neither too old nor too young,

free from desire for all gains and honors, celibate, and compassionate— such a person does not speak falsely even out of mere greed, nor for the sake of enjoyment, nor for the sake of conciliation; how much less so for trivial forms of greed or delusion?

One who is firm in his vow, impartial toward all beings, compassionate, generous by nature, and one who has performed the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*); one who recites your secret mantra, who has mastered the sciences through prior service, and who has entered your maṇḍala in the proper sequence; one who knows the world, knows the ritual rules, is benevolent, capable of action, and discerning; one who is intent on the highest good, fearless, undaunted, free from hesitation, and possessed of firm vigor.
One who is free from disease, not habitually indolent due to any illness, and born of a very high family—
endowed with these qualities, one becomes a master of the mandala.
The practitioner, being either equal to or slightly inferior [to the master] in some of his limbs [of practice], should request such a Maṇḍala Master and pray:
"I wish to enter the samaya of the Great Bodhisattva, the Youthful Noble Mañjuśrī.
Therefore, may the Master, out of compassion for us, with a mind intent on our welfare and full of mercy, speak [to me]."
Then, that mandala master, having examined the disciples according to the previously described procedure as before, should cause them to enter;
having bestowed the empowerment as before,
he should give the mantra.
One should demonstrate the commitments (samaya) in their proper order and sequence.
Furthermore, the secret tantras, mudrās, and ritual actions (karma) should be revealed only after a long period of time, having thoroughly examined [the disciple] and known their disposition.
This rule is proclaimed: that the ritual actions regarding all tantras, mantras, and so forth, are not for others.
Then, the disciple should offer himself and his possessions to the mandala master according to his ability, or whatever else might please the master.
Thereupon, that mandala master should regard him as a son.
"One should behave toward her as toward a son,
and one should provide for her needs.
Then, that practitioner, having taken up a certain mantra, should go to a secluded place in the location previously specified.

The elaboration: with those very same mantras, the invocation, dismissal, offering of lamps, perfumes, incense, and food-oblations should be performed extensively according to the procedure taught for the mandala.

Having invoked [the deities] and offered the *argha* and the seat, one should perform the recitation during the three junctions of the day, bathing three times and changing one's garments three times.

One should perform [the rites] there daily; that which is called the time of *saṃdhyā* begins from the end of the night until the sun has risen by the distance of a yoke (*yugamātra*). Within this interval, it is called the first *saṃdhyā*.
And at midday, when the sun is at both ends of the sky at the measure of a yoke’s distance, the solar disc resting in the firmament is called the middle *saṃdhyā*.
And at the time of sunset, when only the length of a yoke remains, it is called the third twilight.
One who is endowed with moral conduct and vows, a teacher who is skillful and wise, born of a noble and high lineage, and possessed of firm vigor in every respect.
Dedicated to mantra and tantra, with an intellect skilled in all undertakings,
subtle and proficient in the knowledge of mantras, he is always a bearer of the dharmadhātu.
Possessing great energy and brilliance, disregarding worldly dharmas,
and having faith in this dharma of the supreme sages, one should avoid those things belonging to the world.
One who has performed the recitation, who knows discernment, who practices the preliminary service,
who knows the mantra of Mañjughoṣa, and who is intent upon having witnessed the signs of efficacy.
One who knows the application of worldly mantras spoken by the Buddha,
having performed protection, possessing firm strength, and always delighting in pure conduct— Mmk_11.5.
Following in every respect the path taught by the Buddha,
I am diligently engaged in this mantra-recitation, which is praiseworthy and extolled by the Victors.
Constantly perceiving the fruits of karma in this world as well as in the next,
one should be fearful of all evils, even those as small as an atom; likewise, one should be pure, skillful, unwearied, intelligent, and pleasant to behold.
The mantras taught by the Ones Possessed of Ten Powers, as well as those by the Sons of the Victors,
and whatever worldly mantras there are— even those of the Vajra and Antaka families—
to them he has constantly applied his efforts, upholding the meaning of their texts and treatises.
Free from disease, not lacking in power, devoid of both old age and childhood,
having perfected mantras, likewise protected, he is swift-acting in every respect.
Not procrastinating, likewise modest, and especially skilled in discerning gestures;
a celibate student of great wisdom, wandering alone and free from attachment.
One who has received initiation and is a hero in this Mañjubhāṣita tantra, who is devoted to the completion of recitation and likewise accomplished in the vidyā-mantras; Mmk_11.11 //
Possessing great majesty, knowing the world, contemplating the reality of the states of existence,
devoted solely to the highest good, he is a giver and delights in the welfare of all beings.
Likewise, such a distinguished preceptor must always be entreated;
the mandala of mantras written by him attains accomplishment.
By giving an empowerment in this manner, one obtains great fruit;
and he who desires accomplishment should always be honored by his disciples like a sage.
His word must be diligently obeyed by the disciples;
they should provide him with enjoyments according to their available means. (Mmk 11.15)
Whether it be very little or abundant, by whatever means one attains satisfaction—
for the sake of the body and life— one should regard the mind as the body does for a father.
In the same way, the disciple who knows the Dharma should give wealth to the preceptor;
he shall obtain fame, accomplishment, long life, and indeed good health.
The disciple who honors his guru attains an abundant goal;
moreover, his mantras become effective through the demonstration of the path of ritual procedure.
Through serving, honoring, and even worshipping them,
all the Buddhas as well as the sons of the Victorious Ones are likewise pleased.
All the gods are indeed pleased when there is always proper honor shown toward the guru;
all this has been told concerning the gurus who perceive the mantras.
For the practitioner who has previously entered the samaya,
whether the person [to be initiated] is equal to him, similar to him, or even superior— if such should be the case— Mmk_11.21.
One must never despise the guru, whether he be equal to or even superior to oneself;
for by him alone is the instruction always given in this tantra.
The mantra-attainment should be performed for this disciple, as shown according to his capacity; one should not harbor envy toward this disciple who has been previously prepared. Mmk 11.23.
The eye that follows with affection toward those embodied beings who are well-established—
out of concern for the disciples, the teachers should make such a person their disciple.
Wherever there is a continuous stream of affection that follows one another, and where the succession of those who are affectionate maintains it, there indeed one should impart the mantra.
In this manner, both the teacher and the disciple should always remain eager upon seeing one another, due to their state of apprehension.
For them, the path is indeed constant in the observation of mantra practice;
both the father and the son are knowers of mantra who follow it with fruitful results.
Both the disciple and the teacher always attained steadfastness and contentment;
thus, a son who is ever devoted to the Dharma must always be protected with great effort.
For those Buddhas who have severed all constituent parts, suchness indeed exists within them;
in their absence, one should bestow the mantra as prescribed upon those who are protectorless.
The practice of mantra is superior for all sentient beings, and especially so for those who are poor and those who are weak. Mmk 11.30.
One should perform [the rite] at all times— whether it be inferior, superior, or middling— and always, with respect to all phenomena, one should act for the sake of bestowing grace. (Mmk 11.31)

One should bestow [the gift] even upon those who desire it, for the destiny and birth of one who remains inactive depend upon it; however, the disciple himself, having received the mantra from him according to the prescribed rule, [should proceed].
One who desires accomplishment should strive in that [practice] which is supreme among others, following exactly the path taught by him and not otherwise. Mmk 11.33.
Having bowed with one's head as to a father, one should depart from there at will;
then, having gone to a solitary place, one should recite the mantra in brief.
A mendicant monk, subsisting on alms and observing silence, should recite [the mantra] three times a day;
thus he shall proceed according to the path as previously described.
Then, following that [instruction], the practitioner should frequent places of residence and sanctuaries,
as well as great forests, mountain peaks, and likewise pure riverbanks.
In a cow-pen, in a great city, or in a secluded place devoid of people; in an empty temple, at the foot of a tree, or on a mountain peak.
On the delightful banks of a great river, or on a sandy shore, or at a lamp-lighting site,
and in various other charming locations previously specified.
In these and other locations, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind,
accompanied by friends who possess the auspicious marks and are experts in the meaning of mantras and in logic.
By those who know the truth of gestures and physical expressions, who are like themselves in character, who are heroic, victorious in battle, virtuous, and patient; Mmk_11.40.
In this teaching proclaimed by the Jina, those who possess faith should practice the mantra-conduct with companions who are praiseworthy, endowed with auspicious marks, and patient.
For him, all ritual actions are accomplished without any effort at all,
provided that he rises from bed in the morning and bathes in pure water.
In water free from living organisms, originating from a river or a great lake,
the knower of mantras should rub his body with powdered earth and cow dung.
Then, having purified the clean and stainless water with mantras, the practitioner of recitation, with a disciplined mind, should bathe; he must not let the proper time pass by.
Then, having risen and stood on the bank, he should wash his hands with earth twenty-one times— seven, seven, and again seven.
Having sat down there, one should then use a tooth-stick;
after discarding the tooth-cleansing stick, one should then pay homage to the Protector (Tāyin).
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, one should perform a delightful worship,
praising him again and again with various offerings of hymns. (Mmk 11.47)
Having offered argha with fragrant flowers to the Teacher, the reciter should then bow his head to the Buddhas and those born as disciples.
One should perform confession before those Lords of the World,
and offer food there in front of the central painting.
Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, remaining there with a composed mind,
one should perform the recitation continuously using that rosary.
One should indeed recite only the mantra as it was received, and not another mantra at that time;
one should avoid what is excessively inferior or excessively superior.
The practitioner who observes the vow should always recite the mantra with a moderate tone during intermediate rites;
he should carefully avoid speech that is excessively loud, as well as any other [inappropriate] speech.
The medium [recitation] is praised for medium rites and is extolled by the Victorious One;
one should always perform the medium recitation, which is neither too high nor too low.
This speech was spoken by all the former Buddhas for the sake of those seeking the highest good:
one should never recite [the mantra] in the presence of others or while engaged in the activities of others;
rather, one should recite the *madhyama* mantra in a secluded place known to oneself.
Likewise, if someone well-versed in the meaning of mantras should find that their recitation has been interrupted,
they should recite that mantra again if they desire middling accomplishment.

Therefore, in a secluded place free from living beings, where the true meaning of mantras is well-heard and where there is no commotion, the reciter should indeed perform the recitation of the mantra.
In the fourth part of the night, at its very midpoint,
when the sun has risen just a yoke’s length above the horizon, glowing with a coppery-red hue.
Thus has the first twilight been described by the preeminent sages;
the middle one is proclaimed to be four cubits, the measure of a *yuga*.
Therefore, when the sun has risen into the sky, one should then cease the recitation of the mantra;
having ceased the mantra recitation, the practitioner of the vow offers the arghya water and performs the dismissal.

Then, during the remaining time, one who is devoted to this wholesome teaching of the Sage [should perform] the recitation of the true Dharma and so forth, such as the Prajñāpāramitā and other [scriptures]. (Mmk 11.60)
The books known as the *Daśabhūmika* should always be honored and recited; having arrived at the proper time, one should indeed bow down to those foremost of Jinas.
Then, having [recited] his own mantra and the Lord of Mantras, he should not seek a livelihood;
thus disciplined as a "wandering at night" practitioner, eating at the proper time, and with senses conquered.
A practitioner who is righteous, diligent, and devoted to the Buddha’s teaching should enter among the villages while observing silence and always remaining intent on pure conduct. (Mmk 11.63)
The reciter should always enter for alms the house of a righteous being, where water free of living organisms has been prepared and which is considered pure. Mmk 11.64.
In such a family, where the Buddha’s teaching is serene and accompanied by right view, one seeking alms should always receive alms.
Just as a warrior, well-armored, might enter the perils of battle, constantly crushing his enemies and never being slain by them; Mmk_11.66.
In this manner, the practitioner who subsists on alms should always enter the village;
likewise, upon seeing a pleasing form or hearing auspicious sounds, he should remain composed.
For the sake of pacifying passion, one should meditate on the foul and the pure,
having seen the body among women adorned with the conduct of youth.
One should meditate upon the body as impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome—dripping with worms, situated in a cemetery, impermanent, and suffering. Mmk 11.69.
Wherein the foolish and deluded indeed wander through the five destinies,
bound by the threads of karma that have shone for a long time.
But those deluded beings who are shrouded by ignorance, like those blind from birth, are the cause of their own suffering;
being of perverted intellects, they sink into that wherein they are attached.
Adorned with various garments and colored in many ways,
they are seen going back and forth, mounted upon long swings.
Indeed, those beings who are intent on dancing and whose movements consist of the gestures of their feet will sink for a long time upon the path where they are devoted to impurity.
Those born from the waters of the ocean of existence are like the buckets of a waterwheel;
their births, submerged in the floodwaters of suffering, never come to an end.
For it has been declared by the Buddhas, as well as by the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas, that woman alone is the root of suffering.
This great ocean, difficult to dry up and unshakeable— the sea of existence—
in which beings sink, their consciousness deceived by women.
The hell realm, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts along with that of the asuras,
the human world, and indeed the divine and celestial realms— these are always his destinies.
Indeed, being powerless and deceived by women, they wander everywhere;
they sink into the great mire of the prison of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Foolish men attached to women are like jackals drawn to a corpse; wherever beings are constantly indulged, they indeed endure intense suffering. (Mmk 11.79)
Having entered the teaching of the Buddha, those whose pure qualities have been utterly destroyed prevent all sufferings within the ocean of existence.
Those who are devoted to the practice of mantra-recitation, who possess the eyes of Maheśvara,
who are wise, radiant, and have conquered their enemies— for them, no suffering exists.
For those who are self-restrained, who know Brahman and the truth, who worship their gurus and deities,
and who are devoted to their mothers and fathers, no suffering exists regarding women.
For those who pursue the ultimate truth, the female body is impermanent, suffering, and empty; for those who recite mantras, it is like a tumor or a thorn. Mmk 11.83.
One who is passionate, foolish, and of corrupt intellect, who has not fled from saṃsāra and is constantly addicted to women— for him, there is no accomplishment.
For a reciter here who is of immoral conduct, there is no superior destination, nor a middling one, nor even the lowest accomplishment. Mmk 11.85.
The Lord of Sages has not taught the accomplishment of mantras for one who is immoral,
nor has he shown the path that leads to the city of Nirvāṇa.
How indeed can mantras be accomplished here by a fool in this contemptible state?
Furthermore, there is no happy rebirth for that person of immoral conduct in this world.
Nor indeed does one attain the vault of heaven, nor become devoted to happiness;
how much less could one achieve such success with the mantras spoken by the Jinas?
Furthermore, when a palmyra tree has been cut down at its very top, it is incapable of becoming green again;
likewise, it cannot produce sprouts once more.
Thus has the accomplishment of mantra for the deluded been proclaimed here:
how could the king of mantras be accomplished by one who is of bad character, a doer of evil deeds, always attached to women, and associated with non-virtuous friends? (Mmk 11.90)

Therefore, one who is self-controlled, always reciting mantras, and not dwelling on the faults of women should avoid attachment to them; for it is toward such [practitioners] that success is ordained.
Success is not declared for others—namely, for the foolish who are infatuated with women;
rather, it belongs to the wise one who delights in being undistracted, who is pure, skillful, and free from attachment.
One who is of noble birth, firm and brave, friendly, and pleasing to behold,
and who knows how to discern between dharma and adharma— for such persons, success is not difficult to attain.

Having proceeded in this manner, the knower of mantras should enter a village for the sake of alms; having gone to whatever place he desires, he should go to a location previously prepared there. (Mmk 11.94)
Having gone to a suitable place, one who possesses a pure mind regarding the alms-bowl should eat what is permissible after having set it down in a clean location.
Having washed his feet and gone outside from that dwelling,
he should first wash only his shins in water that is free of living organisms.
Secondly, having embraced the shank with the left hand and rubbed it,
one should again perform the rite with the right hand (apasavya) and wash the hands with earth-clods.
Then, using seven pure and clean vessels previously prepared,
one should place that which has been purified by mantras and made clean into a vessel that is bright and stainless.
Having taken excellent cow dung from a tawny cow renowned for its purity,
one should prepare a circular maṇḍala for the Teacher in water that is free of living organisms.
First, one should especially construct [the image] of the Best of Sages (the Buddha) measuring one cubit;
second, that of the Lord of the Excellent Mantras (Mañjuśrī); and third, that of the Family Deity.
Furthermore, whenever the mantra-reciter performs that [fourth mudrā],
it is always proclaimed as the enjoyment for all sentient beings.
To the right of the Maṇḍala of the Lord of the World, one should always construct here for the Triple Gem that square Maṇḍala.
The second belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas, and the third to the sons of the One Possessing the Ten Powers;
thus these seven mandalas are square on all sides.
The reciter of mantras should perform this daily in a secluded place for a span of one cubit or half a cubit; thus, day by day, it shall destroy all sins.
Then, having risen, the mantra-practitioner should again diligently wash his hands and perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) in water that is clean, pure, and free from living organisms.
In a pure and stainless vessel, carefully brought from a great lake, a spring, a pond, a natural pool, or the flowing current of a river; Mmk 11.106.
Having approached a pure place and having taken [the earth] with the hands of a pure person,
the mantra-practitioner should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) two or three times.
Then one should touch the face, as well as the ears and the two eyes,
the nostrils, and the two arms.
One should touch the head and the region of the navel with auspicious water;
one should perform this five or seven times, doing everything according to the prescribed rule.
Endowed with pure conduct and having become clean, the reciter should take his alms-bowl and go to a body of water. (Mmk 11.110)
Wherever water flows downward or wells up, one should always wash the alms-food from rivers, springs, and the like. *Mmk* 11.111.
Then, having risen, one should go again to the monastery or the dwelling;
one should enter that very place where one previously resided and remained under control.
Having gone to that place, the reciter should set down the vessel;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), he should quickly take up the vessel once again.
One should present the offering to the Teacher in a vessel made of clay, leaf, silver, gold, copper, or even bark. Mmk 11.114.
The King of Mantras should again offer the sacrificial food (nivedya) to the Teacher with his own mantra;
having approached on a single lunar day, he should give according to his ability even to those who are suffering.
One should not offer an excessive amount of oblations in any respect;
the knower of mantras should not act with self-interest, but rather should always act with proper application in all things.
One should always maintain the measure of the body as being only the size of the belly;
for one who is afflicted by hunger and thirst is not capable of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra.
Neither one who eats excessively nor one who eats too little is capable of following the mantras;
for this very reason, it was said by the Lord of Jinas for all embodied beings: Mmk_11.118.
Food is the sustenance of sentient beings, by which humans live,
as well as gods, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and kinnaras.
Rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, bhūtas, uṣṭrārakas, and grahas—none of these exist who can look upon one who is focused [on the practice]. Mmk 11.120.
The Tathāgata has declared that beings who consume gross, formed, and solid food are called coarse eaters, whereas those who consume subtle food are indeed subtle eaters.
The divine beings of the form realm subsist on the nourishment of meditative absorption and engage in activities characteristic of that realm;
the gods of the formless realm indeed consume the fruit of their meditative concentration.
Beings in the intermediate state are proclaimed to subsist on the food of intention;
likewise, beings in the desire realm consume various kinds of food.
The gods and asuras are desirous and subsist on food consisting of mouthfuls;
for this very reason, it has been taught by the Lords of Jinas through the causes of the Dharma.
It is proclaimed that for all sentient beings, sustenance is the basis of existence;
for one who is constantly disciplined in recitation, the act of eating should be done with moderation.
For one established in this diet is capable of practicing the mantras;
being pure in conduct, he is skilled in the life of a celibate practitioner.
And for one who knows the proper measure regarding food, success is not difficult to attain,
just as a cartman succeeds when he lubricates his cart with oil.
Just as those [oxen] are for the purpose of enduring a long time and for the sake of bearing a burden,
so too the mantra-knower, the minister, gave food for the sake of stability.
The practitioner of recitation should always nourish the body for the sake of its maintenance and health,
for the purpose of accomplishing mantras, and as a cause for the accumulations of enlightenment.
Likewise, in the world of mortals, one should recite the mantra for the sake of benefiting the worlds;
for this very reason, the most excellent sage of great splendor spoke thus.
In former times, on this earth, one named Kāśyapa always recited this mantra for the sake of the welfare of all beings.
It was spoken for the sake of all those in the world who suffer, who are wretched and exhausted by poverty, who are weary from toil, and who are afflicted.
For the welfare of beings who have come into this cycle of existence, one should recite this supreme mantra for the sake of providing sustenance to those beings. Mmk 11.133.
"Listen, all you disciples and those who rely upon the Bodhisattvas;
receive this mantra, my word, which destroys disease."
But those beings who are afflicted by the disease of hunger, and those who are thirsty—you who desire the stages [of practice], listen for the sake of pacifying all suffering! Mmk 11.135.
Having spoken thus, that Kāśyapa of great splendor, who resembled a sage,
addressed that Lord with his disciples, their minds filled with joy.
Speak the mantra, O Knower of Dharma, King of Dharma, Great Sage;
you who have compassion for sentient beings, the supreme time has now arrived.
Having spoken thus, the sages should recite the mantra in detail at the beginning;
its resonance is like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, with a sound like a drum or a thundercloud.
The Conqueror has a voice like Brahmā, possesses great heroism, and is indeed the foremost of the Brahmas;
let all the hosts of beings who have gathered here listen!
Whether they be footless, many-footed, two-footed, or four-footed— in brief, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall proclaim this mantra that brings about happiness.
Sentient beings of the past and future, and those of the present who have come here—I shall speak of them in brief; listen, you who desire the truth! Mmk 11.141.
Thus it is said.
Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: *Oṃ gagane gaganagañje ānaya sarvaṃ lahu lahu samayamanusmara ākarṣaṇi mā vilamba yathepsitaṃ me sampādaya svāhā*.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kāśyapa became silent.

In that interval, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, the words of the knowledge-mantras were recited in full detail; the entire sky was seen filled with clouds of most precious food, and the whole of this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system was seen with its celestial vault covered by clouds of food.
To whatever being desired food according to their disposition, whatever nourishment they took pleasure in, that very thing was provided for them.

For the sake of allaying the suffering of hunger, the act of eating was performed with foods according to their preference; and for those who were thirsty, the drink and water—consisting of a stream of water endowed with the eight qualities—fell right there as they desired.
At that time, at that very moment, all sentient beings had their every hunger and ailment pacified and all thirst removed.
That entire assembly, filled with wonder and joy, having rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished right there.
Both the Blessed One Kāśyapa and the Tathāgata remained dwelling in the dwellings of a Tathāgata; and this has now been spoken and approved by me, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, as well.

In this supreme king of kalpas, for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst— especially for those who recite mantras— the practitioner must first accomplish this mantra. If one is unable to go out for alms,
one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it six hundred thousand times, subsisting on the three white foods or consuming only milk.

Then, having installed the medium-sized cloth painting (*paṭa*) of the noble Mañjuśrī on that very mountain peak, one should perform a great worship as before and offer a most magnificent *bali* oblation.

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood fuel using this very mantra spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, [one should offer] fresh *audumbara* wood fuel— measuring a span (*vitasti*), smeared with curd, honey, and ghee— as well as *śrīphala* wood fuel.
Or one should offer eight thousand oblations.
Then, at the time of midnight, a great circle of black clouds and wind will arrive;
one must not be afraid,
nor should one rise and depart.
One should perform self-protection and the binding of the mandala using the eight-syllable heart-mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, as well as for one's companions, as previously described.
Then that black whirlwind of wind disappears.
And all the women, adorned with every ornament, garlanded with light, illuminating the directions, appear before the practitioner.
"Arise, O Mahāsattva! I have attained success. Having said this, she departs. The practitioner should offer an *argha* oblation with scented water mixed with *jātī* flowers.
Then she vanishes right there;
on that very day, she provides for herself and her twenty-five companions, or as many as desired, whatever food they wish for,
and she supplies all necessary articles according to their needs.

Then the practitioner, having dismissed [the deity] and offered the *argha* water, should circumambulate the cloth-painting three times, take up the painting, and prostrate to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
he should then go to a desired place suitable for practice as previously described— a great forest, a mountain peak, or a place devoid of humans.
There, one should dwell having constructed a dwelling with companions.
While dwelling in that place, one should perform such deeds as traveling through the sky.
Then, the practitioner, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass as before, should install the middle cloth-painting, having installed it.
As before, having kindled a fire with khadira wood, one should offer eight thousand white flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days.
Then, at the time of midnight, at the conclusion of the fire offering, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
he grants the desired boon.

Whether it be traveling through the sky, invisibility, the stages of a bodhisattva, the state of a pratyekabuddha, or the state of a śrāvaka; whether it be the five superknowledges, long life, great sovereignty, great wealth, or being beloved by kings— in brief, whatever one desires while practicing the mantra together with the noble Mañjuśrī, he grants all of that.
Whatever one asks for, that he bestows; or he obtains all the substances necessary for spiritual accomplishment;
and he performs the summoning of great beings.
"In brief, whatever is spoken, he performs it all;
he purifies either past karma or transgressions," so said the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, there is another intermediate practice suitable for ritual action:
first, in a distinguished place, a pure location, or on the sandy bank of a river, having performed everything as previously described,
one should install the cloth painting facing west and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east.
The passage should be expanded in detail as before.
One should recite [the mantra] six hundred thousand times during the three periods of the day.
Upon the completion of the recitation, one should perform one hundred thousand oblations with *karṇikāra* flowers mixed with white sandalwood or saffron.

As before, having kindled the fire in that same manner, at the conclusion of the *homa* offering: if the cloth (*paṭa*) trembles, one attains the status of a mantra-master (*mantrin*); if a ray of light shines forth from the cloth and a beam issues out, one attains kingship; if the cloth is enveloped in a garland of flames on all sides, one attains the kingship of the Caturmahārājakāyika gods; if speech issues forth from the cloth, one attains the status of Śakra, the lord of the Thirty-three (*tridaśeśvara*); and if the cloth issues forth a teaching of the Dharma, one attains the status of a Bodhisattva, the lord of the three realms.
Upon touching the head of Paṭabāhu, he attained the five supernormal powers, reached the seven stages, and was destined for the attainment of the ten powers in successive order.

Then, when the practitioner has accomplished the mantra spoken by the Blessed One Kāśyapa and has attained the means for warding off hunger and thirst, he should practice the dharma conducive to accomplishing the purpose of the mantra-conduct according to that very same procedure and with those very same requisites; otherwise, there is no success.
In this way, following the gradual practice of mantra-conduct according to the rules, one will certainly achieve success.
This applies to substances, implements, medicinal herbs, and all other precious gems as previously described.
The mantra-knower, reciting the mantra, with his mind focused on the prescribed rite,
the practitioner of mantra in that place at that time [should eat] white rice produced from pure [grain].
Having eaten with a satisfied mind and always with fully nourished faculties,
one should secretly take that remainder of the vessel and go to a river of pure water.
Having set it aside in a secluded spot, the observer of the vow gave it to the animals;
and having given it to the animals, he diligently washed the bowl.
Furthermore, one should carefully subject an earthen vessel to firing;
then, one should prepare the remaining vessels so that they are free from grease and devoid of meat.
Having discarded even the scent [of food], the excellent sage should leave the remainder in his bowl;
in whichever bowl he wanders for alms, he does not eat from that one.
One should never eat solid foods there; rather, one should always consume edible fruits.
One should not eat from a lotus leaf, nor even from those produced by the *kuvalaya* water-lily.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid fragrant flowers; he does not eat there those leaves which belong to the *kaumuda* or those originating from the *plakṣa* and *udumbara* trees. (Mmk 11.148)
Nor [should one use] leaves from the *vaṭa* tree, nor those of the *karṇaśāka*, *gaulmin*, nor likewise those from *āmra* leaves, nor those produced from the *pālāśa*.
With śāla leaves and śirīṣa flowers produced from the Bodhi tree,
where that Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, sat.
One should avoid that tree with great effort, nor should one even dig up its wood;
one must not strip off the leaves from *nāgakesara* trees.
Nor should one ever eat at any time when these [periods] are all avoided by the wise;
nor, out of delusion, should one ever step over the leaf-huts of the sages.
The mantra-practitioner falls from his commitment by eating from those leaves;
the practitioner should not eat food there using any other leaves.
One should always take up the food in vessels made of clay, those specified as being of copper, likewise of silver, of gold, of crystal, or of stone. Mmk 11.154.
One should not eat from the backs of leaves, nor likewise from the palms of the hands;
those leaves produced by the offering [of food] belong to the Ten-Powered One, the enemy of Māra.
The reciter should avoid the leaves of those who are Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of Śrāvaka individuals, and he should not step over them with his feet.
The mantra practitioner should not, even with effort, take any of the various kinds of cakes, drinks, or food that have been offered. Mmk_11.157.

The practitioner of recitation should always avoid giving [offerings] to the Jinas, those who follow the conduct of the Jinas, as well as to the individuals who are Śrāvakas, even if they belong to the Three Jewels.

Even the slightest mantras do not succeed for embodied beings who [neglect this]; how much less so the divine [mantra] which is esteemed as the source of all auspiciousness and the highest good? Mmk_11.159 //
The rites for nourishment and pacification, which fulfill all hopes—
these rites for nourishment and pacification that fulfill all hopes will not succeed for one who eats the offerings presented to them.
The mantras of one who is pure, skillful in character, compassionate, and likewise righteous, and who is devoted to cleanliness and proper conduct, succeed everywhere.
Having first given food to all there, the reciter should not eat;
he should not consume any other food, but should eat only that which has been offered by others.
One who knows the mantra and proceeds with even a small amount of food that has been offered by oneself will have success resting in the palm of his hand. Mmk_11.163 //
By this method, the practitioner who maintains the vow and performs the recitation should take his food;
for this is praised by the sages as the practice for the accomplishment of all mantras.
In brief, [this is] the procedure prescribed for all acts of eating.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the mantra for the purification of all things.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), the reciter should always recite this mantra;
then, having recited it seven times, the practitioner of mantra effects the purification of the body.
Listen, O assembly of beings and deities, to the detailed explanation of its meaning:
having touched the entire body, the Sage spoke this mantra. (Mmk 11.166)
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, O destroyer of all sins, destroy, destroy all that is employed by the wicked; remember the pledge! Hūṃ Jaḥ Svāhā!
With this mantra, whatever rice-meat (*bhikṣodana*) or other food one consumes should be eaten after having consecrated it with the mantra.
Having eaten and performed the ritual rinsing (*upaspṛśya*), as before, one should rub the entire body starting from the head; then one should rest.

After resting for a moment, or for half a watch (*yāma*), or even a quarter of a watch, one should then pay homage to the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and recite the books of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of all the Buddhas.

One should recite any one of these: the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*, the *Āryacandrapradīpasamādhi*, the *Āryadaśabhūmaka*, the *Āryasuvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the *Āryamahāmāyūrī*, or the *Āryaratnaketudhāraṇī*. Having recited them while standing at the height of a yoke, with the sun at its zenith, and having dedicated the merit according to one's ability, one should set aside the book and cover it with a clean cloth.

Alternatively, having paid homage to the True Dharma, one should then go to the bank of a river or to a great lake to bathe; having taken earth free of living organisms and consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should pour water [over it] with this mantra.
With which one?
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, paralyze all evil ones, hūṃ! O you who hold the blue lotus, you who assume the form of a sporting youth, bind, bind! Remember the pledge! Sphaṭ, sphaṭ, svāhā!

Having performed protection with this, one should perform the binding of the directions, the binding of the companions, the binding of the maṇḍala, and the binding of the mouths of all the wicked and malicious ones.
It effects the summoning of all things and the binding of semen; by tying a thread over which the mantra has been recited seven times around the waist, one may wander everywhere.
During all times of recitation and at every time of bathing, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times for the purpose of destroying and pacifying evil obstacles.
Thereafter, one accomplishes all rites.
One should place the great mudrā of Pañcaśikha in all rites;
it accomplishes everything, and it does not turn out otherwise.
Then the practitioner, having taken earth, cow dung, powder, and so forth, should bathe as he pleases;
he should bathe with water free of living organisms.
And in all rites everywhere, he should perform them using only [materials] free of living organisms.
Then, having bathed with applications of clay and cow dung, or other various fragrant substances and special requisites, he should not discharge phlegm, urine, excrement, or the like into the water;
nor should he discharge a stream of saliva or water.

Nor should he play, even while feeling compassion, having reflected upon all sentient beings and himself as being overwhelmed by sensations obstructed by suffering, empty, and selfless—like a creature distressed by separation from its mother.

Thus, the knower of mantras who is devoid of the means of accomplishment should behold himself situated in the depths of the ocean of saṃsāra, obstructed by the foundations of suffering such as being cut, fallen, scattered, and destroyed;
and having observed himself as one without a dwelling, without a mantra, without refuge, and with a dejected mind.

One should meditate while standing in water reaching up to the neck, or while standing in water reaching up to the navel; indeed, having established one-pointedness of mind right there in the midst of the water.
First of all, there was a great lotus stalk, endowed with great lotus flowers, adorned with great lotus petals, beautiful to behold, composed of jewels,
with its stem made of lapis lazuli, its leaves of emerald, its filaments of ruby, and its thousand petals of crystal, which was in full bloom.

Then, one should meditate upon the Blessed Buddha seated there upon a lion-throne made of jewels, adorned with many gems, beautified by flowers of crystal and ruby, and covered with a pair of fine cloths; one should meditate upon him as he teaches the Dharma,
white as gold, garlanded with flames on all sides, adorned with a halo of light, and of great stature like [the sun] in the sky.
He is depicted in the cross-legged posture.

To the right is the noble Mañjuśrī, endowed with all the finest ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, holding a fly-whisk for the Blessed One; he stands and does not sit, his body being reddish-fair or the color of ground saffron. And to the left is the noble Avalokiteśvara.
White as an autumn stalk of rice, with a yak-tail whisk held in his hand—thus one should meditate on these eight bodhisattvas:

Ārya Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha, Ārya Vajrapāṇi, and Sudhana; these ten bodhisattvas [along with the two previously mentioned] are on the right, while one should meditate on the eight Pratyekabuddhas.
Candana, Gandhamādana, Ketu, Suketu, Sitaketu, Ṛṣṭa, Upāriṣṭa, and Nemi—these eight great śrāvakas were also present in that very place. They were as follows:
the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍolabharadvāja, Pilindavatsa, the noble Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa, and the noble Ānanda.
In this way, one should meditate upon an infinite community of monks in the presence of these great śrāvakas;
one should meditate upon an infinite number of pratyekabuddhas in the presence of the pratyekabuddhas;
and one should meditate upon an infinite community of bodhisattvas in the eight locations of the great bodhisattvas.
In this manner, one should meditate upon the surface of the sky adorned with the great mandala of the assembly.
And oneself, standing in water reaching to the navel, [should visualize] various kinds of flowers— divine and human, such as *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*,
*padma*, *mahāpadma*, *dhātu*, *kārika*, and *indīvara* blossoms— in various forms, of great size, and forming vast heaps.
One should perform worship of the Blessed One with baskets of flowers;

one should perform a delightful worship for all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas with powders, parasols, banners, and flags, both divine and human, and with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps.
Likewise, all offerings and services such as food-oblations, incense, and edible offerings, whether divine or human, should be presented as ritual requisites.

One should meditate on oneself being illuminated by a ray of light issuing from the *ūrṇakośa* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. For the practitioner who has just entered this meditation and recites the mantra, there is the attainment of the fruit of Brahma-merit; he will certainly be destined for enlightenment.
Thus have these meditations been described by the foremost beings in the world for the sake of the welfare and benefit of all beings and of practitioners of mantra.
Then, for the benefit of all mantra-practitioners,
that foremost and principal sage, the most excellent of beings, spoke this meditation to the sentient beings.
The first [chapter] spoken by the Sage concerns the mandala-form and that aversion;
the second is the mandala, and the third is the doctrine of mantra thereafter.
In the first [case], there is supreme accomplishment; likewise, in the middling, the next best;
and in the inferior, there is minor accomplishment—thus spoke the bull among sages.
Likewise, there is the banner-like meditation, which is superior, middling, and inferior;
in brief, that meditation is the destroyer of all evils.
Beyond this, the wise should not resort to other forms of meditation;
for his mantras, being well-established in this meditation, truly attain accomplishment. (Mmk 11.172)
Having meditated upon the meditation as described according to the ritual procedure as desired,
the reciter should indeed dismiss the mantra there, having offered an *argha* offering at his ease.
Having crossed over that flood of water, one should then proceed at ease to the previously designated place, which is prescribed by rule and well-restrained.
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra according to the previously described ritual;
having dismissed the mantra there, the invited deities should likewise be dismissed.

Then, having likewise performed the protection for his companions, he—being skilled, knowing the reality of the ritual acts, and devoted to the performance of the rites—is considered [fit]. Mmk 11.176 (= “177”)
Having praised the Supreme Person with various offerings of hymns,
as well as his own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the rhinoceros-like horn.
Then, rising again from that seat, the mantra-reciters [beheld] the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who are capable of bestowing grace upon the three worlds.
Having gone far from his dwelling to a place sheltered from the wind,
he should void his urine, excrement, phlegm, and nasal mucus.
During the day one should face north, and at night one should face south;
the reciter of mantras should never contemplate worldly matters while in that state.
One should not recite there a mantra spoken by one's own family for their specific rite;
rather, having sat upon the ground, one should do so when it is auspicious according to the signs of the [proper] course and other such indicators.
Having sipped water that is pure and strained through the hem of a clean garment,
one should wash both feet up to the knees with exactly seven applications of clay.
In the case of seminal emission, one should take seven [handfuls];
in the case of the discharge of feces, thirty; at both ends [of the anus], two each;
and likewise, two for the discarding of phlegm and two for nasal mucus.
Then, having touched water, one should go from afar toward the dwelling on the ground;
likewise, having gone [there], one should proceed by means of a mere sound or by the casting of arrows along the path.
Beyond that, one may proceed as desired toward the southern direction and its outskirts,
[encountering] chasms, fallow fields, barren lands, and likewise places strewn with sand.

One should avoid the further bank of a river—excluding [the case of] a *caitya*—as well as places with refuse heaps or impurities; rather, one should dwell confidently in a secluded spot at the edge [of a forest], devoid of people.
At that time, however, the minister of the rite should perform the evacuation of impurities;
the reciter of the mantra, knowing the proper time, should restrain his natural urges. (Mmk 11.187)
Then, having gone as desired to a pure region in a secluded place according to the rules,
one should construct a hut or a spring in that location as is comfortable.
In the morning, in a secluded, covered, or secret place upon the earth,
one should always discharge urine while observing silence and remaining free from attachment.
Once the urine and feces have been eliminated, the observer of the vow should always perform purification using clay that is soft, pleasant to the touch, well-ground, and free of living organisms.
Having likewise taken water three times and once, one should always [wash] the anus at both ends, as well as the hands; first, it was thus prescribed by the Mantra-knower on earth.
Having diligently washed his feet, and specifically the right one first,
the practitioner of recitation (japin) should always keep his feet joined together with one another.
The detailed purification for those who recite mantras has been explained previously;
however, the purification consisting of being free from odor and stains was taught by the pure ones of old.
Thus has purity for those who follow the mantras been briefly explained.
Purity through the removal of odor and stains is indeed constant purity;
this is seen in all these tantras—so said the Lord of Sages.
Having performed the ritual ablution, the ascetic practitioner, devoted to the rites of accomplishment,
should recite [the mantra] according to the previously mentioned procedure with a mind that is inwardly pure.
Purity is declared to be fivefold for practitioners in all tantras:
physical purity, as well as [purity of] speech, mind, and meditation;
the fourth is the purity of truth, while water is said to be the fifth.

Those who possess the true Dharma, have conquered anger, know the tantras, perceive the treatises, are skilled in the meaning of subtle reality, know the mantras, and are diligent in ritual action; Mmk_11.197(=“198”) //
For those who are skilled in the causes and in internal [meditative] cultivation, accomplishment is not difficult to attain among them;
one should not speak of false worship that is devoid of truth and the Dharma.
Cruel and even more cruel, utterly devoid of truth,
inciting hatred, wrathful, harsh, and piercing the vital points.
But one who is devoid of truth and righteousness, who oppresses other beings, is malicious, possesses a defiled mind, and is abandoned by all virtuous qualities— Mmk_11.200(=“201”) //

One who constantly practices violence, one of immoral conduct, or even one who follows the path of righteousness—such a person must always be avoided by one reciting mantras; likewise, so too is vulgar sexual conduct.
False speech and anger are indeed censured by all the Buddhas and by the wise Bodhisattvas for one who is exceedingly fearful of the next world. (Mmk 11.202)
Furthermore, among the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the sword [of wisdom], among the Śrāvakas,
and likewise in this world among those on earth who desire the attainment of supernatural powers, falsehood is always present.
The speaker of false speech goes to the most terrible hells;
furthermore, he is always reborn among animals, as well as among pretas, and again in the world of Yama.
The evil-minded one who lives by falsehood shall dwell eternally right there in the fierce and blazing Tapana and Kālasūtra hells.
In the Sañjīva, the Asipatra, and likewise in the Śālmalīvana hell,
a living being who speaks falsehood shall dwell for many kalpas.
How indeed could the mantras be accomplished for one who speaks falsely?
Deluded by false speech, he causes living beings to tremble;
thus, that person of deluded action will certainly not see the accomplishment of the mantra.
And thus, for one who speaks such words, there is no success for practitioners of mantra;
how could success ever accrue to him, even through many millions of eons?
He by whom the teaching of the Buddhas has been rejected upon this earth will,
therefore, fall into a terrible state of great fear due to ignorance.
In the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, and Pratāpana hells,
he shall dwell for a great eon (mahākalpa) due to his destruction of my True Dharma (saddharma).
Foolish people, having despised the true Dharma and being shrouded in blinding darkness, are cooked in the most terrible hell.
Out of ignorance or childishness, deluded and possessed of false pride,
those who indeed despise the King of Vidyās fall into a terrible hell.
Therefore, one should not commit evil, nor engage in despicable and false actions;
for indeed, the disparagement of the true Dharma and false views are both censurable.
Therefore, always being faithful, one should constantly practice the ritual procedures of the mantra;
speaking the truth, knowing the mantras, and always intent on the welfare of sentient beings,
the knower of mantras should devote himself to the mantra— for him, success is indeed certain.

One performs various actions—superior, inferior, and middling—for it is action (*kriyā*) that accomplishes the rite (*karman*), not non-action; for action is always beneficial. For one who is fully engaged in action and rite, success (*siddhi*) shall always be attained.
Because all objects have action as their purpose, action is always the object of action; thus,
that which has no action as its purpose and that which has action as its purpose are both appropriately joined with action and the object of action.
And may his ritual action be fruitful; always perform the ritual action itself.
Thus, the duty, the action, and the fruit— this triad of duty, action, and fruit— is always such that the fruitless attains fruitfulness, and the fruit itself becomes ever-fruitful.

Whether fruitless or fruitful, all indeed arise from fruit; through conjunction the mantra is accomplished, for conjunction is the means of accomplishing the mantra. Disjunction is the absence of conjunction, yet disjunction is that which accomplishes conjunction.
But the relationship between the goal and the means is not established among them;
for substances that have already achieved their purpose are everywhere contradictory causes for further accomplishment.
For those who have mastered the mantras, the mantras are not unestablished, for they are the cause of accomplishment.
That which the agent most desires to reach is the *karman*; when one intends to act upon an object, it arises from the action.
One should not perform non-action among all actions, for there are causes for action;
one who is endowed with the meaning of mantra and tantra should undertake every rite.
One should undertake the action that has been begun, and likewise not undertake that which is not to be done;
for those who do not undertake the performance [of rites], the mantras do not succeed for any embodied beings.
Long ago, this was sung by the most excellent sages who proclaim all the true Dharma;
it reveals the commitment of the sons of the Conquerors regarding the practice of mantras.
The practitioner, knowing all mantras, [should follow] this other path taught here in the King of Rituals (Kalparāja) in the form of mantras as the cause for awakening. Mmk_11.224(=“225”) //
"All my mantras will succeed wherever there is always proper application;
he shall attain his desired accomplishment in a very short time."
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, the Perfectly Awakened Ones have proclaimed [this] through various forms for those who are destined for the city of Nirvāṇa.
Likewise, the path to awakening is eternal, fulfilling all actions and purposes;
Buddhahood is the primary state, its ultimate consummation and final resort.
In this state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), one shall attain accomplishment here with its fruits;
for those who know the various karmas and dharmas, there shall be the performance of mantras.
This attainment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and liberation has been briefly explained by the foremost of Jinas as the means for accomplishing all goals.

One shall obtain abundant wealth and the basis for the highest state; likewise, O Lord of Yakṣas, one who constantly acts for the sake of sovereignty shall attain the lowest [state]. Mmk_11.230(=“231”) //
He shall attain sovereignty over all the practitioners of mantras among the worlds of humans, gods, and asuras;
likewise, he brings their activities to fruition.
Endowed with purity and proper conduct, always delighting in ethical discipline and meditation,
the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra spoken among all mantras.
He performs various rites— superior, middling, and even inferior— accordingly,
as he desires prosperity for his ministers.
For the reciter, there is an increase in enjoyments in the lowest [case], and for embodied beings in the middle;
however, by means of the highest [practice] alone, one attains the most excellent [result].
At the conclusion of the recitation, the mantra-practitioner should rest for as long as he deems necessary;
there, at the appropriate time, the reciter should perform the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

Nevertheless, all rites are accomplished therein; for by the constant recitation [of mantras] and the destruction of the sins of men, the practitioner of mantra performs the ritual action according to the rules, which has been established throughout the succession of rites.
Success remains possible for that person whenever he attains completeness;
therefore, the reciter of the mantra should again recite the mantra for the sake of destroying evil and, consequently, for the destruction of karma.
May the mantras be effective—those that are supreme, as well as those that are middling or inferior, which are honored by the world;
through their recitation, they destroy without remainder whatever evil has been committed throughout a succession of births.

Thus, the sins of all embodied beings are destroyed; he creates a beautiful woman adorned with various ornaments on her limbs, endowed with all excellent qualities, who dwells eternally as a queen among the Yakṣas. By reciting the mantra of the Tathāgatas, they attain the accomplishment of all aims. // Mmk_11.239(=“240”) //

Thus concludes the fourth chapter, the detailed exposition on the procedures for all rites, including the methods of accomplishment, the stations of ritual action, the rules for recitation, fire offerings, meditation, purification, and conduct, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, from the eleventh section of the detailed exposition.
(Vaidya 86) Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the procedure for the rosary (*akṣasūtra*)—by which mantras are recited, or by which they are caused to be recited—for all beings who follow your vidyā-mantras and are engaged in the welfare of all sentient beings. This applies to all mantras in all tantras that serve as general means of accomplishment.
Listen to it well and keep it thoroughly in mind.
"I shall speak. When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Excellent, Blessed One! Please speak that for our sake, out of compassion for us, for the benefit of those beings who have entered the observance of all mantra practices, and for the benefit of all sentient beings."
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, and I shall explain in detail and with full analysis that by which beings devoted to all mantra practices accomplish all their aims."
And what is that?
First of all, there is the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāmacintyādbhutarūpiṇām*. (Homage to all Buddhas of inconceivable and wondrous form.)
It is as follows: *Oṃ kuru kuru sarvārthān sādhaya sādhaya sarvaduṣṭa-vimohani gaganāvalambe viśodhaya svāhā*.
With this mantra, one should perform rites upon all rosaries;
one should perform such rites as cleansing, piercing, grasping, and purging on the rosaries, and first, one should consecrate the tree [from which the beads were taken].
Then, having performed the protection ritual thirty-seven times and observing the vow, he should sleep there for one night; and in his dream, he sees this.
Whether it be a non-human being endowed with beauty or one who is deformed, O son of Sumitrā, he shall cry out for him after a long time, as if grasping his own wealth according to reality.
Then, having risen early in the morning, that practitioner should go to that tree;
moreover, he may see a dream that is either deformed or extremely fierce.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid that tree, or else go elsewhere;
first is the rudrākṣa, and after that, the indrākṣa.
One should climb a tree that bears fruit—whether it be the *putrañjīvaka*, the *iṣṭa*, or another—accompanied by assistants who are fully skilled in climbing trees. *Mmk* 12.5.
In the absence of companions, the reciter may ascend by himself;
[he should remain] upon the fruit-bearing branches of a tree that grows upwards.
Furthermore, having emerged from the upper branch,
one should grasp the fruit from the upper branch and employ the upward-directed rite.
The supreme accomplishment is declared by the foremost of persons for the highest [level];
for the middling, the middling accomplishment; and for the lowest, indeed, the inferior one.
Having always gathered fruit from those trees without causing harm to living beings,
and having obtained [the fruit] from the trees in the western direction, the purposes of the substances are accomplished.
In the north, one should bring together the deities, such as those born of the yakṣa lineage;
this rite known as "attraction" is for the sake of pacifying the purposes of all beings. (Mmk 12.10)
Devas, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and rākṣasas—
O Ordainer, they perform their actions well for the nourishment of the welfare of all beings.
It renders fruitful all actions performed on earth without exception;
those branches situated in the eastern direction are the source of fruit.
One should always apply effort toward those [sites], for they are the causes for the sake of long life;
therein one performs various forms [of rites] where success is always attained through the fruits.
But that branch which goes toward the south, abounding in leaves and shoots,
the reciter of mantras should avoid it, because it is a taker of the life-force of sentient beings.
Those fruits which have grown high upon the branches extending toward the south should be recited over with the same number of seed-syllables; this destroys the sins of one's enemies.
The reciter should avoid with great effort those fruits that are proclaimed to hang from the lower branches, for they are causes for the loss of much merit.
By means of those [fruits], one may go to Rasātala and to the women of the Dānavas;
a rosary made of those fruits is proclaimed as being "grasped" (gṛhītā). Mmk 12.17.
Whichever lower abodes there may be, by that [mantra] one shall go to Pātāla;
having entered there, the reciter indeed attains divine happiness.
If one is possessed by the female spirits of the Asuras, one shall remain so for an eon;
having grasped all the seeds of the *akṣa* tree, the reciter should then descend from that state.
Having performed the protection rites together with his companions, he should then proceed at his ease;
having gone there, he should always remain in a pure place far away.
The mantra-practitioner should remain there and purify the beads produced from the *akṣa* tree; taking hold of the beads, he should be intent upon them and thoroughly purify them in every respect.
Having thoroughly purified the eyes on all sides, one who possesses the mantra should pierce them twenty-one times—either three, seven, eight, or once. Mmk 12.22.
One who knows the mantras and the beings should always purify [the site] with the primary mantra;
when it has been recited seven or eight times, purification is then considered complete.
The practitioner of the vow, provided with five triple-strands made from thread spun by a maiden and derived from lotus stalks, should prepare a wick.
One who knows the reality of mantras should take that [thread], which is fine, well-rounded, without holes, always free from insects, unblemished, and not contemptible. Mmk 12.25.
One should likewise [use] a rudrākṣa that is beautiful, of lovely color, without holes, and uncracked,
or one with a living seed, or even the fruit of the indrākṣa. (Mmk 12.26)
The mantra practitioner, as prescribed, should always diligently string together a rosary that is auspicious, beautiful, ever-free from defects, and esteemed for its efficacy.
It is prescribed that it may be made of gold, silver, ruby,
crystal, conch-shell, fine sandalwood, or even pearl.
One should fashion various garlands and rosaries from coral,
and one may also fashion auspicious garlands from other divine jewels.
With a focused mind, one should string together round, earthen beads upon a thread;
or otherwise, some other beads made from fruits or derived from minerals.
One should diligently prepare a string of kuśa grass tips for the reciter;
[the number of knots] should be one hundred and eight, twenty-five, or fifty for the middling [recitation].
The mantra-practitioner, being composed, should string together this rosary;
he should make the superior rosary consist of one thousand and eight beads.
This fourfold garland is to be strung constantly by practitioners;
then indeed, the garland should be strung with three or two measures.
One should, in brief, string the garland with bracelets made of flower-metal (puṣpaloha), or of gold, silver, or even copper. Mmk 12.34.
Then, having made a noose at the end, one should place it in that sequence;
one should encircle it until the end of the three junctions so that it remains bound.
Then, having made the appearance of the mandala clearly manifest,
one should surround it with all objects of enjoyment in their respective forms and adorn it.
Having bathed in auspicious water or in a pure river, [one should wear] that which has the appearance of a pearl necklace, fashioned in the form of a neck-ornament (kaṇṭhikā).
Having bathed as before, one should emerge from the water;
having sipped water according to the rule, one should take up the domestic [mantra] recited over the rosary.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as well as with powdered clay,
and having rinsed it in pure water, one should anoint it with fragrant unguents.
Having carefully washed [the image] with excellent pigments, white sandalwood, and saffron, one should then proceed from there to the sacrificial pit (uḍaya).
Having gone to the proper place where that middle-sized painting is located—
wherein is the best of Jinas, the foremost Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men.
Likewise, one should always [perform it] before an image of the Teacher, or before the excellent relics of the Jina on earth, or in the presence of [the Buddha’s] attendants. (Mmk 12.42)
Having established [the deity] upon that cloth and standing before it,
one should recite [the mantra] one thousand eight hundred times, and one hundred and eight times in a single session.
Having fasted for a day and night and performed the recitation previously according to the prescribed measure, he offered a garland to that best of sages.
Having recited the mantra over the rosary, the knower of mantras should then deposit it right there at night; he should sleep right there on the ground upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
If, in a dream, he sees a beautiful vision,
then the success indicated by that dream is ordained for him as fruitful.
If anything is seen in a dream by a Buddha, a Śrāvaka, or a Pratyekabuddha, the practitioner of mantra will certainly achieve success; his ritual performance will surely bear fruit.
If, having seen in a dream a child in the form of a youth, variegated and beautiful to behold, he likewise offers a garland,
his mantras will unfailingly succeed, accomplishing all aims.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for rosaries, from the *Madhyama-paṭavidhāna-visara* within the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 90) Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having once again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, there exists your own specific ritual procedure for the fire-offering (*homakarma*) as set forth in the entire chapter on mantras, which is employed by the practitioner of the *vidyā* who is engaged in the practice.
It is that wherein all beings devoted to the conduct of the *vidyās* are established and apply themselves.
And what is that?
The mantra-words of the secret vidyā are as follows: Oṃ uttiṣṭha haripiṅgala lāhitākṣa dehi dadāpaya hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ sarvavighnāṃ vināśaya svāhā.
This, O Mañjuśrī, is that supreme heart-mantra of fire, which performs all rites and grants all desires.
First of all, the practitioner, having recited this Heart of Fire once, should offer three oblations of clarified butter into the fire;
thus the fire becomes summoned.
Now, for one who has not yet performed [the preliminary], there are three kinds of fuel-wood for the rites of pacification, enrichment, and ferocity.
For the purpose of pacification, aśoka wood that is moist is especially recommended;
it should be one span, one cubit, or even three finger-breadths in height.
This procedure is prescribed for one who is praised for having a glossy appearance;
[the site] should be without hollows or cavities, and likewise resemble a parrot’s wing.
One should avoid [wood] that is green, white-colored, or black-colored;
one should also avoid that which has been eaten by insects, and one should employ wood that is free of hollows.

One should employ wood that is of any color but excellent, free from defects, and devoid of unrighteousness; it should be neither too dry nor too moist, and one must not begin with wood that is burnt.
One should avoid that which is putrid, crooked, or excessively high;
likewise, one should construct the fire-pit as a square on all sides.
Then one should diligently dig downwards with a measurement of four cubits,
or three cubits, two cubits, or likewise even one cubit.
It should always be devoid of living beings and established in the form of a lion;
then, the altar should be shaped like a lotus, circular in form on all sides.
One should also carefully fashion it as a square, or likewise in the shape of a bow;
resembling the form of a thunderbolt, with two points and three prongs.
One should prepare this fire-pit, two cubits wide,
in a pure and well-swept place, such as an excellent riverbank.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with great fervor in a solitary place, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, and likewise on a mountain peak.
Always in an empty temple, and likewise in a great forest—
those places for practice which have been described by the supreme persons. (Mmk 13.11)
These locations have been described in every respect as the places for performing the fire sacrifice (homa).
Then, having stood at a distance of one cubit, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
There, the knower of mantras should especially perform the rite of homa;
by means of these, success will quickly be established in these very places—of this there is no doubt.
Facing either the east or the north, the mantra-practitioner should perform rites for pacification and nourishment;
however, he should avoid performing those rites of a fierce nature toward the south.
Success in rites for pacification is attained when facing east, and likewise for rites of enrichment when facing north;
with these orientations, the mantra-practitioner should always begin the recitation of mantras.
One should perform rites for nourishment using wood from the *vilva*, mango, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* trees;
for malevolent rites, one should use wood that is dry, bitter, sour, or pungent.
One should always avoid all those things forbidden by the sages;
for rites of pacification and enrichment, wood that is still moist is recommended.
Likewise, such actions as those involving cruelty are always avoided by the sages;
in the absence of such [sacrificial] materials, one should instead prepare wood for them.
One should arrange it so that it is strewn with kuśa grass on all sides, with the tips pointing in both directions,
using blades that are green, glossy in appearance, and resembling the neck of a peacock.
One should always perform rites for pacification and nourishment with such *kuśa* grasses,
as well as with dried blades of grass that resemble the color of emerald or the sky.
One should perform the rites of fire here, which have been prohibited by the supreme Victors,
provided the water is always stainless, pure, and free from worms.
