Then, having sprinkled water all around and performed a circumambulation,
one whose mind is disciplined should kindle the fire after touching water according to the ritual rule.
One should fashion a torch from clean grass stalks according to the proper measure;
having made it the size of a fist, one should then carefully ignite it with fire.
Nor should one ever [recite] with the breath from the mouth or with the edge of a garment;
it must be avoided while wearing lower or upper robes, and not while naked.
Nor should one strike it with the wind from the hand, nor with a fan for one's own pleasure; likewise, one should cause it to be fanned with a clean fan, or with cloth, or even with leaves.
When the fire has been kindled and the wind has been stirred up by these [means],
the one who knows the mantras and desires to perform the oblation (homa) should, being well-composed, cause it to blaze.
Then, having sprinkled [the water] three times while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder,
one should indeed offer three oblations there into clarified butter derived from a cow.
Then one should indeed perform prostration to all the Buddhas, the Protectors, and to one's own mantra and the Lord of Mantras; thereafter, one should pay homage according to one's desire.
Then, having recited the mantra within the heart of the fire, one whose self is united with the fire should always invoke him with fragrant flowers alone.
The wise one who knows the mantra should always summon [the deity] and provide a place;
having given a seat and a location, he should do so with that very mantra and no other.

For the purpose of worshipping the fire, one should offer three pieces of fuel wood soaked in curd, mixed with clarified butter, and anointed with honey, throughout the entire ritual action accompanied by mantras.
At that time, one should perform [the rite] situated in both [places], with fuel-sticks mixed with substances,
combined with clarified butter and honey, and likewise mixed with curd.
The practitioner of secret mantras should prepare a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or even one hundred and eight [offerings]; having thus recited the mantra once, he should cast them into the fire.

One should perform the rite of pacification (śāntika) when the fire has garlands of flames or even a single flame; likewise, one should perform the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) when it is free of smoke.

If, when performing the rite of fire-offerings (homakarma) as prescribed by the Conqueror— though it be censured and involve fierce rites amidst smoke— the color of the fire should become [unfavorable], [it portends ill].
For pacification, a white color is always praised by the supreme Victors;
indeed, mantras are accomplished there for one who offers oblations into a white fire.
Likewise, a red color is always desired for the accomplishment of nourishing rites (pauṣṭika);
while black, smoke-colored, or even tawny indicates a malevolent (pāyika) result.
Thus, this threefold accomplishment is set forth in three ways:
as having other colors, as being cloud-colored, or as described in various forms and colors.
Furthermore, there is no accomplishment of mantras upon this earth for those who possess such a complexion or are described as having various forms and colors.
But having seen the fire blazing, one should again undertake the rite;
if the mantra-siddhi has not yet been attained, one should perform the recitation once more.
One should again perform the fire-oblation according to the ritual procedure as prescribed;
having performed the dismissal and the invocation, one should utter the mantra to the fire.
In this very maṇḍala previously prepared according to the ritual rules,
he should indeed perform the fire offering (homa) for the rites of dismissal and invocation.
One should perform all rites with that very [mantra] in that very rite;
likewise, one should begin the fire-ritual (*agnicaryā*) in such a manner before the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). (Mmk 13.43)
"Mantras indeed attain accomplishment there, as previously stated by the Tathāgatas;
one should perform the rites praised by the Jinas there, and not [perform them] anywhere else."
One should not perform other actions, especially sinful ones,
which are censured by the supreme Victors and contrary to what is despised by the world.
Arise as a universal monarch, or a bodhisattva, or a sovereign of the earth;
likewise, upon attainment, one achieves the five superknowledges or even the state of a deity.
On this cloth, one who is constantly disciplined and skilled in the rite of fire-offerings may attain lordship over the underworld or the power to move through the atmosphere.
One always attains the state of a terrestrial deity or a yakṣa in the summoning of a yakṣī,
whether for sovereignty, lordship, or within this very realm or village.
One attains the state of a Vidyadhara and an Asura, bringing all sentient beings under one's control,
and the power to summon spirits and great-souled Mahasattvas.
By means of the rite of homa, one can summon even the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas who abide on the ten stages; how much more so a human being on this earth?
Likewise, one shall attain the rank of general in the world, as well as sovereignty in particular,
the subjugation of all beings, and even the status of a king.
For the purpose of subjugating all beings or even a king upon this earth,
one should likewise constantly perform all rites everywhere by means of fire-oblation (homa).
One whose self is entirely endowed with all [qualities] should undertake every ritual action;
for him, that action will certainly succeed, leading to the highest welfare.
Furthermore, middling and even inferior rites are accomplished;
all substances therein are likewise said to achieve success in three ways.
When the fire-offering rite (*homakarman*) has been undertaken, success is seen to be fruitful, provided one binds the five-crested mudrā and recites the Keśinī mantra. *Mmk* 13.55.
One who possesses the wisdom of self-protection should perform all rites;
however, when engaged in the rite of *homa*, one should then recite this mantra.
In this ritual, it should always be recited seven or eight times.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded.
That is to say: *oṃ jvala tiṣṭha hūṃ ru ru viśvasambhava sambhave svāhā*.
By means of this application of the mantra, one who knows the mantra should repeatedly recite it over pieces of wood and offer them into the fire, either twice or seven times.
Or one should sprinkle flowers, incense, or all kinds of perfumes from every direction with water over which this mantra has been recited. (Mmk 13.58)
Then one should undertake all rites according to the prescribed method;
indeed, in all rites, they must be performed by means of the preliminary practice itself.
Having bound the glorious Mahāmudrā with the five preceding finger-tips,
and having then performed the protection ritual, one should always recite the mantra of Keśinī.
Those who are confident should undertake all ritual actions for the sake of accomplishment,
provided that auspicious omens are seen and sounds are always favorable.
His mantras are indeed successful in granting boons as desired;
when applied in the initial rites, they proceed by means of the mantra.
In them, every success is ordained to be fruitful;
there is the sound of the word "Victory," the beating of drums, and the resonance of kettledrums.
Success is indeed declared to be everywhere for one who relies upon the rite of fire-oblation (homa),
as well as when other excellent omens appear or when the auspicious cries of birds are heard.
Various kinds of sounds and meanings have been described by the Victors;
they are praiseworthy, divine, auspicious, celestial, delightful, and manifold in their resonance.
Parasols, banners, and flags, as well as adorned women,
a full water-jar, and likewise the sight of half-moons, are causes for success.
Or those that possess many excellent forms and colors, which are praiseworthy and honored by the world—
for them, the mantras of various domains are accomplished upon being seen.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 95) Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, there exists one who is authorized in all the mantras that serve as the means for accomplishing the secret vidyās of your own [mantra system]; he is the master and the most senior of all mantras— both mundane and supramundane— which have issued from the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, which have entered the cloud of Dharma, and whose nature is like space, just as a prince is among all beings.
In this regard, the Tathāgata is proclaimed as the most senior, the most excellent among gods and humans, the bull among men, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

For in this way, O Youth, this King of Vidyās is proclaimed as the foremost and most excellent of all mantras, as previously designated by the Tathāgatas—those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whose merit is equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā and who are ineffable. [It belongs] to the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
It is the supreme heart-essence, the supreme secret, esteemed as all-auspicious, praised and extolled by all Buddhas, the consoler of all Buddhas and sentient beings,
the destroyer of all evils, the granter of all desires, and the fulfiller of all hopes. And what is it?
In that interval, from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there issued forth a ray of light named "Exhorter of All Buddhas.

Having illuminated all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, above and below, and having gladdened the minds of all sentient beings, it vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s head.

And from the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Blessed One, there issued forth the King of Vidyās named Ekākṣara, whose form was adorned with flames on all sides, who was unobservable by any sentient beings, invincible, arisen from great majestic power, his body adorned with a halo of light, possessing various forms and the form of a Great Universal Monarch (*mahācakravartin*).
Having emerged and illuminated the entire expanse of the sky, surrounded by all the kings of vidyās, preceded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vidyās,

being honored by all the supramundane sovereigns of the vidyā-wheel, being praised by all mantras, and being empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— those great beings who have attained the ten stages— he filled the entire expanse of the sky.

With a body adorned with great maṇi-jewels and embellished by divine gems, possessing a beautiful form and exceeding brilliance, emitting hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of emanations in various forms,
uttering the single-syllable sound, and releasing a great web of light rays,
he stood in the sky above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, gazing directly at him and surveying the entire realm of the Pure Abodes.
And he illuminated the great circle of the assembly.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [spoke] the single-syllable sovereign of vidyās, the heart of all Tathāgatas, named Ratnaketu—
the supreme heart and most profound secret of the Tathāgata [Ratnaketu], which was established by all the Blessed Tathāgatas:
Sālendrarāja, Amitābha, Duḥprasaha, Sunetra, Suketu, Puṣpendra, Supināntalokamuni, Kanaka, and other Tathāgatas.
And it has been uttered by me, and it has been spoken and approved by all the perfectly awakened ones of the past.
And what is that?
It is as follows: *bhrūṃ*.

This, Mañjuśrī, is that supreme heart-mantra of all the Tathāgatas, the single-syllable great purifier known as the Vidyā-Cakravartin of all virtues. By means of this being accomplished, all mantras are perfected.
It is your own, O Youth, the most excellent king of manuals, conforming to all mantras, the supreme secret, the foremost, and fully authorized.

It is the purifier of all karmic obscurations; indeed, one must necessarily accomplish [the rites]. O Youth, within this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*) of yours, all worldly and supramundane mantra-tantras among all mantras are to be accomplished. Having performed protection by means of this, [one should proceed].
"He becomes unassailable by all beings," meaning he is not overcome by any obstacles, whether mundane or supramundane.
And when this was spoken by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lord of Universal Jewels, the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
all the Buddha-fields were illuminated, and all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, assembled together.

In that assembly circle, all those seated in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, as well as all the bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages and are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, along with all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and all beings of great supernatural power, shall come under his control, impelled by the rays of light of the King of Vidyās.
Furthermore, many other beings established in infinite and boundless world-systems— who were dependent upon the miserable destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts—
being touched and illuminated by that great radiance of light, their sensations of suffering which had been fully awakened subsided;
with minds gladdened by happiness, they would certainly become established in the three vehicles.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that great circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī, to this King of Knowledge (vidyārāja), who possesses great supernatural power, who is the solitary hero, who performs all rites, who is the universal monarch of all kings of knowledge, who fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings, and who is fully integrated into the extensive ritual manuals of your own mantra-tantras throughout all the detailed kalpas."

For the practitioner of all mantras, this is the common foundation for those of great renown, great energy, and heroic beings; it is the means for purifying the entire path to enlightenment through skill in wisdom and method, and for establishing the sequence of entering into nirvāṇa, ascending to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and becoming skilled in the accumulations [of merit and knowledge].

In brief, this is the detailed ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the cloth-painting (*paṭa*), the mandala, and the methods for accomplishment, following the conduct of the former mantra-practices, wherein established beings shall accomplish the Great Wheel-Turning King, the Vidyārāja, the Great Being.
The supreme lord of all mantras, the light-maker, the fulfiller of all hopes, the Vināyaka who acts for the welfare of the entire world,
appearing like the Buddha himself in person, the self-existent one, the performer of all rites— whether superior, middling, or inferior—
he is the bringer of security, auspicious, peaceful, and the destroyer of all sins.
The god of even the gods, the bull among sages of the sages.

I shall proclaim the supreme ritual manual of that Buddha, who is like the sun, boundless, pure, renowned throughout the world, the knower of the intrinsic nature of all actions, the stainless limit of reality; listen, you who desire prosperity! Mmk_14.2 //
First of all, one should paint upon a divine cloth that is free of hair, devoid of adhesive substances, new, white, and especially provided with a fringe;
it should measure two cubits in length and one cubit across.
Likewise, on a cloth that is auspicious, pure, beautiful to behold,
white, made of wool, bright, well-prepared, and free from black fibers.
On a cloth that removes impurities, whether it be white, made of fine silk (dukūlaka),
dyed with *ātasa* fibers, or made of bark, provided it is pure and free from loose threads.
In that which is not produced by worms or wind, which causes no harm to living beings, which is not made of silk, and likewise whatever else has been praised as excellent; Mmk_14.6 //
And upon such an excellent cloth, one should have a temple painted;
having depicted the image of the Teacher, encircled by a garland of light-radiance.
Then, having drawn him of golden complexion, garlanded with flames, alone, hidden in secret, situated on a mountain, and of great splendor; Mmk_14.8 //
One should indeed fashion a canopy of silk bound with garlands of jewels;
above it, one should depict the two deities as being held aloft. (Mmk 14.9)
Indeed, one should fashion a garland of jewels upon the mountain,
adorning it on all sides with pearl necklaces and half-necklaces beneath a canopy.
Having carefully drawn everything above the king of mountains,
one should likewise draw it below the mountain as submerged in the great ocean.
And on the edge of the cloth, one should likewise draw flowers all around:
*nāgakesara*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, and *yūthikā*.
The *mālatī* flower, as well as the *priyaṅgu*, the *kurabaka*,
the blue lotus (*indīvara*), the *saugandhī*, and thereafter the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Various kinds of flowers as well as others possessing fragrance;
these very flowers [are used] for... [the ritual].
And for the sake of worship, they should offer what is pleasing to the Teacher upon a superior cloth-painting,
according to the previously prescribed ritual.
A weaver of thread and likewise a painter are considered suitable;
one should have [the image] painted on the most pure day during the fortnight of miracles.
When the time has thus arrived and the recitation is underway,
one should perform everything exactly as previously prescribed for him.
One should paint the universal form of the Teacher, radiant with color, richly adorned, endowed with manifold aspects, and possessing a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower. Mmk_14.18.
One should draw [the Buddha] with a radiance like that of the campaka flower, depicted in the color of gold;
having thus drawn the Sage, who is endowed with these features and born from jewels.
One should paint that jewel of a Buddha, the highly fortunate Ratnaketu, the most excellent bull among sages, who has attained mastery over all dharmas.
Seated upon a mountain of jewels, adorned with precious caves, he sat cross-legged, imparting instructions on the Dharma.
Having depicted the hero with a slightly smiling face outside the cave, with his mind fixed on the object of meditation, one should likewise draw him below and all around.
The practitioner is seated at a corner of the edge of the cloth, with his knees covered in camphor,
his hands occupied with incense, and his body slightly bent forward.
One should arrange him wearing the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), according to his attire and characteristics,
beneath the Blessed One on the right, even below the surface of the great ocean.
One whose self is ever-disciplined and who seeks the highest good should have the mantra-master painted;
this procedure for the cloth-painting has been taught by those honored by the world. (Mmk 14.25)
Now, the maṇḍala of that deity shall be explained;
at that time, the mantra-practitioner, skilled in mantras, should be properly equipped with the mantras.
Having always performed service to the mantra and practiced it for the sake of perfecting the recitation,
one is then consecrated into this mantra-ritual spoken by Mañjughoṣa.
One who is perfected in the conduct of the maṇḍala and is constantly consecrated is himself consecrated for all mantras and is confident within this maṇḍala.
Those who possess reason are always considered beneficial for self-protection according to the Tantra;
likewise, one of great splendor should carefully examine his companions by means of those [mantras] that destroy obstructors.
The teacher is highly energetic, one who has undertaken and observes the vows;
he is possessed of great wisdom, very affectionate, glorious, and always compassionate.
One should likewise prescribe the characteristics for all the companions:
one, two, three, or even eight, or others as well.
One should accept disciples who are well-endowed, and one should avoid those who are numerous;
furthermore, one should always perform the previously observed rites within this maṇḍala.
Those maṇḍalas first described, proclaimed by the One Endowed with the Ten Powers, belong to Mañjughoṣa; they are not for another, nor through another ritual action.
I shall now declare the measurement for the mandala of great splendor:
it may be four cubits, two cubits, or likewise eight cubits and beyond.
In a pure place, on the bank of a river, and especially on a mountain peak,
one should perform the ritual as previously observed using powder of five colors.
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
having four corners, level, divine, and possessing a radiance equal to divine conduct.
One with good companions should undertake [the rite] that is brilliant in color, variegated, beautiful in hue, very splendid, fragrant, and well-formed.
Silent, observing the conduct of his vow, practicing the eightfold path, with an unafflicted mind, knowing the proper measure, righteous, and always engaged in recitation.
Having undertaken deeds free from evil, performing rites for pacification and nourishment,
one should enter with a neutral mind and draw the Teacher’s form with colored pigments.
First, all of that should be drawn, adorned with various jewels:
the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, of great splendor, seated within a cave.
One should paint him upon the cloth exactly as he is: seated in the paryanka posture, turning the wheel of Dharma, and honored by the *śāstu*. (Vaidya 99) Mmk_14.41.
One should decorate it with three rows of lines and also with mudrās,
covering every row on all sides.
One should place the great lord, the Universal Monarch (cakravartin), in the midst of them, both individually and collectively, without confusing his specific attributes.
Exerting great effort, one should draw the one who follows the Great Wheel, who has the form of a youth and is radiant like the risen sun.
Having the appearance of a great king, adorned with a crown and ornaments,
wearing a diadem, that Great Being is embellished with every kind of decoration.
He is wrapped in a beautiful half-scarf, clothed in variegated silk,
wearing a garland, possessing a gentle complexion, and adorned with flowers and garments.
Smelling the *vakulamālaka* with his right hand alone,
[he beheld] the Lord, of great heroism and sovereign power, whose face was slightly smiling.
Indeed, he is of beautiful and lovely form, devoid of both children and the elderly;
his left hand always holds a wheel, and he wears a blazing garland while grasping [it].
One should paint that figure, seated comfortably in the half-lotus posture with one arm resting [on the knee],
possessing a divine complexion, beautiful in form, and endowed with exquisite beauty.
Seated upon this fragment of jewels, the Great Radiance,
the Bestower of Boons, who is the source of all mantras and the supreme benefit for all beings, is ever present.
Blazing with the form of fire, adorned by a mandala,
and encircled by a garland of flames on all sides, it blazes forth when stirred by the wind.
Thus, by means of the applications of mantras, such a being of great heroism, the accomplisher of all mantras, is ignited among humans on earth.
For whoever beholds [it], that righteous soul is liberated from all sins;
even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, is of immoral conduct, or is dull-witted.
Indeed, all sins are pacified and one is liberated by the mere sight of the Lord;
merely by seeing the mandala of the Wheel-bearer, the God of gods.
At that very moment, one is liberated from those other sins which have been proclaimed;
then, having purified the eastern gate with the mantra of the Lord himself.
Having completely encircled it with archways and adorned it all around with plantain trees,
one should fashion a clearly manifest maṇḍala that is beautiful in form in its entirety.
One should always respectfully perform the offering of bali, incense, lamps, and pure perfumes and garlands, according to the very same procedure as previously described. (Mmk 14.57)
One who knows the mantras should place a full water-jar in the center, directly in front of the practitioner of the wheel; that jar is called "Victorious," and he must not move it.
Likewise, one should first prepare the fire-pit according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule;
the commencement of the fire-offering rite must be done with the *vibhu* mantra and no other.
One should perform eight thousand fire offerings with a fire fueled by *khadira* wood,
as well as with *pālāśa*, *śrīkaṇṭha*, *bilva*, *udumbara*, and *cākṣaka* wood.
Likewise, one should diligently offer apāmārga in all rites,
or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and saturated with the fragrance of burnt incense.
In all rites, one should always perform the oblation one thousand and eight times at the three junctions of the day; as previously specified, this includes bathing and the wearing of garments.
The wise have declared the Triśūla to be an auspicious constellation;
it is suitable for the previously mentioned rites, as well as for recitation, fire-offerings, and other such practices.

Endowed with great power and purpose, this solitary hero, ever supreme,

All ritual manuals— those worldly and esteemed by the world, as well as those supramundane ones— are accomplished, along with the great heroic Vidyārājas of great ascetic power.
Indeed, all mantras are accomplished through this ritual manual;
for it was these very mantras that were taught by the sages and likewise by the sons of those who possess the ten powers.
By Śakra and the other world-protectors, by Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Brahmā,
as well as by the Moon and Sun, and likewise by other lords of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
By the mahoragas and kinnaras, as well as by the best of sages on earth,

Those mantras which have indeed been spoken attain accomplishment here;

He possesses mastery over all mantras, is the director of all rites,

This single-syllable mantra makes the recitation of all practitioners bear fruit; merely by being recited, it attracts all the deities.
The Great One-Syllable [Mantra] possesses mastery over all ritual procedures; it produces various forms, manifold and well-described by the virtuous. (Mmk 14.73)
One who has applied oneself correctly shall accomplish worldly mantras;
having made the cloth-painting perfectly clear and beautiful to behold in its entirety.
One should place it in a pure location, on a riverbank, or on a mountain peak;

The practitioner, facing the east and seated upon a bundle of *darbha* grass, should perform the recitation undisturbed, according to the ritual procedure as prescribed.
Neither too loud nor too soft, and not with a mind intent on something else—

With a mind of loving-kindness, [he should always regard] those in the world who are suffering, wretched, always without a protector, dejected in mind, afflicted by calamity, and extremely weak.
Then, filled with compassion for those fallen into this terrible saṃsāra, one attains success;
one should always diligently perform great worship before the cloth painting.
One should contemplate or indeed perform the mental, human, and divine rites arising from the heart of the Universal Cloth of the Lord of Jinas.
In that very place, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedures should construct a fire-pit according to the rules of reality;
there, indeed, he should offer oblations into the well-prosperous fire.
One who knows the mantras, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron mixed together as worship, shall blaze with light within six months.
One should constantly kindle a powerful fire using wood produced from the *khadira*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, or *pālāśa* trees. *Mmk* 14.83.
In the absence of these woods, one should procure another wood—
such as that of the *picumarda*, the *kadvama*, the sour [wood], or likewise that produced from the *madana* tree.
All those with thorns [on their palms] are declared to be excluded from sinful rites;
one should perform rites for pacification and nourishment using the single-syllable mantra alone. For such a person, success will come quickly even if they were to commit a sinful deed.
For here, all mantra-holders, together with their rituals and extensive manuals, should be employed with non-conceptualization; they always attain accomplishment.
Then the mantras are drawn forth and indeed become bestowers of boons.
Of fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or indeed *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha*,
smeared with ghee, mixed with curd, and combined with honey, one should remain composed.
On this earth, a mantra-practitioner desiring sovereignty should offer oblations everywhere;

Desiring sovereignty over the Vidyādharas and the gods,
one should offer thirty-six hundred thousand lotuses together with their filaments.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, one should indeed present the respectful offering (arghya) and make an announcement to the Teacher;
there, the supreme cloth painting marked by the Victor will blaze forth on all sides.
And as soon as it is touched, one shall fly up to the abode of Brahmā,
reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven and down as far as the collection of netherworlds (pātāla).
In this interval, he always becomes the king of all the siddhas;
possessed of great heroism and firm vows, he puts all malevolent beings to flight.
Krama will always be the king of the Vidyādharas in the accomplishment of rites;
furthermore, he shall live for the duration of a kalpa, traversing the long path.
Having passed away at that great time, he is certain to be destined for enlightenment;
this other [type of] karma, which is constant, has thus been described both in brief and in detail.
Having gathered white lotuses combined with white sandalwood, one should offer them in oblation one hundred lakhs of times; he shall behold Ratnaketu.
Having seen that supreme Jina, one shall then possess the five superknowledges;
one shall live for a long time, a great kalpa, and become an attendant of the Buddha.
And then one beholds the Buddhas residing throughout the infinite directions;
one should constantly worship them and dwell together with them.
There is a single realm named Ratnāvatī where that Blessed One dwells—
the supreme sage, the most excellent and foremost Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
There he dwells eternally, purified by mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, another desired rite has been taught by the foremost persons.
The mantra practitioner, having combined nāgakesara, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron in equal parts, should then perform seventy-eight hundred thousand oblations.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, O God, you arrive here with your discus;
always pleased and ready to grant boons, you touch the practitioner upon the head.
As soon as he is touched by that, the practitioner becomes the lord of the seven stages;
he is called a Bodhisattva, the legitimate son of the Victors.
He will certainly be prophesied as destined for the culmination of enlightenment;
from that time forth, whatever knowledge and object of knowledge belongs to the Son of the Victor [is his].
I know the course, majesty, and power of all mantras;
by merely seeing this king of mantras, one shall possess the five superknowledges. (Mmk 14.104)
When he is always devoted to the performance of worship, he constantly assumes various forms of embodiment endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
At that very moment, he becomes intent upon the work of awakening;
in a mere instant, he then goes to the world-systems of the Buddha-fields.
Then, thousands of world-systems, like cosmic eggs, wander everywhere; they behold the conduct of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He hears the Dharma and is intent upon performing worship for them;
furthermore, there is another rite here concerning the arising of the Victorious Wheel-turner.
One should offer a lamp characterized by a pure wick and ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. Mmk 14.109.
When the lamp has been kindled by men of a hundred thousand measures, placed by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of sailors; Mmk_14.110 //
Men, excluding women, with lamps in their hands on all sides,
should present the cloth [painting] known as the image of the Teacher during the rite of worship.
When all have proceeded equally and are consecrated with the single mantra, one should offer [the oblation] with the mantras of the Teacher; at that very moment, one should declare success.
There was a roar resounding on all sides and the sound of kettledrums;
indeed, many hosts of gods let out cries of "Well done! (sādhukāra).
Then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, stationed in the sky, remained there and said:
"Excellent, excellent! O wise one, you have performed a well-done deed."
Do you not see again the suffering submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra?
Having taken refuge in Buddhahood, which is secure, auspicious, and fearless, [you shall find] nirvāṇa.
O you who are protected by the single-syllable wheel, you have entered the auspicious, stainless, eightfold path practiced by the virtuous in the form of mantra.
Furthermore, there is karma alone which is based upon the supreme destination;
it is known for its great power and purpose, as proclaimed by all the Buddhas.
Taking wood made from the *nimba* tree, one should fashion a three-pronged vajra;
both its tips and its middle sides should be fashioned according to the characteristics of a thunderbolt.
Then, having purified it with mantras before the cloth painting in the lower [section],
the mantra-practitioner, having touched it, should recite the mantras with a concentrated mind.
When sixteen hundred thousand [recitations] are completed, success is desired;
then that Vajra, becoming a single flame, blazes forth on all sides.
From there he rises up in an inconceivable manner, for he ascends;
from there he goes to the Brahma-world or to another realm equal to the gods.
Then, one shall travel through the sky as the foremost among all accomplished ones;
indeed, one exercises sovereignty over the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others.
Then, in the presence of the deity, that king becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) and performs various kinds of physical gestures.
Remaining for ten intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*), he shall not be moved;
always partaking in happiness, worthy of worship, and always possessing a beautiful form.
One whose conduct is the thought of awakening becomes free from the suffering of birth;
indeed, such a person becomes a god or a siddha, entirely devoid of all evil.
Having passed away from there, that mortal shall be devoted to great happiness;
traversing all states of existence, he becomes one who is intent upon awakening.
In this king of mantras, infinite and diverse rites, honored for the sake of many worlds, are recited according to the detailed extent of the ritual procedures and their variations.

Or whatever form of manifold aspects is spoken of here,
