Having ascended the cross-legged seat at night and reciting the inconceivable [mantra], the practitioner of the vow attains accomplishment at dawn; the reciter shall become possessed of the five superknowledges.
Having stepped upon a corpse in a cremation ground, the practitioner, remaining motionless, should recite that single-syllable mantra of great significance; success is sought at dawn.
If one staying in a cremation ground recites this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power,
he attains accomplishment within six months and achieves whatever result he desires.
Whether in this place or that, when recited, it possesses great supernatural power;
staying there, it brings about accomplishment for practitioners who apply it correctly.
A white parasol, as well as a sword, a jewel, sandals,
earrings, necklaces, armlets, a cloth, and a ring.
A waist-thread, as well as a garment, a staff, a water-pot, a sacred thread, a turban, armor, and also a shield; Mmk_14.135 //
The deerskin, the lotus, the rosary, and the sandals—all these are the most excellent ornaments; in this world, both are equal. (Mmk 14.136)
By means of gods, mortals, and others as well, all ornaments indeed bring about success for the reciter before the cloth painting.
All kinds of substances, as well as minerals, ornaments, and even jewels—
all these various weapons were arranged before the cloth painting.
Chanted once, it is then completely purified; when consecrated eight hundred thousand times, it blazes forth when combined with all [substances]. By touching it, the reciter rises up.
Furthermore, the innate natures of sentient beings, appearing in various forms,
may be ornaments or weapons, either fashioned from clay or existing by their own nature.
Those beings who are renowned as having beautiful forms, movements, and natures— even more than various flocks of birds—
whether they be artificial or natural.
Whether conceived as a sentient being or as devoid of consciousness, they are accomplished when honored with mantras;
they are arranged with various substances and fashioned from various elements.
Or else, the one who is highly honored among the destinies and wombs,
having been placed before this cloth-painting according to the previously seen procedure.
Having touched that [object], the mantra-practitioner should recite it six hundred thousand and seven hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, when those [objects] blaze forth, he attains abundant accomplishment.
As soon as they are touched by those [mantras], one shall rise up in the four directions;
one shall live long and obtain the long-lasting happiness of the gods here in this world.
In whatever manner this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power is applied,
in that very manner he shall be pleased and shall always become a granter of boons.
But those engaged in other activities are swiftly perfected by those very rites through the extensive rituals, as is the Vidyārāja of great supernatural power.
One who is pure, whose mind is pure, and who always delights in pure deeds—
the knower of mantras— attains pure accomplishment in a pure place.
One should know that action corresponds to its fruit; from superior [action] comes superior [fruit], from middling [action] comes middling, and what follows is considered inferior.
A rite that bestows abundant wealth produces the activity of a spirit;
however, if it is not accomplished, the success of the rite yields only a very small result.
And by the mere constant recitation, one becomes possessed of great enjoyment and great strength; it always brings the practitioner the favor of kings and the status of a minister.
The king of mantras, when recited even once, destroys his evil;
when recited twice or seven times, it becomes a great protection for oneself. (Vaidya 106) Mmk_14.152
Recited eight times, it provides protection for one's companions from all sides;
furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should then consecrate both garments with the mantra.
Both garments, when consecrated with these mantras, liberate one from all diseases;
by touching them, the fever of embodied beings is destroyed.
Or, if one carefully consecrates water with a mantra and sprinkles it upon the eyes of an angry person,
that angry one will be destroyed by the mere sight of the mantra-reciters.
And as for those hosts of spirits who are wicked, harmful, and performers of evil deeds—
one should gaze upon their faces with this king of mantras recited thirty times.
And one should consecrate one's own hand again and again;
by directing a blow with it toward them, all embodied beings are liberated.
One should constantly perform the bathing, drinking, and feeding of children with the excellent, supreme mantra, which has been recited sixty times and is worshipped by the gods. (Mmk 14.158)
All the wicked ones— the flesh-eaters, the mothers,
and the planetary spirits— being terrified by the mantra, perish and always abandon the foolish.
In this manner, he performed many such deeds upon the surface of the earth for human beings; thus he acted, and always swiftly established [them].
Whatever beings there may be that have crept forth, whether various stationary or moving,
whether poisonous or non-poisonous— they are destroyed when addressed with the mantra.
Whatever various sufferings there may be, whatever sensations experienced by sentient beings,
when applied by the King of Mantras, they quickly bestow peace.
The various sufferings of exhaustion and the calamities of great pestilence are thus swiftly destroyed by the recitation of the mantra six hundred times. Mmk 14.163.
One should perform the fire-offering rites with blue lotuses that are fragrant and honored eight thousand times, mixed with honey, liquor, and clarified butter. Mmk 14.164.
Through the sesame seeds, the spirits attained peace and the people regained their composure;
such were the many various [rites] that have arisen over many eons.
When properly employed by practitioners, it indeed swiftly accomplishes everything;
merely by recitation, one may effect the destruction of the anger of enemies.
For those who are endowed with the meaning of many mantras and for the extensive ritual manuals,
the method prescribed therein is said to be the means for attaining accomplishment in this world.
One certainly accomplishes minor rites through the recitation of mantras;
indeed, by means of such recitation, one always swiftly achieves all goals. (Mmk 14.168)
For the purpose of subjugating all beings, recitation is prescribed at the three junctions of the day;
one should also constantly perform the rite of fire-offering with *mālatī* flowers.
When prepared with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
the mantra always brings fruit for the excellent reciter.
Through constant fire-offerings (*nityahoma*), the reciter shall accomplish his desired aims;
indeed, the constant fire-offering is prescribed as being performed with camphor and other such substances.
One should accomplish various rites as they are conceived according to one's desire;
from even a very small rite, a vast abundance of prosperity arises.
Success is always proclaimed for intermediate rites when performed in the middle [period];
therefore, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all ritual actions.
Thus [it is said].

Thus concludes the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the mandala and the means of accomplishment concerning the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 108) Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present, having assembled right there in the midst of the assembly.

Having sat down, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-expounded [is this]."

This is the well-illuminated, supreme, and sublime teaching, issued from the great Dharma-cloud of the application of spells and mantras; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, the sovereign wheel-turning king of great vidyās, which fulfills in every way the extensive great ritual manual (*mahākalpa*). It is fruitful, the unsurpassed path to enlightenment for those who follow the practice of vidyā—including the distinctions of ritual action, the junctions of time, recitation, and fire-offerings—and it is the certain final goal that leads to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), being skilled in treading upon the ten powers through causes and signs produced by the conditions of karma with visible results, and through great wonders.
Therefore, may the Blessed One, the Teacher, please speak of the signs of the time for the vision of dreams that are conducive to the accomplishment of mantras,
so that beings who follow the practitioners of *vidyā* may undertake the rites for the sake of the signs of success, and so that all *vidyās* and their ritual signs may become fruitful.

When this had been said, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Yakṣas! You have set out for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, and for the sake of all practitioners of vidyā-mantras."
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak to you.
First of all, having gone to a place free from attachment for all activities— the commencement of prior work—
whether on a mountain peak, by a riverbank, or in mountain caves and courtyards,
one should construct a hut in a pure location.
Having installed [the image] on a cloth and performed a great worship,

by that very same procedure as before for all rites— either during the bright fortnight or the fortnight of miracles— one must certainly, on an auspicious day, during the first watch of the night, combine white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
and kindle a fire with *khadira* wood.

In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee that has been strained, using a vessel measuring four cubits, into embers that are smokeless and devoid of flames. At the conclusion of that fire-offering, one should offer eight thousand lotus flowers anointed with white sandalwood.
And at the end of the offering, having formed the mudrā of the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), one should offer a seat for one's own mantra by means of that very mantra.
With this mantra, one should perform the fire offering (homa): *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāmapratihataśāsanānām*.
Tadyathā: *Oṃ kumārarūpiṇa darśaya darśayamātmano bhūtiṃ samudbhāvaya svapnaṃ me niveda yathābhūtam*.
*Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having performed the protection with this mantra, one should carry out all other ritual actions during the fire-offering (*homakarma*).

Then, having spread out *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing toward the danger, one should lie down not too far from and not too close to the front of the painting, using a bundle of *kuśa* grass as a pillow for the head, while devotedly engaged in the practice of wakefulness during the first watch of the night before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Having prostrated and confessed one's misdeeds, one should offer oneself to all the Buddhas;
thereafter, one may fall under the power of sleep as is comfortable.
Those dreams which occur during the first watch are known to arise from phlegm; those in the second watch, arising from bile, are censured as being produced by worldly [influences]. (Mmk 15.1)
In the third [dream] one should recognize it as being caused by wind; in the fourth, as arising from truth.
But in the case of a dream dominated by phlegm, one should always see such things as these.
He sees heaps of jewels and strings of pearls on all sides, as well as a vast mass of water in which he himself is immersed. (Mmk 15.3)
Surrounded on all sides by flowing rivers and submerged in the great ocean— standing there, one should behold [the deity] who resides within one's own body, wherever that may be.
There, that place was filled on all sides with lotus ponds,
as well as boats, water-wells, taverns, and dwellings.
And one should see the Himālaya mountain or likewise a great river situated in crystal, being carried away on all sides by floods of water. Mmk 15.6.
He sees a mountain, a rock, and a king, all piled together with crystal, covered with nets of pearls, and heaps of pearls.
That bearer of the *kahā* sees a great rain and a flood of water,
as well as a white, bright umbrella or even a pale ornament.
A dream of an elephant white in form is said to indicate phlegm;
likewise, the sight of a white yak-tail whisk, a man, or even a garment [indicates the same].
One should touch from all sides rock salt and other such salts,
as well as cotton, linen cloth, iron, silver, and likewise agallochum.
In dreams associated with phlegm (śleṣman), touching or swallowing [substances] such as mung beans, puffed rice, sesame flour, and jaggery-rice is desired. *Mmk* 15.11.
For one with a predominance of phlegm (kapha), dreams of eating various kinds of black gram (māṣa) are desired;
likewise, svastika cakes, other types of cakes, kṛsara, and milk-rice (pāyasa). Mmk_15.12 //
For one with a phlegmatic constitution, the consumption of these in a dream is prescribed;
likewise, *śaṅkulī* cakes, *parpaṭa* wafers, and various kinds of soups.

Through touching and eating [the substances], as well as in dreams, there is an increase of phlegm and impurities; these consist of various kinds of foods previously considered fit for eating and consuming. Mmk 15.14.
Through eating or touching them, one experiences the activities of dreams characteristic of a person with phlegm (kaphin);
likewise, food, bedding, vehicles, and mounts originate from the [corresponding] elements.
If dreams involving touching, ascending, or seeing [the deity] are seen during the first watch of the night, all of this is said to apply to one characterized by phlegm (kaphin).
Dreams of this kind that involve activities arising from water,
or various visions of foods and drinks, as well as those pertaining to phlegmatic [conditions], [are auspicious].
Having indeed seen their activities in dreams, those characterized by phlegm [are described];
for other inconceivable dreams have been taught by the Leaders of the World.
Furthermore, for those embodied beings with a predominance of bile (*paittika*), there are dreams during the second watch of the night:
[dreaming of] a blazing form of fire, or [jewels] produced from various gems. (Mmk 15.19)
A person who, being overwhelmed by bile, sees in a dream a firebrand or a great meteor blazing in every direction, is indeed afflicted by that [disease].
One should recognize the sight of a ruby, or another gem born of precious substances,
in a dream as belonging to a person of bilious temperament (paittika).
In dreams, those overwhelmed by bile see various yellow-colored things due to contact with fire, its touch, or even its consumption. (Mmk 15.22)
One who, fainting with the heat of bile, sees in a dream the sun always blazing and its rays perpetually harsh; Mmk_15.23.
If one sees in a dream that the sky has a golden color and the surface of the earth is yellow, it arises from a deficiency of bile.
For a person overcome by bile, during this time of dreaming, one sees fire blazing on all sides, illuminating the expanse of the sky.
At that time, the ground, the mountain, or the mass of rock shall be gold-colored;
likewise, the great elephant and the vehicle shall all be made entirely of gold.
Constantly remaining in a state of sleep, one who is overwhelmed by the activity of bile sees everything as consisting of golden vessels, vehicles, ornaments, and mounts.
Furthermore, sitting or lying upon a seat or bed made of gold,
and from touching or ascending such objects, there occurs a dream-vision characterized by bile (paittika).
Clad in yellow garlands and garments, adorned with yellow cloth,
rich with yellow radiance and fragrance, and wearing a yellow sacred thread.
And he who perceives himself in a dream as having a yellow appearance does so because of the onset of a bilious fainting spell, due to the vision occurring during the second watch of the night.
Various dreams of such kinds as have been described,
or those that appear yellowish and diverse, arise from bile.
In the middle watch, they are indicated for those embodied beings who delight in bile;
appearing in many forms, they arise with a yellow luster.
The dreams arising from bile have been described by the foremost of the world;
now those dreams arising from wind are described during the third watch:
all the directions are seen as radiant on every side.
And also traveling through the sky, even horizontally across the expanse of the heavens.
For it constantly wanders everywhere through the sky and the firmament; such a dream is declared to be caused by wind (*vātika*), and it is described as being of this nature. (Mmk 15.34)
Jumping, leaping, and climbing trees;
the recitation of all the treatises, and especially of the mantras.
Excessive talking and chatter also occur in one of windy temperament (vātika),
as does the climbing of thorny trees and the eating of extremely bitter things.
In cases of wind disorders (vātika), one should consume pungent and sour foods among all edibles,
as well as fruits that primarily obstruct the wind and aggravate the wind humor.
Furthermore, in dreams, the consumption of those [substances] is indicated as arising from wind;
among the specific foods and substances to be eaten, those that increase wind are [to be avoided].
Likewise, a living being becomes deranged in mind through touch or even by eating [the substance], and likewise,
one enters into servitude to all beings merely by seeing oneself [in that state].
Indeed, those who see such things in a dream are known to be afflicted by wind (vāta);
they exhibit various forms of movements and speak with various signs.
Various terrifying utterances occur in dreams characterized by wind;
such dreams as these have been described by the preeminent ones of the world.
The applications and so forth of those possessed by passion, hatred, and delusion are threefold;
one should know that for those with passion it arises from phlegm (śleṣman), and for those with hatred it arises from bile (pittika).
That which arises from delusion is the wind-element; that which is mixed is the combination of both.
The impairment of dreams called passion is the vision of vulgar conduct.
In a dream arising from phlegm (śleṣman), there would be a count of women therein;
in a dream arising from bile (pitta), there is what is called quarreling with those who are hostile.
Born of delusion, having a sluggish appearance when mindfulness is lost from sight,
dreams are indeed always seen as conjoined with a state of confusion.
Therefore, those who perceive reality have taught that what is called a dream is in every respect devoid of substantiality, and is equal to the time of ritual action.
Those of a phlegmatic nature are said to be beings who possess a fine complexion, are pleasant in speech,
long-lived, dull-witted, of oily appearance, and self-confident.
Fair-complexioned, tall, and well-proportioned, they are always devoted to the company of women;
they are righteous, eternally heroic, and ever delight in great honor.
One born under the asterism designated for birth will be free from envy and unblemished;
likewise, others will become protectors of the earth or established as army commanders.
They will be born in Bhogavatī and live according to their past karma.
The mantra is taught as being determined by the fruit of one's own karma, not devoid of action;
yet the leaders of the world have declared that action is not the primary element of the mantra.
Therefore, it is said that success on the surface of the earth is attained for a being of phlegmatic temperament.
May sovereignty over the earth and great wealth be accomplished for him;
moreover, the reciter should not excessively consume any foods that increase phlegm.
For these dreams, when practiced excessively, arise from the occurrence of impurity;
therefore, the mantra practitioner should not indulge in them, as they are described as being for the purpose of causing division.
At that time, one who is wise and possessed of reason should not sleep;
rather, the conduct of a person of bilious temperament (paittika) is always described as follows.
One who is angry with a form of hatred is black in color and weak;
he is cruel, performs cruel deeds, and is always crooked in disposition.
He is always heroic and daring, endowed with strength and intelligence;
he speaks much, possesses many friends, and has attained mastery over many scriptures.
One characterized by hatred is born righteous, firm in his undertakings, praised for his rising resolve,
high-minded, and possessed of great power.
He is heroic, free from hatred, possessed of great wealth, a knower of the world, and pleasant to behold;
he is liberated, devoid of longing, steadfast, and always difficult to withstand.
He will always be proud, envious, and angry toward women, yet he becomes beloved by them;
possessing great energy and firm resolve in counsel, he is then born with great enjoyment.
Having stepped upon sentient beings according to their attainment of karma,
his mantras that obstruct life-breath are always successful.
For that embodied being who performs actions involving the injury of living beings, even fierce and powerful rites will quickly accomplish their goals; so says the Sage.
Whatever various ritual applications (karma) have been employed by all mantra-practitioners, they succeed when performed with reverence; they do not succeed in other sentient beings' rites.
Those mantras which are indeed hostile and afflict other beings, as well as the mantras of others— these are severed by the one who has attained mastery over the wrathful being.
Krodha mantras are effective for the purpose of seizing the property of others and for obstructing the lives of others; one should not employ them in other types of mantras.
Indeed, this being born of hatred exercises sovereignty;
it is black in color, or dark, or fair, or a mixture of these.
A mortal born under this [influence] becomes prone to anger and is deprived of a golden complexion;
such a man is born with a coarse, smoky, or tawny hue. (Mmk 15.65)
One born in the zodiac sign of Scorpio is brave, cruel, and likewise greedy;
situated in the field of the planet Mars, he belongs to the phlegmatic humor (śleṣman) of Jupiter.
For one who eats little and partakes of pungent and sour flavors, long life shall arise; moreover, he becomes endowed with memory and mantras.
I shall now describe the conduct and the behavior of one who is subject to wind (vātika):
he is discolored and of a dry complexion, yet his stature is not excessively weak.
The wise one’s intellect is constantly lost; his heart is indeed unstable and unsettled;
there is trembling of the limbs, dizziness, vomiting, and excessive discharge.
He will indeed become a glutton, a constant eater, and one of many words;
he is opposed by all the world and thus becomes one with many enemies.
Even one who is of bad character and afflicted with suffering shall be born upon the surface of the earth;
indeed, it is declared that the mantras for invisibility will attain accomplishment for him.
Those foods that provoke the wind-humor (vāta) follow after him;
therefore, one who recites mantras and desires the accomplishment of his rites should never consume them.
For these beings who are overcome by delusion and agitated by wind, these [mantras] born of delusion have been taught; they are accomplished through deluded mantras.
The accomplishment of the delusions of the deluded is always desired in those [constellations],
when a water-born sign is in the lunar mansion and is aspected by a true planet.
One should not perform auspicious deeds when a person of a windy temperament is in a state of fainting;
likewise, one should avoid rites of subjugation, summoning, deluding, and paralyzing beings.
Even among beings dominated by wind, these characteristics of dreams— which arise from the sins born of delusion— are declared to be visions of truth.
For these were described by the sages of old as accomplishing all aims:
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and indeed Leo.
Libra, Virgo, and likewise Scorpio; Sagittarius and Capricorn; Aquarius and Pisces; the elephant, the divine monkey, and the asura. Mmk_15.78 //
The Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others who have been proclaimed among men,
as well as the many classes of beings, have indeed been described by the foremost of leaders.
Of many kinds, with diverse meanings, and described through various types of actions—
in all of those actions, the extensive qualities bear fruit.
Indeed, for embodied beings, it is taught that there is nothing free from the qualities of karma;
and when one is joined with the qualities of karma, one brings about rebirth once again. (Mmk 15.81)

For one who knows the reality of qualities, the practitioner of recitation who understands the virtues and defects of the bonds of karma attains success in mantras that are endowed with virtue, dharma, and purpose.
One does not perform beneficial action if there is no respectful treatment even toward the qualities;
for it is the ritual action that accomplishes the task, not an action devoid of its constituent qualities.
Endowed with the qualities of ritual action, he shall accomplish it;
for ritual action preceded by the prescribed method was taught of old by those possessed of the ten powers.
For these actions, objects, and qualities are seen as the movements of sentient beings;
various forms like those in dreams are perceived, arising from karma.
Therefore, by means of the dream-sign, one should employ extensive ritual activities that are manifold in form,
diverse, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.
Men of great enthusiasm and great heroism who desire accomplishment see obstacles both with form and without form as the causes of their dreams.
Success is ordained among those who are superior, inferior, or middling; however, for those who are fierce and performers of cruel deeds, dreams always yield immediate results.
The supreme worldly rites are for the sake of success in constant tasks over long periods of time; they are capable of producing qualities in the foremost of worldly beings.
Various dreams are seen by those who recite mantras for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi;
however, for the sake of non-attainment of mantras, sleep and lethargy are produced.
At that time, the mantra for destroying obstacles is prescribed;
at that time, the practitioner should employ those mantras which take the form of logical reasoning.
Then, the great wrathful one with six arms and six faces was manifested;
the four-syllable great mantra issued forth from the form of Kumāra.
Of terrible form and most formidable, born from the appearance of a boar, that very King Kālarātri exists for the sake of destroying all obstacles. Mmk 15.93.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent’s coil hanging down,
the great being of immense power, sword in hand, has the form of Kṛtānta.
Compassionless toward all obstacles, the destroyer of the lives of the Vināyakas—
let all beings indeed hear this most formidable mantra in the tantra.
The destroyer of beings who have been seen, the remover of all obstacles, and the accomplisher of all mantras—O hosts of gods, listen to me! Mmk 15.96.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: He he, O Great Wrathful One, six-faced, six-legged, destroyer of all obstacles, hūṃ hūṃ!
Why do you delay, O Vināyaka, bringer of the end of life? Destroy my bad dream!
Leap, leap! Remember your pledge! Phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

As soon as this Great Wrathful King was spoken, all the obstructors and leaders of obstacles— afflicted, terrified, with broken hearts and trembling minds— paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
and they remained steadfast in their commitment.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Pure Abodes and that great maṇḍala of the assembly, spoke thus: "O hosts of gods! This King of Wrath is [the protector] of all worldly and transcendent mantras being accomplished; for whichever wicked being should harass a practitioner of recitation,"
This King of Wrath will subdue his entire family and dry them up,
yet he shall not cause the obstruction of their life-force.
Having scorched and dried it up, he will establish it in its proper state;
he will remain for the protection, preservation, and guarding of the reciter,
and he will cause him to flourish.
For whoever should thus transgress the pledge and harass the practitioner who has been protected by the King of Wrath—
"His head shall split into seven pieces like the cluster of an arjaka flower.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages then addressed Mañjughoṣa.
O Kumāra, [I shall explain] the extensive exposition of all purposes regarding your mantras,
especially for practitioners who have been liberated through the meaning of the mantra-tantras.
The King of Wrath, which destroys all obstacles, was taught in the Tantra;
indeed, in the past, the Lords of the World likewise employed it in this very way.
For the destruction of wicked obstacles and the subduing of the anger of enemies,
this should always be recited at night by practitioners who constantly engage in mantra-recitation.
This [mantra] is for the protection of sentient beings and the destruction of bad dreams;
it has been taught by the leaders of the world for the accomplishment of the purpose of all mantras.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of persons,
among whom the mantras— whether superior, inferior, or middling— are brought to accomplishment.
Radiant, wise, golden-hued, and large-bellied;
broad-eyed, very gentle, with little passion, and free from anger.
One with eyes red at the corners, who speaks kindly, achieves the highest success;
he has thin skin, a darkish complexion, slender limbs, and is not overly tall.
Possessing great energy and great splendor, contented and auspicious in every way,
preeminent by birth, pure, having few desires, and humble.
For such a person, success is seen to be certain and supreme in all rites;
moreover, one who is not deficient in limbs, dark-complexioned from birth, and possessed of great majesty [attains it] everywhere.
With an unafflicted mind, wise, a celibate practitioner always pure,
constantly delighting in dwelling [in virtue], knowing the world, and virtuous in nature. (Mmk 15.107)
He should always have many friends, be generous, and always act with moderation;
he should be pure, skillful in conduct, and always devoted to cleanliness and proper behavior.
One who speaks the truth and is compassionate attains the highest success;
such a person is always of noble birth, virtuous, righteous, and possessed of the full expansion of all excellent qualities.
Devoted to his mother and father, honoring brahmins and guests,
exceedingly compassionate and steadfast— for him too, the supreme accomplishment is attained.
Dark-complexioned yet fair-skinned, gentle, speaking little, always pure,
desiring delicious food, and approaching a pure wife.
One who knows the world, is highly esteemed by beings, and possesses supreme accomplishment—
neither too short nor too tall, with hair like crushed collyrium.
With eyes of a gentle hue, pure, and always devoted to bathing, he was also full of faith in the Three Jewels; for him too, the supreme accomplishment was attained.
Engaged in superior activities, knowing the intentions of sentient beings,
patient, pleasant of speech, and serene toward the Son of the Victor—
then his supramundane accomplishment remains fruitful.
A great being of great heroism, of great majesty, and of great vows;
possessing great wealth, a knower of mantras, and one who knows the reality of all tantras.
By caste, he is a preeminent kṣatriya or a wise brāhmaṇa;
he is always devoted to women and passionate, and by appearance he has the luster of gold.
He is seen to be tall and fair-complexioned, with a prominent nose and mighty arms;
he has long-reaching limbs, is heroic, and desires a great kingdom.
He is well-disposed toward the sons of the Victors, a worshiper of goddesses known as women,
devoted to the Three Jewels, and adorned with the thought of awakening;
he is exceedingly compassionate and steadfast, yet occasionally wrathful and possessed of great splendor.
Possessing great wealth, great generosity, and great splendor, difficult to overcome,
beloved by women, and heroic— he too attains the highest accomplishment.
Delighting in pride, brave, and always attached to women; with a golden complexion, eating little, broad-chested, firm, and pure. Mmk_15.120 //
Compassionate, merciful, skillful, and knowledgeable of the world, he is highly esteemed for his virtues;
he is a constant reciter of mantras and a devotee of the Lords of Jinas, the Dispellers of Darkness.
Among them, the sons of the Śrāvakas and the Khaḍgins are always present; moreover, the foremost leaders of the world appear in color in the second auspicious [mandala]. (Vaidya 117) Mmk_15.122 //
He is free from physical defects in all his limbs, yet always cruel and impetuous;
he is generous by nature, has conquered his enemies, and is a judge of what is dharma and what is adharma.
Neither too stout nor too thin, neither too tall nor too short—the person of medium build is the best; for him, too, the highest accomplishment is attained.
With copper-colored nails and very glossy palms that are red, he is pure;
from the tips of his feet they are red and glossy, adorned with wheels and svastikas.
A person endowed with hundreds of thousands of marks sees on his hands and feet banners, arches, fish, flags, lotuses, and water-lilies.
Such a person is considered supreme; he is conceived as having the foremost accomplishment.
His teeth are white, his nose is without perforation, and he is tall like a mountain peak.
He has a prominent nose and large eyes; his eyebrows and chin are well-knit and auspicious;
he possesses the marks of a cowherd’s eyelashes, black eyes, and is adorned with pupils.
He whose forehead is broad, whose head is auspicious and shaped like a parasol, and whose head is likewise shaped like a *uṣṇīṣa*, and whose ears are beautiful and auspicious; Mmk_15.129 //

His jaw is always shaped like a lion’s; his two lower lips have a luster like that of a ripe bimba fruit; his tongue is seen to have the reddish hue of a lotus petal, and his palate is likewise intensely red.
The neck resembles a conch shell, the shoulders are well-developed and thick, and the armpits and chest are auspicious; likewise, the breast is broad and excellent.
The navel region is slightly deep, broad, firm, and auspicious;
the navel is deep and clockwise-rotating, without a network of veins.
With long-hanging arms and mighty shoulders, he is marked by the sign of a lion on his hips;
his thighs are rounded, and his elbows are free from deformity.
His shanks are like those of the eneya antelope, and they are celebrated as being perfectly formed and rounded;
his feet are fleshy and elevated with well-proportioned toes.
The two [feet] are red, with red nails, glossy, elevated, and adorned with flesh; moreover,
the two heads are like the surface of the earth, beautiful, lovely to behold,
unjoined, pure in color, praiseworthy, and marked by the signs of the world.
Furthermore, above those [shoulders], the network of veins is not protruding.
The two channels for the discharge of excrement are deep with rightward whirlpools;
they are praised when very slight, and the testicles are always round and auspicious.
It is proclaimed as being both limited and unlimited, and indeed manifold;
when it is purified within the physical body, it rests at the end of passion. (Mmk 15.138)
If, during the time of sleep or while consuming food that increases virility,
one's semen is seen to be blue or red in color, [it is an omen].
For those beings characterized by auspicious marks who exude profusely and possess a moist nature, the highest accomplishment is desired when such [conditions] are present.
One who voids excrement and urine three times [daily], who is devoted to pure conduct and is clean,
and who indeed goes to sleep at the end of the watch and rises in the morning— such a person, O beings, [attains purity].
Its purification is always seen as most excellent, effective for all rites,
yielding various kinds of fruits or, moreover, abundant prosperity.
One characterized by middling marks shall be an enjoyer [of wealth],
as will one born under the lunar mansions Puṣya, Revatī, or Phalgunī.
Under the asterisms of Maghā, Anurādhā, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and Kṛttikā,
the progenitor is seen situated there, capable and marked by planetary signs.
Success is seen among those who are born at the time of dawn;
likewise, at midday, in the morning, and at the end of the day, the pure planets [bring success].
Śukra, Soma, Śukra, Pītaka, Budha, and Bṛhaspati gaze upon all living beings for the sake of accomplishing their power and purpose. (Mmk 15.146)
And in this interval, for those humans who have been born as performers of auspicious deeds,
mantras succeed without effort in accomplishing all their aims.
At midday, in the afternoon, and always at sunset—
at this interval, cruel planets always gaze upon embodied beings.
The Sun, Mars, the cruel planets, Ketu, Rāhu, Saturn, and those who are the chief among the grahas, as well as those accompanied by earthquakes, thunderclaps, and meteors— Mmk_15.149.
Tārā, Ghoratama, Kṛṣṇa, Ariṣṭa, as well as Kālamārakuru and Raudra, are seen at that time due to the influence of the age.
At the time of sunrise, Mercury beholds the earth;
at a height of one *ratha*—the measure of a yoke—he beholds it as Jupiter does.
When the sun is in the Yuga constellation, Śukra and Dhanādhyakṣa appear beyond it;
from noon onwards the moon becomes full, and this is the time for the appearance of those who possess a lunar body.
During the time of Mercury, there shall be sovereignty; during that of Jupiter, it brings wealth and enjoyment;
during that of Venus, there is the attainment of riches, a great kingdom, and an abundance of enjoyments.
O long-lived one, likewise, when the moon is in its fullness, sovereignty is fruitful;
and when the sun is at midday, it is said that the central gaze is attained. (Mmk 15.154)
When midday has passed, the sun always gazes toward the direction;
it is described as being at the height of a yoke, neither high nor low—such is the characteristic of Ketu.
Rāhu and Śanaiścara, as well as Tama, Kāla, and Yugāntaka;
thereafter, in the period of decline, there will be the Niṣṭa, the iṣṭa, meteors, and earthquakes.
When the sun has set, appearing coppery and colored like a mass of vermilion,
that chief of planets appears in the form of a young child.
With a spear in hand, he is exceedingly fierce, appearing like glowing embers;
then, when the sun has reached the end of the eon, the origins of the auspicious planets [arise].
One born under Ādityadarśana will be cruel and impulsive;
one born under Satyakāṅgāraka will be wrathful, greedy, and conceited.
From smoke-colored flames, the birth of diseases arises;
people will always be impoverished, afflicted by illness, greedy, and arrogant.
The time of darkness and earthquakes, of meteors and the malevolent planets; of tremors, thunderclaps, and stars, as well as the blazing thunderbolts. Mmk 15.161.
Likewise, for the bear and other such creatures, it is ordained as the Vajra-ariṣṭa;
however, the terrible appearance of Rāhu is seen by all living beings.
Human beings are always born as the poor, the helpless, and the immoral; they are men who are sinful thieves, suffering mortals afflicted by disease and life-threatening ailments,
as well as those with leprosy, many other maladies, blindness, lameness, and scabies.

Eunuchs, impotent men, those childless, the unfortunate, and women who are despised; likewise, men, women, and others who are loathed for their appearance or their grasping—[these are excluded]. Mmk 15.164.
Worlds are born in many ways from the very birth-charts (jātaka);
among them, the white and yellow planets are the most excellent, as they bring about the auspicious arising of one's birth.
In terms of color, those with white and yellow lusters are praised and extolled by the Victors;
these four are the foremost of the planets: Venus, the Moon, Jupiter, and Mercury.
For the sake of accomplishing the vision of those [deities] in all rites by the reciter,
and for the sake of foolish beings, birth itself is always auspicious.
All forms of prosperity are said by the foremost beings in the world to be always sweet,
even for a mere moment, or for the blink of an eye, or even for the snap of a finger.
The birth of these has been briefly described by the leaders of the world;
this alone is the measure for the planets who contemplate the world.
Thus they constantly arise at this very time in reality; for these evil ones, through their lack of excellence, always wander like a wheel. (Vaidya 120, Mmk 15.170)
They always perform auspicious and inauspicious deeds here through the mantra as one;
they have indeed resorted to the world of the gods.
Among these, in certain instances, some degree of evil intent arises;
furthermore, due to their lack of attachment to the fruits of good and evil, they arise again in many ways.
They say that this is the vision of these planets who consume karma;
they move swiftly toward sentient beings because of their rapid movement.
The movement of the eyes is rapid, lasting for a visible moment, an instant, or a flash;
from these, time is calculated,
and this measure of time has been demonstrated by those of supreme intelligence.

Henceforth, I shall always explain the twelve muhūrtas that occur during the fixed birth-moment (jātaka), which are the causes for each respective time; I shall also declare those who are unworthy vessels, whether they are causes for success or not.
Furthermore, by the repeated observation or non-observation of omens among the people,
one may discern the ruin of the kingdom, famine, and the prosperity or misfortune of the king.
At that time, O noble one, the people always experienced [the effects of] the right and wrong times;
moreover, there were tremors of comets, thunderclaps, and meteors accompanied by smoke. Mmk 15.177.
The movement of the constellations, days of the week, and stars, both auspicious and inauspicious;
the conduct of all beings, and the activities of Śiva and Śivā.
I shall likewise describe the conduct of the flesh-eating mothers, those of fierce nature who cause harm, and other malevolent beings who subsist on meat.
Where the deities are well-pleased with those whose minds are fixed upon the supreme jewel of the Dharma—
those who are ever engaged in virtuous deeds and possess hearts of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those whose actions, goals, and intellects are virtuous, and who rely on the fulfillment of others,
they are drawn in by the utterances of mantras for the purpose of medicinal food.
I shall describe in detail their conduct, upon which their characteristics depend;
having entered into the bodies of others, they remain there as those who have passed into human existence.
Furthermore, the gods spoke thus to him, and the asuras did so for the sake of pride;
those gods and asuras present there were of two kinds among the retinue.
They also go there in two ways, being either cruel or common;
they also go there in two ways, [entering] the fivefold destinies of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Residing there, they proceed through three types [of realms]: twenty, thirty, and the innumerable;
reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, including the Indras, the Yāmas, the innumerable Abhūpas, and the others.
As far as the realms and worlds are infinite, so too are their virtues and non-virtues;
as many as there are worldly beings, and as many as there are noble Śrāvakas.
Of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their legitimate sons,
the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas established in the ten stages.
All sentient beings are likewise eternally dependent upon the womb of existence; all foolish creatures are dependent upon the wombs of their various destinies;
while for the Buddhas, who are liberated from the serpent of saṃsāra, there is the state of all the Noble Ones.
I shall explain in detail their constant characteristics and conduct in all respects, as well as the truth regarding their speech and gestures.
All beings are drawn forth by means of mantras, tantras, and proper methods;
one who knows the mantras for summoning and drawing in perceives them as having entered and taken refuge within another body.
By those who are virtuous, who know wholesome actions, who are heedful, who practice recitation,
whose conduct is undeluded, and all of whom are capable of both restraint and favor—
by such mantra-reciters, the worlds upon the surface of the earth have been drawn forth within the human realm.
I shall explain everything regarding the signs of their accomplishment according to reality,
for the sake of conforming to the bodies of those humans who are constantly afflicted by disease.
This is always intended for the sake of the ultimate Dharma and for the sake of liberation;
therein lies the restraint of the wicked and the honoring of the pure.
In this way, the mantra and tantra are prescribed for both restraint and favor;
here, the threefold action for wind, phlegm, and bile is likewise threefold.
For them, one should prescribe pacification; indeed, a threefold sequence is considered appropriate.
In that regard, one should always perform the medical treatment for humans by means of mantras.

The conceptualization of the great elements (mahābhūta-vikalpa), however, is traditionally held to be "become" (bhūta) and "excessive with respect to the elements" (bhūtādhika). Likewise, that which is overcome by the elements is called "overcome" (adhibhūta).
When a living being produces ill-health through a spirit, then that spirit is to be understood as being of two kinds: the primary spirit and the secondary type of spirit.
Likewise, it is eternally conceived as being sentient and also as being insentient;
so too are bile, phlegm, vitality, and whatever others there may be.
The four great elements and the fifth, space, are recognized;
water conjoined with fire, and earth conjoined with wind.
"The wise always say that he is not reckoned among sentient beings;
for the one of great splendor said, 'He is the foremost lord of the pinnacle of the world. (Mmk 15.200)
"For that which is non-human is reckoned as non-sentient;
yet the one of supreme intellect, the best among speakers, declares it to be a human being."

Whether it be non-human or human, including all beings counted among sentient creatures as well as the gods, the speech of the Omniscient One is for the sake of the welfare and excellence of all beings. Mmk 15.202.
Thus has karma, which gives rise to pure and impure fruits, been taught by the Buddhas of the past, the future, and likewise those of the present.
The mere word of the Buddhas necessarily brings about the result;
because of that cause and the commonality of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), success is indeed clearly perceived.
They call it omniscient knowledge—secure, peaceful, and ever-pure;
it is held to be liberation, the ultimate reality, the final goal, and pure selflessness.
That very path among sentient beings is proclaimed in this sūtra;
therein, he spoke the entire discourse on mantras, seeds, and medicinal herbs.
It is the reality that has been and will be, eternally honored by all scriptures;
it is the supreme state in the world, the selflessness of phenomena, the ever-peaceful and auspicious ground.
This word of the Omniscient One is the ultimate; it is his supreme state.
However, both [the means and the result] are conceived as arising from the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
The power of all the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas,
as well as the accomplishment of mantras in all rites, is demonstrated everywhere;
for this very reason, the King of Rituals was proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.
Proceeding by this path in the form of mantra for embodied beings,
one reaches the city of Nirvāṇa, which possesses the wealth of peace and freedom from decay—
free from sorrow, stainless, secure, culminating in awakening, and eternally auspicious.
This tantra, which is the teaching of all the Buddhas for those who recite mantras,
has been explained on the surface of the earth in its entirety for those who recite mantras.
All knowledge and the objects of knowledge are bound by the cause of karma;
all this, however, is the meaning of mantra, which flows toward the threefold awakening.
In this eon, the complete knowledge of the Buddhas has been revealed;
for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, it has been set in motion throughout all worlds.
Whatever is found in this *Kalparāja* is not seen in other *kalpas*; and whatever has been taught in other *kalpas* by the sons of the Sage, those best of sages, [is here as well].
Indeed, they possess the extensive ritual manual (*kalpa*) for all mantras; for this very reason, it was taught by the Lord of Jinas for the sake of all embodied beings. (Mmk 15.215)
And upon the surface of the earth and within these three worlds,
there is nothing that has not been brought under control or mastered by this sovereign king of rituals.
When the Moon of Sages has set and the circle of the earth is empty,
he will act for the sake of the teaching while this world remains in this eon.
The Youth Mañjughoṣa, ever auspicious among all beings,
shall likewise perform the work of a Buddha in this world and in this teaching.
Having heard the power of this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), those who have long desired it will gain faith in it even upon hearing it once; for them, success shall always be attained.
This auspicious speech is always unfailing for all beings,
as well as for those mantra-practitioners who are constantly devoted to recitation and fire-offerings among all beings.
Whatever knowledge operates among the three types of triple-knowledges,
that very same [knowledge] operates in this supreme king of rituals.
The establishment of mantras is declared here as the teaching of the Buddhas;
yet that mantra is free from conceptual construction, though it is spoken here within this realm of conceptual construction.
It effects the welfare and misfortune, the auspicious and inauspicious, for all sentient beings;
likewise, it determines the destinies, the intellects, the nature of beings, and the prosperity and adversity of the worlds.

This very [reality] is elaborated upon in the ritual manual (*kalpa*); yet the Tathāgatas are free from such elaboration. Though they have transcended the world and are self-awakened, they are spoken of here for the sake of the world.
Surpassing all phenomena, for it transcends the worldly dharmas;
the practitioner performs various and manifold rites that are honored by the world.
The King of Mantras, engaged in ritual action and likewise beneficial to the multitude of beings—
that Mañjughoṣa Kumāra performs the work of a Buddha.
Its meaning is the accomplishment of qualities and the foundation of the world, both auspicious and inauspicious;
I am indeed the requester and the speaker, for one who does not request is not said to speak the Dharma.
"Exclusively for the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall proclaim that which was spoken by the Buddhas and was indeed spoken by all the Buddhas of the past."
One who has faith will ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas remains uninterrupted;
for them, the wisdom of the omniscient one shall arise in all activities of the mantra-practitioners.
However, only that single action which proceeds from the wisdom of the Omniscient One is praised;
one's own prior karma in this world is what is now being experienced.
Therefore, one should perform difficult deeds in this life;
thus, even here, the bonds of karma will be severed and the mantras will be accomplished without effort. (Mmk 15.231)
Success may be attained here even through action in this very life;
therefore, all the Buddhas have praised action alone.
But that rite performed according to the rules brings success quickly even in this world;
yet foolish beings, being utterly deluded, wander about deprived of the proper method.
