it is prescribed by rule in the seventh [chapter] regarding the attainment of mantras for those who recite them.
The seventh [chapter] should be understood according to its seven meanings;
one should apply the various explanations of sequence to the seven meanings of the seventh.
Sixty groups of mantras, as well as their constituent parts, are proclaimed;
indeed, due to the connection between the mantras, two signs are applied.
Its transformation is said to be manifold, consisting of six types;
among these, one should employ the sixth, which possesses the female gender, within the eight mantras.
The five types of mantras are those that strive for the fivefold purpose;
the meaning of mantras with neuter gender is said to be devoid of the purpose of the Dharma.
Those mantras that have issued forth there, joined for the purpose of seizing,
are all remembered as life-takers;
they issue forth from the lips and teeth through the conjunction with the sound of the head (the letter *m*).
Those for whom the tongue is pressed down here, who obstruct the breath of sound,
and who are stilled through equal cognition— they are joined with the element of tranquility.
One should apply this mantra to those who have taken refuge up to the end of their hands;
for the sake of nourishment, those elements which are words beautifully adorned with the meaning of suffixes [should be used].
Those others who have been proclaimed by dividing them according to their respective places are known as being employed in rites for nourishment and in cases of withdrawal.
Nourished by words and syllables, O Element, they blossom clearly;
likewise, mantras in the masculine gender are endowed with great power and purpose.

The syllable adorned with the fourth [vowel] and the two [anusvāra and visarga] is said to be at the beginning of the *pavarga* group; it is the foremost, the most excellent, and effective for all rites.
Arising from the combination of the letter *repha* and the suffix, then the beautiful letter *u*,
the central mark which is the *visarga*, and the letter *bha* adorned with movement.
They know the preeminent word, which accomplishes all ritual actions and purposes,
as being invariably established upon the path of the ultimate goal when applied to a Bodhisattva.
They call this the unsurpassed sound, the path that is the way to great enlightenment;
by reciting it, a human being will swiftly accomplish all mantras.
Therefore, the fifth meaning is declared to be marked by a single syllable;
the wise always know it as that which arises from the end [of the alphabet], belonging to the *pavarga* class, and ending with the letter *ma*.
Human beings call the second [mantra], which is the foremost in the world, "Sound" (śabda);
it is not merely a conjunction of sounds, nor is it adorned by an emission at the end.
He was born as the preeminent mantra, supreme and born from the source of sound;
he is the Buddha, the Teacher of the World, the most excellent, characterized as the Chatra-uṣṇīṣa.
O Teacher of the World, the triad of mantras has been taught at the beginning of the *ta*-group;
indeed, this foremost mantra, accompanied by sound, is honored by the world. (Mmk 23.39)
That which ends in the letter *a* signifies the meaning of case-inflection; that which ends in a *visarga* is understood as the middle gender;
that which ends in the sound *sa* is masculine; and that which ends in a word is adorned by its own term.
They know that sound to be the supreme mantra worshipped by the gods,
for those who are engaged in the fifth sense-object, which arises from calculation in the context of enumeration.
For these, having the fifth [vowel] as their division, are the *sup* endings for the meaning of case-divisions;
infinite are the mantras thus described, infinite are those spoken by the Jinas.
The mantras are the uṣṇīṣas, the hair of the Victor’s head;
they should be known as infinite, knowers of sound, and sounds that bring about the fulfillment of all aims.
One should employ the mantra endowed with sixty-four [qualities] and joined with sound.
That sound is the most excellent of all; it is the fourfold word-group in which the four *m*s are joined together and placed at the end.
Those with sound are indeed the primary mantras; they accomplish the purpose known as the parasol.
This is declared to be the fourth enumeration, the division born from the source of sound.
The mantras for the purpose of making offerings, which have attained a dual gender as their basis,
are taught by the Lotus-Born One for the sake of nourishment and the attainment of wealth and purpose.
The fourth [section] describes the mantras employed in four ways:
the sounds of the four syllables, namely the head-sounds (mūrdhan), the sibilants (ūṣman), and the palatals (tālavya).
It has been explained in the third [chapter] on the designation of sounds;
one should apply it for the purpose of expansion regarding the clear elements, and then apply it to the suffix and the gender.
The sound that exists at the beginning and at the end—that sound is honored by the world;
it is the excellent mantra known as the primary, properly applied.
That sound is indeed said to belong to Puṣṭin, arising from Abdaketu;
it ends with *tra*, is the conjunction of the three, and its middle portion is highly extolled.
That sound is the foremost among the leaders of the world; it is always preeminent in its meaning.
One should employ it in its true sense, endowed with the elements and possessing the constant form.
Then he chose Uṣas as the deity;
listen to that [mantra] which is endowed with sweet syllables and joined with the vocative particle *ut* in the masculine.
That sound, the foremost in the world, is called the supreme mantra;
that syllable is to be avoided in the fourth [vowel], while it is proclaimed [to be used] in the second.
This should be known as the supreme one spoken by the Buddha for the purpose of pacifying desired aims;
it is the third labial sibilant (*ūṣman*), devoid of any other conditional suffixes.
Always engaged with the signs of nourishment and joined at the end with the earth element (bhūdhātu), that mantra spoken by the Buddha has an upward-pointing mark and is likewise rotated. Mmk_23.55.

In the third [section], regarding the meaning derived from the case endings of the words *bhūti* and *saśabda*, the first should be understood according to the syllables; it is peaceful (*śāntika*) when ungrasped and brings about prosperity (*pauṣṭika*) when arisen.
The second [case] is declared for the object (karman), and likewise the third for the instrument (karaṇa);
it should be known that the king of mantras consists of both these case-endings along with the word "sa."
They say that the first [element] is the action (karman), and the agent (kartṛ) is that which is independent.
Likewise, the Victors, the Lotus and Vajra families, the mantra, and the lords of mantra are beneficial;
all those ending in case-terminations and those born from verbal roots ending in suffixes should be known as beneficial in every respect. Mmk_23.58.
The meaning should be understood through its characteristic marks; it arises from the sentence and from the words.
The mantras are said to be primarily those born from the Victorious One, O Lord.
The mantras of the Jina and Lotus families, as well as those of the Vajrin and the worldly ones,
grasp the meaningful elements and their transitions.
The mantras, indicated by both the acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents, are to be understood as the means for accomplishing the intended purpose;
they consist of those ending in a feminine gender suffix, and having offered oblations in the middle, they are likewise raised up.
One should employ the sound that is without beginning or end, as well as those mantras ending in *ni* or *la*, joined with the letter *ra*, and expanded in detail.
Between the word denoting the object to be bound and the word [denoting the agent], that which is heard with gender and case endings—
endowed with the *svarita* accent— one should quickly apply that gender in the mantras.
The power of death is joined with the preceding syllables;
that meaning which arises from the middle of the two words is known as the "word-famed" (śabdaviśruta).

Therefore, for the sake of full comprehension, that mantra spoken by the Buddha— which is well-formed, described in beautiful form, and brings about the highest welfare through its fruit— is to be understood.
Time is proclaimed as being by nature non-existent, and as being by its own nature;
the cessation of these two is the peaceful state, adorned with the meaning of the Dharma.
The speech from another is supreme, peaceful, meaningful, syllabic, and auspicious.
This mantra spoken by the Buddha, praised by practitioners, should be known by the mantra-adepts;
it is this single-syllable Brahman, adorned with the meaning of the word "Oṃ."
He should be known as one who possesses form, pure, praiseworthy, and bringing auspiciousness;
for he is said to be the accomplisher of welfare, praiseworthy, and endowed with blessings.
That mantra has been declared by the Lords of the World as the foremost;
it possesses various meanings and is the primary expression of sound, as well as the supreme word among all others.
That sound is the excellence of the substratum; those mantras, arising in the sequence of action and time from the Solar Lineage, are adorned with radiant words and meanings.
The mantras, whether designated as gentle or fierce, blaze within the fire when properly applied;
they are always beautiful in form, possess gentle minds, and are characterized by the names of the lunar mansions.
The mantras arisen in this moon are expressed through sounds arising from lunar syllables;
they are declared to be well-arranged, stainless, single-syllabled, and supreme.
Renowned as being beyond measure, of beautiful complexion, and possessed of great supernatural power,
these mantras are declared by the sons of the Jinas to be the most excellent Uṣṇīṣas.
The applications of various forms remain like the satisfaction of yoga;
they are always serene and pure, as taught by the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
The mantra of the two Pratyekabuddhas is praised for rites of pacification;
these mantras, ending with *svāhā*, are honored by the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*.
That mantra, which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas, possesses the designation "one or two" and should always be employed for all rites with the highest benefit. (Mmk 23.76)
It should be known that [the mantra] is joined with *ananta*; the beginning and middle are as before.
The mantras possess many signs, and the syllables have the meaning of many mantras.
For these elements are indeed manifold; they are understood to end with the letter *ṣa*.
As for the accomplishment of those mantras, the first letter belongs to the *ta*-group.
Those born from the lotus-mantra should first strike the end of the syllable *repha*; [then recite]:
"O Avalokiteśvara, out of compassion for these, deliver the suffering beings! (Mmk 23.79)
That indeed is the foremost *tāra* (oṃ), while *ananta* and *mantra* are indeed *ture*;
between the sounds *tvaryāccha*, the *pavarga* is known as *māmakī*.
In the *pavarga* [consonant group], she is the renowned goddess, the Mother of the Family who accomplishes all aims;
she is the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī, whose white insignia is well-known for its purpose. (Mmk 23.81)
Tārā was previously described; one should employ her for the sake of protection.
The mantra of the warrior is abundant in the letter *la*, ends with the word *gaccha*, and arises from those three.
The sound produced from the limbs of the Victor is called the goddess Locanā;
one should apply this sound, which is the syllable of meaning, as the accomplishment in all mantras.
This [mantra], renowned throughout the families of the Victors, Vajras, and Lotuses, should be employed at the very beginning of all mantras for the sake of pacification. Mmk_23.84.
Locanā is renowned on earth; there, the foremost mantra is to be accomplished.
Therefore, one should know that "all" is to be applied to the initial mantras.
For the sake of the accomplishment of mantras and for the purpose of self-protection,
one should know that the goddess Jinalocanā is everywhere fully accomplished.
Mantras, indeed possessing manifold forms,
always resound within the letters at the beginning, the middle, and among the sixty-four syllables.
One should employ mantras and tantras everywhere among all the classes [of beings];
and in all initial positions, the *tavarga* consonants belong to those two classes.
One should employ all those declared to be peaceful in three ways;
among the letters of the natural order starting from *ta*, those ending with *la* are born from all wombs.
Those are the colors for nourishing rites (pauṣṭika), while others are for malevolent rites (abhicāruka).
Furthermore, they should be known as threefold: fierce, pacifying (śāntika), and nourishing.
Thus, those three types are indeed as they have been described, threefold and threefold;
those infinite ones, moreover, are again threefold through the application of yoga.
Know that the gentle syllable leads to peace; one should separate it from that [context].
For some syllables are granters of boons, while others are middling and cause prosperity.
One should know that the supreme syllable ending in *ha* is fierce and brings about evil;
it is thus adorned with these applications and words.
Know that the syllables are indeed infinite, and the deities of the mantras are infinite;
in this manner, through this yoga, one should apply the infinite mantras.
They know that king of mantras to be masculine, which accomplishes all aims;
that syllable which is joined with the letter *e* is a sound adorned by mantra,
and they know that mantra to be neuter— one should employ it in intermediate rites.
The syllable accompanied by the letter *i* is known and proclaimed as the mantra;
it is well-established among other mantras for minor rites. (Mmk 23.96)
Furthermore, all these [mantras] here are adorned with various sounds;
one should employ that threefold and triple variety in all ritual actions.
That which is known as the masculine gender, the person (puruṣa), is considered by all to be the meaning; they know that to be the *puruṣa-mantra*, and one should employ it in all ritual actions.
Know that mantra which possesses a neuter gender to be neutral;
it shall bring about the arising of all happiness and well-being in all rites.
Know that any mantra designated as feminine is always a woman;
though they perform all rites, one should constantly employ them for protection.
These mantras perform infinite deeds, possess infinite purposes, and are the source of all sounds.
Indeed, various sounds and the like, joined with mantras from diverse tantras,
likewise succeed quickly and without effort when practiced in this manner.
The cognition of sound has been explained as the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras;
now, the calculation thereof is proclaimed by the wise.
O gods, know that this was spoken for the sake of the welfare of those who recite [mantras];
through the application of these [elements], it is said to extend up to a hundred [recitations].
Ten times five thousand is twenty thousand; understand that.
Ten thousand is the number proclaimed as "ayuta."
Ten times ten thousand is likewise always called an ayuta; a hundred thousand is called a lakṣa; a thousand lakṣas is a koṭi; the place beyond that is known as an arbuda.
Ten arbudas are to be known as nirbuda, and beyond that is samudra;
ten times [samudra] is to be known as sāgara, which is applied to tenfold increase.
One should know Akṣobhya in the next [position], and Niḥkṣobhya beyond that;
the wise proclaim that Devarāj is the marriage for all.
Merchants say that if it exceeds ten digits, it is a sword; the minister knows that as "without-sword" (nikhaḍga), and also "sword-bearer" (khaḍgin) when it is without-sword.
Beyond that is the Śaṅkha [number], and beyond that is its reckoning;
that should be known by me as the final Mahāmāyā when calculated.
Those mortals who know the incalculable [mantras], and others born of divine origin—
all these are multiplied by five and joined with ten and a half.
Beyond that, what is possible and even what is impossible and difficult to conquer—
when honored and accumulated in the proper place, the wise know it to be a station of vision. (Mmk 23.111)
Then there is the superior and inferior [knowledge] born from infinite and boundless wombs;
beyond that is the knowledge of the Buddhas, as well as that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The sons of the Buddha are great-souled ones, and even those gods who know reality;
for their destinations are infinite, yet their supreme station is one of calculation.
The abode of those possessing infinite knowledge is not for those dwelling upon the surface of the earth;
this has been declared by the mantra-experts who know calculation as the place established in calculation.
For those engaged in the accomplishment of mantras,
the application [of the number] at the time of recitation should be known as the authoritative standard for calculation, for the purpose of the mantra-recitation.
For those who recite the meaning according to the ritual injunctions, the measurement of the number of recitations is prescribed;
one whose mantra is perfected shall enter the Vindhya mountains, while for one who has attained success, it brings benefit even in a cow-pen.
Likewise, one who has perfected the mantra should always go to the Himavat mountain;
for that embodied being who has perfected the mantra, movement is according to his will.
If the minister, for the sake of recitation, should go to the Himālaya while unaccomplished,
he will not withstand the unbearable army nor the coolness of all dualities.
Success in price is declared to come from those with little vitality and little application;
[one should seek it] on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains, abounding in many flowers and fruits.
Therefore, he sent [the practitioner] to the Vindhya mountain for the purpose of properly reciting the mantra;
thus, the Vindhya is always prescribed as the place for preliminary service (*pūrvasaṃseva*) on account of the recitation.
Therefore, one should know that accomplishment is found in the mountain caves of the Vindhya range;
on the southern side of the Gaṅgā, one should employ everything within the Vindhya.
One should point out the Himavat mountain in the northern region;
from there, one should accomplish mantras as they have been declared for those who are pure according to their desire.
The perfected one goes to the Himavat, the perfected one [goes] to the slopes of the Vindhya;
[he dwells] in mountain caves and along their banks, in dwellings and mansions within the caves.
Whether always on the bank of the lord of rivers or upon its shores,
one should accomplish mantras everywhere in a manner that is pleasing and beneficial.

Thus concludes the twenty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the teaching of the names and the calculation of the knowledge of sounds, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which is an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*.
(Vaidya 205)
Then follows the twenty-fourth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed all the constellations, planets, stars, and luminaries included within all world-systems, situated in all directions, who possess the most excellent and supreme great supernatural powers.
"Listen, worthy sirs! In order to demonstrate the power and your own words regarding the influence of all the planets and constellations, may you accomplish the purpose of all mantra-practices.

In this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*) within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, and in other King of Rituals hereafter, may you be diligent for the sake of attaining accomplishment. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [spoke] concerning the entire conduct of the planets for the benefit of sentient beings and for the sake of their welfare."
The meaning of the mantra for all reciters has been established;
I, the All-Knowing One, shall now explain everything regarding that. Mmk_24.1 //
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā—
these three lunar mansions are indeed marked by the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars).
Regarding those [signs] declared to be Aries, success does not arise;
only superior, middling, or inferior success is seen.
One who is obstructed by malefic planets should not travel on any path whatsoever.
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, and Ārdrā are said to be the lunar mansions; Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Aśleṣā are likewise proclaimed.
Both Maghā and Phalgunī, as well as Hasta and Citrā;
likewise Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla.
The two Āṣāḍhas are auspicious and highly praised, beneficial for those who recite mantras;
the constellations Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭha are for cruel rites.
Both the constellations Śatabhiṣaj and Bhadrapadā are causes for success;
one born under Revatī becomes illustrious, skilled in battle, and wise.
But the remaining principal constellations do not arise in this lowest of ages;
Abhijit and Sucarita alone are proclaimed as meritorious for the attainment of success.
Tiṣya, Upapada, Kaniṣṭha, and Niṣṭha; likewise Bhūta, Satya, Loka, and Āloka are proclaimed.
Aniruddha bestows enjoyment and auspiciousness, while Ruddha likewise [bestows] fame, splendor, sovereignty, and the world.
The constellations are said to be manifold, numbering sixty-four thousand;
yet in this lowest of ages, their power does not exist at this time.
This has been taught solely for the sake of knowledge in the *Kalparāja* that brings about happiness;
for at that time, in the Kṛta Yuga, sentient beings indeed possessed the power of self-origination.
All were capable of traveling through the sky and were free from old age and death;
at that time, there were no lunar mansions, nor sun, moon, or stars.
In the world at the beginning of time, during the most excellent age, there were neither gods nor asuras.
There is neither perception nor lineage, neither the lunar day nor the birth horoscope;
there is neither fasting nor mantras, nor indeed any action, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
These beings roam about according to their own will; there is neither food nor eating.
For these beings are pure, free from affliction, and equal in many ways. Indeed, the notion of the "receptacle world" arises within this [state].
Then, drawn by their former karma, they go to the earth,
where there are divine palaces situated upon the ground, along with gods and asuras.
Then, from that [state], they arise in the intermediate [age];
when the intermediate age has arrived, they have taken recourse to human bodies.
For those greedy for food and drink, that radiance is destroyed;
there is indeed a roughness in the limbs and the manifestation of both auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Then indeed the days and months were obscured by the light of the planets;
from that time forth, whatever knowledge of the luminaries there is, all of that was created by me for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Mmk_24.19 //
In ancient times, this was indeed the attire of the sages; then it was the attire of the wise Brahmā;
or again, having assumed the form of Maheśvara, or the attire of Viṣṇu, or having taken on the form of Garuḍa, [it was used] against Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Vāris.
"I declare that those born again and again would indeed possess a *paiśācī* body;
however, the Bodhisattvas are skilled in those various births."
By the power of rebirth and for the sake of accomplishing the practice of awakening,
I myself was that very Bodhisattva in that former age.
For previously, I was a fool, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance;
whatever forms of knowledge or artistic crafts exist in this world, [I was ignorant of them all].
In the treatises, as well as in ethics and the Purāṇas, there is likewise the Veda and grammar, prosody, astrology, mathematics, and that which is recognized as the Kalpa.
False knowledge, as well as true knowledge, and likewise false conduct—
all such teachings were sung by me in the world long ago. Yet,
I did not attain that knowledge by which this sage has become so tranquil.
For the sake of the cause of awakening and liberation, and likewise for the purpose of release,
I am confined in the prison of saṃsāra and not yet liberated from my karmas. (Mmk 24.26)
Buddhahood is stainless, peaceful, the unshakable state of nirvāṇa;
it has been rightly attained by me, that which was long desired.
Now, through the proper application of ritual actions, I have myself reached it.
The primordial wisdom of Svayambhū, previously revealed by the Victors, has been attained;
I do not see any such state that can be obtained through an external path.
Wandering in the wilderness of saṃsāra, I did not attain the knowledge such as this which belongs to the Self-Existent One, for the causes of awakening are difficult to find.
Now I have attained nirvāṇa, being engaged in action and delighting in what is auspicious;
however, this compendium of treatises is indeed being spoken by me alone.
And no causes for accomplishment are found apart from karma;
this long thread of saṃsāra is a bond bound by karma.
This is the greatness of its power: it ripens both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
these [omens] merely indicate the movements of the constellations, planets, and luminaries.
No such sign is seen among other people who are unrighteous;
therefore, it is joined with the planets and so forth, and is to be understood as auspicious or inauspicious according to its influence.
The four world-protectors are proclaimed as being composed of water, earth, wind, fire, and lightning;
these great elements are the causes for the gathering of all beings.
When impelled by the mantra for the sake of gathering sentient beings,
the accomplishment of the mantra arises through the regulation of their timing.
In those recitations, one must indeed strive to protect [the mantra] from both auspicious and inauspicious influences;
it is held in high esteem by the leaders of the world, such as Śakra and the other lords of the gods.
At that time, during the end of the age,
those mantras conceived for the final age will achieve accomplishment through diligent effort, even in this lowest of ages.

For this very reason, Mañjughoṣa, the greatly wise one, who was conceptualized as a youth by the Lords of Jinas, wanders through this entire world in the form of a young boy, capable of bestowing grace upon sentient beings.
At that time, the accomplishment of Mañjughoṣa will be seen;
at that time, there will be knowledge of the stars and astrology.
In that lowest of ages, twenty-seven lunar mansions, the muhūrtas,

The Magadhan king, the lord of all, shall fall from his kingdom;
these are the signs said to appear when Rāhu approaches.
In whichever directions one perceives the lunar or solar disk,
in those respective regions, auspicious or inauspicious events then arise.
Whatever tremors of the earth have been described as marked by worldly signs,
one should understand that [the same] auspicious or inauspicious results apply there in the case of an eclipse of the planets.
If there is smoke for five days at the end of the day, it will be the cause of rain;
thereafter, for half that duration, there will be anxiety among the people concerning Tīrabhukti.
All inhabited lands, which are the abodes where diseases arise, will perish;
and even the king on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā shall perish.
Likewise, Himavat is situated in the belly; the ill-fated ones and those afflicted by fever are placed there, and the kings and the Kohupālas are stationed all around.
Then, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, that lord of the Tīrabhukti region,
the ruler of men, shall die from various sorrows and torments.
That lord of men perishes together with his sons and wife;
indeed, one should predict smoke during those constellations in which an earthquake occurs.
In all directions, terrible clouds appeared even without rain;
five days passed, during which there was constant and abundant divine rain.
Mortal beings born of human lineage would perish through one another;
there, the mutual gaze of humans does not proceed.
One should know that there will be great danger therein; it shall destroy the king along with his kingdom, wherever such a trembling occurs accompanied by the falling of meteors on all sides.
Furthermore, if there is a terrifying arrangement of two or three [omens], or if there is a rainbow at night, or a crow with white wings; Mmk_24.233.
Then a white-colored one appears as black, and a black one appears as white;
the colors of the birds are reversed, and the sounds of the seasons are inverted.
Wherever birds appear in reverse order, there is great danger for all— bipeds, quadrupeds, those with many feet, and even those without feet. (Vaidya 221) Mmk_24.235.
If birds fly horizontally, it portends a great danger;
likewise, if dogs howl repeatedly with their muzzles turned upward,
whether by day or by night, there will be great peril wherever that occurs.
Wherever many such portents of various kinds are manifested,
there shall be drought and the king’s wheel of power shall perish.

Just as the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] of living beings are declared in the rite of birth (*jātakarman*), so too do portents (*utpāta*) arise from that [same source] and produce good or evil results here in this world.
No sign whatsoever is seen to arise otherwise than from a prior cause; obstacles and the occurrence of portents do not manifest without a cause.

Thus concludes the twenty-second detailed chapter on the light of knowledge regarding omens from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 222) Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed the hosts of planets, lunar mansions, stars, and celestial luminaries.

"Listen, all of you! This King of Rituals (Kalparāja) of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta— concerning the procedures for mantras, tantras, empowerments, and mandalas, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, observances, and the accomplishment of vidyās— is not to be transgressed by the vidyādharas who are engaged in this excellent ritual, and who possess mastery over the lunar days, constellations, conduct, calculation, and supernormal knowledges."
O constellations, you must not create obstacles;
and by all the hosts of gods, protection must be afforded there to those engaged in this teaching. Furthermore, all malevolent beings must be restrained.
They should be obstructed,
they should be disciplined;
none of them at all should be killed.
And they should be established within the various classifications of this teaching of the Ten-Powered Ones.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the meditative absorption named Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣābhyunnata for the sake of warding off all malevolent beings among all sentient beings.

As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had entered that absorption, all those Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions beheld the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, in the abode of the Pure Abodes and approached him.
Having approached, through the inconceivable personal empowerment of the Buddha, he addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, for the arising of the welfare of the worlds, as all mantras and their tantras proceed according to the ritual rule! Mmk_25.1 //
This King of Vidyās of great supernatural power, the single-syllable, supreme, and foremost, was taught by all the Buddhas for the time when the Kali Yuga has arrived.
The most excellent of all mantras, spoken by all the Buddhas,
is the King of the Uṣṇīṣas, possessed of great heroism, and the warder-off of all malevolent spirits.
He is the restrainer of the planets, the constellations, and the malevolent mātṛs;
likewise, he is the subduer of all obstacles in the world and others who possess evil intent.
For the sake of favoring sentient beings and for the arising of happiness for those who recite [mantras],
he is indeed the foremost in this entire teaching— the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of great supernatural power,
the King of the Uṣṇīṣas, possessed of great heroism, the supreme lord over all.
"Speak now, O Tathāgata, regarding the time for this.
Thus addressed, those Buddhas remained silent.

Then, through the gathering of those Buddhas, the entire great trichiliocosm and the world-receptacles of all sentient beings became a single mass of flame; yet not a single being experienced any suffering.
By the empowerment of the Buddhas, great radiances were seen.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Pure Abodes, addressed those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of gods residing there, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas gathered in the great assembly of the Blessed One: (Vaidya 223)

May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, all the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Noble Śrāvakas, attend to me! I shall once again proclaim the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the Lord Uṣṇīṣarāja Cakravartin— at this time, in this degenerate age (*kaliyuga*)— of that one-syllable Vidyā-Cakravartin who stands above all the Uṣṇīṣas of the Tathāgatas, whose teaching is unimpeded, and whose strength and prowess are immeasurable.

Now, I shall again declare the mantra of the Blessed One, whose teaching is difficult to transgress, the Teacher of the three worlds, honored by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites; in the Kali age, at the time when the teaching is on the verge of disappearing, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin will become the protector of the teaching.
And he shall attain accomplishment;
at all times, and even at the time when the teachings of all the Buddhas have disappeared, this Blessed One, the Buddha, will act for the benefit of sentient beings.
This Blessed One is a protector, endowed with the Dharma-treasury of all the Tathāgatas.
Listen, O assemblies of gods and all sentient beings! Bhrūṃ!
This Blessed One, the omniscient one, established by the Buddhas in the form of mantra,
the Great Compassionate Teacher, wanders among all embodied beings.
The glorious Lord of Mantras, renowned and honored as Uṣṇīṣa,
having descended from compassion, abides here as this syllable;
having emerged from the dharmadhātu, he abides here in manifold forms.
For just as the relics derived from the bodies of the Buddhas have appeared among people—
those accompanied by material offerings are honored by the world, while those free from material offerings are especially so.
The spheres of the True Dharma are said to be free from worldly attachment and are the causes for the world;
those with worldly attachment are said to reside within the bodies of the Greatly Powerful Lords of Jinas.
The Moon-like Sages, free from outflows, have proclaimed various elements—
both with and without worldly attachment— which have spread forth for the sake of the world.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Lord of the World, the Maker of Light, remains in the form of mantra, thoroughly permeating the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
He, possessing all forms and omniscient, is indeed seen upon the surface of the earth;
this mantra, which accomplishes all aims, was spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is the mantra in brief; when recited by oneself according to the ritual procedure, it indeed always accomplishes every action that is desired, making it fruitful.
Furthermore, its ritual procedure shall be explained in brief for the future time:
when the Tathāgata, the best of sages, has passed away at the end of the age,
the accomplishment of the rite will then be declared to be the accomplishment of mantra.

Now, the ritual manual for the single-syllable [mantra] of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin— formerly set forth in detail, but here presented in brief— is that of the Blessed One, the Cakravartin Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa; it destroys the application of others' rites, is victorious over the unconquered, is the sovereign of all mantras, and is authorized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
First of all, in whatever place this is recited,
within a distance of one *yojana* from that place along the path, all malevolent planetary spirits (*graha*) flee.
Even all perfected mantras have no power over him;
all the gods abandon their presence;
and except by the will of the practitioner, he robs other practitioners—whether worldly or supramundane—of their accomplishments.
It liberates mantras employed by others from being cut, broken, or pinned down.
Desiring to sever the spell himself, one should take a handful of green kuśa grass,
empower it with eight hundred recitations of the mantra, and cut it with a weapon while directing the rite toward that spell.
She becomes severed;
having made an image [of her] with this [substance],
one should strike it in the heart with a stake.
It becomes pinned down.
One should make a knot with a thread dyed with safflower that has been recited seven times;
it becomes bound.
One should seal it with a shallow dish over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times;
she becomes restrained.
One should split the heart in two with a weapon.
It becomes split.
One should dye it with mustard seeds colored with poison and blood; it becomes stained.
One should strike it with a *karavīra* creeper.
She becomes afflicted;
she performs all magical rites (*abhicāruka*) according to her will.
Having bathed [the image] with milk from a pearl-white cow, one performs every rite that fulfills [one's desires].
One should perform the *homa* for pacification (*śānti*).
By means of a *homa* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the pacification and nourishment of all [beings] is accomplished.
By clenching the fist, one paralyzes all mantras.
One liberates by means of the mind;

one who desires to accomplish a mantra should accomplish it by obstructing it with this very [mantra]; if one wishes to accomplish another ritual manual (*kalpa*), one should accomplish that as well with this very [mantra].
It is accomplished.
By this very mantra, the invocation is performed; again, by this very mantra, the dismissal is performed.
Even he for whom protection is performed by this very [mantra] becomes invisible;
and whatever mantra does not succeed, [it succeeds through this].
Or, if he does not grant a response,
one should recite [the mantra] together with him;
then it is quickly accomplished.
Or he gives a refusal;
if it does not succeed,
he provides a refusal, and then he dies.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for seven days, while reciting the specific mantra intended;
whoever that mantra refers to will come under one's control and will perform whatever task is commanded.
Or, if one desires to bring the gods under control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *devadāru* wood;
within seven nights, they become submissive.
If one desires to bring the *nāgas* under control, one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*).
They become submissive.
If one desires to bring yakṣas under control, one should offer curd-rice as an oblation; they will become submissive.
One who desires to bring a yakṣiṇī under control should offer curd-rice as an oblation.
One brings a *gandharva* under control with all types of perfumes.

With *aśoka* and *priyaṅgu* wood-samids or flowers, one subdues *yakṣiṇīs*, *nāgas*, and *nāga-grahas*. With *rājikā* seeds, one subdues kings; with *siddhārthaka* seeds, Brahmins; and with a flower-homa, a Vaiśya, using curd, milk, and ghee.
One should subdue a Śūdra with chaff and dust; a woman with an oblation of salt;
and a widow with an oblation of black gram and jambūlika.
By offering parched grain (*lāja*) one brings a maiden under control; by offering ghee and oil, one brings everyone under control everywhere for seven nights during the three periods of the day.
Having said this, the Supreme Victor became silent.
Then, amidst the assembly of gods, that bull among sages, the seventh [in the lineage], who knows the ways of the world, laughed; having attained wisdom, he was then liberated.
Then the supreme sage addressed the eldest;
he then chose Mañjughoṣa, the bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
This ritual procedure has been proclaimed by me as but a single portion for the wielder of the wheel,
that wise Lord, the God of Gods, whose [power] is vast.
The measure of his [merit] cannot be expressed even by the Jinas throughout eons;
nevertheless, for the sake of the welfare and prosperity of human beings, I shall describe it to you in brief.
When this had been said, the glorious Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great supernatural power,
then made a formal request to that Buddha who was stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, Perfectly Awakened One, Supreme among Humans!
At this lost time, at the end of the age, [speak] for the arising of happiness for human beings.
How is it that the king of mantras of this one of great majesty and great heroism is seen to grant the accomplishment of the cloth? And how is the ritual procedure for the cloth performed swiftly?

Thus concludes the twenty-third chapter, the detailed exposition on the emergence of the One-Syllable Universal Monarch, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 226) Now follows the twenty-sixth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the brief procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) of the One-Syllable Universal Monarch of great majesty;
it has been explained at length previously.
Now, in brief: in this degenerate age, sentient beings are of little vigor.
Those of little wisdom and dull intellects are unable to accomplish the application of the cloth's dimensions in detail.
Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I shall speak in brief so that those practitioners of recitation may attain the accomplishment of the supreme goal. Mmk 26.1.
One who desires to perform the supreme sādhana should have the Blessed One painted on an unbleached cloth that has its fringe intact, is free of hair, and is colored with non-staining pigments.

He is the King of Dharma, the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma, the Sovereign of all worlds, the Supreme Person, the Foremost among bipeds, the Jewel of the Tathāgatas, the Supreme Victor named Ratnaketu, teaching the Dharma,
and surrounded by a halo of blazing light on all sides.
Below are Brahmā and the noble Vajrapāṇi;
above are two sons of gods bearing garlands;
and below is the practitioner.
In front of it, burning agarwood incense at the three junctions of the day, one should recite the mantra one million times;
thereafter, the ritual activities will succeed.

Desiring to perform the first wheel-sādhana, one should fashion a twelve-spoked wheel made of *puṣpaloha* metal; then, during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), burning agarwood incense before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day, one should recite [the mantra] one million times.
At the conclusion, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship, [one should proceed].
Having firmly grasped it with the hand,
one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth.
Having taken it, one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas;
by those who see him,
and those whom he sees—
He flies up together with them.
Now, one who desires to accomplish the parasol should have a new, variegated white parasol made,
marked with a golden wheel and draped with silken cloth; having placed it upon his head according to this very procedure, he should recite the mantra.
Knowledge itself will manifest spontaneously.
Furthermore, one should recite this mantra ten hundred thousand times before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day.
At the end, on the full moon day, having performed a magnificent worship, [the knowledge will appear].
One should hold it firmly with the hand and recite [the mantra] until it blazes;
having grasped it, one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas.

Month after month, on the full moon day, it is accomplished within five fortnights during the fortnight of miracles. Then, as soon as it is accomplished, all dharmas become manifest before one; one attains all the superknowledges (abhijñās).
Rejoiced in by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, his entry into the realm of all sentient beings becomes perfected;
even in another world-system, he becomes a universal monarch with a retinue of a thousand.
Then, one desiring to accomplish the uṣṇīṣa should fashion a staff one cubit in length made of gold, silver, copper, or precious gems; one should recite the mantra until it blazes.
Having grasped it, one wanders at will and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
He lives for a great eon.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*) should fashion a golden auspicious jar, fill it with all kinds of seeds, jewels, and medicinal herbs, and wrap it in white cloth; one should accomplish it by means of this [mantra]. One should begin the rite during one fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), and it is accomplished during the other.
Having placed it in that hand, one obtains whatever one desires;
it becomes inexhaustible.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the Cintāmaṇi-ratna should fashion a golden staff with a genuine gem and a crystal gem, or a golden [staff] hung with cloth, and accomplish it by this very procedure;
whatever one thinks of, all that is accomplished.
And by holding this among gods and humans, one becomes possessed of unimpeded strength and prowess.
Then, if one recites [the mantra] ten million times for the Blessed One,
one flies up with one's own body and lives for many great divine eons.
Or whatever other [rites] there may be, such as those resembling the black parasol and so forth— even those rites are accomplished by this [mantra] when recited one million times for the Blessed One.
Thus, this unimpeded Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣa succeeds in whatever way it is employed, even according to the ritual procedures of other tantras.
If recited one million times, this sovereign of all vidyās and mantras, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin of the Blessed One, accomplishes everything without delay.
Then, desiring to accomplish the vajra, one should fashion a single-pronged vajra made of red sandalwood,
or alternatively, one made of flower-metal (puṣpaloha),
and wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having performed a magnificent worship before the cloth painting,
having lit lamps of ghee,
and having washed [the image] with scented water,
The yakṣas become submissive.
Having dedicated oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
one should perform protection by means of this King Uṣṇīṣa together with his retinue, or by means of the Tejorāśi-sitātapatra.
Having performed the binding of the mandala and the protection of one's companions,
and having taken a vajra in the right hand,
one should sit during the second watch after the first watch has passed and recite with a one-pointed mind until [the desired result].
Until it blazes forth—
during this interval, all the Vidyādharas, as well as all the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas, assemble;
and all the kings of the Vidyādharas arrive.
Being praised by them, he goes to the city of the Vidyādharas and becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
Possessing a body like that of Vajrapāṇi and strength equal to Vajrapāṇi, he goes to the Akaniṣṭha celestial realm in a mere instant, a moment, or a brief hour.
Abiding for a great eon, he beholds the Blessed One, the noble Maitreya,
hears the Dharma,
and after death, goes wherever he desires.
He is reborn there;
if he so desires, he is born from the presence of Vajrapāṇi.
Then, desiring to accomplish the sword rite, one should take a flawless sword, fast for a day and night, and perform a grand worship of the Blessed One.
One should recite until,
once it has blazed and been accomplished, one flies up together with one's retinue.
With his hair curled in ringlets, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, he does not yield the path and is inaccessible to all Vidyādharas; he lives for an intermediate kalpa.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the practice of realgar (manaḥśilā) should purchase it through a "hero's price" (vīrakraya). Having fasted for three nights during the conjunction of Puṣya, he should feed alms designated for the Saṅgha and cause them to grant him permission. Once permitted, he should enter the place of practice.
Having performed a magnificent worship,
one should light a thousand lamps of ghee.

Having fasted for three nights, having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and having offered oneself, one should take realgar and recite the mantra as many times as required.
Up until the threefold accomplishment is attained,
one should first contemplate the stages of heat, smoke, and blazing.
Having applied a tilaka that is like the heat of unliberated accomplishment, one should proceed.
All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, and so forth, as well as the beings dwelling in Jambūdvīpa, become his servants; they become his attendants. He lives for a thousand years.
Having applied a tilaka while it is smoking, one becomes invisible;
if one so desires, one becomes invisible even to the gods.
In a single moment, a brief instant, or a muhūrta, he is seen;
then he vanishes again.
He becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility.
For three thousand years he lives, and by means of the blazing [mantra], he becomes a vidyādhara;
together with his retinue,
he flies up and becomes a king of the vidyādharas.

Possessing the body of a divine youth, he becomes invincible to all the gods, let alone to the vidyādharas; he remains for an entire kalpa and, upon passing away, is reborn in the Tuṣita realm of the gods.
Now, one desiring to accomplish the trident should fashion a trident made of flower-metal and recite the mantra for one year.
Then, having fashioned a stupa made of sand the size of a hand,
having performed a great worship for it, and having offered a magnificent sacrificial oblation,
Holding a trident with the right hand,
one should recite the mantra until, having assumed the cross-legged posture, it vibrates.
It blazes,
emitting thousands of rays of light.
In the meantime, the gods, headed by Maheśvara, arrive;
all the vidyādharas rain down a shower of flowers.
Then, surrounded by them, he sees as many [beings] as there are.
And with those by whom he is seen, he flies up together with them.
Having three eyes, like a second Maheśvara, he is honored by all the Vidyādharas; remaining for a great kalpa, he causes those of evil intent to fall by his mere glance.
He becomes unassailable by anyone in the world including the gods, let alone by the vidyādharas; and upon passing away, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Now, as for accomplishing the Vetāla:
having taken a man with uninjured limbs and seated oneself upon his chest, which has been secured with four stakes of khadira wood;
One should offer an oblation of powdered jewels;
then, a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇiratna) will appear at the tip of one's tongue.
Having grasped it, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the vidyādharas.
Whatever weapons he thinks of, those appear by means of his mind alone;
he illuminates a hundred yojanas with his radiance.
He passes away according to his wish;
he goes wherever he wishes.
Even in another world-system, one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas;
upon passing away, one is reborn in the world-system Vimalā.
The second is the accomplishment of the vetāla:
having seized a vetāla with its limbs unimpaired, one should pin it down with stakes of jujube wood.
One should offer iron powder into his mouth;
his tongue comes forth,
and having cut it off, he flies up with a retinue of a hundred.
He lives for an intermediate kalpa;
he plays and delights upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
When he dies,
At that time, he becomes a regional king.
Now, one desiring to accomplish the goad: having fashioned a goad out of *kuśa* grass,
and having washed it with the five products of the cow on either the full moon or the new moon day,
Having stayed for one night, the handle of the goad should be made to the proper measure.
Having performed a magnificent worship,
one hundred lamps of clarified butter should be lit for Vajrapāṇi.
One should fashion a vajra in the same manner as for the Sitātapatrā; protection for oneself must be performed.

With the *Tejorāśi* [mantra], one should perform the binding of the maṇḍala, and having consecrated seven stakes with the *Vikaraṇa* [mantra], they should be driven into the ground in the four directions.
Then, having secured the place and made it free from obstacles,
one should, during the second watch, sit cross-legged with a one-pointed mind,

worship the hook (aṅkuśa) with perfumes, flowers, and incense, perform the protection ritual, and pay homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Taking the hook in hand, one should recite the mantra until, in the meantime, [the beings] belonging to the hells...
The sensations of the gods are pacified;
having paid homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
he flies up as a king of the Vidyādharas with unimpeded movement, his hand grasping a hook.
All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, upon seeing him even from afar, pay homage;
when he who abides for an eon passes away, he goes to the Vajra-abode.
He beholds Vajrapāṇi;
if he accomplishes the cloth-painting,
by means of that blazing [image], he becomes a vidyādhara.

Having grasped the name of the mantra for whichever rite (*kalpa*) one wishes to accomplish, one should recite it one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion, having fasted for one night and performed a magnificent worship, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
At the end of the fire-offering (*homa*), [the deity] arrives.
Whatever wealth he desires, he gives it;
he remains under control, subject to the will of his servants.
Then, desiring to become Maheśvara, one should perform a great worship of Maheśvara, kindle a fire with *arka* wood at the southern image, and offer eight thousand oblations.
A sound of "hā hā" will arise.
One must not be afraid; then he will come and say, "What should be done? May all the *vidyās* of Maheśvara be accomplished for me."
Whatever boon he desires, that he grants;
having said, "So be it," he vanishes.

In this manner, one attracts Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others; and for whomever one desires [to attract], this same procedure must be performed. The rite should be carried out by one who has established protection.
Now, one who desires to summon a yakṣiṇī should take her name and offer oblations of aśoka flowers for seven days. She will come and grant a boon; on the seventh week, she will certainly arrive.
Whether it be a mother, a sister, or a wife,
if one does not go when requested,
his head shall split asunder.
For one desiring to attract a *nāgī*, this same procedure applies using *nāga* flowers.
For one desiring to attract a *yakṣa*, one should offer curd-rice as an oblation for three months.

At the conclusion, having fasted for one night, performed worship of the Blessed One, and presented the *yakṣa*-bali offerings and incitements, one should mentally resolve, "I shall perform the attraction of the *yakṣa*," and [offer] fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should perform eight thousand oblations.
In the meantime, Kubera and other yakṣas arrive;
an offering of water (argha) is presented to them with red flowers.
They will ask, "What should be done by you?
One should say to them, "On each day, send a yakṣa who carries out your commands.
Then they will provide one yakṣa each day.
His command must be obeyed;
they bring women even from a hundred yojanas away and lead them back to that very place at dawn.
They provide food for him when he is surrounded by a hundred [attendants];
having mounted his back, he goes wherever he desires and leads [others].
She bestows the elixir of rejuvenation;
when commanded, she performs everything.

Now, one who desires to accomplish Vajrapāṇi should perform the preliminary service fourfold or sevenfold; having performed a complete and most magnificent worship during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), and continuing until the full moon, on that full-moon day, having performed the worship and fed the monks designated for the Saṅgha, one should offer a blessing of rejoicing (*anumodana*) specifically to the Noble Vajradhara; thereafter, having performed a magnificent worship—

When the first watch has passed, having sat down in the lotus posture during the second watch and formed the mental resolve, "With one-pointed mind I shall behold Vajradhara," one should offer oblations of guggulu resin pills the size of jujube seeds for one watch of the night.
Thereupon, the garland of the Blessed One will begin to move.
The earth trembles;
the clouds rumble;
and all the vidyādharas rain down a shower of flowers.

In the meantime, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi approaches, surrounded by all the vidyās; surrounded by the vidyārājas headed by Vidyottama; and surrounded by all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and bodhisattvas. He approaches.
At that moment, the intense sufferings of the beings in the hells cease.
One should offer water scented with perfume as an *arghya* offering;
having prostrated, one should stand, and then Vajradhara will say: "What boon shall I grant you?"
One obtains from the presence of that very Blessed One whatever one desires: the status of a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, entry into subterranean caves, a kingdom, or invisibility.

Alternatively, if one desires the status of a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, one becomes a sovereign over all *vidyādharas*, possessing a vajra-body like Vajrapāṇi; by mere thought, all weapons arise, and one remains for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
When he dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode.

This same procedure applies in brief to other vidyādharas as well—namely, those rituals taught by the Blessed One in the *Vajrapāṇi-kalpa*, those in the *Avalokiteśvara-kalpa*, those in the *Brahma-kalpa*, and those in the *Maheśvara-kalpa*. In short, this is the rule for all of them.
Whatever is to be accomplished through mundane or supramundane rites is accomplished by this very means alone;
great mantras that are being practiced do not fail to succeed.
These [mantras] should be recited together with this one for seven nights; it will certainly grant a vision.
If it does not grant it, he perishes.
If one recites them in the presence of the gods headed by Maheśvara, it grants a vision within seven nights.
If he does not give, his head will split into twenty-one pieces.
During a lunar or solar eclipse, one should prepare clarified butter, vacā, collyrium, purifying staffs, wooden rods, sacrificial threads, yellow orpiment, realgar, and so forth.
Now, for one desiring to accomplish the ritual substance (*dravya*), one should take realgar (*manaḥśilā*), grind it with human milk, and form five pills.
Having placed them in a casket of agarwood, one should perform the rite together with white *siddhārthaka* mustard seeds.

During a lunar or solar eclipse, having performed the offering of bali-oblations, when the mustard seeds crackle and pop, then [the mantra] is first accomplished; by that which subjugates all people, everyone belonging to the mundane world becomes obedient.
Whatever is commanded, it performs all of that.
Then, when it smokes, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility;
one lives for an intermediate kalpa.
When it blazes, one then possesses the body of a divine youth with the splendor of the rising sun and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas.
He lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
In this same manner, substances such as yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and yellow arsenic (*haritāla*) are to be accomplished.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the ointment (*añjana*) should take *śrotāñjana*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *kuṣṭha*, and sandalwood (*candana*), place them together in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it emits smoke. With eyes anointed by that, one becomes invisible; able to assume any form at will, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility.
Then, one desiring to accomplish the sword rite should take a flawless sword and, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,

having performed an elaborate worship of the cloth painting and the offering of oblations, and having established the protection, should hold the sword in the right hand and recite the mantra until it vibrates.

When it blazes and flickers, one becomes a solitary *vidyādhara*. By means of its blazing, one becomes the king of all *vidyādharas*, possessing unimpeded strength and prowess; and together with those who see him and those whom he sees, he flies up into the air.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra made of *puṣpaloha* iron, sixteen finger-breadths in length, with three prongs on each side; having anointed it with red sandalwood, beginning from the first day of the fortnight of miracles, one should perform a grand worship of the cloth painting and recite the mantra daily, while feeding an increasing number of monks.
Having fasted for three nights, having installed the cloth-painting in a shrine containing relics, having performed a grand worship, and having lit a hundred lamps of ghee,

one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and, grasping the *vajra* with both hands, recite the mantra until it blazes. Grasping that [blazing object], one shall fly up together with seven attendants.
He becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas,
possessing prowess equal to that of Vajrapāṇi; he lives for a great aeon (mahākalpa),
and upon the dissolution of his body, he goes to the abode of Vajrapāṇi.

In this manner, all weapons such as the trident, the discus, the arrow, the spear, and so forth, as well as the cloth, the sandals, the staff, the wooden [implement], the sacrificial thread, and others, are to be accomplished according to the ritual procedures of their respective manuals;
for all of these, there are three kinds of accomplishment.

Desiring to perform a rite for pacification (*śāntika*), one should prepare an altar in the shape of a lotus, kindle the fire with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and offer eight thousand oblations of the finest cooked rice mixed with curd, honey, and ghee using a *sruva* ladle.
Within three nights, peace is attained for oneself or another;
within seven nights, for a village or a city.
During a great epidemic, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
During a drought, one should offer oblations of *udumbara* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhu*).
In all circumstances, supreme peace arises.
One who subsists on alms-food should recite [the mantra] three million times.

During the fortnight of miracles (prātihārakapakṣa), on the full moon of the bright half of the month, having fasted for three nights, one should drink black cow’s milk that has been consecrated eight hundred times during a lunar eclipse; it becomes a potent elixir (rasāyana) endowed with excellent qualities.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of young durvā grass tips smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for ten nights; untimely death is pacified,
and one becomes long-lived.
One should consecrate the banner, conch, and other objects with mantras.
Upon seeing or hearing the enemy army, one paralyzes it.

Having prepared a new jar filled with all kinds of grains and scented water, one should touch and bathe a person afflicted by Vināyakas with that jar over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times.
One who is consecrated becomes possessed of fortune;
by this consecration, one is liberated from all sins and performs the rites of the mandala.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one destroys all poisons with a peacock feather;
by that same means, one destroys fevers, eye-pains, diseases, and the like.
With a thread, combined with the mudrā and the mantra, one destroys all fevers and strikes down the mechanical devices of the asuras.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of khadira wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
it bestows a great treasure.
Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away. One obtains a treasure equal to that heap of lotuses,
which remains inexhaustible even as it is being given away.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one thereby attains enjoyments.

Desiring to bring the gods under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *agaru* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one nights. One should then offer rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, combining them together;
thus, food becomes inexhaustible.
For the subjugation of yakṣas, one should offer oblations of guggulu pills smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
With *aśoka* wood fuel, [one subdues] yakṣiṇīs; with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, nāgas; with *agaru* wood fuel, the noble Vajrapāṇi; with *damana* wood fuel, vidyādharas;
and with *agaru* wood fuel smeared with turuṣka oil, gandharvas—by means of these offerings.
For the *pretas*, one should perform a *homa* with *śrīvāsaka*; for the *kinnaras*, a *homa* with resinous *sarjarasa*; and for all the *vināyakas*, a *homa* of one hundred and eight [offerings].
For seven days, one should offer one hundred and eight [oblations] of royal mustard seeds soaked in oil before a king.
Reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times facing the sun for seven nights at the three junctions of the day, one shall be liberated from all sins.

Desiring to master all branches of knowledge, one should subsist on cow urine and barley gruel, fashion an image out of *uśīra* root, worship it with white flowers, and offer eight hundred oblations of milk.
One should also bathe the image with milk and offer incense of *agaru* wood consecrated with eight hundred recitations.
One becomes nourished;
by reciting it twice, protection for oneself is accomplished; by reciting it thrice, protection for another or for an object is accomplished.

Desiring to perform the restoration of those [mantras] that are severed, split, lost, or pinned down, one should fashion an image out of *uśīra* root, worship it with white flowers, and before a painted cloth,
offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee while reciting this *Uṣṇīṣarāja*.
Directed toward the *vidyā*, it becomes unpinned.

Having ascertained that the knowledge [contained] therein surpasses that of wicked people, one should write it on birch bark with *gorocanā* pigment; then, having consecrated one's own mantra eight hundred times and performed a magnificent worship of the Blessed One, one should recite it eight thousand times together with this Blessed One and sleep right there upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
Having approached in a dream, she tells one what is deficient or excessive.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the lotus rite should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood, perform a grand worship, and remain fasting for three nights. Taking that lotus in the right hand, he should recite the mantra until, accompanied by a retinue of twenty, he flies up into the air and becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas.
Possessing unimpeded movement,
when he dies, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī.

(Vaidya 232) Now, one who desires to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra from earth mixed with anthill soil and sand. Subsisting on alms, observing silence, and not looking back, he should take the vajra and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
a single-pointed vajra must be made.
Having placed that vajra in the midst of white mustard seeds at the end of the mantra, one should remain during a lunar eclipse;
one should recite the mantra until the mustard seeds crackle and pop.
Then the vajra becomes accomplished.
With that vajra grasped, one performs all activities:
one pulverizes mountain peaks and dries up the lakes of the nāgas.
It causes rivers to flow upstream,
puts the nāgas to flight,
and renders poisons harmless.
It paralyzes all living beings, deludes them, and causes them to fall.
It pulverizes machines and brings to a standstill vehicles such as carts,
crushing them to dust.
He performs all such actions as these;
this is the sādhana of the single-pronged vajra.
For one who accomplishes the practice of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, no one whatsoever is able to create an obstacle;
for even Mūrdhaṭaka himself [is powerless] if it is done according to the ritual procedure, but not if it is done contrary to the procedure.
And during the time of reciting this, one should constantly recite Buddhālocanā both before and after.
In this way, gentleness arises,
and accomplishment becomes manifest.
Then, having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; Śrī comes and grants a boon,
and bestows a kingdom.
Then, if one should offer three hundred thousand [offerings],
one becomes a universal monarch;
one becomes the sovereign lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Having installed the cloth painting in front of the opening, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
all magical devices will fall away,
and one may enter without hesitation.
Having entered, it extracts the essence and the elixir;
then, if one remains right there, the fear of Viṣṇu’s discus arises;
but if one enters, by the mere act of recollection, [the enemy] is reduced to ashes.
He causes it to arise by means of the mind;
he never enters into it at all.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should strike the big toe of the Blessed One three times a day with *jātī* flowers over which the mantra has been recited once;
this should continue until a ray of light issues forth from the big toe and dissolves into the body of the practitioner.
At that very moment, his hair becomes curled like a ringlet;
he flies up together with his retinue and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas, remaining for an eon.
Then, having installed the painting facing west on the shore of the ocean and kindled a fire with *nāga* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand *nāgapuṣpa* flowers dedicated to the ocean.
Waves will come from the ocean;
one must not be afraid of these signs of accomplishment.
This shall continue until the Ocean arrives in the guise of a brahmin and asks,
"What should I do?
To which he should reply:
"Be subject to me!
Then he does everything that is commanded.
Having drawn a thousand-petaled lotus on the ground and sat upon it, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Then, having split the earth, one rises;
surrounded by a thousand followers, one flies up and becomes a king of the *vidyādharas* who remains for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
One who gives without expectation illuminates five yojanas with splendor.
During the fortnight of miracles, one should offer one hundred thousand jasmine flowers (*jātīpuṣpa*) above the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One;
each flower should be consecrated with a single recitation until a ray of light issues forth from the *uṣṇīṣa*.
It dissolves into the body of the practitioner;
at that very moment, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*).
When recited one million times, in whatever way it is employed, if the *vidyā* is recited together with this very Blessed One, she will certainly come.
If she does not come in person while this is being recited, his head will split or wither.

And this Single-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is the Tathāgata himself in person; who else in the world with its gods could be the king of all mantra-vidyās? It is the Tathāgata alone, whose retinue is headed by Sitātapatra and Tejorāśi.
The entire procedure for the practice of all the Uṣṇīṣa Kings should be applied right here;
and all the Uṣṇīṣa Kings are to be accomplished by means of this.
One who desires the supreme accomplishment should employ it at the improper time;
if employed [at such a time], the supreme accomplishment will not occur.
In brief, all deities are summoned by this.
Then, one opens the treasure-chest:

having gone to where the treasure is located, one takes the jar of untimely death (akālakalaśa), smears it with all kinds of perfumes, pours white sandalwood water into the jar, consecrates it eight thousand times with mantras,
and places the treasure there.
If the treasure remains [buried], then that ground cracks open.
If the treasure remains at the height of a man, it should be touched with water;
having dug down a cubit's depth, it should be taken up.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the lion [sādhana]: having fashioned [an image] from the clay of an anthill, having anointed it with *gorocanā*, and having installed it upon a pedestal, one should perform a grand worship and recite [the mantra] until it moves. Once it has moved, success is attained;
mounting its back, with hair curled like a ringlet, one flies up into the air as the fifth person including oneself.
He lives for nine thousand years with the lifespan of Brahmā,
having attained the state of all vidyādharas.
In this same way, elephants, horses, and buffaloes are to be accomplished;
when one utters the lion’s roar, then the gods tremble in their seats.
Having gone to a lotus pond, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one will obtain the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.
One should perform a fire-oblation of a hundred thousand buds of red karavīra flowers.
One obtains a princess.
By casting one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers into a river flowing toward the ocean, one obtains whatever maiden one desires.
All these are supreme methods for accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Wherever that Uṣṇīṣacakravartin goes, even Indra offers him his own seat;
and all the kings of the gods, seeing him from afar, become afraid and terrified;
moreover, he eclipses the radiance of all the kings of the gods.
He performs it within a range of one hundred yojanas.

"This Tathāgata Cakravartin—in the world of the gods and throughout the entire aeon—all [deities] are under the control of the Blessed One, the Sole-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. All mantra-tantras, together with their ritual manuals and extensive details, are inclined toward him. Thus spoke the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion, the Supreme among Men.

Thus concludes the twenty-fourth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual procedures for the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and the hosts of deities residing there, [spoke].
Then all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once again:

"Mañjuśrī, this treasury of Dharma, which is the very essence of all the Tathāgatas and resembles a wish-fulfilling gem, has been taught for the sake of fulfilling the intentions of the world; it is intended for that time of the degenerate age, when the Buddha-fields are empty and the Tathāgatas have passed into parinirvāṇa."

At the time when the guidance of the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas is about to disappear, at that very time and on that occasion, for the sake of protecting the treasury of mantras of all the Tathāgatas, this One-Syllable Universal Monarch (Ekākṣara-cakravartin) shall become a hidden treasure within this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) consisting of your own mantras and tantras, O Mañjuśrī. When recited according to the prescribed rite, it shall be the essence of all the mantras and tantras of the Tathāgatas, and it shall be the foremost within your own King of Rituals as a youth.
By reciting this, all the Tathāgata-kings of vidyā-mantras become as if recited.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in your own King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), there was previously a single-syllable [mantra] that was a treasure-trove, the very essence, the foremost, and the most senior. In the past, in a time long gone— sixty-two eons ago, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed one.
The Charioteer who subdues men, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—
by the mere recollection of him, or by the simple utterance of his name, the five deeds of immediate retribution are brought to exhaustion;
and many beings who shall hear even his name alone will certainly be destined for enlightenment.
How much more so for those who seek the accomplishment of mantras!

Indeed, all practitioners of mantra must first of all bring to mind this Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja, and must speak these words: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra!"
Then, having paid homage to Amitābha, Ratnaketu, and all the Buddhas, the mantras should be recited according to one's desire;
they will swiftly bestow accomplishment.
For this reason, the proclamation of the names and the salutation of the Tathāgatas' mantras leads to the increase of great merit.
And he becomes fixed in the measure of all the Tathāgatas, destined for enlightenment, and perfected in the accumulation of merit; he enters the ranks of the Bodhisattvas,
and the mantras grant him swift accomplishment.

By the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, this single-syllable mantra— the heart of all Tathāgatas, esteemed by all mantra-tantras, and the accomplisher of all rites— is the supreme secret and most profound mystery within your *Kalparāja*, O Mañjughoṣa; it should be employed by the world for its own benefit.
And also toward one who is not a disciple, one who is unrighteous, and likewise toward one who has no faith in this teaching of the Teacher proclaimed by the Victor. Mmk_27.1 //
It should never be employed against one who is wicked, arrogant, a violator of the Teacher’s instruction, or lacking faith in the sons of the Jina.
To those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who are incapable of receiving worship and favor, one must certainly not give the mantra; for them, no accomplishment is seen.
The Bodhisattva is likewise always faithful, gentle-minded, and serene toward the teaching of the Jina, being intent upon worship and bestowing favor.
Success in this mantra shall be achieved here in this great,
exalted ritual manual— the single-syllable great mantra dedicated to Mañjughoṣa.
Therefore, that Lord of the World bestowed this mantra which brings happiness;
it is the heart of all Buddhas and the source of all mantras.
