In the past, seventy-six crores of mantras were sung by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the welfare of embodied beings who are deluded by evil. (Mmk 27.7)
All mantras have set, having taken refuge in the image of the Teacher;
among them, this king of vidyās, possessed of great supernatural power,
is the very essence, and it proceeds as a single, eternally established syllable.
This abides as the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi) for the Buddhas who act for the welfare of the world;
relying upon the guide of the Dharma, this remains as the single syllable.
This mantra accomplishes all aims and wards off wicked kings;
it performs a variety of rites and brings all activities to fulfillment.
And it certainly performs eight thousand rites;
likewise, by means of the ritual action as prescribed by the rules, it bestows manifold prosperity.
This syllable *ma*, conjoined with the mantra, is the heart of Mañjuśrī; known as eternally present within the syllable *u*, it has been set forth in the world for the sake of blessings.
The King of Infinite Life and Wisdom has revealed the definitive meaning;
this was set in motion by the Buddha for Mañjughoṣa through the cause of his mastery.
Therefore, at the end of this age, when the Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa,
one will swiftly attain accomplishment through the ritual action prescribed by the rules.
The buddha-field named Amitāyus was envisioned;
there, that Blessed One, the Buddha, turns the wheel of Dharma.
He remains for immeasurable eons, having empowered his lifespan;
for this very reason, his name is Amitāyurjñānaviniścaya.
This Tathāgata, the lord of kings of all worlds and possessed of great supernatural power,
shall bestow the foremost and supreme mantra upon the wise son of the Buddha.
The eldest son of the foremost of sons [was established] in a great station of vast supernatural power;
thereafter, this was entrusted by that son to Samantabhadra.
Then that son of the Buddha indeed gave it to Mañjughoṣa;
now I, the Tathāgata, shall proclaim its foremost ritual manual.
This is indeed that foremost of mantras spoken by the King of Dharma; for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he proclaimed this mantra. (Mmk 27.20)
Homage to the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha; homage to all Buddhas, beginning with Śālendrarāja, Rāma, Amitāyus, and Ratnaketu.
Having paid homage to these, the single-syllable mantra should be recited three times.
And what is that? *Muṃ*.

This, O worthy ones, was spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, while residing in the world-system Amitavyūhavatī, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all beings, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit of the great multitude,
and having regard for future generations, knowing that the time for the disappearance of the teaching had arrived.

At the end of this lowest of ages, for the sake of warding off wicked kings who harm the Three Jewels, he gave his eldest legitimate son to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, [the embodiment] of all Tathāgatas;
by the empowerment of the Buddha, he gave him to Samantabhadra.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra gave [this] to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Then, for the sake of favoring all sentient beings and through the power of great compassion, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta established it within his own form, residing in his heart.

Looking toward future times, at the time when the teaching is disappearing during the lowest of ages, he thought: "In the wicked time of the Kali Yuga, as the final Tathāgata, this one will act for the purpose of protecting my teaching."
The supreme mantra.
I shall explain its ritual manual (*kalpa*) in brief.
Listen, O Mañjusvara of beautiful voice, to this greatness of yours, the detailed expansion of the ritual manual;
I shall explain it even more extensively for this sovereign king of ritual manuals.
First, having ascended a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] two million times;
thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.

One should subsist on milk, observe silence, direct the mind toward nothing other than the mantra, take refuge in the Three Jewels, generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and undertake the vows of the *moṣadha* precepts as well as the vows of the bodhisattva discipline.
It should be recited;
from that, the rites come to be effective.
First of all, a cloth painting (paṭa) must be caused to be painted.
A painter who observes the *upoṣadha* vows, using non-adhesive pigments and a clean piece of cloth or a wooden board treated with sandalwood,

camphor, and saffron, should have it painted by a pure painter in a clean place— while the painter himself is dressed in clean garments, eats the three white foods, and is clad in pure clothes— on the fifteenth day at the time of sunrise when the moon is full and the lunar mansion is pure, continuing until midday.
One should avoid [these] from others;
thus, day by day, until it is completed.
First, one should paint the world-system of Amitāyusvatī upon a cloth;
on a cloth measuring one cubit, or on a rectangular panel of one Sugata-span, one should depict the world-system of Amitāyusvatī on all sides,
adorned at the bottom and above by mountains of ruby, sapphire, crystal, and emerald.

They saw the form of that place adorned with great jewel-palaces and the form of its lofty structures adorned with banners and flags; and there, in the center, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, was the Tathāgata Amitāyur-viniścaya-rājendra, teaching the Dharma, garlanded with a blaze of universal light, slightly reddish-white in hue, and [they saw] the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta seated upon a jeweled stone at his left side.

To his right side is the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, standing upon a jewel-stone; his left hand holds a *bījapūra* fruit, while his right hand is occupied with a fly-whisk (*cāmara*). He gazes toward the Tathāgata, his body is dark-complexioned like a *priyaṅgu* flower yet radiant, adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded by a halo of flames. His white hand is raised and gracefully positioned as he waves the fly-whisk.
With his left hand holding a jewel, [he is] adorned with a crown of jewels as all his ornaments, fair-complexioned like a dark-yellow priyaṅgu flower,

clothed in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a sacred thread of pearl necklaces and gems, and encircled by a garland of flames on all sides; at his right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, standing upon a jeweled stone, in the form of a youth, adorned with five locks of hair.

The head [of the child] should be depicted adorned with the ornaments of a young boy, golden in color, dressed in a blue silk lower garment, wearing a sacred thread interspersed with strings of pearls and jewels, possessing the gaze of a Tathāgata, with a slightly smiling face, gentle in appearance, beautiful in form, with palms joined in reverence, and endowed with all the most excellent characteristics.

Below that, the practitioner, wearing the appropriate attire and bearing his characteristic marks, should be depicted holding a lotus garland, resting on his knees and elbows with his head bowed toward the corner of the cloth;
above the Blessed One, four Blessed Buddhas should be depicted.
In the southern region, two [Buddhas] should be depicted: Amitābha and Puṇyābha.
On the upper left side, two Tathāgatas should be depicted: Sālendrarāja and Ratnaketu.
They are all-pervadingly radiant, with flames all around, golden-colored, endowed with the excellence of all marks, and strewn with all kinds of flowers.
Seated upon lotus thrones alone and not on any other seats, they teach the Dharma, sitting cross-legged with gentle countenances like those of the Blessed One.
Above, one should have depicted the Tathāgata named Sunetra, emerging from within a cloud while raining down a shower of flowers;
he is endowed with all excellent marks, garlanded with a halo of blazing light, granting a boon with his right hand, and holding the corner of his robe with his left hand.
This is the ritual procedure for the cloth painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra.
This is the single-syllable mantra (*ekākṣaramantra*) of that very Blessed One.
He is the King of Uṣṇīṣas, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, who rivals [the Buddha], possessing equal vigor and equal power.
The extent of its qualities, power, and majesty is inconceivable; it possesses great supernatural efficacy and great majesty.
In brief, it performs all those extensive ritual manuals (*kalpa*) that have been taught for the Single Syllable, the Great Universal Monarch who is the Uṣṇīṣa King of all Tathāgatas.
Even when not yet fully accomplished, it performs its activities through mere recitation.
How much more so, then, when it has been accomplished;
it bestows the perfection of fruits according to one's wish,
and that which is desired comes to pass.
Whatever is desired by the mind, through the mere sight of this painting, one certainly becomes destined for enlightenment.
By the empowerment of that very Blessed One, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, he is called the Heart of All Tathāgatas; he is called the Uṣṇīṣarāja of All Tathāgatas;
he is called the Cakravartin;
he is called the Mahācakravartirāja.
It is called the heart of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
it is called the single syllable. In brief, its power is inconceivable.
For the empowerment of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable;
the miraculous display of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

Even one who has not accomplished [the practice], even one who has not performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), even one established in all domestic undertakings, and even one who indulges in all kinds of food, intoxicants, meat, and vulgar pleasures—provided he excludes those who lack faith and have not generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For these individuals— those who have harmed the Three Jewels and those who have injured those who assist them— there is no accomplishment;
even their minor rites do not succeed.
What need is there to mention middling or supreme accomplishment?
For one who engages in the practice of enjoying all desires and conducts, eight thousand rites—along with the minor rites—will be accomplished when applied.
And what are they?
First, recited once, it is self-protection; recited twice, it is protection of others;
recited thrice, it becomes great protection.
Even a great Bodhisattva established on the ten stages cannot disturb it,
let alone other beings.
One should wrap [the amulet] around the waist with a five-colored thread that has been recited over four times.
The retention of semen is accomplished;
furthermore, he shall not suffer any impairment from dreams.
However, except by his own will, if he so desires, it may be done alone during that very night; otherwise, it should be performed day after day.
Alternatively, if ash does not please [the practitioner], one should empower it seven times with mantras and touch the region of the navel;
thus, the binding of semen (*śukrabandha*) is accomplished for three weeks.
Having meditated upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and recited the mantra five times, whomever one touches becomes submissive.

During a lunar eclipse—that is, during the seizure of the moon—within the lunar disc, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and, even without a cloth, offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter while facing the east.

The ritual of homa should be performed near a royal palace, separated by a river, or in a temple; it should not be performed in a place that is not separated [by such barriers]. In whichever region the king resides, the ritual should be performed in its vicinity. At dawn, the king becomes submissive.
He performs everything that is told to him;
but when he does not see [the teacher], his mind becomes distracted or he becomes dull-witted.
If the mind becomes distracted,
it must be brought back again;
one should offer eight thousand oblations of milk.
At whatever time this may be,
from that moment on one becomes healthy.
This rite must not be performed for those who possess faith, who have clear confidence in the Three Jewels, and who have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
If one performs even greater merit, one would cause an even greater mass of demerit to follow; therefore, one should act toward others who have done one harm,
and one should grant audiences day after day to those with malicious minds and those with cruel intentions.
They become gentle-minded;
if they do not, they are deprived of great wealth and their lives are reduced to mere breaths.
Furthermore, there is another ritual:
during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter.
At dawn, one becomes the king and lord of the land; whatever is to be deliberated upon, he shall deliberate.
He demonstrates his true nature;
within six months, he bestows a village with a thousand households as the object of instruction.
If one performs the fire-oblation at midnight, [the result is attained] in three months.
If one performs the oblation throughout the entire night, one obtains [the fruit] in one month;
if one performs the oblation for one month, every single night one obtains a kingdom,
or a village equal to a kingdom, or any other kind of wealth.
Enemies do not prevail;
even if they should prevail, it is again karma that comes to pass.

During a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into the fire of a Brahmin enemy.
At the conclusion, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *picumanda* leaves smeared with pungent oil.
At dawn, the gentle Brahmins will cause the king to become hostile.
There is another rite as well:
during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with whatever wood is available, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter.
At the conclusion of the homa, one should cast that ash in the direction where the lord resides.
He becomes submissive;
at whatever time he chooses, whether it be this or that, he provides extensive wealth and assistance,
and he bestows a very small or even a large village, or a province.
And accomplishment becomes unfailing, certainly within six months.
Then, with a mind full of anger, a member of any of the four castes may go to some place of transformation, or by means of a strange and prominent sign,
he approaches one who is devoted to another deity among worldly beings; in whichever direction they reside, that very house he enters for him, and he departs to another region, becoming agitated.
If he flees at night,
or if his family breaks apart,
one should offer eight thousand oblations of milk for the sake of reconciliation.
He becomes established in his own nature.

There is another ritual as well: during a lunar eclipse, according to that same procedure, one who is pure, dressed in clean garments, and has fasted for a day and night, should perform the rite with water free of living organisms before an image of a Buddha or a Bodhisattva, or a cloth painting, or a book of the True Dharma, or a stūpa containing relics.
One should prepare that site with fragrant dry flowers and filled with sandalwood and saffron, and fumigate it with camphor incense.

There, one should perform the rite: having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood for an enemy who is a Brāhmaṇa, with *aśvattha* wood for an enemy who is a Kṣatriya, with *khadira* wood for an enemy who is a Vaiśya, and with other woods for an enemy who is a Śūdra, one should perform that very rite.

At the conclusion of the *rājya-homa*, one should perform the ritual with *palāśa* fuel-sticks for a Brāhmaṇa, *aśvattha* fuel-sticks for a Kṣatriya, *khadira* fuel-sticks for a Vaiśya, and *apāmārga* fuel-sticks for a Śūdra; or otherwise, with whatever [fuel] is available. Likewise, the Great King should likewise offer fuel-sticks from the roots of the Aparājita tree.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee, and at the end of that, one should cast that very same ash in whichever direction the Great King resides,
or toward where one with a wicked mind approaches; having formed the single-syllable mudrā of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, one should cast it.
Or, terrified, he turns back with his *utpala* seal;
or his wheels break,
or some other great portent occurs.
A great affliction and instability of mind, by which his speech is brought to an end.
These or other desired rites may be performed.
Having consecrated a garment with mantras, one should wear it;
one becomes fortunate.
Having consecrated the eyes with mantras, one should apply ointment;
one will become beloved by all people.
One should perform this after sevenfold consecration.
Having placed his eyes and mouth everywhere, he should gaze at the face of one who is angry;
that person will become submissive.
Furthermore, having consecrated seven times a gentle flower, fruit, or anything else fragrant, he should present it to the king.
Merely by smelling it, one becomes submissive;
or whatever other being there may be, that being becomes submissive merely by the sight of it.
For all types of bodily aches, having consecrated [the water] one hundred and eight times, one should bathe with warm water.
He becomes well;
he should perform these actions, but not for the sake of suffering beings.
One who has faith in the Three Jewels may perform such an act for one who is destitute, fallen, impotent, or even for one who observes vows here in this teaching.
One should certainly not perform the ritual for women, nor for children, the elderly, or the sick;
nor for the poor, the suffering, those of little strength, or those born of improper wombs.
One should not perform such an action [against] a Mahāsattva;

rather, one should employ it against those who are brave, reckless, greedy, possessed of a great faction, or great wealth, as well as those who are excessively arrogant and fierce. One may perform such an action [against them].
For one who hates the teaching, for one who is angry, for one who steals the property of others,
for one who lacks faith in all mantras, medicinal herbs, and yogins— [these are ineffective].
One should employ ritual action against those who are arrogant, evil-minded, unrighteous kings, and those despised by the world; one must avoid employing it against those who are righteous.
They say that another rite is devoid of intellectual deliberation;
indeed, the reciter, when enraged, casts that very ash toward whichever direction he desires.
Those enemies dwelling there become enraged, and even the king perishes;
furthermore, those people will certainly fall into a state of long-lasting exhaustion.
Furthermore, if a great plague or calamity is seen in that region,
one should not perform the rite at all, even if one has fallen into dire straits.
Within three weeks, all those rulers of men there will perish;
however, when that karma is fully exhausted, he shall withdraw them within two weeks.
In the first [week] there is distraction of mind; in the second week, however, there is illness; likewise, in the third week, death occurs; therefore, one should avoid it. (Mmk 27.30)
In the first [week] they flee; in the second, there is the ruin of the country;
and in the third week, there is destruction. One should not perform such a rite.
The leaders of the world have taught that [this method] is intended solely for those beings who are to be disciplined through courage;
for these Buddhas, whose minds are pure, do not [rely] excessively upon material success.
All Buddhas have condemned any action that obstructs the vital breath;
therefore, one who recites mantras and desires supreme accomplishment should not perform such an act.
Rebirth in hell is seen to occur only within these very realms of desire;
however, this which has been proclaimed is solely the arising of the fruits of black and white karma.
The majesty of the diversity of karma is as it has been seen by the best of bipeds;
it is capable of producing constant auspiciousness, and even that which is dark brings him good fortune.
Likewise, mixed karma is taught as being indeed mixed;
thus has this variety of karma been demonstrated by those who perceive reality.
The reciter should avoid that which is black or even mixed karma;
he should resort to the white, auspicious [karma] that brings about the arising of the fruit of virtuous action.
But by suppressing the vital breath, the reciter goes again and again to hell;
therefore, the dharma of non-violence for the sake of its cessation is the supreme action.
Heaven, as well as the accomplishment of mantras and an auspicious destiny, are attained through well-performed deeds; conversely, the opposite is said to result from contrary actions.
I have declared dharma and adharma, and the conduct that leads to omniscience; one who constantly recites auspicious mantras should undertake [the practice] with the desire for accomplishment.
The mantras of that reciter shall be accomplished when he abides in auspiciousness;
for him who is devoted to white karma, liberation is indeed irreversible.
The Tathāgatas declare that success comes through the welfare of the minister;
however, for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, the diversity of karma is taught.
One thousand rites, or even slightly more than eight hundred, will be accomplished as desired;
however, one may perform minor rites, but the supreme one will not be obtained.
The middling [attainment] is accomplished somewhat through effort consisting of recitation and fire-offerings;
the inferior [attainment] is accomplished quickly by means of ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
Three kinds of action have been taught: superior, inferior, and middling.
One who possesses an excellent form and is an ascetic likewise attains the superior [result].

Likewise, one who performs a moderate number of recitations shall obtain moderate success in their actions; likewise, one who constantly performs a small number of recitations shall be occupied with minor tasks. (Mmk 27.46)
One attains only a minor accomplishment (kṣudrasiddhi) and does not obtain any other accomplishment;
furthermore, the number of recitations for the fire sacrifice (homa), determined by the duration of time, is seen to be threefold.
In those of middling capacity, success is seen to be middling;
in those of lesser capacity, only a small or even very slight result is obtained, which is known as a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*).

Thus concludes the twenty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the cloth-painting and the heart-mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, concerning the single-syllable root mantra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 242) Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Mañjuśrī, there is yet another procedure for your cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) which serves as a means for accomplishment and achieves the purpose of all rites.

By means of this very one-syllable heart-mantra, or by your six-syllable root-mantra ending with *vāma*, or by your six-syllable heart-mantra beginning with *oṃ*, or by the one-syllable mantra, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for this [painting] is performed before the cloth.

In the future time, in the future age, when I, the Tathāgata, have passed into parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha-field has become empty, when the lowest of ages has arrived, and when the world is without protection, without refuge, and without resort— this very King of Rituals (Kalparāja) shall become a protection,
a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort.
And what is that?

First of all, on a previously unwashed cloth, free of hair, seven cubits long and three cubits wide, with its fringes intact, and treated with saffron and sandalwood paste, one should depict the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma and looking toward Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
On the right side, one should depict Sudhana, Subhūmi, Āryākṣayamati, and Mañjuśrī, all paying homage to the Blessed One.
One should have Samantabhadra depicted on the left side, appearing as a youth with his limbs adorned with all ornaments, along with Āryāvalokiteśvara, Bhadrapāla, and Suśobhana;
the image of the Blessed One should be depicted as somewhat shorter [than them].
The noble Avalokiteśvara and Sudhana should be depicted with fly-whisks held in their hands;
and below them, the Earth should be drawn, with hands holding jewel-caskets emerging from her upper body. These are to be painted.
Above, two young *vidyādhara*s holding garlands should be depicted, as well as clouds raining down with lightning.
All the *bodhisattvas* should be made to appear scattering flowers while gazing at the face of the Blessed One;
they should be adorned, with serene gazes, and depicted sitting with their upper bodies slightly bowed.
Having placed such a cloth-painting (paṭa) in a shrine containing relics, one should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times while facing westward.

For this practice, one should observe silence regarding wood, bathe three times a day, change into three sets of robes, constantly maintain the *poṣadha* vows, and subsist on a diet of vegetables, barley-gruel, or whatever alms-food is obtained.

Having divided the food into four parts, one should offer one part to the Three Jewels, another to Mañjuśrī, and the remainder to all sentient beings; then one should consume what is left for oneself.

With an unyielding body, having brought the Blessed One to mind, and with a mind that takes all sentient beings as its object, one should reflect: "I do nothing, nor will I do anything, for my own sake, but solely for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having thus meditated, one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*).
One should also offer bathing water, incense, flowers, incense smoke, sacrificial offerings (*bali*), and lamps.
One should constantly offer the bathing of the cloth-image, as well as perfumes, flowers, and sacrificial offerings below it.
One should first offer these to them right there;
thereafter to the Three Jewels, then to Maitreya, immediately after that to Avalokiteśvara, and then to Ārya Samantabhadra.

Having first offered incense, flowers, incense smoke, and an oblation to the noble Ākāśagarbha, the noble Akṣayamati, Kumārabhūta, Candraprabha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the noble Vajradhara, the noble Tārā, the noble Mahāmāyūrī, the noble Aparājitā, and the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā, one should afterwards offer them to the cloth painting.
Afterwards, in a certain spot outside, one should fashion effigies of camels, donkeys, horses, and elephants out of anthill earth and offer them all of these.
Without forgetting, one should avoid oil-cakes, flour, sesame preparations, horse-gram, fish, meat, radishes, eggplant, lotus leaves, and bronze vessels.
Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, weary from that very exertion, one should cultivate the recollection of all the Buddhas.
One should perform the recitation mentally.
Elsewhere, in a secluded place, one should prepare a bed upon a layer of kuśa grass.
One should avoid excessive drinking, excessive eating, excessive wandering, excessive sightseeing, and excessive sleeping.
One should practice the recollection of the Buddha three times a day, maintain the retention of the vital essence,
and not disclose auspicious dreams to anyone else.
One should inform the Blessed One.
In this manner, proceeding in due order and with haste, one should recite one hundred thousand syllables;
and at the conclusion, one should cause the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā to be recited.
At the time of recitation, one should perform the *japa* while gazing at the face of the Blessed One or Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; the syllables and words should be articulated without confusion.
At the end of the rosary, having performed a prostration, one should offer the dedication.
Having performed the preliminary service according to this procedure, one should place the cloth painting in some healthy location and carry out the ritual where there is satisfaction of the mind.
The ritual for the cloth painting is completed.

Afterwards, one should have an image of the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī made of white sandalwood, seated upon a lotus throne, holding the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā in one hand and a fruit in his right hand.
Having placed it in a clean spot facing west, one should construct a fire-pit before it;
for all rites, it should be square, measuring two spans, and one should cast fragrances and all kinds of grains beneath it.
One should construct it above that.

Having generated the new fire according to this procedure, one should take fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *aśvattha* wood—or alternatively, of *aśoka*—and having brought together clarified butter, rice mixed with water, milk, curd, and honey, and having placed them all in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times and offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Afterwards, on another day beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the rite: having kindled the fire with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks and seeing that it is free of smoke, one should invoke the fire (*agnim āvāhayet*).
Come, O tawny-hued one with a flaming tongue and red eyes! O tawny-hued one, give, cause [them] to be given! Svāhā!

With this mantra, one should offer three oblations. Afterwards, one should invoke the Blessed One: "Come, come, O Youthful One! I am intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings; provide me with assistance. Accept this incense, flowers, and perfume, svāhā!"
Whatever one gives, that should be given by this [mantra].
To the one who has arrived, an *argha* offering should be presented with fragrant flowers and water; afterwards, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should cast a single oblation.
In this manner, for seven days, one should perform nourishment with ghee and rice, as well as with sesame and barley gruel.
Furthermore, within this very interval, one will certainly see the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks, each two finger-breadths in length;
day by day, this brings a hundred lords of the earth under one's control.
One should offer one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers;
the king will become submissive.
One should offer one thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains wealth.
Having kindled a fire with *śamī* fuel-sticks, one should offer sesame seeds;
one becomes a lord of riches.
One should constantly offer water into water.
Having risen in the morning, one becomes beloved by all people.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains a village consisting of a thousand households.
One should offer oblations with the *bahuputrikā* mantra;
one obtains whatever daughter one desires.
One should offer oblations of *apāmārga*; this pacifies disease.
Having kindled a fire with wood from milk-producing trees, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds.
Whatever one performs while focusing one's mind upon it, that one obtains.
One who desires a kingdom should offer one hundred thousand lotuses;
he obtains a kingdom.
By offering one hundred thousand barley grains, inexhaustible food is produced.
One should offer guggulu and priyaṅgu together with clarified butter into the fire;
one will obtain a son.
In the absence of kākoli, one should offer jasmine flowers into water as an oblation.
Within seven days, one obtains a village.
Taking each flower of the *jātī* jasmine one by one, one should offer them into water.
Whosoever is given the remaining fragment for their sense of smell becomes submissive by that mere act of smelling.
Having placed saffron, musk, and clove flowers in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra;
whoever one converses with becomes submissive.
Having consecrated black pepper eight thousand times and placed it in one's mouth, even if one is angry, one becomes beloved by means of one's speech.
One should bind the topknot with this very [mantra];
one becomes invisible.
Upon seeing Śakra, if one recollects [the mantra] mentally, one becomes free from anger.
By constant recitation, one becomes beloved by all people.
Rising at the great dawn, one should offer water together with *jāti* flowers upon the ground in a clean place;
thus, one becomes a master of mantras.
His word is not to be transgressed.
When fear arises, one should bring him to mind;
then fear will no longer exist.
Even toward one who is angry, one should cultivate loving-kindness and, having recollected it, look upon their face;
thus, that person becomes free from anger.
One should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with all kinds of fragrant flowers; whomever one performs it for will become submissive.
One should drink water consecrated seven times at dawn;
it exhausts karma that is to be experienced in this very life.
By rinsing one's mouth with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one becomes beloved by all people.
Having consecrated flowers with mantras, whoever one gives them to becomes submissive.
Through a single hundred-thousandfold oblation of rice grains, one attains the status of a teacher;
through sesame seeds, one attains the status of a regional ruler; one should offer a thousand lotuses.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras.
Having combined guggulu, sarjarasa, gandharasa, and śrīvāsaka—purchased with heroic effort—one should perform oblations.
On every fifth day for six months, when that period is complete, one obtains a thousandfold return.
Having fashioned an image out of all types of perfumes, one should cut it repeatedly with a sharp, single-edged blade and offer it as an oblation.

By using the right foot of a man or the left foot of a woman [as the cutting tool], whoever one desires becomes submissive. For seven days, at the three junctions of the day, one should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers as an oblation.
One obtains cattle;
with *arka* wood one obtains grain; with *śirīṣa* flowers, horses; with *aśoka* flowers, gold; and with *vyādhighātaka* flowers, one obtains garments.
Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished by means of an oblation of *jātī* flowers.
If one offers flowers of whatever color into water at sunrise,
one obtains garments of that same color.
Having consecrated a vessel with seven recitations, if one goes for alms, one receives inexhaustible alms.
Having risen during the night and recited [the mantra] over oneself, one personally beholds auspicious dreams.

Then, desiring to bring a king under one's control, one should take the dust from his feet, mix it with mustard seeds and oils, and offer it as an oblation for seven days at the three junctions of the day; thus he becomes submissive.
Desiring to bring a queen under one's control, one should combine *sauvarcala* salt, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vārāhī* together and offer them as oblations;
after seven nights, at the three junctions of the day, she becomes submissive.
Desiring to bring a royal minister under one's control, one should fashion an image out of *bhallātaka* nuts, sesame seeds, and *vacā*, and offer it as oblations.
For seven days and seven nights, he becomes submissive.
One who desires to bring a royal priest under control should combine *brahmadaṇḍī* and *śatapuṣpā* together and perform oblations;
for seven nights, at the three junctions of the day, he becomes submissive.
One who desires to bring Brahmins under one's control should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee;
all will become submissive.
Now, if one desires to bring a Kṣatriya under control,
one should offer oblations of boiled rice with ghee for seven days.
For the subjugation of Vaiśyas, one should offer barley-gruel mixed with molasses;
they will become submissive. One should offer oil-cake as an oblation.
Śūdras become submissive.
Having gathered them all together, one should offer oblations; then all become submissive.
By offering a bali-oblation at a crossroads or in a solitary house, whoever is afflicted with illness becomes liberated from it.
If one touches the face while reciting [the mantra], the fever departs.
By tying a lock of hair with the mantra recited one hundred and eight times, one is liberated from all diseases.
Having tied a *mūśraka* [amulet] and performed the binding of the topknot (*śikhā-bandha*), one should go to sleep, thereby being freed from all ailments.
All diseases depart;
one seized by illness is liberated by mere recitation.
In the case of throat-obstruction, one should apply an ointment after consecrating anthill earth with the mantra.
The disease departs.
In the case of eye disease, one should offer oblations of indigo buds;
it will be pacified.
This is the ritual procedure for the preparation of the cloth-painting (paṭa).

According to the previously described procedure, upon an unbleached cloth from which the hair has been removed, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta should be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, red in color,
having the form of a youth, and seated upon a lotus throne;
on his right side is Āryāvalokiteśvara, and on his left side is Samantabhadra.
Slightly smaller than that of Noble Mañjuśrī;
having placed that cloth painting [in a shrine], one should recite the mantra ten million times,
and one becomes a king.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks smeared with saffron;
one becomes a king.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of agarwood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One becomes a king.
One should offer ten million *jātī* flowers smeared with ghee;
one becomes a king.
One obtains a heap of dināras equal in measure to the heap of lotuses that one offers as an oblation;
as long as he does not accept [the reward] while reciting the mantra, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*.

If one performs a hundred thousand oblations of *bhallātaka* fruits, one is given a thousand *dīnāras*. If one performs a hundred thousand oblations of *vyādhighātaka* fruits, one becomes a great lord of wealth. By performing eight thousand oblations with *guggulu* fuel-sticks, one obtains grain.
By performing a continuous homa of sesame seeds, one obtains grain without interruption. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of cow-rice;
together with curd, one obtains a thousand cows.
Having placed the fruits of the *bahuputrikā* and the fruits of the *śamī* together, one should offer them as oblations;
whatever maiden one desires, that one obtains.
One should offer *śamī* leaves as oblations.
One becomes a granter of all desires.
One should offer agasti flowers smeared with milk;
this is for the subjugation of brahmins.
One should offer white *karavīra* flowers for the subjugation of a *kṣatriya*. One should offer *karṇikāra* flowers for the subjugation of a king.
One should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers for the subjugation of a Śūdra.
One should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One is completely liberated from all diseases.
By this very rite, one should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers at the base of the feet;
one will become eternally happy.
Having kindled a fire with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks, one should offer a thousand *śamī* flowers as oblations.
The affliction of the constellations is pacified.
Having written the mantra with *gorocanā* and bound it upon one's head, one may enter into battle;
one will not be touched by weapons.

Having placed Mañjuśrī at the forefront of the army upon the shoulder of an elephant, the enemy force is broken by the mere sight of him. Having fashioned the image of the Youth (Kumāra) at the top of the banner, seated upon a golden peacock throne, one should enter the battle;
by the mere sight of it, the enemy force is broken.
One should offer one hundred thousand jasmine flowers at the base of the feet;
there, upon a bed of kuśa grass, one should prepare a couch.
In a dream, [the deity] will speak according to one's desire.
Having offered a thousand lamps, having made a single lamp with a wick of lotus fiber and having wrapped it with licorice root, one should light it; thus one sees Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta as he truly is.
The second procedure for the cloth painting is completed.

Having fashioned a youth out of gold or silver, with the right hand in the gesture of granting boons and holding the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā in the left, one should place such a figure before oneself together with a casket containing relics and recite the syllables one hundred thousand times.
One should perform worship during the day;
young boys and girls should be fed in his presence,
and one should engage in singing, instrumental music, and the recitation of scriptures.
Upon the completion of the recitation (*japa*), one should offer an *argha* with three flowers and dismiss [the deity].

Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the recitation while forming the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).

With the banner mudrā (*dhvajamudrā*), one performs the circumambulation; with the swastika mudrā (*svastikamudrā*), the seat; with the full mudrā (*pūrṇamudrā*), the *argha*; and with the single-liṅga mudrā (*ekaliṅgamudrā*).

One should offer flowers with the *manorathamudrā*, a lamp with the *yamalamudrā*, incense with the *mayūrāsanamudrā*, perfume with the *yaṣṭimudrā*, and the *bali* offering according to this procedure, night after night, day after day, until the completion of the recitation; thereafter,
one should perform the ritual activities.
One should float a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers upon a river flowing to the ocean;
one will obtain a kingdom.
Having made a heap of *jātī* flowers at night, one should sleep before the Blessed One.
One sees the Blessed One teaching the Dharma, surrounded by bodhisattvas; one should perform that very rite intended for him and not perform it for anyone else.
One who observes the *upoṣadha* vows, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, should offer incense of *śrīvāsaka* mixed with honey; he shall obtain a kingdom.

If one recites it ten million times, one sees Mañjuśrī himself; he performs the teaching of the Dharma for one, and if one converses with him, he speaks face-to-face, and one becomes an irreversible Bodhisattva.
The third procedure.
One should have an image of the Youth made of red sandalwood, with Priyaṅkara on one side and Vīramatī on the other, both resting against an Aśoka tree. Having placed that [image] on one side,

one should prepare a replica of the red sandalwood image mixed with salt and *sarvaparājikā* (all-conquering plant), and having cut it up again and again, one should offer it as a sacrifice in the name of whomever— that person becomes submissive.

He whose name one offers as oblation with *udumbara* fruits becomes submissive; one should offer *kākodumbarikā* fruits in the name of whomever one desires, and that person becomes submissive. For the subjugation of a Brahmin, one should offer *śṛṅgāṭaka*; for the subjugation of a Kṣatriya, one should offer lotus roots; and for the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer *kaśeruka*.
For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*) and bringing others under one's control (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should offer lotus roots (*śālūka*) as oblations.
For the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt and sugar.
By offering these at the three junctions of the day for seven days while reciting the name of a specific person, that person becomes submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of nimba leaves smeared with pungent oil at the three junctions of the day for seven days; he in whose name this is done becomes submissive.
Through every such fire-offering (*homa*), subjugation is achieved.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *bṛhatī* flowers, and one obtains gold.
One should offer eight thousand *kālāñjanikā* flowers; one obtains a large village.
One should offer *pāṭala* flowers; one obtains inexhaustible grain.
One should offer *śrīparṇī* flowers; one obtains gold.
One should offer oblations of *vacā* grass smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one will become a superior debater in all disputes.
Having placed the juice of *brāhmī* together with ghee in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and then drink it; one will conquer all debaters.
If one takes a clod of earth, consecrates it eight thousand times, and throws it before someone who is angry, that person will release their anger.
The fourth procedure:
On an unbleached cloth free of hair, a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast should paint the noble Mañjuśrī using non-sticky pigments.

He should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma. To his right side is the noble Mahāmekhalā, and to his left side is the noble Prajñāpāramitā, engaged in recitation, adorned with all ornaments, and dressed in white garments.

Below that is a lotus pond filled with various kinds of flowers; from the two sides of the stalk emerge the two Naga kings with their hands holding the lotus stem. On one side is the Noble Aparājitā, destroying the obstacles and impediments, with a face like a flame of fire and eyes knit in a frown; on the other side is [the goddess].
The noble Parṇaśabarī has her hands occupied with a noose and an axe; her eyes are black and red, and she is mounted upon the back of a peacock, protecting the practitioner.
The practitioner, his hands occupied with a lotus garland, gazes at the face of the Blessed Mañjuśrī. Above them, two sons of the gods should be depicted holding chowries, flower garlands, and drums.
Having placed that cloth-painting facing west in a shrine containing relics, one should recite the mantra ten million times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed a great worship and recited the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, one should perform ten thousand recitations while gazing at the face of Mañjuśrī;
thereafter, the cloth painting will tremble.
One obtains a kingdom,
one obtains sight,
and one becomes a vidyādhara.
By laughing, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin);
by speaking, one becomes a bodhisattva who has attained the first stage (bhūmi),
and one hears his teaching of the Dharma.
In front of that very cloth painting, one should take cow's ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, place it in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra until it becomes warm,
emits smoke,
and bursts into flames.

By drinking it while it is steaming, one becomes supremely intelligent and possesses a retentive memory; when it is smoking, there is invisibility; and when it is flaming, there is the power of traveling through the sky. Having placed *vacā* root inside a hollowed-out earthenware bowl and wrapped it with *jātī* flowers, one should recite the mantra until it sprouts.
Having consumed that, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
If one recites another ten million times, one beholds Mañjuśrī in person and hears his teaching of the Dharma.
And he resolves upon that.
Having had a hundred-petaled golden lotus fashioned and having placed his right knee upon the ground, he should recite the mantra until it blazes.
As soon as it is grasped by him, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*, invincible by others.
Having placed realgar, yellow orpiment, or collyrium in a casket made of *śrīparṇī* wood, one should recite the mantra until it makes a *khuṭ-khuṭ* sound.
As soon as it is grasped, one becomes the invincible lord of the earth-dwelling *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*.
Taking a sword that is free of blemishes and endowed with auspicious marks, one should recite the mantra until it stands with its blade raised like a serpent spreading its hood.
Having taken that, the Wheel-Turning King of the Vidyādharas— unassailable and possessing a lifespan of an eon—
should wrap realgar (manaḥśilā) in the three metals, place it in his mouth, and recite the mantra until it makes a *culuculā* sound;
then he becomes invisible.
The sword-wielder becomes invisible and performs all deeds associated with virtue,
with the sole exception of those associated with sensual desire.
Taking the heartwood of an *aśvattha* tree growing upon a *śamī* tree, wrapping it in three metals, and placing it in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra until it makes a *culuculā* sound.
He becomes invincible and lives for a thousand years.
Having fashioned a silver wheel, one should recite the mantra before the entrance of the asura cave until the wheel pierces the asura mechanisms and enters;
at that very moment, asura maidens emerge.
Having entered together with them, he remains for an eon (*kalpa*).
Having fashioned an iron trident, he performs the recitation (*jāpa*) at that entrance to the subterranean opening; there, all mechanical devices are shattered.
He enters together with as many [companions] as he desires.
He remains for an eon and beholds the Blessed One Maitreya.
The fifth method for preparing the cloth painting.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of white *arka* wood and the size of a thumb, one should offer a hundred thousand *arka* flowers;
one will obtain a neighboring kingdom.
Having fashioned [an image] from the root of white *karavīra*, likewise the size of a thumb, one should offer ten million of those flowers; one becomes a master of mantras (*mantrin*).
Having had an image made of *karahāṭa* wood measuring only one span (*vitasti*), one should offer a hundred thousand of its flowers;
one will obtain the rank of commander-in-chief.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī out of white sandalwood measuring only one span, one should offer a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers.
One obtains the office of domestic priest.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of aśvattha wood and measuring one finger-breadth in size, one should offer a water-pot during a time when no crows are present;
thus, one becomes esteemed by many people.

Having fashioned [an image] out of all kinds of perfumes and having offered all kinds of fragrant flowers, one obtains whatever one desires. If the practitioner of mantras offers oblations of *agaru* (aloe) fuel sticks continuously and constantly, he becomes esteemed by many people.
By constant recitation, he dispels the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
At the time of death, one beholds Mañjuśrī,
who delivers a teaching of the Dharma to them;
by rising again and again and reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one becomes invincible to all beings.
Having recited the mantra over one's eyes, one should look at the master;
he will become well-disposed.
For whomever one performs this rite, if that person is located nearby, [the result is achieved] in seven days; if they are in another village, in twenty-one days.

One performs all rites— except for those connected with sensual desire and those of a malevolent (ābhicāruka) nature— within four months if the object is located in another region, and within six months if it is separated by a river, according to the ritual procedures of one's own lineage or the procedures of other mantras.
The sixth procedure:
Thus has been spoken that which was intended for the end of the eon, as well as [that which was taught] by the Sage in the past for the benefit of beings of little merit. Mmk 28.1.
When the teaching of the Teacher, the ascetic Śākyasiṃha, has disappeared,
one will attain accomplishment during that fierce and most terrifying time.
Indeed, the seventh [chapter] will be spoken here in this auspicious ritual manual (kalparāja); I have taught this ritual manual for that most terrible time. Mmk_28.3 //
This path has indeed been set forth for the sake of beings with little merit;
it serves as the cause for the equipment of awakening and flows toward the way of the three vehicles.
At that time, in this age, I manifest skillful means for the sake of sentient beings;
for indeed, sentient beings are deluded by craving and agitated by passion and hatred.
To them, who follow the sway of craving, I show this path;
yet they remain bound by the fetters of craving, performing either wholesome or unwholesome actions due to their causal motives.
Likewise, the substances to be accomplished for the sake of spiritual attainments, as well as the mantras and tantras,
were taught by the Leaders of the World for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings;
such is the majesty of this ritual for practitioners who recite the mantra.
Having spoken thus, the supreme sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men,
explained in detail the power and efficacy of the mantras and tantras.
At that time, in this debased age, the Supreme Victor revealed unfailing accomplishment; then the hosts of gods chose Śuddhāvāsa.
"O worthy ones, this which has been proclaimed at length as the King of Rituals (Kalparāja), the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, is for the sake of the welfare of all the world."

Thus concludes the twenty-sixth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual procedures for Noble Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 249)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, within the section on the ritual procedures of your *kalpa*, there is a seventh procedure for the preparation of cloth-paintings (*paṭakarma*). Those who shall accomplish it at that time, in that age, at the end of the eon, their success will be unfailing."

It will be fruitful, bringing about happiness and resulting in happiness; it will be experienced in this very life, warding off all miserable rebirths, and its accomplishment will certainly lead him toward enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke the heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—
the six-syllabled mantra which is the essence of liberation from the six realms of existence, inconceivable, peerless, and unequaled, possessing great supernatural power;
it is the deliverer from the ocean of all existence and from the bonds of the fetters of existence consisting of the three types of suffering.
Unbearable to all beings, it is anointed by all the worlds;
unassailable by all beings, it purifies the path of existence.
It brings about the attainment of the Buddha-qualities, wards off all that is evil, is rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, and produces all prosperity;
it is the most excellent among all mantras in the teaching of Mañjughoṣa. (Mmk 29.3)
And what is that? Om vākyeda namaḥ.
The ritual procedure for this is as follows:
subsisting on a diet of vegetables, barley-gruel, or alms-food, bathing three times a day and changing one's garments three times, one should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times;
thus the preliminary service is accomplished.
Then, on a cloth with uncut fringes, a painter observing the *poṣadha* vows should depict the noble Mañjuśrī using non-adhesive pigments.

He should be seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, adorned with all ornaments, appearing in the form of a youth, and wearing a loose upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*). To his left is the noble Avalokiteśvara, holding a lotus in one hand and a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in the other; to his right is the noble Samantabhadra.

Above, two vidyādharas wearing garlands should be depicted as emerging from the interior of a cloud; below, the practitioner with a censer in his hand should be painted, and all around, mountain peaks should be depicted;
at the bottom, a lotus pond.

Having installed a cloth painting facing west before a reliquary containing relics, having performed extensive worship and lit lamps of ghee, one should empower eight thousand *jātī* flowers one by one with mantras and strike Mañjuśrī’s face with them.
Thereupon, a great and profound sound of "Hūṃ" will be heard.
Or, if the cloth trembles,
by the sound of the syllable *huṃ*, one becomes a sovereign king;
if the cloth trembles, one becomes a superior debater among all disputants.
He becomes the sole knower of all the world's scriptures;
furthermore, if he does not achieve [supernatural] success, he becomes capable of performing all rites.
This is the first ritual procedure:
one should offer as oblations sticks of *agaru* incense, measuring one and a half finger-breadths, soaked in *turuṣka* oil, upon smokeless coals of *khadira* wood for the entire night;
at the rising of the dawn, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī.
He grants him whatever boon he desires,
with the exception of that which is connected to sensual pleasures.
In front of that very cloth painting, burning sandalwood incense continuously throughout the entire night, one should recite the mantra.
Then, the noble Mañjuśrī will appear in person and teach the profound Dharma.
He resolves upon that;
having resolved upon it, he becomes liberated from all diseases and attains mastery.
Having fashioned a lotus made of red sandalwood, six finger-breadths in circumference and complete with a stalk, and having smeared it with red sandalwood paste,

one should perform a thousand oblations of the *sampāta* and consecrate it a thousand times with mantras. Then, on the full moon day, having placed it upon a lotus leaf in front of the cloth painting and grasping it with the hand, one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth.

Having grasped it, one becomes a divine youth (*devakumāra*) with the form of a sixteen-year-old, possessing the luster of molten gold and a brilliance that surpasses even the sun; honored by all the *vidyādharas*, he lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
When his body perishes, he is reborn in the Heaven of Delight (*nirmitāvatī*).

During a lunar eclipse, one should take white *vacā* root, wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and support it with *aśvattha* leaves. One should recite the mantra until it emits heat, smoke, and flame.
When it smokes, it brings all people under one's control and grants victory over all disputants; when it flames, one attains invisibility and lives for thirty thousand years.
When it blazes, one attains the power of traveling through the sky and lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).

Having taken the ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, and having placed it in a copper vessel upon seven *aśvattha* leaves, one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
By drinking that, one gains the power of retaining all that is heard (*śrutidhara*), invisibility (*antardhāna*), and the ability to travel through the sky (*ākāśagamana*).
Having placed a lotus seed in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it makes a *culuculu* sound.
Having encased it in the three metals (*triloha*) and placed it in the mouth, one becomes invisible;
when it is spat out, one becomes visible again.

Having placed the scent of cloves in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times; whoever he speaks to becomes subject to his will. Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite it one hundred thousand times, and one becomes a Vidyādhara.
Subsisting on alms and observing silence like a log, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and becomes invisible.
If one recites it ten million times, Noble Mañjuśrī teaches the Dharma in such a way that one becomes a bodhisattva in his final existence.
Through constant recitation, there is an increase in all goals.
Having fashioned an image of someone with all kinds of fragrances and having cut it up, one who offers it as an oblation becomes subject to their will within seven nights.
One should offer one hundred thousand pills of *guggulu* resin, the size of jujube seeds and smeared with clarified butter; one obtains one hundred thousand *dīnāras*.
Having descended into a river that flows to the ocean, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one will see a great treasure equal in size to a heap of lotuses,
which never comes to an end.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds anointed with saffron;
the king will become submissive.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds anointed with curd, honey, and ghee.
One becomes a great householder who gives everything.
Having made a mandala with fallen cow dung and having scattered loose flowers upon it, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times.
Then, one should cause a volume of the True Dharma to be read.
Within one month, one becomes supremely intelligent.
Having performed the recitation of *rocanā* one hundred and eight times, one should apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*);
one will become beloved by all people.
Having performed the rite of binding the topknot (śikhā) after reciting [the mantra] seven times, one becomes invulnerable to all sentient beings.
One should offer ten thousand oblations of *kirimāla*;
one is then liberated from all diseases.
One should recite it seven times every day;

this exhausts karma that is to be experienced in the future. Furthermore, by reciting it one hundred and eight times at the time of death, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī in his entirety before one's eyes.

Thus concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, the seventh detailed section on the ritual procedures for the Mañjuśrī cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 251) Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, in your mantra-tantra there are places for the accomplishment of all mantras, beginning with the Vidyārājas such as the Cakravartins and headed by the Uṣṇīṣas of all the Tathāgatas; in brief, throughout the northern region, the Vidyārājas of the Tathāgatas attain accomplishment.
In China and indeed in Mahācīna, Mañjughoṣa himself is terrified of him;
and whatever mantras he possesses will truly attain accomplishment there.
Indeed, the accomplishment of the Uṣṇīṣa Kings is seen everywhere there—
in Kāpiśī, Vakhala, and likewise throughout Udiyāna.
In Kaśmīra, in the land of Sindh, and at the junctions of the Himalayan mountains,
having gone out toward the northern direction, mantras that lead to excellence are accomplished.
Those songs which were sung by the Buddhas of the past, those now being set forth,
and those yet to be uttered by the future Perfectly Awakened Ones, are the causes of peace.
All indeed attain success there in that auspicious and blessed land arising from the lap of the Himālaya mountains; I shall begin to perform peace for the welfare of the people.
Likewise, these mantras born of Padma attain accomplishment in the Middle Country;
furthermore, success is seen there even within the Gaja and Umā families.
The mantra of the yakṣa Pañcika, that of Hārītī born of the yakṣa womb, and those mantras belonging to the gandharvas— their accomplishment is fully proclaimed.
Then, [it shall prevail] constantly in the city of Kāśī, throughout Magadha,
as well as in the land of Aṅga, in the eastern regions, and throughout Kāmarūpa.
On the delightful bank of the Lauhityā, throughout the regions of Vaṅga,
there shall be the accomplishment of Jambhala, as well as that which arises from the Maṇikula.
On the shores of the ocean, on islands, and everywhere where there are bodies of water,
the mantra deities are accomplished in the delightful city of the Siṃhalas.
Bhṛkuṭī, and likewise [the others], the illustrious Mahāśrī and Yaśasvinī— these four maidens, known as the White Ones, are all mantras within the great ocean.
They indeed attain success in that region throughout the eastern quarter,
as well as in the interior of the Vindhya mountains and all around Agra and Indraprastha.
Then Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī attain accomplishment everywhere— in the mountain peaks, the depths of the valleys, on the slopes of Kukṣādri, and in the forest caves.
There, success comes from the Vināyakas; they are the creators of obstacles for those who recite mantras.
They possess the form of hands, have many tusks, and are endowed with great majesty. (Mmk 30.14)
Likewise, there are many horse-headed ones who possess various forms;
they are the divine daughters of Īśāna, manifold and creators of obstacles.
Therein are seen the fields of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) where those mantras previously taught are joined with their applications,
as well as Mothers of various forms and most terrible planetary spirits (graha).
Those assigned to the realm of pretas, those who subsist on human food, and the nairṛtas—
this field of accomplishment is declared to be commanded by the King of Pretas.
One should designate that as the field of accomplishment for all beings from the very beginning;
indeed, the Vajrakrauñca of great heroism attains accomplishment in that direction.
The foremost mantras of the Asuras, as well as other worldly ones,
indeed achieve accomplishment there, for they are based in the southern direction.
Likewise, one should always assign [the rites] to Yama, the King of the Pretas;
for then the mantras of the various castes, as well as those of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, will attain success.
Cruel mantras, commanded by Vajrapāṇi and others, are ineffective when applied to non-cruel rites, fields, and so forth; they are intended for cruel deeds.
Having gone to the southern region, those who have committed evil deeds attain success;

Thus concludes the twenty-eighth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules for the fields and times, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 255) Now begins the thirty-first chapter.

"It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would speak concerning those beings who have entered the bodies of other beings—whether they be noble ones, divine beings, *etis*, *siddhas*, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, *mahoragas*, and so forth;
those whose bodies are fashioned by various karmas, who reside in various destinies, who possess diverse forms and manifold marks, and who are human or non-human."
“The times for the mental dispositions of beings; the Blessed One is the time; the Sugata is the time.
Now is the time, as you deem fit.
When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta remained silent on his own seat, having entreated Gautama, the best of Jinas, the supreme Leader of the World.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke on the knowledge of the signs of the mental conduct of sentient beings, their characteristics, and the [appropriate] time.
A being who has gone to another world, drawn by the application of mantras,

Then mortals should be possessed by those who are free from passion and possess great supernatural power (maharddhika),
in a pure place and among pure people, under auspicious lunar mansions and stars,

The sign of one who has entered existence, though free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power,

[there arise] various divine and incomparable sounds, as well as those like the Brahma-sound, which are pleasant to the ear.
That great being speaks wherever he stands with a mind intent on causing pain;
drawn by the uṣṇīṣa mudrās, he falls to the surface of the earth.
Standing without touching the ground, one should immediately offer arghya water mixed with jasmine flowers, white sandalwood, and saffron.

For when that being, whose mind is free from envy, is requested,

Having bound the five-crested mudrā and another arising from the uṣṇīṣa,
one should then perform the binding of the directions— above, below, and across.
Then he will proclaim the entire account from beginning to end—
the beginning, the middle, and likewise the time— whether past, present, or future.

likewise, he [knows] the accomplishment of success, the substance, the womb, the collection, and the destiny.
It is certain for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, arhatship, and great awakening;

Marked by the *samaya*, that yogi shall speak the truth regarding everything— the lack of lineage, the time, and the sentient being who is destined for success and possesses great supernatural power; he shall speak merely according to the characteristics and shall not wait for another time.

Whatever one may pray for with a well-disposed mind, all that is swiftly obtained in this very moment; one attains the complete perfection of the mantra and every prosperity desired according to one's wish.
Having quickly dismissed them and offered the approved *argha* water, the mantra-practitioner should perform the protection of the vessel according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules.
Considering the fallen body lying upon the great earth,
one should employ the mantra appropriate for the Victor, conjoined with the uṣṇīṣa mudrā.

then, with a healthy body, the being [should remain] on the ground with the remnants.
This protection has been devised for all beings who have entered [the mandala];
indeed, malevolent beings are powerless to harm those who rely upon such a worthy vessel.
Indeed, this is a great protection for living beings arising from the vessel;
his speech is proclaimed as neutral in the Middle Country.
Having resorted to the divine womb, these and other signs belonging to those born of form are seen among the gods of the Form Realm, beginning with Akaniṣṭha.

Residing within the womb of the Himalaya mountains and on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā,

Rākṣasas, tārakas, pretas, the deformed ones, and likewise the mātṛs;

For the sake of protection, the youth Viśvasambhava should be employed;

it will become a great protection established upon the five garments.

Thus concludes the twenty-ninth chapter, the detailed exposition of the rite for the activity of the possessed, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 260) Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, I shall explain according to the authoritative measure the causes of accomplishment—the reasons for the continuous emergence of the fruits of various qualities and portions [of practice] over time, as well as the secrets of all vidyās that enter into all your mantras within all tantras. They are as follows:
accomplishment may be attained in another birth; accomplishment does not depend solely on the cause of time.
The application of its measure, however, arises from what was previously connected.
Success comes from being attentive to what is beneficial; it arises from rational investigation.
The principle of taking refuge in your son is seen by all embodied beings.
In this context, previously performed karma is designated as "yukti" (reasoning/application).
Through its application, by means of yukti, the steadfast one shall attain supreme accomplishment.
An unaccomplished rite is brought to accomplishment, for there is no accomplishment without action;
when joined with both the object and the agent, accomplishment is conceived through their union.
He attained the supreme state through causes joined with ritual procedure;
he did not choose a mantra from the minister, for one who lacks a mantra cannot be a minister.
By practicing the conduct of silence, one attains abundant accomplishment;
the reciter who accumulates the seed-syllables brings forth the supreme intellect.
One shall attain the first goal, the most excellent state of space;
through the realization of the non-existence of space, being established in one's own nature, one shall attain the wealth of the immortals.
In brief, for one who desires success at an improper time,
there is no success in mantras even for Śakra himself, regardless of the signs.
Furthermore, for one who acts harmfully toward living beings and invades [the ritual time] at the wrong hour,
no success is seen, even for a high-souled Brahmin.
Overcome by lethargy and thirst, possessed by intoxication and pride, characterized by laxity and agitation, he is constantly devoted to vulgar company.
If one is lazy and joined with a partner, how could there be success for him?
For if they are the teachers of the gods, then they are likewise the teachers of the asuras.
They too are unable to accomplish the mantra if it is devoid of the prescribed ritual;
likewise, a rite lacking the proper procedure causes confusion of the mind.
Therefore, one should not mutter that mantra without the proper application and ritual procedure;
for such [practices] produce a delusion of vision in the ignorant.
But the foolish, being utterly deluded, fall thereafter into the most miserable state;
from there, those mantra-holders rescue them once again.
Then, in due order, they grant success and a fortunate rebirth;
thereafter, those mantras establish the reciter upon the immovable mountain of Śiva.
Thus, the Tathāgatas have declared that the recitation of mantras is unfailing;
it is indeed appropriate for the purpose of benefiting the mind, even when one's view is deluded.
These indeed are the spiritual friends; these are those who are affectionate toward sentient beings.
For them, the auspicious equality of the three vehicles is taught as the accomplishment.
Therefore, with all effort and with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra;
for mantras employed by mantra-reciters through improper application [fail].
Liberation from saṃsāra is held to occur only after a long time;
it is seen that the accomplishment of mantras is achieved only after a very long period has passed.
For mantras employed according to the prescribed ritual rules will swiftly attain accomplishment;
one perceives the fruition of the result, for a mantra is not said to be fruitless.
In this very life, the mantras are perfected, arising together with their fruits;
there is no accomplishment without the performance of ritual acts, nor is a ritual act intended to be fruitless.
The fruit arises from the conjunction with karma; thus karma is said to be fruitful. That which is born from its recitation is produced in the sky as a manifestation of non-existence.
The auspicious state indicated by the world is attained through the liberation of peaceful being;
such is the greatness of the destination reached by those who follow the path of the Buddhas.
Even in this time of the degenerate age, success is seen for him as well;
success may occur in this very life, or it may manifest at the end of this birth.
Until there is the ultimate peace, the unconditioned path of Śiva—
that which is designated by the World as the pure and stainless state of Śiva.
Buddhahood, however, is luminous and revealed in every way by all people;
the attainment of mantra-siddhi is said to be its very limit, indeed its end.
The non-existence that is unmanifest, which arises within each individual,
has been described in the world as mantra by the Moon-like Sages of great supernatural power.
The direct accomplishment is ordained for embodied beings even in this very life;
in the empty field of one who knows reality, the mantras shall enter into Buddhahood.
At the time of the onset of the Kali age, when the Knower of Reality has attained peace,
mantras will not swiftly grant success to those who desire their goals.
At that time, one who knows the mantras and tantras should accomplish [the goal] through application and ritual action as prescribed by the rules, according to the teaching spoken by the Sage.
Success is maintained when the Tathāgata is present, and it is held that the highest success is swiftly attained;
likewise, during the intermediate period, middling success is proclaimed.
When the time of the end of the eon has arrived, it is called the lowest accomplishment;
whereas in a beautiful eon and at an auspicious time, there is likewise the power of flying through the sky.
The accomplishment of all mantras has been taught by the leaders of the world;
at that time, that foremost of the families of the Lords of Jinas will be successfully accomplished.
Success belongs to the Lotus family in the middle age, but to the Vajra family at the end of the age;
however, by the power of their former aspirations, certain mantras always bring success.
Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, and the King of Yakṣas—
all the yakṣas who move among māṇicaras— attain accomplishment at all times.
Those mantras and others that are employed by all the deities, even though they are passionate,
achieve success in the Kali age, as do those worldly ones that are well-marked.
It was proclaimed by gods and humans, by lords of the Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as by Ṛṣis, Garuḍas, Piśācas, hosts of Bhūtas, and Grahas.
Both human and non-human beings, belonging to the realm of desire—
those possessing great supernatural powers, those endowed with merit, and those of cruel and most dreadful deeds.
By Śakra, Brahmā, and likewise by Rudra, by Īśāna and others,
and by Viṣṇu along with all the beings, mantras of great supernatural power have been proclaimed.
Even they attain accomplishment for those who recite [mantras] at that end of the eon;
likewise, accomplishment in fierce rites occurs at that time of great terror.
On this earth, the accomplishment of subjugating, attracting, and [controlling] flesh-eating spirits is seen to be fruitless and condemned in the world beyond.
Therefore, at that time of great terror, the Lord of Jinas,
intent on favoring sentient beings, was instructed by Mañjughoṣa.
Then those beings who are devoted to this teaching and are worshippers of the Three Jewels will perish by means of the mantra-forms of those who recite them.

Thus concludes the thirtieth chapter, the detailed section on the rules for rituals and the timing [of rites], from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 263) Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, spoke.
