in this extensive chapter on the excellent jewel-sūtra authorized by the supreme secret of the Tathāgata, while the mantra is being accomplished through its ritual application..."

The expansions of the cries of all beings serve as means for accomplishment, separated by signs, knowledge, marks, time, and measure; they are the sounds of the designations of both sentient and non-sentient beings.

It is said that there is verbal knowledge, and non-verbal knowledge is likewise proclaimed; furthermore, there is mixed [knowledge]. Thus, the ritual action of mantras and logical reasoning is threefold.
Endowed with divine sounds, employed for the sake of impermanence,
forever free from corrupt words, and adorned with the meaning of refined linguistic formations.
In all the established doctrines, the noble mantras are proclaimed;
they are eternally devoid of referential objects, yet they are divided into three kinds.
Adorned with heavy, light, and medium syllables,
that mantra-deity shall be further embellished by vowels and meters.
The discourse on the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the meaningful and the meaningless, according to others;
likewise, the meaning of the elements (dhātu), the logical reasoning, and that which is adorned with the meaning of the mantras of the destinies (gati).
The speech of all worldly mantras is characterized by a profusion of conceptual elaborations;
their meter consists of one or two syllables and possesses the *āścarita* and *ālaya* rhythms.
The accomplishment of the letters is held to occur at the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, as well as the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth [vowels].
These syllables, which are the causes of all letters, are joined with ten vowels;
indeed, these syllables are seen on the surface of the earth as being tenfold.
From one hundred syllables down to twenty, and even unto a single syllable—
mantric perfection is composed of such measures of phonemes.
The mantras spoken by the Victorious Ones, which accomplish all aims, are endowed with four feet; they are indeed the eldest, the most excellent, and the noblest of mantras.
But those which are middling or inferior were then spoken by the sons of the Victor, his own progeny; these are indeed the middling ones.
Those mantras which are indeed spoken by all worldly beings are inferior;
those mantras spoken by the Nairṛtas are said to be base.
The measure of these mantras spoken by the Noble Ones and the Victors is ten, eighteen, twenty-eight, or even up to more than one hundred.
The number of syllables in the mantras proclaimed by the Bodhisattvas may range from one or two up to five hundred syllables, according to their extent. (Vaidya 264) Mmk_33.14 //
The application of mantra is declared to be the arrangement of words within those syllables;
it is adorned by the meters joined with vowels and the meanings of the verbal roots.
Indeed, even a well-employed statement endowed with the principles of tantra may sometimes result in success, provided it is not deprived of the proper sounds and accents.
Accompanied by mudrās and sounds, [the practice] proceeds from the head to the end of the sibilants (ūṣman) and the palate;
the sound emitted from the teeth, lips, and throat is the ritual of accomplishment.
But that which has emerged from the unmanifest is declared to be well-applied;
one who employs it correctly will accomplish the word that is complete in its phrasing.
A mantra that deviates from the prescribed rules, is devoid of ritual action, and is separated from its words and meanings will not achieve success quickly; it requires a long period of time.
For that practitioner of recitation, success is never fruitless; his mantra-recitation shall not be in vain.
Even in another birth, the granting of boons through the perfection of mantras is seen.
Through the power of that mantra, and because of the long duration of recitation by those who chant it,
the mantra makes the ritual action unfailing for people who know the mantra and possess it.
All worldly mantras, including those belonging to humans, are inferior among all mantras;
so too are those mantras proclaimed by all the bhūtas, as well as those that are characterized by envy.
Their syllables are said to be one, two, or three in number,
expressed through various barbarian languages as well as those proclaimed in the divine tongue.
They are always strung together in rows, intermingled by their sounds;
they range from one thousand, eight hundred, or eight, down to even a single syllable.
That which consists of four feet or half a foot is declared to be prose or verse; by means of the *daṇḍaka* meters alone, it is composed as *śloka*, *gāthā*, *skandhaka*, or *pañcika*.
The reasoning of the meaning of the counter-position is adorned with the meaning of a thousand stars;
it conceptualizes words in Apabhraṃśa and Saṃskṛta as being devoid of meaning.
The unmanifest, devoid of manifestation and lacking [sensory] measures, is joined through the dissociation from the destination and location; that is called the accomplishment of mantra.
This is the characteristic of all mantras:

those mantras that abound in the letter *śa* and are adorned with the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*, and which abide in the tantra characterized by the letter *ta*, their accomplishment will certainly be achieved.
Those mantras which begin with the syllable *oṃ* and end with the letter *ma*,
when joined with a thousand *śa*s, are likewise unfailing and auspicious.
It has the form of a square with the letter *ta*, and is devoid of the final letters of the pratyāhāra.

Within the square of the letter *va*, the syllables are capable of accomplishment:

beginning with *ma* and *na*—that is said to be the supreme mantra. (Mmk 33.31)
That mantra in which the letter *ta* is seen to abound in all tantras is said to be gentle (*saumya*); that which is adorned with *huṃ* is called Yāmya;
and that which abounds in the letter *bha* is called Aindrāvāyavya.
They say that the letter *ca* belongs to Varuṇa and is beneficial and nourishing in this world;
while a mantra in which the letter *va* predominates is seen to belong to Mahendra.
The first mantra is the going for refuge to the Three Jewels; by performing this salutation, it becomes a cause for peace and brings about happiness.
That other [mantra] is employed for the purpose of paying homage to all the deities;
that mantra, together with its own mantra and the Lord of Mantras, is effective for all rites.
Any mantra that abounds in the syllable *ḍa*, and which is uttered with *huṃ* for the purpose of *phaṭ*,
these mantras are extremely fierce, radiant, and possessed of great power.
Because it immediately obstructs the life-force when employed against cruel beings,
one should therefore not perform sinful deeds, especially those that involve such violence.
The reciter should avoid that [place], because it has always been avoided by the sages;
for even in both matters, the mantras for pacification and enrichment are accomplished.
In an instant, these well-recited mantras, which are powerful and possess great supernatural efficacy, accomplish all the rites as many as have been described.
One should perform pacifying rites with those [mantras] spoken by the Jina;
however, one should perform all enriching rites within the Kokanada family.
All evil deeds are employed in malevolent rites (*ābhicāra*);
one should perform all such malevolent acts by means of the Vajra family.
Though forbidden by the Lords of the World, they have been revealed by the Lord of Yakṣas.
For the sake of disciplining sentient beings, the arising of the majesty of mantra has been explained in three ways throughout all the three families.
As for those eight foremost families proclaimed by the Sage himself,
within them success has proceeded in three ways; they are declared to be of three types.
It is divided into three types: superior, middling, and inferior.
Pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), and also the malevolent rite (ābhicāruka) are intended;
however, the application of mantra alone is declared to be the application of tantra (tantrayukti).
The great power of the movement of mantras is employed for malevolent rites;
however, this action is base and is censured by the Omniscient Ones.
One should not perform an action that obstructs life, even when fallen into hardship;
however, this has been described in brief solely for the sake of illustrating the greatness of ritual action.
The extensive ritual procedures of the Tantrayukti, along with the mantras and the detailed expansion of rites,
are taught here in the Karmarāja, yet they are also seen in other tantras.
One who is proficient in all mantras should not employ that which is devoid of ritual action;
this applies to as many worldly mantras as there are, whether they be with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*).
All those who are supramundane possess these very qualities eternally;
their mantra-accomplishment is incalculable, and it is proclaimed as such.
Although it has been stated that [the numbers] begin with one and go up to twenty, nevertheless,
from there [follow] thirty in brief, and another forty.
Then, they say that sixty-three multiplied by seven, plus ten,
and another ten, makes a total count of eighty.
They say that ten times ten is ninety, and a full hundred is ten times more than that;
the number one hundred is thus reckoned, and ten times that is a thousand.
Ten thousand is an ayuta; ten ayutas are a lakṣa;
ten lakṣas are a vilakṣa; and ten vilakṣas are a koṭi.
Ten times ten million (koṭi) is indeed arbuda;
ten arbudas is said to be nirbuda, and ten times that is held to be khaḍga.
Ten *khaḍga* is a *nikhaḍga*; ten *nikhaḍga* is held to be a *kharva*. Ten *nikharva* is likewise a *padma*, and ten *padma* is a *mahāpadma*.
Ten padmas constitute a vāha; likewise, ten vāhas are another [unit], mahāvivāha. Ten mahāvivāhas are seen as a māya.
The tenth of those is Mahāmāyā, and the tenth beyond Mahāmāyā is Samudra;
these have been designated by the Leaders of the World for the knowledge of calculation.
Thereafter, one should accomplish the Mahāsamudra for twenty-five [days];
thus indeed is the Mahāsamudra described, and then the Sāgara with ten [days]. Mmk_33.58 //
They say that twenty-five [units] constitute a *mahāsāgara*;
by multiplying ten *mahāsāgaras*, it is indeed called a *praghara*.
Ten *pragharas* are said to be one *ghara*; that is proclaimed as such. Ten *gharas* are also called by the name *nāma*, and all of that is described in its entirety.
When the remainder is multiplied by twenty-five,
that which results is called "innumerable" (asaṅkhya) as the measure by the leaders of the world.
They say that ten times the number is "asaṅkhya" (incalculable); when that is multiplied, it becomes [the next stage].
Beyond that, in the same manner... // Mmk_33.62 //
That world is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than Amitā;
beyond that world is Mahāloka, which is multiplied by the same factor as Mahāloka.
Then, that which is called "complete darkness" is said to be light by means of darkness;
having multiplied the light of light, that great mass is so designated.
From a great heap comes what is called a "great heap"; regarding the heap, it is said to be profound.
They say that the profound is stable; from the stable, one should proceed to that which is even more stable.
Beyond that, by means of great esteem, a highly esteemed state is described;
those who are heroic in the knowledge of calculation say that this state is a state superior to other states.
One should then go to the Great Place; that Great Place is considered to be "Measured.
Having made the measured equal to the measured, it is proclaimed as being of great significance.
From there, one should go to the Mahārtha-susthāna, which is like a great ocean;
they say it is the first after the great ocean, for it is indeed more primordial than the first.

They say that in the first [case] it is "excellent" (śreṣṭha); from "excellent" it is called ending in "eldest" (jyeṣṭha). That which follows "eldest" is named "essence of the temple" (mandirasa), and it is proclaimed as inconceivable.
The inconceivable is the most excellent among those seeking the inconceivable; from the terrible, the kingdom is desired as more terrible.
Beyond the kingdom is the secret place (nidyasta), and beyond the secret place is the auspicious.

Beyond the auspicious, the Great Consciousness (mahācetas) will bring about consciousness; that which is called "consciousness" (cetas) is described as the mental distraction of the mind (citta) that can be expressed in words.
The expressible and the inexpressible are proclaimed as *viśvara*;
beyond the universal (*viśva*) is the Great Universal (*mahāviśva*), which is called *asvara*.
From *asvara* comes the station of *mahāsvara*; likewise, from *khava* comes *adhigarvita*.
Those who have reached the further shore of calculation have declared *śreyasa* and *śānti* to be stations. *Mmk* 33.73.
From that comes Mahādhṛṣṭa, and then Dhṛṣṭa; here Odaka is spoken of.
Odaka is the state of mental distraction, and another supreme station is [also] mentioned.
Beyond the highest [level], the Buddhas do not have an object belonging to a lower stage;
however, for humans, the calculation of the world's formation is impossible.
Beyond that, it is considered the domain of the Buddhas; no other [domain] is known, except for the Buddha-fields which are said to be as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
The Leaders explained that atoms are divisible;
for this is presented as an illustration, since it falls within the domain of inferential knowledge.
A substance is established by its cause; it cannot be determined by those who rely on mere enumeration.
This is the measure [of the rite] which I formerly attended upon the Fully Awakened Ones.
Having propitiated them for me during this mindless eon,
I previously existed as a bodhisattva for an infinite duration of time.
Having fully awakened for the sake of sentient beings, one should enter into Buddhahood;
in various places, I have taught tantras and extensive ritual manuals.
This is the supreme and most excellent ritual manual; this has been spoken by the Buddhas.
This is the authoritative standard taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, as I myself declared it of old.
Now, O Kumāra, at the end of this age of birth, I have proclaimed all the worldly mantras and the beautiful kings of rituals (kalparāja).
Whether supramundane, divine, or human— including those of the gods and asuras—
the application of the tantras is declared for all mantras.
But this King of Rituals, possessed of great supernatural power, is authorized everywhere;
through the performance of their ritual procedures, Mañjughoṣa attains accomplishment.
By this very method, Mañjubhānin,
the powerful one, has declared the accomplishment for all of them.
How much more so in the human world those who are other mantra-deities;
all supramundane mantras and mundane ones possessed of great supernatural power.
By means of this application of ritual according to the King of Kalpas, one attains accomplishment;
it is declared that all mantras are mastered through every rite.
But Mañjuśrī, this one is authorized here in this supreme king of manuals regarding whatever worldly arts and sciences are recognized by the world.
The omens of knowledge regarding signs are characterized by the science of astrology;
through the practice of the knowledge of signs, the auspicious and inauspicious are determined by sounds alone.
The cries of all beings, their conduct marked by the mind, the elements, the sense-bases, and the substances— [these are the objects of knowledge]. // Mmk_33.90 //
They say that bodily gestures, omens, the extraction of minerals,
as well as mathematics, grammar, the sciences, weaponry, sequence, and ritual procedure [are included therein].
The inner science, medicine— which brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings—
and likewise other sciences such as logic and grammar were set forth.
The classification of perfumes, the art of music, and the formulation of fragrances have been proclaimed by me, a Bodhisattva, for the benefit of sentient beings. Mmk 33.93.
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings dwelling in the ocean of saṃsāra, I spoke these words to you previously.
I have indeed dwelt for a long time in the dense wilderness of saṃsāra;
I act therein in accordance with the needs of those beings who are to be trained.
In whatever way sentient beings indeed undertake beneficial action,
in that very way I perform for their benefit an action that is a foundation of virtue.
The various states of beings, which are the sources of their welfare, are produced by diverse karma;
indeed, they are fashioned in manifold ways, corrupted by the source of diverse objects.
I shall likewise bring about for them that manifold perfection of form, described in the treatises as having various purposes and joined with diverse karmas.
I shall likewise assume various guises with diverse limbs, both my own and those of others;
out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I manifest manifold forms.
In the past, I likewise created Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and the others, as well as Viṣṇu, Dhanada, and Nairṛta, along with the various planets in their embodied forms.
With minds permeated by great compassion and perceiving the dispositions and spheres of sentient beings,
I shall indeed gradually establish them in the auspicious state.
I have wandered through saṃsāra for a long time,
observing the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings, which is taught in the form of mantras.
The sequential knowledge of the mind and the ritual manual of mantras have been set forth;
after wandering for a long time through births, I have now taken my place within the lineage of the Buddhas.
I have no creator, nor even a master;
having relied upon the fixed lineage, I am the Buddha who has attained supreme awakening.
I have attained security, the ageless, the peaceful, the sorrowless, the stainless, and the auspicious; I have reached extinction and tranquility, and I am liberated from the bondage of birth.
Now that the wheel has been set in motion, resting upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
I shall indeed demonstrate this ritual manual (*kalpa*) of mantra-discourse in full detail. (Mmk 33.106)
The reciter should not perform the ritual procedures in detail in vain;
for all worldly mantras and their ritual manuals have been described in this manner.
All of them are to be honored and revered, and contempt for them must be avoided; therefore, the mantra-practitioner should not despise them, even if their ritual procedures are extensive.

One should not perform these signs, the application of knowledge, and the astrological calculations proclaimed by the science of jyotiṣa in vain; they have been set forth for the sake of auspiciousness.

Thus, the medicinal substances and so forth that bring success in this very life are accompanied by worldly gain and are a lure for attachment; therefore, such success is called a mere "auspicious omen."
It is praised with verses of the Jina and adorned with verses of auspiciousness;
it is performed on excellent, primary days of the bright fortnight, clearly marked by favorable signs.
When joined with the most excellent white planet, one should begin the practice of mantra;
likewise, when joined with such auspicious [planets], one should avoid those that are inauspicious.
Since this was previously taught by me alone, it must therefore be accepted by those who recite [the mantra].
Whatever skill in the knowledge of astrology there may be in this world, [it all derives from this].
Or others there who are experts in policy, possessing the causes and reasons thereof,
well-connected with the treatises on logic, acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
All that has been spoken by me alone is to be grasped by those who recite mantras;
this path, the cause of accomplishment, has been shown by the seers of reality.
For whatever has been taught as the cause of liberation in all the scriptures without exception,
by that very means one should establish the path of mantras, which are the causes of accomplishment.
The practitioner of recitation should not perform the application of mantras in vain;
for all worldly mantras as well as those proclaimed as supreme are included therein without exception.
One should employ all those that are supramundane as well as divine;
one should not cause the mind to be false, nor should one ever corrupt the mental faculty therein.
All mantras are indeed to be honored; they are proclaimed as those who know the samaya.
In this teaching of the Teacher, which is for the equal benefit of all Buddhas, let it be so.
The sons of the Victors are established, drawn in, and introduced into the mandala of the Moon-like Sages; those who know the samaya are proclaimed here.
Those [mantras] brought forth by the mantras are always fruitful when entered into the heart;
one should not bow down to other mantras, nor should one act with contempt toward them.
But those mantras which are indeed non-noble are proclaimed to be fruitless.

However many worldly mantras there are— those of lower status, arising from recitation, accompanied by afflictions, and ending with the path of vision— they are indeed fruitful for those who perform the recitation.
One should not pointlessly agitate the mind with anger or wrath;
one should not show favor or devotion toward that which yields fruitless action.
For since [the success] depends upon the mind, one should never offer submission to it.
But one who employs a single mantra, remaining disciplined and concentrated, constantly performs the recitation;
he obtains the entire fruit exactly as described by the rules of the ritual procedure.
Having made the mind steady, one should recite that single mantra;
for one with a single-pointed mind, the mantras that accomplish all aims are perfected.
For one whose mind is distracted and whose self is deluded, success is not seen;
however, one shall attain the complete production of results and a vast state.
For one whose mind is eternally pure, who truly possesses faith in the teaching and is devoted to the Three Jewels, the desired accomplishment is proclaimed.
Thus [it is said].

The thirty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of the knowledge of signs for the ritual procedures of action, extracted from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, is completed.
(Vaidya 272) Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī, to your *mudrā-tantra*, which is together with its secrets, most supremely secret, and not to be revealed to those beings who lack faith, who have no devotion to the teaching of the Tathāgata, who have not been authorized by the *samaya*, who do not act to preserve the lineage of the Three Jewels, and who are under the influence of non-virtuous friends."

O Youth, in this eon characterized by a desire for merit yet defiled by association with wicked people, seized by evil friends, far removed from the Buddha-dharmas, and rendered fruitless, you have been consecrated— despite the absence of a teacher’s instruction— into the most supreme secret maṇḍala.
This is not to be revealed to those who have not seen the samaya, nor to those outside the Tathāgata family, nor to any beings whatsoever, even if they follow your mantras.
One who lacks faith in the Buddha's teachings is indeed far removed from awakening; one should not cause such a person to receive the mudrās, nor should one show them the tantra. Mmk_34.1 //
If, due to negligence or being utterly deluded by ignorance, one causes [the rite] to be performed out of greed and so forth,
the tantras and mantras will certainly not succeed for that practitioner who recites them perversely.
If one forms the mudrā and recites the mantras otherwise than this,
one will not quickly attain accomplishment and will even be deprived of one's body.

One should reveal the Tantra of Mudrās to those who are gentle, whose minds are intent on the śrāddha rite, who perceive reality at the proper time, and who are engaged in the practice of tantras and mantras.
One should reveal the mudrās to those who worship the Three Jewels, who have faith in the teaching of the Jina, and who have observed the prescribed applications.
One should reveal the mudrā to those who know the ritual of the bodhicitta, who are adorned by the bodhicitta, and who always abide on the path to enlightenment.
One should reveal the mudrā to those who have applied themselves to the tantras and mantras, who have perceived the higher and lower within the samaya, and who are intent upon great awakening.
One should reveal the seal to those who are devoted to the Sons of the Victors— those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— for whom the fruit is visible in this very life.
One should reveal the seal (mudrā) of those who possess faith, who are free from envy regarding the unconditioned dharmas, and who understand the logic of the Teacher’s words.
For these mudrās are indeed sealed; they stand at the measure of one hundred and eight. Neither more nor less, they have been revealed directly by the Buddhas.
In the ritual manual of Mañjuśrī, the mantras are indeed equal to him;
it is said that there are one hundred and eight mantras proclaimed as being equal to him,
and the seals (mudrās) numbering one hundred and eight were likewise taught by the best of sages in the past.
This is the measure for the emergence of mudrās and mantras within a kalpa;
it is proclaimed as the treasury of all Buddhas, the treasury of mantras. (Mmk 34.12)
When combined with the mudrās and mantras, it brings about swift action; for without a wheel, no motion can arise in a chariot, even if it is joined [with other parts]. Mmk 34.13.
In the same way, among all mantras, one that is devoid of mudrās does not perform the ritual action;
mantras joined with and accompanied by mudrās accomplish the action swiftly.
For these indeed cause all the three worlds, including the gods and asuras, to revolve;
how much more so in the human world regarding other conditioned activities?
For the fruit of these is seen in this very life within the mudrās and mantras;
when combined with both and shown according to the prescribed rule, they are pure in every respect.
The foremost of Jinas, together with their sons, cause the turning back of all beings;
the mantra, the mudrā, and the austerity—these three types of action reside in the hand.
In this way, the practitioner of recitation shall obtain all perfections as desired;
the mudrās are sealed by the mantras, and the mantras are likewise sealed by the mudrās.
A mantra devoid of mudrā is ineffective, nor is a mudrā without its corresponding mantra;
however, when mudrā and mantra are joined together, they are empowered for all ritual actions.
For these are mutually the fruit of one another, arising as mutual fruits;
when the practitioner applies the proper method, no adverse action exists alongside it.
Indeed, all mantras of those possessing form are accomplished when joined with mudrās;
for a mantra applied according to the prescribed rite is [efficacious] when accompanied by its seal.
There is no place to be found where one who is drawn [into this practice] does not achieve success;
from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, one traverses the entire world-system.
There is no being whatsoever to be found who, once possessed or drawn in, cannot be brought under control or made to turn back. Mmk_34.23.
Even Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are drawn in by the chanting of the ritual;
even Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages are rendered powerless.
Whether to break through protective rites or to obstruct the accomplishment of ritual actions,
those who rely upon mantras and mudrās are invincible to all beings.
For whoever among all beings relies upon the mantra,
these applications of mudrās indeed arise as protection.
The manifestation of all mantras is seen within all mantras;
from the mantra arise all mudrās, as they are mutually dependent upon one another.
The procedure for the recitation of forms is employed on the path in the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*);
therefore, the accomplishment born from that is seen in the mantras through the *mudrās*. (Mmk 34.28)
For one who constantly recites, always diligent and ever established in those [practices], all mantras are indeed accomplished; the word of the Munis is never in vain.
The speech of all the Buddhas, who act for the benefit [of beings],
has been otherwise rendered by those who are well-versed in the logic of the mantra-tantras.
"O Youthful Mañjuśrī, I declare this again and again: by those who have performed the rite through the complete application of mantra and mudrā, [liberation is attained]."
The liberation from all mantras without exception is found in the mudrā; therein lies the arising of benefit.
I pay homage to that which brings about deliverance and the production of fruit in this King of Ritual Manuals.
The most secret and beneficial *mudrā-tantra* has been extracted from the world;
therefore, that glorious and patient one [is the master] of those who possess the form of a child.
With a face adorned by a slight smile, the youth who is the source of the universe—
the Bodhisattva of great heroism, who has attained the ten stages— [spoke].
O Blessed One, bestow upon us that supreme sage, the Buddha, kinsman of the sun,
who has been described in this world as the cause of mantras.
"That which was previously taught to me by the former Perfectly Awakened Ones—
why has it now been revealed by the Lion of the Śākyas?"
This doubt has arisen within me; explain it, O best of sages, you who are wise, possessing the voice of a kalaviṅka bird, and born from the thundering of Brahmā.
But he spoke to the Bodhisattva established on the ten stages:
"In former times, for many eons, I wandered through saṃsāra."
This sovereign king of rituals was obtained from the Sage named Saṅkusumita;
there, in various places, I have performed great benefit for sentient beings.
Having come under the power of compassion, I then made this vow:
"When I indeed become a supreme Buddha in this most degenerate age."
Having indeed fulfilled the purpose of the teaching and set the wheel of Dharma in motion,
when I am about to pass into nirvāṇa on this earth during the final age,
I shall reveal this King of Rituals (Kalparājendra) in your presence.
When I have passed away, when the world has become empty,
when the Teacher’s treasury of Dharma has receded far away in the Kali age,
this King of Rituals shall act for the sake of protecting sentient beings.
This king of rituals, in its full detail, is bestowed upon you alone;
at that time, you shall be intent upon the welfare of sentient beings.
At that time, during that terrifying period, sentient beings will be most unrighteous;
kings will be constantly unstable and possessed of wicked minds.
Both humans and non-humans who are hostile to my teaching will destroy the entire treasury of Dharma proclaimed by me.
For the sake of their discipline, this treasury of mantras has been proclaimed;
O Youth, this was your vow in inconceivable past eons.
For as many Buddhas as there may be who have entered parinirvāṇa, those kinsmen of the world, for the sake of their teaching, I shall act in age after age.
I shall wander everywhere in the form of a young boy;
through the form of mantras, I will then and there discipline sentient beings.
O youth, this very vow was made by you in the past;
it has now been attained, O boy, and for that very reason I shall explain it to you.
Then, in a Buddha-field that is empty and where people have no refuge,
you, though appearing as a fool, should instruct sentient beings by means of mantra-forms.
You shall discipline many beings, bestowing all forms of prosperity;
you are the granter of boons to all sentient beings at that time, in this debased age.
For when I have passed into nirvāṇa and the surface of the earth has become empty,
you yourself, in the form of a child, shall perform the work of a Buddha.
"Then, in that delightful great forest born from the womb of the Himalayas,
on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, my nirvāṇa shall take place."

The thirty-second chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual for the invocation of mudrās as taught in response to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
is hereby completed.
(Vaidya 276) Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, entered the samādhi called "The Exhortation of the Treasury of the Great Mudrās of the Tathāgatas."
Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s entry into meditative absorption, a great ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows.
Accompanied by a retinue numbering in the hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of rays, that web of light illuminated countless buddha-fields, exhorted all the Buddhas,
and then vanished back into the circle of hair between the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s eyebrows.
Immediately upon being thus exhorted, all the Blessed Buddhas entered the meditative absorption whose nature is space and stationed themselves in the expanse of the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having paid homage to all the Buddhas, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the ritual procedure for the chapter on the treasury of mudrās, which is empowered by all the Buddhas of the future."
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and bowed to all the Buddhas, addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata:

"It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain the chapter on the treasury of the mudrās of all the Tathāgatas, which is most supremely secret. If you deem it the right time, let it be so; for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of people—both gods and humans—it will become a source of happiness for all sentient beings."
Having a pleasant ripening.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having been entreated by the Blessed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, looked upon all the Buddhas, took hold of all sentient beings in his mind, gladdened all the Bodhisattvas, pacified all the Pratyekabuddhas and noble Śrāvakas, incited those whose minds were intent on the purpose of all mantras and spells, and warded off all the wicked and the terrified.

Having comforted all those situated in calamity and having established all who suffer in the secure, auspicious state of nirvāṇa, he spoke this ritual procedure for the chapter on mudrās for the sake of the happiness of all:
"Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī, I shall speak the chapter concerning the mudrās."
In the beginning, there is the five-crested [mudrā]; that is considered the Mahāmudrā.
One should know the second to be Triśikha and the third Ekacīraka;
the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the fourth Utpala.
The fifth is seen as the Svastika; the sixth is called the Dhvaja;
those well-adorned with the knowledge of mantras say that the seventh is the Pūrṇa.
The eighth is designated as the staff by the Lords of the World who have conquered their enemies;
the ninth is designated as the parasol, and the tenth is called the spear.
The eleventh, however, the Perfectly Awakened Ones prescribe as *sampuṭa*;
the twelfth is said to be *phara*, and the thirteenth is likewise *gada*.
The fourteenth is designated as the sword, and the fifteenth likewise as the jar;
the sixteenth is said to be the noose, and the seventeenth is remembered as the hook.
The eighteenth is the Bhadrapīṭha, while the nineteenth is the Pīṭhaka;
the twentieth is said to be the Mayūrāsana, and the twenty-first is the Paṭṭiśa.
The *ekaliṅga* consists of twenty-two, while the *dviliṅga* consists of twenty-three;
likewise, the *mālā* is twenty-four, and the *dhanus* is twenty-five. (Vaidya 277)
It is declared that twenty-sixty (one thousand six hundred and twenty) are prescribed for the *nārāca* [arrow] formation;

That upon which the past perfectly enlightened ones relied and attained peace,

This is taught as the invocation mudrā for Jātavedas:
the tips of the two index fingers are bent and joined together with the two thumbs.
The dismissal (*visarjana*) is observed in all rites within the blazing fire;

When fully endowed with these mudrās and properly applied to the fire-mantra,

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, there exists a most supreme secret of yours, consisting of the characteristics of the root mudrā together with its retinue; it is to be employed in all rites, bestows all prosperity, is fruitful, follows after all mantras, and accomplishes the purpose of all activities.

Having formed a fist with the fingers interlocked,

*ṣṭhoṃ*.
O worthy ones, this is that heart named the Single Syllable (*ekākṣara*).

Of all those mundane and supramundane, of all beings—*kūṣmāṇḍas*, *pūtanās*, *kravyādas*, and so forth; of the constellations, planets, mothers (*mātṛs*), boys (*kumāras*), and girls (*kumārikās*); of humans, non-humans, and all those counted among the *vidyādharas*, sages (*ṛṣis*), and the like; of all sentient beings bound by the threads of karma across all realms of existence;

and of all beings, both those who have been liberated and those free from passion, whether they possess great supernatural powers or do not, who pacify the three defects and are submerged in the three muds.
For the benefit of all sentient beings, this single-syllable mantra becomes the heart-essence of them all;
it performs all rites,
and all mudrās should be bound.
While performing the recitation, the recitation should be performed with this very heart-mantra.
One will then be constantly sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas.

This [mantra] possesses great power and great benefits; it should be applied progressively for all rites, including those concerning mudrās, ritual vessels, maṇḍalas, and the accomplishment of painted cloth-scrolls (paṭas), for the sake of sentient beings.
It accomplishes everything that is desired by the practitioner in his mind.
From that, there are one hundred and eight mudrās.
One should first perform the uṣṇīṣa-mudrā for the Victor who wields the wheel;
after that, O supreme in the world, it is called the padma-mudrā.
The third is the Vajra-mudrā, which belongs to Vajrapāṇi;
the fourth is the Deity-mudrā, which one should designate as the Svastika.
The fifth, however, is said here to be the sword mudrā of the rākṣasas;
the sixth is proclaimed as the club mudrā of the yakṣas. (Mmk 36.8)
The seventh [mudrā] of the asuras is proclaimed as the vajra-fist;
the eighth is the trident mudrā (śūlamudrā), which is recited for all wrathful deities.
The ninth is proclaimed as the Puṣpa-mudrā for the yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs;
one should know the tenth to be Mudgara, and the supreme eleventh is the final one.
The twelfth is designated as the power of Kārttikeya;
for Mañjughoṣa, one should employ the well-known lotus.
This number thirteen has been taught by the sages who show the way to beings.
The fourteenth is the conch (śaṅkha), while the fifteenth is known as the kettledrum (bherī);
the sixteenth should be understood as the hand-drum (paṭaha), and the seventeenth is the great drum (dundubhi).
Likewise, eighteen is called "bound," nineteen is called "the instrument" (karaṇa),
and twenty is specified as "the axe" (paraśu) according to their numerical measure.
Likewise, a white umbrella is proclaimed as the crown (uṣṇīṣa);
the robe is designated as the bowl (pātra), and the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) is considered the supreme [emblem].
Compassion, loving-kindness, as well as wisdom, meditative concentration, and ethical discipline— likewise,
the sixfold set beginning with patience and generosity has been taught by the Leaders of the World.
For these six perfections have been proclaimed by the Buddhas through the hearing [of the teachings];
and thirty mudrās for the Wheel-turner (cakrin) have been proclaimed by the Foremost Ones of the World.
Of the one-syllabled Hero, the sovereign lord of mantras, the pervasive Lokeśvara, twenty-eight vidyās have been taught. Mmk_36.17(=“12“)
The goddess named Sitā, Mahāśvetā, as well as Paṇḍaravāsinī and Bhṛkuṭī— these goddesses are born from the hearts of the Buddhas.
The mudrā of Tārā is said to be the utpala;
the mudrā of the formidable Hayagrīva is known as the vaktra.
O Vajrapāṇi, likewise there are thirty-one mudrās;
all of them are his weapons, standing in various forms for battle.
The four great mudrās are also proclaimed within the maṇḍala of Māra; that which is designated as the trident of Rudra is [the fifth].
The rosary of Brahmā, the discus of Viṣṇu, and likewise [the trident] of Śiva,
and thereafter the staff of Yama, which is supreme.
All this— the mudrās of all the gods, all the lords of yakṣas and men, and likewise of all bhūtas— is based upon all sentient beings.
The supreme element exists in three ways for those with passion and those free from passion;
it pervades all the world in three ways, consisting of the stable and the moving.
For all those beings who speak of reality throughout the countless realms known as *dhātus*,
it is here said that there is but a single mudrā for them all.
Thus, one hundred and eight [mantras] have been proclaimed;
their qualities, extent, and power are now described here.
Just as for humans there may be accomplishment joined with the application of mantras,
it is performed through other applications and adorned with the fingers.
Placed between the two hands, this supreme [mudrā] swiftly grants wealth;
I shall first explain it for you—listen, O you who desire prosperity!
First of all, in a clean place, wearing white garments and pure clothing,
practicing pure conduct, and remaining devotedly in a clean place,
one should stand facing east in front of a stūpa and perform the binding [of the mantra].
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who practices cruel deeds;
it should be given to one who grants fearlessness and has entered into the samaya.
To one who is devoted to the sons of the Victors and to the teaching of the Buddhas,
even if they have not yet generated the [awakening] mind, the perfection of the mudrās is not to be withheld.
One should always offer [this] to the devoted sons of the Conquerors, the wise Bodhisattvas, and to the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who have been honored.
The teacher, always highly esteemed, is firmly established in the conduct of awakening;
he is always preeminent in the application of all mantras.
Therefore, the mudrā should then be given to the disciple who is free from doubt.
Likewise, the preceptor should be one who knows the application of mantras, pure, skillful, and of noble lineage; he should be righteous, wise, consecrated, and have seen the maṇḍala.
The mantras have been thus demonstrated; the disciple who knows the tantra should be accepted.
The disciple must likewise show love for the guru as he does for the Buddha;
otherwise, there will never be success with the mantras or with any of the mudrās.
First, having become pure and facing the east, one should rub the hands with white sandalwood;
first of all, the Samaya-mudrā must be bound—
the mudrā of the Blessed One’s Uṣṇīṣa.
Both hands, with palms joined in the *añjali* gesture, slightly hollowed, slightly bent, and shaped like buds— though not yet fully opened lotuses—
this is the *samaya-mudrā* of the Blessed Buddha.
Those same hands, extended and held in a hollowed position, with the form of a blooming lotus, is the *mudrā* of Avalokita.
Having encircled both hands as before, one should press down with the little fingers positioned inside, over the index fingers.
This is the *utpala* mudrā of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Contracting those same two little fingers as before, one should display the form of a lotus bud with the index fingers joined with the thumbs while remaining in that very position.
This is the mudrā of Tārā for all limbs;
contracting that very same [mudrā] and forming the shape of eyes,
this is the mudrā of Ārya-Bhṛkuṭī.
One should apply that very same [mudrā] to the forehead;
this is the Eye Mudrā of the Goddess.
Again, contracting those two [thumbs] with the middle fingers and forming the shape of a pair of tongs, one should place it above the head.
This is the single-syllable great seal (mahāmudrā) of the Blessed One, the Wheel-Turning King, which performs all rites.
One should place that same [seal] on the forehead; it is the heart seal (hṛdayamudrā) of the Blessed Buddha.
One should place it on the eyes.
That very same [gesture] is the eye-mudrā of the Cakravartin;
one should place that very same [gesture] upon the face.
That very same [gesture] is the face-mudrā of the Vidyādhipati Cakravartin Ekākṣara.

In this manner, up to the mantra-practitioner’s arms, knees, shanks, feet, and so forth, there are twenty types of mudrās; eight of these are great mudrās (mahāmudrā) that should be employed in all ritual activities.
That same hollowed palm gesture is formed by curling the middle fingers and making the little fingers into needles, with both thumbs positioned like the awns of barley at their tips.
With the index fingers extended like needles, both hands are hollowed out, made fleshless, with the ends bent inward and well-positioned;
this is the Great Mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma (Dharmacakra-mahāmudrā) of the Blessed Ones.
That same [mudrā], with the thumbs bent inward and the middle fingers extended, [is the next].
This is the seal of the Buddhas for the defeat of the four Māras.
One should display that very same seal placed upon the head;
it is the Great Seal named "The Destroyer of All Afflictions of All Buddhas."
One should place that very [mudrā] on the forehead;
this is the mudrā of all Buddhas called Mahākaruṇā.
Having placed that same [mudrā] on the heart,
The Great Seal named "Extraction of the Arrow of All Views":
one should place both hands in that very same seal.
The Great Seal named "Accomplishment of All Vidyās."
One should place that same mudrā upon the neck;
this is the Great Mudrā named "The Pacifier of All Misfortunes.
One should rotate that same mudrā in every direction.
The Great Seal named "Accomplishing the Purpose of Great Protection" is as follows:
in this manner, there are eight great seals that accomplish all purposes;
they are the seals of the Jayoṣṇīṣa.
That same gesture, with the sprout-like hands extended from the left hand and tilted toward the right,
is the seal of the white parasol (*sitātapatra*).
Those same hands, likewise placed upon the head, are the seal of the Blessed One’s *jayoṣṇīṣa*.
Joining both palms together and placing them upon the head in the shape of a *uṣṇīṣa* is the *mudrā* of the Blessed One Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa.
One should then open that same *mudrā*;
this is the great *mudrā* of Jvālāmālinoṣṇīṣa, which accomplishes all rites and should be employed in all activities during all fears.
One should place that very same mudrā upon the chest;
this is the great mudrā of all uṣṇīṣas.
With those same hands, having remained interlaced and very firm, this is the great armor mudrā (mahākavacamudrā) of all Tathāgatas, which should be employed against all obstacles.
Placing those very two hands with their tips joined in the shape of a book at the center of the chest—
this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the mother of all Buddhas;
one should display it to all sentient beings.
It pacifies all obstacles and all misfortunes;
it accomplishes all goals;
and it produces mindfulness.
Placing those very hands upon the forehead is the Dharma Mahāmudrā, the consecration of all Buddhas;
it should be employed in all consecrations for all sentient beings.
One should place those very hands upon the forehead in a variegated form;
this is the Great Mudrā named "The Dispeller of All Māras.

Those same hands, with fingers drawn together and interlocked, are positioned in the shape of a needle; the middle fingers are extended, forming the mark of a needle, and the pair of thumbs are pressed against them.
This is the great seal (mahāmudrā) of the Blessed One’s Mass of Radiance (tejorāśi). Placing that same seal above the head, this is another great seal of the Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa-Mass of Radiance.
Placing both hands on the forehead in that very same manner, this is the Blessed One’s third seal, the Eye-seal (netramudrā).

Those same two hands, made beautiful on both sides, placed one above the other for the sake of offering, or positioned in the form of a hollowed cup with the left hand, with the thumbs and little fingers of each entwined around one another—
this is the fundamental mudrā of the Great Vajra Seat of all Buddhas. Those same hands, shown at the crown of the head, is the mudrā of the root of the Great Bodhi Tree.

That same [mudrā], with the hands joined together and turned back, is called the mudrā named "Destroyer of All Māras of All Buddhas. That same [mudrā], with the hands interlocked, one should place them at the neck;
it is called the mudrā named "Subjugator of All Bhūtas."
One should hold that very same [mudrā] at the throat;
this is the Great Mudrā named Sarvabhūtavilokanī (Beholder of All Beings).
One should place that very same [mudrā] upon the knees.
The Great Seal named Purifier of All Evil Destinies:
one should throw that very same [hand] upward.
The Great Seal named Accumulation of the Arising of All Deities.
Those same two hands, both in the gesture of granting fearlessness, are the great mudrā named Śani, which has the domain of all enjoyments.
Placing those same hands in the form of añjali at the crown of the head is the great mudrā named Sarvabuddhakṣetrākramaṇī (Traversing All Buddha-fields).
Placing both hands in that same manner against the ears with palms open is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Sarvanāgadamanī.
Keeping both hands in that same manner, one should form a hollowed cup and hold it at the tip of the nose.
The Great Seal named the Object of Support of All Buddhas:
one should place that very seal upon the crown of the head.
This is the Great Seal named the Uṣṇīṣa Exalted Above All Buddhas.
In this manner, there are innumerable mudrās of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas.

By means of the innumerable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, there is an innumerable lineage of Cakravartins and innumerable Cakravartins. Their sovereign is the Single-Syllable Cakravartin, the Lord of Mantras; and there are innumerable Kings of the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas, and innumerable extensive ritual manuals (*kalpavisara*) among all mantras.
Their mudrās will be explained in brief; here, there is but one heart-mantra for all of them, the single-syllable Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
Its root-mudrā is described right here among the mantras, which are taught to possess great power and immeasurable majesty;
by the mere binding of which, all mantras become manifest.

All the Blessed Buddhas bestow accomplishment and grant their empowerment to the practitioner of the vidyā. Merely by recollecting the Lord of Mantras, the single-syllabled and peerless one, he becomes one who has acquired the roots of merit of ten billion buddhas.
Even for one who has committed the four root downfalls, that karma which would lead to birth in the great hells is exhausted merely through recollection.
What need is there to mention the recitation?
Even the five deeds of immediate retribution go to destruction;

what need is there to mention other unwholesome acts? Therefore, with every effort, this sovereign king of vidyās, the Single Syllable, should be remembered, recited, meditated upon, kept in mind, and worshipped.
One should constantly propitiate him.
Homage to all Buddhas!
Bhrūṃ!
Friends, this is the root mantra of all the *uṣṇīṣas* spoken by the Tathāgata.

By means of this very sovereign of mantras, the *Uṣṇīṣacakravartin*, which is born from the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, one should perform all rites. When accompanied by its mudrā, it is certain to succeed in all worldly and transcendent mantras throughout the extensive ritual manuals (*kalpavisara*).
And here is the mudrā:

one should hold the two hands in the shape of a hollowed casket, with the middle fingers extended, the tips of all the fingers remaining inside, in the form of a coiled ring, slightly tilted upward, and shaped like a *uṣṇīṣa* above the head.
This is the Great Root Mudrā for the One-Syllable Universal Monarch (*Ekākṣaracakravartin*).
By means of this, one should perform all rites;
it should be employed in the supreme sādhanas and so forth.
It should be employed for the sake of all protection, concealment, and guardianship.
One who employs it for minor accomplishments and the like becomes ignorant of the ritual timing (*asamayajña*),
and for such a mantra-teacher, the mantras will not succeed.
Except for the purpose of providing protection,

for the sake of pacification, and for the purpose of exhausting evil karma, it should be recited constantly in a pure place— on mountains, at rivers, streams, or the banks of oceans— but it should not be recited in other locations, because this King of Vidyās possesses great power and must not be recited in other places.
One should recite [the mantra] with a mind exalted by its power, pervading all sentient beings with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
And here is the mudrā:
having formed the two hands in the shape of a hollowed cup (*karasaṃpuṭa*), one should slightly bend the middle fingers at their third joint using the individual fingers.
One should form the shape of a *uṣṇīṣa*.
This is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed One, the King of the *Uṣṇīṣas*.
Having joined the two hands together in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*), one should slightly incline them downward; this is the third great seal of the Blessed One’s *uṣṇīṣa*.
Oṃ godare vīra svāhā!
This is the heart-mantra of all the Tathāgatas; it performs all activities, accomplishes all aims, and wards off all misfortunes. By merely remembering this, one becomes empowered by all the Buddhas.
One is liberated from all evils;
one stands above all mantras;
and one should be regarded as the Buddha himself in person.
It should be employed together with this mudrā;
it performs all rites even more swiftly.
While this is being recited, all mantras become as if recited.
In whatever manner one applies oneself, in that very manner one performs the rites;
by the will of the reciter, it becomes effective for all rites.
One should hold those same hands, positioned in the hollowed-palm gesture (*karasaṃpuṭa*), over the head in the shape of a triple-pronged pin (*trisūcī*).
This is the second heart-seal (hṛdayamudrā) of all the Blessed Buddhas. And the mantra for this is:
oṃ gerure vīra svāhā.
This is the heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā) of all the Blessed Buddhas;
it performs all activities, wards off all misfortunes, accomplishes all goals, possesses great power, and is to be practiced in all mantra-rituals.
No doubt should be entertained in this regard.
"In whatever manner it is applied, in that very manner it is accomplished.

Furthermore, with those same hands placed in the hollowed-cup (sampuṭa) gesture, one should firmly encircle them with the inner fingers, extend both index fingers, slightly bend them, and place them above the head; this is the great mudrā of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas.
And there is a mantra for this: Oṃ ṭrāṃ bandha svāhā.
This is the root mantra of all uṣṇīṣas; it performs all rites and should be employed in all bindings, directing [the power] from every direction.
And one performs all ritual actions:

during the time of accomplishment and recitation, in fire offerings (*homa*) and so forth, whether for one’s own protection or the protection of others; and regarding all substances and all mantra-rituals—whether mundane or supramundane—that have been taught, protection must be performed entirely by means of this alone.
Great protection is thereby established;
it should be employed with all mantras,
and it succeeds in all ritual actions.

The chapters on the vehicles and the means of accomplishment, as well as the mudrās and mantras, for all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas— the great sovereign wheel-turners and lords of vidyās, such as Tejorāśi, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, and others— all these should be applied in their entirety and in detail; likewise,
all the extensive chapters on the arrays of mantras and tantras, both mundane and supramundane, and infinite mudrās.
And there are mantras for this occasion: *Oṃ jvalitogradeha vibhinda hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the supreme heart-mantra of the Blessed One, the Buddha Tejorāśi; it is to be employed in all rites, in every way, and for all purposes among all mantras.

That very same [mudrā] is formed when the two hands are joined together, the middle fingers are extended, and the index fingers encircle them in the shape of a bracelet, forming a noose; both [hands] are made into the full expanse of a maṇḍala.
This is the Khaṅkhara mudrā of the Blessed Buddha, and here is the mantra:

Oṃ dhuna jitāraṇa hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Khaṅkharaka mudrā of the Blessed Buddhas; it should be employed in all rites. It awakens all mantras according to one’s desire, brings all spirits under control, provides consolation to all sentient beings, invigorates all substances, and is the subduer of all evils.
It is a complete dryer.
Just as this eight-syllable mantra of the Tathāgata is applied, so too does it accomplish all ritual actions (*sarvakarmāṇi*).
Having formed the hands into a hollowed vessel-like shape by curling them inward...
This is the bowl-mudrā of all the Tathāgatas; it should be understood as the "Tathāgata’s Bowl.
One should hold it at the region of the navel, for it becomes capable of performing all rites.
And here there is a mantra:
Oṃ, empowered by the world-protectors, hold, hold, maintain, O you of great majesty, the bowl of the Buddhas! Svāhā!
This is the mantra of the seal of the Tathāgata’s bowl for the Blessed Buddhas; when joined with this, it shall be capable of accomplishing all activities.
It performs a variety of actions honored for their greatness and their course;
it accomplishes all rites spoken of in all mantras.
By the desire of the practitioner, it acts swiftly here—of this there is no doubt.
Those mantras belonging to the Tathāgatas, and those also belonging to Avalokiteśvara,
as well as the preeminent mantras called Vajra, which are worshipped by various deities;
They all attain accomplishment when united with the vessel of the Buddha.
Indeed, there are various groups of foremost female messengers, as well as groups of male and female servants;
and there are the leaders of various attendants, including yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kaśmalas.
Likewise, there were female messengers who carry out all commands and perform all tasks for the various eminent kings born from the lineages of gods and gandharvas.
The mantras [were mastered] by the accomplished vidyādharas, as were the world-protectors of great supernatural power,
and by the foremost gods, such as Śakra and others, headed by Brahmā, who are wise.
Whatever mantras there may be that are spoken by Kinnaras and Garuḍas, as well as those of great supernatural power (maharddhika),
they all attain accomplishment when uttered from the vessel of the Buddha.
It has drawn forth all mantras, relying upon their movement and form;
it is brought under control by the King of Mantras, the Master, the Lord, the most excellent one of great splendor,
and is pointed out as the foremost of all mantras by those who perceive reality.
That mantra, residing within a worthy vessel, is like a wish-fulfilling gem in three ways;
it performs a variety of actions according to the desired wish of the practitioner.
It produces a greatness of diverse qualities and a supreme excellence of power;
it performs miraculous feats difficult to surpass, which cannot be overcome by any other mantra-practitioners.
Even one who is unworthy becomes worthy when abiding in the mantra described by the Best of Sages.
The vessel, when empowered by mantras and endowed with mudrās,
brings about a manifold expansion of qualities arising from ritual action.

It shall destroy all diseases from every side and bring about abundant enjoyments for the beings belonging to the three births— the gods, daityas, and lords of men. When employed in all rites, it shall swiftly bring about prosperity.
Thus it is said.
One should place those very hands, formed into the shape of hollowed palms and bound with various beautiful braids, upon the region of the forehead.
This is the Citrahasta; it is the great mudrā of the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇiratna) of the Blessed Buddhas.
And here is the mantra:
Homage to all Buddhas! Oṃ, blazing with splendor, accomplisher of all aims, succeed, succeed, O wish-fulfilling jewel of accomplishment, hūṃ!
This mantra of the wish-fulfilling jewel accomplishes all aims;
it shall accomplish desired objects and also the mantras in their full detail.
It brings about the greatness of one's virtues and accomplishes even that which is intended;
it also makes the prosperity described in the well-spoken mantras and tantras bear fruit.
One should accomplish the ultimate goal, which is likewise fixed upon Buddhahood; thus,
by one's own will, the hand was placed in action and so produced.
I shall accomplish all the various forms of prosperity, whose fruits arise immediately through ritual activity,
and which have been mastered by myself for all mantras and tantras.
Furthermore, [one may attain] the state of a deity, or the state of Śakra, or even the embodied state of Brahmā;
likewise, the beautiful forms of those belonging to the Ābhāsvara realm who possess similar bodies.
"Through this practice, one attains a physical form consisting mostly of gods—the foremost of gods, the best of gods, the Bṛhatphala, and the Akaniṣṭha. // Mmk_36.52(=“47”) //
For contemplation is said to be the foremost of mental activities, providing an extensive exposition of the meaning of the mantras;
it is abundant among the mudrās and accomplishes the goals of the dharma for one’s destiny.
The accomplishment of the meaning of all phenomena, the realization of the purpose of all mantras,
for the sake of all qualities and enlightenment, having its basis in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This which has been taught in the form of mantra, honored by Ratna and Cintāgra, one shall especially attain;
indeed, one shall obtain the support of the very forms of heaven.
Through its practice, one shall attain heaven and the extensive goal of the meaning of the mantra.
In that same manner, both hands are placed over the shoulders, with the right and left held up halfway; they are interlocked, grasping one another, with the bases of the palms well-joined.
This is the *cīvara-mudrā* of all Buddhas. And here is the mantra for this occasion:
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa! May all the Buddhas empower my robe, svāhā! This is the mantra for the robe. Having consecrated one's own robe with this, one should put it on.
He becomes invincible to all beings.
A consecrated Kṣatriya great king, acting as a bringer of confidence to all, should empower his own garment with this mantra seven times and enter the battle;
upon seeing him, all enemies will be paralyzed.
Or they turn back;
and all beings, upon merely seeing him, become submissive.
His pride and arrogance are gone, and no weapon falls upon his body.
Furthermore, he has no fear of humans or non-humans;
neither poison nor fire falls upon his body,
and he has no fear of disease.
Nor does he have fear of untimely death;
nor is he slain by a hostile army;
nor is he harmed by *ḍākinīs*, *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *gandharvas*, or by various hosts of spirits who steal away vitality.

Indeed, it is impossible for those with fierce minds, flesh-eaters, or any carnivorous beings who are harmful, who torment other sentient beings, or who engage in evil deeds— including kings— to cause harm or inflict injury [upon this person]. How much less could they— without such protection— break through all ritual actions and substances, or deprive them of life?

Indeed, there exists no sentient being, nor any class of sentient beings, nor mantra, nor mudrā, nor poison—whether stationary or moving—nor weapon, nor various implements of attack; nor rākṣasa or rākṣasī, yakṣa or yakṣī, yakṣa elder or yakṣa elderess, yakṣa attendant or yakṣa attendantess—[this applies] to all sentient beings; the same should be expanded in detail by way of analogy.
This is impossible: therefore,

by means of the Tathāgata’s seal, robe-mantra, and the performance of protection, or merely through recitation or remembrance, no one else has the power to break it— not even by the mantras of the Tathāgatas or by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Except by the will of that very practitioner.

Thus, this mantra possesses great power; it accomplishes all rites, fulfills all aims, destroys all malevolent beings, is endowed with all auspiciousness, completes all objectives, purifies all miserable rebirths, eradicates all afflictions, and brings the qualities of a Buddha to perfection.

In that same manner, with the hands as before, one should bend the middle fingers downward, place the tips of the ring fingers [upon them], curve the thumbs, keep the thumbs separated at the third joint, bend the little fingers, and having formed two wheels complete with spokes and hubs, one should place them at the position of the head.
This is the Dharmacakra-mudrā of all the Buddhas. And here is the mantra: Oṃ chinda chinda hana hana daha daha dīptacakra hūṃ.
This is that mantra of the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas;
it destroys all afflictions, cuts off all means of falling into the miserable states of existence,
and kindles all the qualities of a Buddha.
It illuminates the darkness of all afflictions,
dispels all sufferings,
and accomplishes all karmas.
It liberates from all sufferings and illuminates all substances.
This Blessed One, the Wheel of Dharma, [neutralizes] the mantras taught by wicked beings who perform supreme sorcery and take the lives of living creatures.

Whether they are harmful, fierce, or in a state of transformation, he cuts them, splits them, cooks them, dries them up, and eradicates them according to the wish of the practitioner; he uproots them, liberates them, and establishes them in their proper place.
In whatever way this Blessed One is applied, in that very way he performs the rites—except for malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*) and those associated with sensual desire.
It should be employed in all rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings in every respect, it should be employed with great protection (*mahārakṣā*) and so forth.

In all accomplishments (*sādhana*), whether mundane or supramundane, in all rites—whether of pacification or enrichment—as well as in all mantras, mudrās, and rituals described in the *kalpas*, great protection must be employed by means of this very [mantra].

With that same [posture], one should brandish the two hands, the right hand raised with its fingers pointing upward and the left hand threatening with the index finger; the corners of the mouth should be slightly bared with the teeth clenched, the left foot placed upon the knees, and the right foot extended and slightly lowered while remaining seated. This is the Mahāmudrā of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā.
And there is a mantra for this: Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā!
This is the Aparājitā mantra of all the Buddhas, which destroys all Māras.
It pacifies all obstacles and increases longevity and health.
It is the most excellent among all mantras for the performance of protective rites,
and it is supreme for generating good fortune in men, women, and youths.
Humans and non-humans, as well as others with the minds of wicked beings—
rākṣasas, uṣṭārakas, pretas, skandas, apasmāras, and guhyakas.
The hosts of *mātṛ*, *bhūta*, and *graha* spirits, as well as those produced by *yoga* and mantras;
pains, afflictions, and diseases arising from various humors (*dhātu*).
Snakes, mice, spiders, insects,
and boils shall not afflict the body, except as a result of past karma.
In disputes concerning travel, and in the face of kings, thieves, water, or fire, one shall obtain victory, security, auspiciousness, and peace; of this there is no doubt.
Having written it on birch bark, or on cloth, or elsewhere,
one should carry it on the head, or on the neck, or on the waist, or on the arm, or in the hand.
Whoever, having tied a cloth-binding and a topknot-binding, shall constantly wear a garland of knots, for him there will be well-being.
Whoever recites this upon rising in the morning and while falling asleep,
having passed away in happiness, will remember seven lifetimes.
Possessing a beautiful form and perfected in ethical conduct, with a mouth fragrant as a blue lotus,
he will be beloved and his words will be accepted in birth after birth.
And here there are effective mantra-words known as mantras which accomplish the purpose as stated: namely—
bhañjane stambhane dhā dhā dhā dhatsa yā yā yā yate hā hā hā hate parakaraṇi vīryevīrye guṇatejabhūtakari bhadrakari raudrakari kumbhavati viṣakumbhavati sarvabale bhūtabale.
Protect, protect me from all poisons and from all obstacles! Namely:
Siddhakari, Siddhārthe, Siddhamanorathe, Siddhakārye, Phuru, Nurūpe, Svaste, Praśaste, Siddhi, Siddhārthe, Dhairyavati, Samane, Tapane, Śaraṇe, Bhadre, Bhavati, Śānte.
O Dānta Śiva, perform the *hūṃ* [mantra]; provide complete protection, provide total acceptance,
and provide thorough guardianship.
Bring peace, bring auspiciousness, and grant protection to me and to all sentient beings, svāhā!
This is the heart-mantra of Aparājitā;
it is the root-vidyā.
The practitioner must necessarily be intent upon the side of wholesome qualities.
It should be recited three times a day;
or even better, one should have it read from a book once, for this alone constitutes a virtuous practice.
Furthermore, there is a subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) here: *Namaḥ saptānāṃ samyaksambuddhānāṃ saśrāvakasaṅghānāṃ sarvavairabhayātītānām*.
Vipaśyin by his splendor and supernatural power, Śikhin likewise,
Viśvabhū by his wisdom, and Krakucchanda by his strength.
Through the training of Kanakamuni, through the virtues of Kāśyapa,
and through the heroic power of Śākyasiṃha, may there always be auspiciousness for me.
Namely: *Jaye vijaye aparājite mārasainyapramardanīye svāhā!
Sarvārthasādhanīye svāhā!* This Blessed Lady, the accomplisher of all aims, however she is employed, [accomplishes them].
In such and such a manner one performs the ritual actions;
she should be employed in all protective rites,
and must certainly be brought to mind by the practitioner.
It destroys all obstacles,
disperses all the deeds of Māra,
and brings all mantras to manifestation.
One fulfills all the qualities of a Buddha;
one attracts all mantras, both mundane and supramundane;
and one perfects that which is deficient or excessive.
It fulfills all hopes,
wards off all malevolent beings,
and, in short, accomplishes everything according to the desire of the practitioner.
At the time of death, he grants him a vision face-to-face;
he dries up all miserable states and evil destinies;
and through constant recitation, he exhausts the five deeds of immediate retribution.
It attenuates even all four root downfalls;
by mere recollection and through recitation alone, it uproots them.
It establishes one in rebirth among all the gods and among humans.
She directs one toward all the practices of a bodhisattva and brings all the qualities of a Buddha to fulfillment.
Thus, O Blessed Lady, you possess immeasurable virtues and benefits, great power, and are uttered from the mouths of all Buddhas for the destruction of all Māras.
It has been spoken by all the Tathāgatas as that which dries up all afflictions; it is unimpeded in all activities and should be applied for the sake of all protection, shielding, and guarding.
This is the thunderous roar of all the Buddhas; this is the Great Lion’s Roar.
This is the basis for all conduct;
this is the enlightenment of all Buddhas;
this is the natural outflow of the great samādhi.
This is the supernatural power of the great miracle;
this is the state of surpassing all;
this is the state of universal peace.
This is the abode of all Buddhas; this is the state of nirvāṇa;
this is the state of auspiciousness.
This is the word of the ineffable; this is the word of the limit of reality;
this is the word of the nature of non-existence.
That is to say, the mantra-word is the word for the empowerment of all Buddhas.
One should place that very [mantra] on the forehead with both hands joined in the hollowed-palm gesture (*karasampuṭa*), with the middle fingers of both hands pointing upward.
This is the second mudrā of Aparājitā; when applied together with the root mantra, it fulfills all hopes and accomplishes all rites.
Placed at the location of the heart and conjoined with the heart-mantra, it destroys all demons and annihilates all states of misfortune and miserable rebirths.
This is the third heart-seal of the Blessed One Aparājitā:
the same hands as before, hanging down from the region of the navel with the palms turned downward.

This is the fourth subsidiary heart-seal (upahṛdayamudrā) of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā. With the heart-mantra, it performs all rites; it is esteemed as all auspicious things, and it provides all peace and well-being.
Having consecrated water with mantras, this bathing brings about supreme good fortune, removes misfortune, generates prosperity, and bestows glory and success.
One should place those very hands at the region of the face;
this is another great mudrā of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā, and it is the fifth.
In this manner, there are thus incalculable mudrās,
and they are to be employed among all the *parājita* mantras.
That very same hand is cast out to the right, slightly clenched into a fist and pressed against it by the left hand, which is held in a firm fist.
This is the Great Power Mudrā of all the Buddhas.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayine phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ svāhā.
This Tathāgata Power Mantra should be employed against all wicked beings.
And when great dangers have arisen, whether in a village or elsewhere, this mudrā should be employed in all rites.

During afflictions caused by planets and constellations, and for those seized by any vetāḍa-graha, as well as those possessed by any yakṣa, rākṣasa, piśāca, marut-graha, brahmarākṣasa, and so forth—the mantras should be recited while binding the mudrā;
[the victim] will be liberated at that very moment.
And it should be employed at the entrances to all great cremation grounds;
all obstacles will flee, they will run away, and they will cease to exist entirely in every way.
In this manner, one accomplishes various individual great powers of mantra and tantra that manifest in diverse ways for all ritual purposes;
it provides complete protection, shielding, and concealment,
and is a purifier that destroys all demons while increasing longevity and health.

That very same [mudrā], with both hands joined in the hollow of the palms, the middle fingers slightly bent, the little fingers encircled by the ring fingers, and the two thumbs pressed against the eyes in the shape of eyes—this is the Tathāgata-locana-mahāmudrā of the Blessed Buddhas.
Displayed in the region of the eyes, it possesses the measure of the supreme qualities of all Tathāgatas; it is the mother who gives birth to all Tathāgatas and to all vidyās.
She is the one who brings forth light, who fulfills all aims, who purifies all wrong views, who generates right view in all sentient beings,

the mother of the family of all Tathāgatas, the sustainer of the families of all mantra lineages, the fulfiller of all mundane and supramundane mantras, the fulfiller of all purposes, and the one who provides consolation.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha Siddhalocane Sarvārthasādhani svāhā!
This is the Great Vidyā of Tathāgatalocanā:
Vacana vacana vacana oṃ Buddhalocane svāhā!
This is that *vidyā* of Vajrapāṇi, which performs all rites for him.

Forming the hands in the shape of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*) as before, the middle fingers are bent downward, the tips of the little fingers are extended and slightly bent, both thumbs are encircled by the index fingers,
and the ring fingers are joined and slightly curved.
This is the ūrṇā-mudrā of the Blessed One and of all Buddhas. One should place both hands with their tips joined at the region of the forehead;
this is the ūrṇā-mudrā of all Tathāgatas.
With those same hands, having formed two loops at the tips of both [fingers], one should place them in the region of the forehead in the shape of a circle;
this is the third, the Urṇāmaṇi-jewel mudrā. With those same hands, both being bent inward, the little fingers are entwined and both thumbs are joined together.
This is the fourth, the Ūrṇā-mudrā. Bending the thumbs in that same manner, one should display them in the shape of a tuft at the forehead; this is the Tathāgata-ūrṇā of all the Tathāgatas.
These five great mudrās are equal in power, equal in majesty, and are effective for all ritual actions.
And here is the mantra for all of them: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatānībhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ / He he bandha bandha tiṣṭha tiṣṭha dhāraya dhāraya nirundha nirundhorṇāmaṇi svāhā*.
This blessed mantra accomplishes all activities for all *ūrṇāmaṇi* mudrās.
This is the Tathāgata-ūrṇā-mudrā, which is unimpeded in all rites and should be employed in every application.
Having made a tilaka with gorocana while reciting the mantra, one should enter the battle with the Tathāgata-ūrṇā;
all enemies will be paralyzed.
Upon seeing him, they flee;
their anger subsides,
and all sentient beings become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit, finding complete relief.
Having seen him, all flesh-eaters and the like are rendered powerless once he has applied the *rocanā* tilaka.
Having seen that Great King, that Great Being, of great renown and great energy, they behold him as if blazing with light.
All those who are wicked and malicious—whether yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, all grahas, bhūtas, or kaśmalas—even those with fierce minds become possessed of loving-kindness (*maitra*).
They depart from that place,
and one is liberated from all calamities and afflictions.

For those seized by all types of *grahas*, by all *mātṛkā* spirits and child-seizing demons, or by *brahmarākṣasas* and the like, one should empower yellow orpiment with mantras, apply it as a mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead, and show it [to them].
As soon as they see him, they all release [their grip], flee, and run away;
in every way, they no longer belong to him and do not take hold of him again.
Even if they were to take hold of him, [they would not remain].
They are destroyed entirely in every way.

This same method should be applied to all planetary seizures (*graha*).
