Whatever various [rites] are described in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of all mantras and tantras—whether mundane or supramundane—such as the prescriptions for maṇḍalas and the accomplishment of cloth-paintings (*paṭa*), those are to be accomplished by this very means.
They are accomplished more swiftly.
Having consecrated *gorocana* with mantras and applied it as a tilaka, one may enter into the midst of enemies;
they will become free from anger.
They cannot be overcome.
One should enter into the midst of a great multitude while reciting [the mantra];
all will become filled with loving-kindness.
One’s speech becomes authoritative;
one cannot be overcome by others and is invincible among all beings everywhere.
Having empowered yellow orpiment with this mantra seven times and applied it as a tilaka mark, one should enter a great cremation ground.
All flesh-eaters flee,
all grahas and mātṛs perish,
and one becomes invincible.
Seeing him as if blazing with the splendor of all human beings, those who steal vitality (ojas) flee from that place;
they do not even grant him their sight,
let alone steal his vitality.
Not even for a moment do they remain unestablished;
having abandoned the great cremation ground, all the hosts of spirits who dwell there depart,
moving here and there so that they cannot even be looked upon.
How much less, then, could anyone take away its vital energy or harm it?
Thus, this Great Vidyā named Tathāgatorṇa—which possesses great majesty and great supernatural power—remains present.
It has been spoken by incalculable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it has been spoken and also rejoiced in.
It has been spoken and approved by Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One;
those who will be the Perfectly Awakened Ones in future times will also speak it.
Thus, having been extolled, praised, and approved by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past and the future, it is now likewise approved by me.
It has been praised, extolled, and authorized by Śākyamuni, and it will accomplish all things for all sentient beings according to the prescribed rites.
In whatever way it is applied, it performs all activities—
excepting those that are malevolent or associated with sensual desire.
Having formed the two hands in the shape of a hollowed casket and having intertwined them so as to be variegated, one should place them at the center of one's chest;
this is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed One Samādhivajra.
By binding it, one becomes irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
It remains fixed.
And here is the mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām / oṃ vibhide cūrṇaya cūrṇaya vajradhika vajradhika hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ jaḥ samādhijaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Though this is brief, it should be applied in its entirety;
it possesses immeasurable benefits.
This Blessed One, Samādhivajra, is the [essence] of all Buddhas.
One should place that very mudrā at the region of the throat;
this is the lotus-lotus mudrā of all the Buddhas.
One should place this same [mudrā] on the left side.
The utpala mudrā: one should place this very same [mudrā] on the right arm.
This is the mudrā of the Blessed Buddha’s compassionate focus and loving-kindness.

With the same hands, the fingers of both hands are interlaced and the middle fingers are extended, forming the shape of a full circle; this, placed at the center of the heart, is the second Maitrī-mudrā.
It performs all activities for all Tathāgatas.
Unobstructed;
likewise, by this very same method, the third [syllable] is on the forehead,
and the fourth is placed above.
When rotated all around, it becomes the fifth, the Maitrī-mudrā;
it should be employed at the time of meditative concentration upon an object,
and then no humans will cause harm.
Neither humans nor non-humans—nor any yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth—can produce any affliction in his body.
And all Māras, though they perform their demonic deeds, find themselves thwarted; and all obstacles become non-obstacles.
And there is a mantra for this occasion: *Oṃ prasphura prasphura kṛtālambanamantrātmaka hāṃ*.
This loving-kindness (*maitrī*) of the Blessed One should be employed.
Having entwined the two hands with one another and formed them into the shape of a braid (*veṇikā*), one should position them over the maṇḍala.
One should place the two index fingers upright at the region of the forehead;
this is the seal of the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Blessed Buddha.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ viśve svāhā*.
It is effective for all activities;
it should be applied to sentient beings,
and they become compassionate in nature.
That very same [mudrā], when the hands are joined at the forehead and positioned in the fearless gesture (*abhaya*), is the Great Sealed Gesture (*mahāmudritā*) of the Blessed Buddha.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ munimuni gagana svāhā*.
This Blessed Lady accomplishes all rites; she fulfills them all when applied with a joyful mind.
She performs everything;
she accomplishes without exception all those rites found in all mantra-rituals, whether mundane or supramundane.

Placing both thumbs upon the fingers of the hands and forming them into a variegated shape, one should display this at the forehead; this is the Blessed One’s Tathāgata-prekṣā mudrā, which performs all rites and accomplishes all aims.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ mahadgate upekṣaya sarvadharmān viśvātmane viśvamūrti jvala jvalaya sarvabuddhadharmān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Furthermore, there are six mudrās for the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Those same hands, with the gestures of granting boons,
constitute this Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Those same hands, slightly contracted from each other, are placed at the region of the navel.
This is the Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Keeping the hands in that same position but lowering them and placing them against the sides of the armpits—this is the Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
One should place the hands in that same manner above the upper arms.
Being perceived through a distorted form, this is the Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

Having formed the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) with those very hands, one should place them above, binding the left over the right; and while seated in the cross-legged posture, one should maintain a gaze directed toward the object of meditation (*dhyānālambana*) out of compassion for all sentient beings.

This is the mahāmudrā of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). That same seal of the perfection of meditative concentration, without breaking the cross-legged posture, takes the form of teaching the Dharma;
this is the mahāmudrā of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One should break that very cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*).
Placing the left hand upon the lap and letting the right hand hang down, one should touch the ground in the form of the vajra-seat (*vajrāsana*).
This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas for their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; this indeed is the Great Seal of all Buddha-dharmas.
The mantras for all [the perfections] are as follows: Oṃ dāne dada dada dadāpaya jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite huṃ huṃ jaḥ svāhā.
This is the great mudrā of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Oṃ śīla śīlāḍhye śāntikaraṇi śive praśaste sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā.
The Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline: *oṃ śānte śrīkari kṣānte kṣāntikari svāhā*.
This is [the mantra] of the Perfection of Forbearance.
*Oṃ vīrye vīryam iti sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā*.
Svāhā! To the nature of non-existence, svāhā!
To the one who treads with the vajra, svāhā!
This is the perfection of vigor.
Oṃ śāntikari dhūdhūdhūrdhari dhairye vīrye gagane ramaṇe dhyānavati svāhā!
This is the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Oṃ dhīḥ dhūḥ! This is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Oṃ! Protect me, O Blessed One, you who are honored by all Buddhas, you who are without objective support, whose nature is like space, who have entered the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and who create light! Dispel, dispel the darkness of all afflictions!
Dry them up! Deliver me!
O you who are formless! Huṃ huṃ! Destroy all karmic actions! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!

This Blessed Lady is the mantra of the great enlightenment of the Blessed Buddhas; she accomplishes all activities, fulfills all aims, and repels all misfortunes. She brings to perfection all the qualities of a Buddha, destroys all afflictions, and annihilates all mantras performed by others. She terrifies all Māras and perfects all mundane and supramundane mantras.
It dispels all evils, dries up all miserable rebirths, and establishes one among all gods and humans in all the qualities of a Buddha.
In brief, in whatever way it is applied, in that very way it performs its functions.

It is not possible, even in ten million eons, for countless Blessed Buddhas to fully describe or praise the greatness of her qualities, nor to speak of the manifestation of power, the transformations of conduct, the empowerment, and the acquisition of supernatural strength through her miraculous feats. Such is the miraculous display of this Bhagavatī, whose majesty consists of an infinite expansion of virtues; it is likewise impossible to detail even the six perfections in their entirety.

In brief, the power of teaching, conduct, and supernatural power (ṛddhi) should be understood everywhere as the conduct established in the lineage of qualities (guṇagotra), or even as the attainment of distinction.
Having the nature of space, one should employ the discourse on phenomena (dharma) which is free from the investigation of existence and non-existence,
for eons upon eons, in the accomplishment of activities.
The wise have declared it to be abundant, arising swiftly from the form of its fruit;
it is the meaning of the mantra whose nature is space, adorned by the manifestation of syllables.
When applied with proper method at the right time, they bear fruit in many ways;
thus has the mudrā-tantra been explained in detail by those who act according to reality.
The course of mantra and tantra, as well as time and the proper application of rules,
should be understood through recitation, fire offerings, and so forth, for the sake of attaining the fruit that arises from reality.
The movement of the substances is not for the sake of a support; it is well-characterized by its defining marks.
O Knower of Mantras, one's own mantra and the family-origins are the sources of equal arising.
For the time of accomplishment is indeed perceived through the arising of the signs of the mudrās.
Having reached the culmination of reality, the mantra-practitioner, composed in meditation, should recite the mantra;
the accomplishments shall reveal the family deity as the cause of success.
These excellent mudrās and the highly renowned mantras have been proclaimed;
when practiced according to the prescribed rite, they are accomplished according to one's heart's desire.
Thus [it is said].

That same [gesture], with the fingers interlaced and the right thumbs bent down and placed beneath the left thumbs, is the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; it is effective for all rites. And here is the mantra: *oṃ trailokyapūjitāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
They accomplish all rites and should be employed in all mandala rituals for the great protection and other purposes of all sentient beings.
In that same manner, both hands are joined with the tips of the fingers tucked inward, and the middle fingers are raised upward.
This is the root mudrā of all the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra: *oṃ da dadātu daṇḍa hūṃ*.
Oṃ sarvasattvāmṛtapradeśikāṅkarāya svāhā. Both the staff and the water-pot are the root mantras. By means of these, one should perform all rites.

And it should be employed everywhere among all mantras as the bestower of all accomplishments; it should be applied in all rites of protection. Those same two hands, with the palms pressed together and the fingers interlaced like a braid, should be placed at the position of the head.
It should be employed for specific purposes.
And there is a mantra for this: *Oṃ jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā*.
By means of this, one should perform all rites within the Tathāgata family.
The stimulation of the substance should be performed with the mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, using either red oleander or jasmine flowers.
It should be applied everywhere with the root mantra of Mañjuśrī;
indeed, it is to be employed in all rites in every respect.
One should place those same two hands, formed in the shape of two interlaced fingers, at the position of the head;
this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Uṣṇīṣa of all Buddhas.
And the mantra for this is: jrīṃ.
This Uṣṇīṣarāja is effective for all rites. Forming the hands in the shape of a lotus and placing them at the heart—
this is the Avalokita-mahāmudrā of the Lotus family, effective for all rites.
And the mantra for this is: *jrīḥ*.
One should place those very hands, shaped like a closed lotus bud, at the center of the navel.
This is another great mudrā of Avalokita called "The Pacifier of All Obstacles."
And here is the mantra: *jiḥ*.
This, which performs all rites, should be employed for protection from all fears.

Having formed the two hands in the shape of a beautiful head (*suśirākāra*) with the fingers interlocked against one another, one should place them upon the forehead; this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas, named "Arisen from the Mind of Radiance" (*prabhāvamānasodbhava*).
And the mantras to be employed here are these four single-syllable ones: *tāḥ*,
*vāḥ*.
*droḥ*, *hāḥ*. These four single-syllable mantras were spoken by four koṭis of Buddhas; they are the uṣṇīṣa-kings of all the Buddhas.

The powers of all those possessing great supernatural knowledge (*vidyā-maharddhika*) are based upon all phenomena; they possess the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*) and the five limbs of conduct (*caraṇa*); they are established in the four noble truths; their heads are inclined toward enlightenment; they are to be cultivated by all through the four liberations (*vimokṣa*), the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and the various samādhis; they are unshakable by any worldly or supramundane mantras and tantras; and they are the supreme lords among all the Wheel-Turning Kings of Knowledge (*vidyārāja-cakravartin*).

Jyeṣṭhā is the foremost of all mantras, inconceivable among all the distinctions of samādhis, and the attainment of awakening by the Mahāsattvas. She is the sovereign of the three worlds, inaccessible through the mantras and tantras of all families, and unapproachable by all Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Thus, she is inconceivable, devoid of intrinsic nature, insurmountable, and established as the sky-like nature, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the untainted realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). In brief, she is to be employed in all ritual activities.
By this very [method], one should perform all rites,
especially those prescribed in the ritual procedures of the *Mūlakalpa* of the noble Mañjuśrī.
One should display that same pair of hands in the form of a hollowed casket at the position of the head.
This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) called "Destroyer of All Poisons" within the family of all Tathāgatas; it should be employed in all rites concerning poison. *Ṭroṃ*.
This mantra, spoken by the Buddha when joined with this seal, quickly renders all beings—both stationary and moving—free from poison. (Mmk 36.75)
It renders venomless the serpents who are intent and arrogant with poison;
likewise, it destroys all defects born of passion and hatred.
Furthermore, when this mantra is joined with the mudrā, it performs various rites arising from poisons and venomous creatures, even those born of delusion.
In brief, this mudrā,
when applied according to the Mantra vehicle, performs various rites arising from poison;
it subdues his karma and brings the poison under his control at will.
Thus, with [the mantra] recited one hundred thousand times;

that very same [mudrā], the hands in the form of the Samaya-vajra, with both [hands] having three prongs, having placed the left hand below and the right hand above in an inverted position, one should place it at the location of the head.
That very heart-seal of the Lord of Vajras is effective for all rites.
And the mantra here is: *hūṃ*.
This [mantra] accomplishes all purposes and is to be employed against all cruel grahas; one should not entertain any doubt otherwise.
Oṃ bhadre bhadravati karaṭe ratna viratna svāhā!
First, one hundred and eight recitations of this mantra should be performed;
then Mañjuśrī will be accomplished.
Placing those same two hands upon the head with the tips of all the fingers slightly curled, this is the *mahāmudrā* of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

It should be employed in all rites and applied for all protections; it accomplishes all aims and should be used first in the *sādhana*s of Mañjuśrī, after which one should perform the ritual action. This is common to the three families.
One should place that very same mudrā on the forehead of the noble Samantabhadra.
This is the great seal (mahāmudrā) of Ākāśagarbha.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *svaṃ*.
One should place that very same seal on the region of the throat.
This is the Mahāmudrā of Vimatela-gata.
And here the mantra for all rites is: LAṂ.
One should place that very mudrā in the center of the sheep.
This is the Mahāmudrā of Maitreya.
And the mantra for this is: *maṃ*.
One should place the two hands at the region of the navel as before.
This is the great seal (mahāmudrā) of Kṣitigarbha.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *kṣiṃ*.
One should apply that same seal to the region of the waist and cast it upward.
This is the mudrā of Gaganagañja. And here is the mantra for all rites: GAṂ.
Having placed that same mudrā on both arms, one should rotate it over the head in the manner of a dance.
This belongs to all bodhisattvas, noble śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
And here is the mantra: *Ghruḥ*.
This [mantra] is to be seen as possessing the expansion of the power of karma and immeasurable benefits through its connection with the greatness of qualities worthy of being beheld from every side.
Having looked up at that very same mudrā and brought it down, one should cast it upward through the yoga of dance.

This is the Great Mudrā for all the gods residing in the three realms, those included within the infinite world-systems— above, below, across, and everywhere— for all sentient beings, including yakṣas, yakṣīs, rākṣasas, and rākṣasīs, and so forth, for all of them.
The one named Sarvatrātālalyā should be employed in all rites;
it should also be employed in all rites such as summoning, dismissal, the procedures for the maṇḍala and its sections, and all methods of accomplishment.
And the mantra here is: oṣṭrai.
One should place those very hands, formed in the shape of the *añjali* gesture, upon the head; this is the Great Mudrā of the Inner Barrier for the Great Binding among all mantras.
It should also be rotated around the region of the hips.
And here is the mantra for this: *gyaṃ jaye kumāri śuklabandhani svāhā*.

One should bind a thread spun by a maiden, over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, around the waist; thus the retention of semen is accomplished. One should then gaze toward all directions.
All obstacles become paralyzed;
therefore, the practitioner should perform this mudrā-binding for protection in all rites from every side.
This is the first application to be performed.
Afterwards, the ritual actions (karmāṇi) are to be performed.
Thus, there are one hundred and twenty-eight mudrās.
The practitioner should employ whichever one he desires among them for all rites, or indeed all of them.

In this manner, by means of this application, there are innumerable mudrās and innumerable mantras. That very same [mudrā] is formed when the two hands are held in the shape of hollowed palms, with the fingers interlaced both together and separately, adorned by both thumbs, and the two hands made into fists in the form of five prongs at the position of the head.
One should place it upon the head.

This is the great mudrā of Noble Mañjuśrī named "The Five Crests" (Pañcaśikhā); it performs all rites. By the casting and spreading of the thumbs, with [the fingers] contracted, there is summoning; by their being spread out, there is dismissal.

In this way, by means of the mind and all applications, one performs all rites. Whether joined with the root mantra, the heart mantra, or the subsidiary heart mantra of Mañjuśrī, or with any of the other mantras, it accomplishes all purposes. That very mudrā has the form of a three-pronged pin.
This is called the *triśikhā* (three-crested) mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
It should be understood as the *ekacīra* (single-cloth) mudrā, formed by making the fingers of one hand into the shape of a needle.
Both hands are placed in a hollowed position (*sampuṭa*), bent inward on all sides, with the fingers well-composed and arranged.

Firmly joined and placed upon the head—this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Mañjuśrī named "Emerging Above All Heads. Then, with the hands in that same position but raised higher with the tips pointing upward and palms facing up, one should hold them at the center of the face; this is the Great Face Seal (mahāvaktramudrā) of Mañjuśrī.
Having brought that very [mudrā] down, one should place it in the center of the heart;
this is another heart-mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
That same [mudrā], with both hands positioned halfway and slightly inclined toward the forehead.

This is another heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*). Raising those same hands, the middle fingers are bent downward; the ring fingers have their tips shown while being bent down; they are encircled by the index fingers and extended along the sides of the thumbs.
This is another great root-seal of the Curved Fangs (*vakradaṃṣṭramahāmūlamudrā*), which should be employed in all great fears.
The two [fingers] are very gently bent;
this is another utpala mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
Those same [fingers], when bound, are lowered and coiled.
The peacock-throne mudrā of Mañjuśrī is as follows:
with that same [mudrā], the index fingers and little fingers are pressed together on both sides, held crosswise in the shape of a seat.
This is another mudrā, the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) mudrā.
That same [mudrā], when the fingers are clenched into a fist with only the index finger raised,
is another, the yaṣṭi-mudrā.
When two [index fingers] are raised, it is the dhvaja-mudrā.
Raised three finger-breadths high, it is the banner mudrā (patākāmudrā); raised four finger-breadths high, it is the bell mudrā (ghaṇṭā).
That same hand, with the index finger positioned on top, is the parasol mudrā (chatramudrā).
When all [fingers] are bent downward, it is the *phala-mudrā*.
*Huṃ*.
When the ring finger is positioned at the tip of the hook-like index finger, it is the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.

That same [gesture], with the index fingers firmly held within the fist, is the *muṣṭi-mudrā*. That same [gesture], with the tips of the [index fingers] positioned horizontally like needles, is the *śūla-mudrā*.
When joined with both index fingers, it is the *mahāśūla-mudrā*.
Raising a single thumb constitutes the *ekaliṅga-mudrā*.
Placing that same mudrā at the heart becomes the *manoratha-mudrā*.
Having joined those same two hands together in the form of a hollowed cup, with one above the other, it is the Yamala-mudrā.
Having opened that same [mudrā] into the shape of a bud and cast it toward the head, it is the Utpala-mudrā.
That same [mudrā], full and in the form of space, is the Pūrṇa-mudrā.
That same [mudrā] placed at the head, but formed downward with the fists, is Mañjuśrī’s Yaṣṭimadrā.
Again, when the two hands are made variegated, it is Mañjuśrī’s upward-pointing Svastika; it is red with jasmine flowers, and everything must be bound together.
That same [mudrā], with the hands entwined in reverse, has the tips of the middle fingers extended.
This is another [form of] the Śakti-mudrā of Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī. The bell and the banner are to be understood as before.
Having joined the two hands together in the hollowed-cup gesture (sampuṭīkṛtya), one should open them.
This is another lotus mudrā of Mañjuśrī:
with those same two hands placed horizontally and made into beautiful eyes, one should form the shape of a svastika;
the four fingers, well-extended and positioned toward the four directions, should be very well arranged in the middle.
This is another *svastika* mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
With the two hands in the shape of leaf-buds (*karapallava*), the fingers are not joined to one another. This is another *pallava* mudrā.
Those same two hands formed into fists;
this is another mudrā, the Sarvabuddhāspada-mudrā.
That same [mudrā] of Mañjuśrī is the Dharmabherī-mudrā.
The same [mudrā], with the two hands joined in a hollowed cup, the index fingers encircling the middle, and the thumbs placed upon the palms at their bases, bent and marked with the shape of a conch—
this is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma-conch mudrā. The wheel is as before.
Having the form of a wheel of Dharma, this is another Dharmacakra-mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
Placing that same mudrā on the forehead and performing the yoga of dance, one should cast it with the leftward (avasavya) motion;
this is another mudrā called Mahākrīḍā-vikurvāṇa.

"By the root mantra alone, when applied against great terrors, they are destroyed without exception. Thus, by this application, there are incalculable mudrās, and incalculable mudrā-kalpas, mantras, and tantras.
And they should be understood as being incalculable;
they arise from the self-existent ones who have emerged with great power,
and all of them should be employed.
In this ritual manual, all [rites] must be performed while wrapped within clean garments,
so that they are not seen by beings who do not know the samaya;
such is the great power [of these rites].
Otherwise, it would be a transgression of the samaya.
These hand-gestures (*kara-mudrā*) suitable for the practice are placed upon the hands; through various applications of dance and song, they become manifold.
Furthermore, they have been explained sequentially according to the specific cries of sentient beings. Now, the great gestures (*mahāmudrā*) suitable for the practice of the mandala are as follows.
Likewise, for all Buddhas, there are stūpas on the ground; for Bodhisattvas, they are on cloth with relics as the supreme element; and for Śrāvakas, they are circular lotuses. (Mmk 36.79)
The square [mandala] of the Pratyekabuddhas is said to have three circles;
it is adorned with various vehicles and diverse ornaments.
Furthermore, various weapons belong to the gods, yakṣas, and grahas;
for kings, it should be a sword; and for sages, a staff and a water-pot.
In these maṇḍalas, one should briefly form the mudrās corresponding to whatever is the constant weapon of a deity, or whatever serves as its vehicle or ornament.
Then one should visualize the sun and moon as mandalas above the mandala;
in brief, whatever ground belongs to whichever [deity], one should mentally invoke that very thing and then place those various living beings upon their respective [locations].
Many types of those designated as "beings" and many mudrās have been proclaimed;
one should perform their rites within the maṇḍala according to the prescribed ritual.

Brahmā’s lotus, Śakra’s thunderbolt, Varuṇa’s noose, Rudra’s trident, Durga’s sharp-edged spear, the sage’s water-pot, Yama’s staff, Kubera’s mace, Kumbhīra’s sword, Hutāśana’s fire-pit, and the Earth’s jar— such are the weapons and ornaments of these and others, as they are seen in the world today.

For one who recollects them all everywhere according to the rule, all of those [mandalas] should be employed in all mandalas; or they should be drawn according to the procedure taught in the *kalpa*. All mandalas should be painted with a mind characterized by the resolute intention for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and out of sympathy for all sentient beings.
By those who have been consecrated in all maṇḍalas, or by those consecrated in the great maṇḍala,
or by one who has seen the maṇḍala and received consecration from Noble Mañjuśrī—
by such a person, others must certainly be made to draw all the maṇḍalas.
The noble Mañjuśrī should be brought to mind.

For what reason? Because I, as well as all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have been consecrated by him; and in the form of a youth, appearing in the form of a mantra, he has taught the Dharma through the method of the profound reality and meaning of all mantras for the benefit of sentient beings.
"You shall do so."
One should not perform that which is joined with mantra and mudrā unless it is concentrated on the Dharma;
herein one should not do what is harmful, nor should one do what is beneficial if it is not desired as wholesome.
When joined with the mudrās and mantras, it wards off that which is harmful;
it always [brings about] everything beneficial and harmful, as well as the warding off of what is harmful.
Every mantra should perform its function when sealed by a mudrā;
however, a mudrā without a mantra should not act, nor likewise a mantra that is unsealed.
When joined with the meaning of the mudrās, it will accomplish its purpose with fruit;
when joined with the mudrās, the mantra brings about the fruit of the mudrās.
One should accomplish the extensive ritual activity through meditation equal to the mudrā;
those mudrās which are for pacification, as well as the mantras for pacification. (Mmk 36.89)
Through the union of mantra and mudrā, one should begin the rite of pacification (śāntika);
and for the mantras of enrichment (pauṣṭika), one should employ the arising of the mudrās.
They say that the mudrā joined with the mantra is called *pauṣṭika* (nourishing);
in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should perform the pacifying rite by means of the mudrās and mantras taught here.
By means of the Victors, the principal mantras of the Victors, and also the mudrās according to their divisions,
one should accomplish all rites during the cool season throughout all times.
The mantras originating from the Lotus family are taught for the sake of nourishment;
likewise, the mantra-tantras [are employed] with the fierce mudrās proclaimed by you.
By means of well-known recited mantras and highly efficacious mudrās,
which have been prescribed for the lotus family and are pure and radiant.
[One should act] with praiseworthy auspicious rites that are fully conducive to health and prosperity,
as well as with mantras and seals described as being joined with wrath.
With those [mantras] prescribed for the attainment of enjoyments and wealth— pure, beautiful,
white, marked with white seals, and joined with the appropriate mudrās.
One should accomplish the mantras that bring about prosperity and enjoyment in this life;
when accomplished with such mantras and mudrās, they result in fruitful success.
Likewise, the wrathful mantras beginning with *mantra* are said to be those that obstruct the vital breath;
they were taught in the *Vajratantra* and originated from the Lotus of the Jinas.
The fierce Tejins, who remove the afflictions of wicked beings and are appointed to the harming of living creatures— a wise person should not perform such acts.
And the mudrās are the staff, the subduer, the vajra-spear, and the battle-axe;
likewise, various weapons and great spears belong to Yamāntaka.
Having quickly joined with ministers, one would certainly perform that which takes away life;
therefore, a wise person should not do that which obstructs all life.
One who knows the mantras and tantras should employ a fierce [rite] marked by ferocity;
the mudrā employed in fierce mantras is said to be even more fierce.
Just as those who practice cruel deeds and follow the ends of violent actions are mastered by cruel beings,
so too does that evil-minded person here experience various sufferings of hell.
One should not perform malevolent rites against those of evil conduct using cruel mantras;
likewise, people should never bestow cruel mantras or mudrās upon anyone.
Since an undesirable fruit is indeed experienced again and again, the practitioner of mantras does not find happiness at that time; [it is] cruel... Mmk_36.105 (=“100”)
Together with the threefold [division], it is seen within the attainments (siddhis) that have been proclaimed. // Mmk_36.106(=“101”) //
The sacrifice (iṣṭa) is dependent upon the desired fruit; [it is employed] for cruel rites. Therefore, one should avoid [ordinary] dharmas in such cases.
The best of sages, through yoga... [the teachings] of the Conqueror born from the lotus are sung, being free from cruel deeds.
In the Vajra family, the songs and mantras are proclaimed to be threefold:
inferior, superior, and intermediate.
"The exposition of mudrās, with its extensive meaning of many mantras, was previously taught by the supreme Victors; those which are now proclaimed here [are likewise]. (Mmk 36.110)
Thus concludes the thirty-fourth chapter, the extensive section on the Great Mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which is included within the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.
(Vaidya 320) Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Mañjuśrī, in your *Mūlakalpa*, there is another mudrā that is most supremely secret;

it is esteemed by all the ritual prescriptions of the *mudrā-tantras* and by all mantras. When combined with all mantras, it accomplishes all activities, purifies the path to perfect enlightenment, destroys the paths of all existence, and is the sustenance for all sentient beings.

It fulfills all hopes for longevity, health, and sovereignty; it perfects all the factors conducive to enlightenment; it brings satisfaction to all sentient beings; it makes fruitful the desires and inclinations of all sentient beings; it accomplishes all activities; it grants success to all mantras; and it is accompanied by all mudrās and mantras.
Listen, Kumāra Mañjuśrī!
First of all, there is the characteristic of the *uṣṇīṣa*:
with both hands extended and palms joined, one should place the ring fingers and the nails within the center of the hands, with nail against nail.

The two little fingers are pressed against the tips of the thumbs; the middle fingers are joined at their tips in the shape of a needle; likewise, the ring fingers have their middle joints touching the nail-tips [of the thumbs]; and the index fingers are shaped like a needle, radiating light all around—this is the Great Seal named *Uṣṇīṣa-mahālakṣaṇa*.
And here is the mantra for this: ĀḤ MAḤ HAṂ.
Moving those same two index fingers, one should touch nail to nail with the tips shaped like needles in a circular form;
this is the Great Dharma-Wheel Mudrā, called "the burning away of the thorns of false views and distortions.
And the mantra for this is: *Oṃ dhuna pātaya chinda cakre vajriṇi hūṃ samayiravo bhāge pradeśinyo nirgugugulyākātṛkaṃ caturmārāriśayanī*.
The Great Seal named Vajravīrā, the Immovable One who Subdues the Earth and the Defilements, has the following mantra: Oṃ vajrānani hūṃ phaṭ.
This mudrā and mantra, when joined together, are effective for all ritual actions.
All obstacles are indeed destroyed, just as autumn clouds are dispersed by the autumn season.
Whatever obstacles created by the four Māras, as well as those involving gods and asuras,
are utterly destroyed merely upon seeing this supreme mudrā.
Aiming the same [mudrā] toward another, with the third finger released,
the tips contracted, and beautiful— this is known as the Tathāgata Fist.
The great mudrā for the triple world is named Mahāmaheśvaragabhastimālinī.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ vijaye haḥ.
There is also the Tathāgatamuṣṭi mudrā.

Having bound any one of these mudrās with both hands, one should recite [the mantra] once during the time of practice or the time of preliminary service, and then perform the recitation as much as desired while either sitting or standing.
In this way, all obstacles and impediments find no opportunity to enter,
and accomplishment becomes manifest.
Having moved those same index fingers so that their tips are joined above the middle fingers, one forms the *Udgatoṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra: *Oṃ jvalojjvala dīptodgatoṣṇīṣa dhuna dhuna hūṃ*.
Moving those same index fingers so that they are always touching the tips of the nails of the middle fingers, this mudrā, shaped like a ring with bent ankles, is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ ma ma ma ma hūṃ niḥ.
Raising those same two index fingers equally upward from there and joining them to the needle-like middle fingers forms the *tejorāśi* (Mass of Radiance) mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ tathāgatoṣṇīṣa anavalokitamūrdhni tejorāśi hūṃ jvala jvala eka eka dara vidara cchinda bhinda hūṃ hūṃ sphaṭ sphaṭ svāhā*.
Those same [fingers], with the tips of the index fingers joined to the middle finger tips in the shape of a circle, form the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ jayoṣṇīṣa jvala jvala bandha bandha dama dama ṅraṃ ṅraṃ ṅraṃ haḥ hana hūṃ—this is the Jayoṣṇīṣa mantra.
Moving the tips of those same index fingers and joining them at the third part above the nails with the middle joints of the middle fingers forms the *cakravartin* mudrā.

Oṃ, homage to the invincible Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa, whose crown is invisible; O Cakravartin, hūṃ! Blaze, blaze! Burn, burn! Shake, shake! Tremble! Terrify! Slay! Destroy! Strike, strike! Aṃ aṃ aḥ aḥ kaḥ kaḥ!

*Proṃkhini proṃkhini kuṇḍalini aparājitāstradhāriṇi hūṃ phaṭ!* Moving those same tips of the index fingers (*pradeśinī*) so that they are joined at the third part below the nail of the middle finger (*madhyama*), this is the mudrā of the Lord of Mantras, Cakravartin. Moving those same tips of the index fingers so that they are joined below the nail of the middle finger, this is the mudrā of the Lord of Mantras.
Moving the tips of those very index fingers so that they are joined between the nail and the joint of the middle finger’s phalanx constitutes the mudrā of the Great Cakravartin.
Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined below the third phalanx of the middle finger in the shape of a coil constitutes the mudrā of the Great Cakravartin.
Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined between the joints of the third phalanx of the middle finger constitutes the mudrā of the Great Cakravartin, the Lord of Mantras.

Those same index fingers, with their tips bent at the third joint of the ankles, joined beneath the middle phalanges of the middle finger-pointers by the third joint, constitute the heart-mudrā of Aparājitā-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin;
and the mantra for this is: oṃ aparājitā dhik.

One should perform all rites using either the root uṣṇīṣa mudrā or any other [mudrā], arranged with the ritual offerings (upacāra). By moving the tips of the thumbs and stroking with the ring fingers, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana).

And the mantra for this is: "Homage to the Blessed One, the Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa! Come, come, O Blessed One, King of Dharma! Accept this water for honor (arghya), perfume, flower, incense, food offering (balya), and lamp."
And protect me with "Svāhā to the one of unimpeded strength and valor!

One should perform the invocation with white flowers; then, in one's own form, offer the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the seat (*āsana*). Then, by means of this very [mantra], one should bind [the directions] in the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, below, and above.
One should wipe those same two ring fingers with the tips of the thumbs, then bend them;
touching the middle joints, one should lift them up.
With the water-offering for dismissal (*visarjanārghya*), one should rotate [the vessel] counter-clockwise for one's own deity.
The mudrās for binding the directions become released.

And here is the mantra: "Homage to the Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa! Go, go, Blessed One, King of Dharma! Accept from me this water for honor, fragrance, flower, and incense; and protect me, O you of unconquerable strength and prowess, with this mudrā, mantra, dismissal, and offering."

Those same two index fingers, joined at their third joints below the needle-like middle fingers, with the thumbs together with the little fingers forming a tightly clenched fist—the two middle fingers are the needle.
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya oṃ oṃ hrauṃ bandha hūṃ phaṭ!
O Apratihatoṣṇīṣa, mass of splendor!*
The mudrās and mantras are employed for all bindings and so forth; they are effective for all ritual actions.
Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, slightly touching the third joint of the needle-like middle finger, form the *Vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra for it: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya vikaraṇa dhuna dhuna hūṃ vikaraṇoṣṇīṣaḥ*.

This is the Great King of Vidyās of the Blessed One, the Lord of Vidyās, in the *Uṣṇīṣa-tantra*, for all purposes such as the destruction of obstacles and impediments, consecration, self-protection, the binding of directions, and the binding of the maṇḍala.
It is employed in all ritual actions.
Those same two index fingers, with their tips opened and slightly bent, moved and drawn back, constitute the invocation of Agni; subsequently, one performs the oblation (*homa*).
This very same gesture constitutes the dismissal when the index fingers are cast apart. This is the *Jvālāmālinī-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā*, which is unimpeded in all ritual actions.
And the mantra for this is: Homage to the Blessed One, the Unassailable Uṣṇīṣa! Come, come, O Tejomālin! To Agni, svāhā!
Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, are joined at the third joint of the middle finger—between the joints of the middle finger—to form the *Balotkaṭoṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra for this: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya, imaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ baliṃ dīpaṃ ca pratīccha hara hara sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite dharmarājāpratihātāya svāhā*.

Regarding the mantra for perfumes and other substances: with the ring fingers reversed, the third finger [of each hand] joined to the thumb, and the index fingers shaped like needles, this is the Vajratejoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
It is unassailable by all Vināyakas.
With this, one should effect the subjugation of companions, as well as of directions and times.

Thus, by means of these mantras and mudrās, protection should be performed during the time of recitation, during the time of practice, and also within the maṇḍala; all rites are to be carried out [in this way].
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvavighnavidhvaṃsanakarāya troṭaya svāhā*.
Placing the thumbs at the bases of the two ring fingers in a circular shape, likewise making the two index fingers needle-shaped—this is the Aparājita-uṣṇīṣa mudrā, which is unimpeded everywhere.
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvatrāparājitāya samaye śānte dānte dharmarājabhāṣite mahāvidye sarvārthasādhani svāhā*.
In rites involving oblations of clarified butter and the like, one should perform the rituals for pacification and nourishment.
When the two ring fingers are bent at their tips against the two little fingers, this is the *Śaṅkaroṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra for it: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣa oṃ śaṅkare svāhā*.
It serves as protection in all ritual activities.

The tips of the two thumbs are pressed against the third joints of the two ring fingers; likewise, the two index fingers [are bent] like needles. This is the *Vajrāpratihatasamayauṣṇīṣa-mudrā*, which is common to all samayas.
And the mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | oṃ saṅkare samayaṃ svāhā*.

The two thumbs are placed upon the middle joints of the two ring fingers; the two index fingers are bent at their tips and joined to the middle joint of the needle-like middle fingers. This is the Unobstructed Great Samaya Uṣṇīṣa Mudrā, which is employed among gods and asuras when established in the samaya.
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya oṃ śaṅkare mahāsamayaṃ svāhā*.
Having performed the binding of the maṇḍala with this [mantra], one should recite [it] over even a universal monarch (cakravartin), saying: "Abide, abide in my service!
One also overcomes other universal monarchs.
Reciting in that very place, one can unimpededly effect the mutual destruction of the power, influence, and strength of all mundane and supramundane spells (vidyā).
In one place, for all those who recite [mantras],
there are such Uṣṇīṣa Kings as these, numbering in the incalculable;
the entire family of all the Tathāgatas should be set forth in detail.
For here, Mañjuśrī, in this King of Rituals (kalparāja), there are immeasurable mantras and various kinds of mudrās;
I shall describe them in brief.
If I were to explain it in detail, it would be impossible for all humans and non-humans to grasp or retain it, even in the span of a thousand eons.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, I shall speak in brief; listen attentively to this summary.
O Sage, the supreme mudrā of the Heart is taught here;
following that is indeed the mudrā of the Universal Monarch, the God of Gods.
Then the mudrās of the wise Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara-candra and of Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the yakṣas, are proclaimed. (Vaidya 323) Mmk_37.5 //
Then, [he should likewise employ] all the other great mudrās of immeasurable power,
as well as the entire host of male and female messengers (dūta-dūtī), and the supreme male and female servants (ceṭa-ceṭī).
Yakṣas and yakṣīs, as well as gods and goddesses, likewise nāgas and other nāgīs, and male servants and female servants, as well as piśācas and piśācīs.
[She is the foremost] among the rākṣasīs of great supernatural power, as well as among other celestial women,
the wives of the daityas, and all those of the siddhas and vidyādharas.
The mudrās for all non-human beings and for all humans as well— those who have emerged from birth within the three realms of existence— have indeed been taught individually for every single creature.
Mantras, moreover, are of various forms and are effective for diverse ritual actions;
in royal families as well as in noble lineages, their mudrās are each distinct.
For Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, both mudrās bring about auspicious results;
for all Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, [the same applies].
The mudrā and the heart-mantra are each proclaimed for the divine yakṣa family, which is honored by ṛṣis and gandharvas.
In the seventh family, the mudrā is said to be based on the Gandharvas;
likewise, in the eighth family, the mudrā is proclaimed from among the [other] families.
All mudrās have been fully explained, as well as those others called Sugata-mudrās,
each belonging to their respective mantras, both worldly and Buddhist.
A mantra accompanied by a mudrā becomes radiant in its ritual activities;
the Vināyakas do not follow after one who is skilled in the casting of mudrās and other such rites.
Now, indeed, follows the definition of these [mudrās], beginning with the Mahāmudrā.
This is the definition of the Heart Mudrā of the Blessed Buddhas:
having joined the fingers of both hands together, one should display the two thumbs.
This is the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Tathāgatas.
This very same seal becomes the seal of Padmadhara when the right thumb is shown individually.
Having first formed a fist with the left hand, one should release the pair of middle fingers and extend them together into the shape of a vajra.
This is the mudrā of Vajradhara.
Having lowered a single prong, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin; raising it once again, one should form the shape of a mandala—this is the mudrā of Gajagandha.
One should bend one joint of both [fingers].
This is the mudrā of Maṇikula.
It should be employed with those very mantras of all the jewel-walkers, such as Jambhala, Jalendra, and others.
The two index fingers, with two joints, are bent and joined with their nails facing one another;
this is the mudrā for the Yakṣa family, for the great-attainment Yakṣas such as Pañcika and others.
One should hold the thumbs joined with each other's nails upon the [other] nails.

In the same manner, having positioned the hands as before, one should raise the pair of middle fingers and form them into the shape of a needle; this is the mudrā of all the gods, the celestial inhabitants of the divine families beginning with Akaniṣṭha. Furthermore, having likewise restrained the hands and formed a fist, one should display the two thumbs.
This is the seal of the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas.
Thus, these eight mudrās are encompassed by the eight families;
however, one single mudrā for all the sons of the Victors shall now be described.
With the palms extended and joined, and then slightly contracted—
this is declared to be the mudrā of the most exalted Bodhisattvas.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the staff, the saṅghāṭī robe, the alms-bowl and the monastic robes, and the fangs with the hand in the gesture of fearlessness— these are the seven seals of the Sage.
The Sugata’s abiding state is the web of light-rays of the vision of loving-kindness, with teeth and a tuft of hair;
this too is that supreme mudrā of the Jina, born from his own body.
These two groups of seven and these five mudrās have been remembered by me;
together with the heart-mantra of the Sage, they are said to be twenty by the self-arisen ones and others.
Indeed, these mudrās were previously taught by the primordial Jinas;
the retinue of the Cakravartin was declared to consist of twenty.
These supreme mudrās and mantras are established as being beyond number.
Having raised [the hands] and coiled them, this is the *cintāmaṇi-mudrā*.
Holding the fists at the shoulder region on the left and right while in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*),
it becomes the *khakharaka-mudrā*.
With the two hands joined together facing one another, it becomes the *saṃghāṭī-mudrā*.
The bowl is held with the hands joined as a support; the robe is held by the left hand; the fang is formed by raising the single left thumb of the heart-mudrā.

The hand of fearlessness (*abhaya-hasta*) is inclined in the gesture of fearlessness, with the robe hanging from the left side. In the joined palms, one should place the two middle fingers together, the two index fingers curved outward, and the two thumbs in the middle.

This is the Buddha-locana mudrā. This very same [mudrā], when the index fingers are bent at the first joint and joined together on one side, is the Buddha-maitrī. Having formed the añjali with the fingers spread apart, one should conceal the index and ring fingers by means of the three needles.
The *māmaki* mudrā is as follows:

having formed the *añjali*, one should bend the third joints of the index and middle fingers outward and join them; the two thumbs are placed separately in the shape of fingers—this is the *bhogavatī* mudrā.
With the left hand, the index and middle fingers form the *vijayā* [mudrā].
One should wear a three-finger-width vajra on the right side of the waist with a cord.
In the same way, having personally bound the Vidyārāja-mudrā upon one's head, one should perform all rites with the eight great mudrās;
or one should scatter flowers at the time of the samaya or within the maṇḍala;
or one should act according to the previously prescribed rule or by this [present] method.
One should cause all rites to be performed according to one's desire.
The pledges (samaya) uttered by means of vidyās and mantras become empowered by mudrās when they are sealed with mudrās; they possess the power of the mudrās.
If one should suddenly bind a mudrā in an improper place, that itself constitutes a violation of his pledge (samayabhaṅga).
That which is a vajra is a trident;
there is no difference between the trident and the vajra.
That which is positioned above becomes the mudrā of Vajradhara.

And below Maheśvara is the lower [level]. In the middle, for the teacher, the preceptor, those worthy of offerings, and all human beings, when one finger is raised, it becomes the mudrā for all human beings— beings established in the manifestations of two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, and footless creatures.
With both hands raised twice, it is the mudrā of all yakṣas and yakṣīs; with them raised three times, it is the mudrā of all vidyādharas and vidyādharīs;
with them raised four times and placed with palms level, it is the mudrā of the gods, asuras, and their women.

The two hands placed in the gesture of joined palms (*kṛtāñjali*), positioned in an auspicious form, constitute the mudrā for all the gods who dwell in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Those same hands [in that same position] constitute the mudrā for the gods who dwell in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

That same [mudrā], with both hands formed into hollowed cups and bound into fists, is the mudrā for all beings dwelling in the desire realm, beginning with the lords of the desire realm, including humans, animals, pretas, and those belonging to the world of Yama. Releasing a single finger from that very same mudrā becomes the mudrā for all piśācas and piśācīs.

With two fingers extended, it is for the *rākṣasa*s and *rākṣasī*s; with three fingers extended, it is for all the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) and so forth, including the *graha*s, *mātṛ*s, *kūṣmāṇḍa*s, and all other meat-eaters, as well as for all the *ḍākinī*s, *vyantara*s, and so forth. With all four fingers contracted, it is the *saṅkucita* (contracted) *sarvakaśmala* mudrā.
With mudrās drawn in, there is attraction; with mudrās raised up, there is dismissal.
One should perform all ritual actions by means of one's own mind.
With these very mudrās, one should employ each respective mantra as desired;
one should not employ those of others, nor cause other rites to be performed. One should apply each mantra to that specific rite for which it was intended.
For these mudrās are not to be transgressed, being empowered by all the Buddhas;
indeed, no sentient beings at all are able to provoke them even upon merely seeing the mudrās.
By transgressing the mudrās, they meet with destruction.

From the destruction of the mudrās comes the violation of the *samaya* and the neglect of all vidyās; in the end, they attain a most intense rebirth in the Raurava or Avīci great hells. However, those who establish themselves in the *samaya* of the mudrās and act as protectors against obstacles, they shall enjoy vast and long-lasting happiness and be reborn among the great celestial beings; and at the conclusion of their course, they will certainly be destined for awakening (*bodhi*).
In brief, many varieties of mudrās have been revealed by the primordial Buddhas and by Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power;
it is impossible to reach their limit, to calculate their number,
or for all sentient beings to master them.
In brief, within the family of the Victors, there is a single-syllable sovereign king of vidyās; for the sake of protection, its mudrā is as follows.
First, having formed fists with both the left and right hands, one should extend the pair of middle fingers together on one side;
then, one should bend one joint of both [middle fingers].
Having bent the pair of index fingers at two joints, with their nails joined to one another, one should hold them over the nails of the thumbs.
This Cakravartin mudrā, the most excellent of all mantras, has been taught by the Protectors of the World as being effective for all rites.

When joined with the previously described One-Syllable Cakravartin, it becomes effective for all rites. Once this has been accomplished, the entire Tathāgata family and all mundane and supramundane mantras become perfected.
By the recitation of this, all mantras become recited.
Furthermore, the practitioner must necessarily first perform eight thousand recitations of this supreme mantra proclaimed in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja).
In this way, all these vidyās become manifest before one, swiftly bestow accomplishment,
and quickly grant boons.
One who is certain to be destined for enlightenment performs all rites when joined with the single-syllable heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara and the Padmadhara mudrā;
or likewise, when joined with the vidyā or mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, one performs all rites in the same way;
or when joined with the mudrā of Vajradhara and his very same single-syllable heart-mantra, one performs all rites in the same manner.
Or by means of the Mahāvidyā of Māmakī.

Thus, in the royal family, all rites are to be performed with the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Rājagandha and with its corresponding mudrā. Likewise, in the jewel family, the yakṣa family, the divine, and the noble families—all rites here are to be performed with their respective single-syllable heart-mantras and their very same mudrās. In this manner, everywhere, all rites are to be performed with all the mudrās and all the mantras.
One should perform the empowerments of the knowledge-mantras according to the proper method;
rituals should not be performed otherwise.
Thus, the mudrā with the right hand placed [forward] is for Svastyudyata; the *ekaliṅga* mudrā is for Maheśvara;
the *cakra* mudrā is for Viṣṇu; the *añjali* with fingers slightly apart and open is for Garuḍa; and likewise, the mudrā with hands raised as if to cast a curse is for the Ṛṣis.

In this same way, for the gandharvas, along with the gods and asuras, the four-kumārya mudrā consists of showing the left hand with the thumb placed inside the palm; it is performed with that very same mantra. Likewise, for Kārttikeya with the *śakti* mudrā, and similarly for Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, mahoragas, and all other beings residing within the three worlds, included in all states of existence, and dependent upon the realm of sentient beings.
The mudrās for all beings—such as the grahas, mātṛs, kravyādas, kaśmalas, and so forth—are prescribed in their entirety;
likewise, the mantras are to be employed in their entirety, sequentially and in due order. Thus, everything comes from everything, and not from anything else.
First of all, O Mañjuśrī, the practitioner must rely upon the auspicious Tathāgata-gati Mahāmudrā and its constituent mantras from this King of Rituals (Kalparāja),
as well as the mudrās of the Noble Samantabhadra, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Vimalagati, and yours;
and the mudrās of these Bodhisattvas must necessarily be employed by the practitioner while standing facing east, with his face toward the sun.

Having risen in the morning, being pure and situated in a clean place, one should bind one of these mudrās and cast it upward over the top of one's own head. One should also recite one of these mantras one hundred and eight times.
Thus, one becomes completely freed from all diseases.
One becomes long-lived and is not overcome by any obstacles; one becomes invincible to all sentient beings,
and all mantras become manifest before one.
They bestow swift accomplishment;
one becomes empowered by all the Buddhas;
and one will certainly be destined for awakening.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta also becomes his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) until he reaches the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
And what are his mudrās and mantras?
First, the Mahāvīra-mudrā will be explained.

Having joined the two hands in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), with the fingers interlaced and the thumbs raised, bent at the third joint like a mountain peak—this is the Mahāvīra-mudrā spoken by all the Tathāgatas.
And here is the mantra: ĀḤ VĪRAṂ HŪṂ KHAṂ.
Combined with this mantra, this mudrā performs all rites.

Having formed those same two hands into a hollowed cup (*sampuṭa*), one should again open them with the fingers so that they are spread wide on all sides in the form of a *vajra*; this is the excellent mudrā called *Vikāsinī*, revealed by the Primordial Buddhas.
And here is the mantra: *Oṃ gaganasambhave dīpta dīpta jvālaya jvālaya buddhādhiṣṭhite vikāśaya vikāśaya sarvabuddhān | hūṃ hūṃ vikāsini phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the Vikāsinī mudrā.
When joined with this mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites;
it brings about the discernment of those possessed by planetary spirits.

It causes one seized by planetary spirits to speak, and it performs all those tasks—whether for those possessed by the defilement of carnivorous spirits or those fainting from poison—in whatever manner it is employed.
In brief, this vidyā, when joined with the mudrā Vidāsini, accomplishes every purpose; even if not yet perfected, it swiftly achieves its objective.
Having formed a hollowed cup with both hands, one should make the fingers level within; this is the heart-mudrā.
Having empowered the heart [mantra] seven times by reciting it over the heart, it should be released.
Thus it is in all cases.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ godare vīra svāhā.
This is the heart-mantra of the Tathāgata.
That same hand-cupped gesture (*hasta-sampuṭa*), with the fingers slightly spread and a hollow space between all the tips of the fingers, is the *uṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra: OṂ DROṂ BANDHA SVĀHĀ. This is effective for all rites (*sarvakarmika*).
Having formed a fist with the right hand while leaving the thumb free, this is the *khakharaka* mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ dhunājitaraṇa hūṃ*.
This *khakharaka* mantra is effective for all rites.
By joining with this very mudrā and placing the left hand holding the robe against the robe, one performs the robe-mudrā.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitātmacīvara svāhā!
The Tathāgata’s robe:
by means of this very mudrā, one performs all rites;
having consecrated the robe with this mantra, one should wear it.
One becomes fortunate;
great protection is established.
All grahas, mātṛs, piśitāśins, kravyādas, and śakaśmalas, as well as all obstacles, flee upon merely being seen.
Having joined the left thumb and the right little finger together, and supporting them below with the hollowed palms, this is the bowl mudrā (*pātramudrā*).
And here is the mantra: *oṃ lokapālādhiṣṭhita dhara dhāraya mahānubhāva buddhapātra svāhā*.
This mantra, when conjoined with this very mudrā, accomplishes all activities; it should be recollected at the time of eating.
All poisons, even those from serpents, have no power over them.
With both hands joined in fists, the two index fingers are bent at the middle joints;
this is the Cintāmaṇi mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ tejo jvala sarvārthasādhaka sidhya sidhya cintāmaṇiratna hūṃ.
The wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*).
When joined with this very mudrā, it performs all auspicious rites.
Having empowered various excellent ornaments and decorations with this [mantra], one should bind them upon oneself; thus, great protection is established.
He becomes supremely fortunate;
having adorned himself and empowered the Dharma with mantras, he may enter into battle, and no weapon shall fall upon his body;
he becomes invincible to all enemies.
He protects his own army and attacks the enemy's army.
One performs these and other such immeasurable rites even while remaining unaccomplished.

Taking any one of the excellent gems, such as ruby or emerald, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times, one should bind it to the top of a banner, upon one’s own head, or on the neck of an elephant when descending into the front line of battle;
then, surely, upon merely seeing it, the enemy army will break without even fighting.
Either great paralysis occurs,
or their armies are broken and their leaders flee in retreat.

Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked, one should bend the two index fingers at their middle joints, positioning them where the middle fingers would normally be; this is the Dharmacakra Mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ chinda bhinda hana daha dīpta cakra hūṃ dharmacakra*.

With the left foot extended and the right knee resting on the ground, with the left hand extended behind him and the right hand raised in a striking gesture accompanied by the sound *huṃ*, he stands firm.
This is the Aparājita mudrā.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā*.
The Aparājitā Dharmacakra is the Aparājitā mantra.
When joined with these very mudrās, it becomes effective for all rites;
in brief, it cuts through all sufferings.
In whatever manner they are employed, in that very manner they perform all activities.
Placing the hand in the same manner upon the lap of the braid, with the right hand in the gesture of teaching the Dharma, there is the Tathāgata-śakti-mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayini phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ.
This is the Tathāgata-śakti.
When conjoined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites;
it paralyzes all obstacles, all malevolent beings, all enemies, and even all gods.
This [mudrā] possesses boundless qualities; in whatever manner it is employed, in that same manner it accomplishes all activities.

In the same manner, with both hands turned upward so that the fingers are interlaced, the tips of the two index fingers are joined in the shape of a needle; turning this position upside down, one should place it upon the forehead.
This is the Ūrṇā-mudrā, revealed by the primordial Buddhas for the Blessed Buddhas.
And the mantra for this is: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ*.
He he! Bind, bind! Stay, stay! Hold fast, hold fast! Restrain, restrain! *ūrṇāmaṇi* svāhā!
This is the mantra of the *ūrṇā* of the Tathāgata.
Combined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites.
Having made a mark on the forehead with bovine bezoar while reciting the mantra, one may enter into the midst of enemies;
one becomes invincible.
He is not harmed by any malevolent beings;
he may even enter the midst of battle and,
upon seeing the enemy army in disarray, brings about its destruction.
One does not perform immeasurable deeds without having seen [the truth],
and it has been spoken by immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Having formed a continuous añjali with the fingers interlocked, one should bend the two index fingers toward each other's middle and join the two thumbs together.
This is the Tathāgatalocanā mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā.

This *tathāgatalocanā* mantra, when joined with this very mudrā, becomes effective for all rites. Having consecrated one's eyes with it, one may enter into the midst of enemies; as soon as they see [the practitioner], they become free from anger.
They become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness and become seekers of welfare;
they attain the state of friendship.
Or, at the front of a battle, having consecrated one's eyes with mantras, if one gazes upon the enemy army, they will become peaceful-minded.
Being incapable of striking back, they withdraw without fighting at all;
for the time being, they provide assistance.
Both hands are likewise formed with the fingers arranged in the shape of a book, their tips joined together and held horizontally;
this is the mudrā of Prajñāpāramitā. And the mantra for this is: *namo bhagavati cārudarśane oṃ tha*.
This Blessed Prajñāpāramitā, when joined with this very mudrā, becomes effective for all rites.
While reciting the mantra, one should touch the heart; thus one becomes possessed of mindfulness.
Reciting it in the midst of wicked enemies, one steals away their minds.
In the midst of battle, she bewilders two-footed and four-footed beings, as well as adversaries,
or causes their minds to become distracted; in short,
this Blessed Lady performs all activities exactly according to how she is employed.
In brief, his qualities are boundless, and his eon is likewise boundless.
The mudrās and mantras of the Tathāgatas are also boundless; as it is stated in the *Sannipātaparivarta*, all those retinues of the Tathāgatas—those very mudrās and mantras—are to be employed here.
Furthermore, there are incalculable eons;
the mudrās and mantras therein should be employed within this King of Rituals (Kalparāja).
Thus, in the Lotus Family, she is accompanied by the lotus mudrā.
The mantra is: *oṃ jiḥ jiḥ jināṅgabhṛdbhayabhedine svāhā*.
This mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, when joined with the lotus mudrā, is effective for all rites.
By the recitation of this, the entire Lotus family is recited;
by the accomplishment of this, the entire Lotus family is accomplished—
whether by means of Pāṇḍaravāsinī or the Great Vidyā.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ kaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṅkaṭe kaṭavikaṭakaṭaṅkaṭe svāhā. One should employ it with a mudrā, either the lotus mudrā or another; it becomes effective for all rites.
Furthermore, protection must be performed by one who has gone to any cremation ground.

In this manner, Tārā, Bhrukuṭī, Candrā, and Hayagrīva— as described in the chapter on the Assembly of the Vidyārājas— all these and the entire innumerable Padma family should be employed with their mudrās, mantras, and extensive ritual manuals.
Thus, the banner of the Vajra family is accompanied by both vajra-mudrās;
and the mantra here is: *hūṃ*.
O Vajrapāṇi, this is the actual [mantra]; when this is accomplished, the entire Vajra family becomes accomplished.
By reciting this, everything becomes recited.
When joined with the previously described double-vajra mudrā, it performs all activities according to the practitioner’s wish—
even those that are contradictory to the supreme Victors— by virtue of the necessity of disciplining sentient beings.
This great yakṣa is exceedingly fierce; he performs all rites for the sake of the Mahāvidyā Māmakī or Kulandharī.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ Kulandhari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ!
This Mahāvidyā named Māmakī, which accomplishes all rites, was taught by all the Buddhas. When joined with the previously employed mudrā of the Mahāvidyā Māmakī, it becomes effective for all rites.

In this introductory chapter on the practitioner’s desire, as previously described, the entire Vajra family, without exception, along with its retinue headed by Vajrapāṇi, should be employed here through the conjunctions of mudrās and mantras.
Thus, the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gajagandha of the Elephant family is: Oṃ gajāhvaye hūṃ khacare svāhā.
When joined with the previously described mudrā, it is effective for all rites.
In this manner, as before, the entire Elephant family becomes accomplished.
Thus is the mantra of Samantabhadra: oṃ samāsamajinasuta mā vilamba hūṃ phaṭ.
The mantra for one who has attained the Great Station: Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha, O you who have reached awakening in the Great Station! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
The mantra of Vimalagati is: oṃ vimale vimale vimala muhūrtaṃ dhaka dhaka samayamanusmara svāhā //
The mantra of Gaganagañja, when conjoined with the mudrā of all bodhisattvas, becomes effective for all rites.

There are likewise innumerable mudrās and mantras for these countless great bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, such as Apāyajaha, Sadāprarudita, Kṣitigarbha, Ratnapāṇi, Maitreya, and others.
In this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), the following are to be applied:

the detailed exposition of all mundane and supramundane matters; the extensive ritual manuals for all mundane mantras and mudrās; and all conceptualizations of rituals that have entered into the Great Pledge (Mahāsamaya) and the non-pledge. These have been taught here, as well as all the mantras to be accomplished therein.
In this same way, they should also be applied within the Jewel family, the Yakṣa family, and the Divine Noble family.
All the mantras and mudrās of all tantras, though based upon the three times, constitute only one single family and no other—namely, the Tathāgata family.
And you, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, are to be seen as belonging to the Tathāgata family.

"Mañjuśrī, you should hold this in mind: all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane mantras—whether with outflows (*sāśrava*) or without outflows (*anāśrava*)—and all mudrās and conceptualizations have entered the families of the Tathāgatas.
Mañjuśrī, there exists no secret of any mudrā-tantra or mantra that has not already entered the family of the Tathāgatas and the samaya of the Tathāgatas.
Mañjuśrī, O Youth, hold it thus: they have indeed entered."

Because the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme, therefore the family of the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme. In this way, Mañjuśrī, this King of Rituals and this Supreme Jewel of the Family was revealed, taught, established, and elucidated by the primordial Buddhas— the Blessed One Saṃkusumitarāja and the Blessed One Śālarājendra.

By the Blessed One Saṅkusumitagandhottamarāja, by the Blessed One Ratnaketu, by the Blessed One Amitābha, by the Blessed One Puṇyābha, Kusumottama, Saṅkusuma, Supuṣpa, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Krakutsanda, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and by the Blessed One Konākamuni.
I too have now revealed it, as was revealed by Śākyamuni, and they shall be revealed [by others] in the future.

Thus it is that this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, has been transmitted through the succession of Buddhas; it is the supreme jewel of the Tathāgata family, possessing great benefits, certain, and based upon the Dharmadhātu.
It is impossible to describe its benefits even in a thousand eons, for its vast array of great qualities cannot be fully recounted in detail.
Whether for all beings to speak of or to hear— those [teachings] to be experienced in the present life and those leading toward enlightenment in future lives—
such as these, there arise immeasurable fruits of the expansion of great qualities, both pertaining to the present life and the future,
for anyone who, being faithful and free from doubt, should uphold, recite, or apply themselves to this tantra even with conceptual thought.
One should accomplish the mantra, or recite it, or even form the mudrā; one should remain constantly devoted to these practices.
In this very life, one obtains eight qualities and benefits:
one becomes unassailable by all adversaries.
Moreover, no fear arises within him;
poison does not affect his body,
and weapons do not fall upon his body.
He is blessed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he becomes long-lived, happy, and wise; and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes his spiritual friend.
At night, they grant him a vision as a sign in a dream;
all mantras protect him,
and they reveal the mudrās to him in his dreams.
He becomes invulnerable to Duṣṭarāṣṭra and to those wicked beings who seek his harm;
he is destined to have enlightenment as his ultimate goal.

These eight benefits are to be seen for one who has faith, is free from doubt, and is diligent—whether they be a householder or one who has gone forth, a woman or a man, and those great beings who assist in the teaching. They do not belong to others who are engaged in evil deeds; for such as these, there is a perverted state below in the Raurava hell and other such places.
As it was stated— that in the forenoon, the binding of mudrās brings long life and victory—
one should honor the mudrās such as the Heart-Uṣṇīṣa and Ālocanā with the retinue of the Tathāgata mantras.
O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, for these are indeed equal in potency and equal in power to your own mudrās and mantras.
Regarding what was said, "by one who is pure and situated in a pure place":
the place is a central area of ground, free from thorns and obstructions, smeared with fallen cow dung, and strewn with fragrant white flowers;
standing there, one should recite the mantra.
One should form the mudrā; otherwise, one should not recite even a single mantra from any other [tantra] unless it is accompanied by its mudrā.

As it has been said regarding "purity": when the sun has set, one should bathe with pure water that is free of living organisms; wearing fresh garments and having performed protection by means of a turban, one should avoid sexual intercourse and remain devoted to purity, cleanliness, and guarding [the precepts], O auspicious one. *Mmk* 37.23.
Having performed protection with the uṣṇīṣa and following the binding of the wheel,
one should meditate there upon the Tathāgatas during the watch of the night that has passed in a dream.
Having taken a thread spun by a maiden or by a Brahmin woman who has not yet given birth, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with this mantra—
*oṃ hara hara bandha bandha śukradhāraṇi siddhārthe svāhā*— one should recite the mantra while joined with the Māmakī mudrā.
Then one should tie a thread around the waist;
having wrapped it three times, the binding of the semen is accomplished.
Even the Lord of the Desire Realm would be unable to cause a disturbance of the mind even in a dream.
How much more so, then, the Vināyakas appearing in dreams?

Whether by proper ritual or improper means, even the daughters of sages—who can assume various forms—are unable to cause mental agitation in one who is free from passion, let alone in a lord of the desire realm; how much less so other women, whether born of humans or non-humans, for those who possess passion?

Having thus risen at dawn according to this rule, having discarded the tooth-stick and rinsed the mouth, and having bathed with pure water free of living organisms, one should, standing facing the east as before,
form the mudrā and recite the mantras according to the prescribed rite.
One becomes long-lived, capable in all undertakings,
liberated from great diseases,
and beloved by all people.
It arises as a counter-force against enemies;
as soon as it is seen, all grahas, kravyādas, kaśmalas, and the like flee away,
and it paralyzes the enemy army.
By mere sight alone, he performs all rites—whether with pure or impure materials, and whether according to the prescribed rule or without it.
Thus, this king of manuals is surrounded by an incalculable multitude of mudrās and mantras;
it has been spoken and will be spoken by incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and it is also now being spoken by me, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.

In the midst of this great assembly, O youth Mañjuśrī, you have been appointed by me for the sake of protecting the teaching and for the sake of long-term preservation of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), once I have entered final nirvāṇa— having relied upon the limit of phenomena (*dharmakoṭi*), having reached the culmination of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and having become stilled— with a mind impelled by great compassion.

For the benefit of sentient beings, this has been spoken by me; at the time when the most terrifying end of the age is occurring, it has been spoken in detail and with full analysis as a king of manuals for the sake of all sentient beings, for the purpose of restraining and subduing wicked kings and evil beings who cause harm to the Three Jewels.
