Thus concludes the thirty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the rules governing mantras and mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 332) Now follows the thirty-eighth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the characteristics of the mudrās and the mantras in detail, as well as the ritual for the maṇḍalas in brief and the observance of the commitments (samaya). Mmk_38.1 //
Furthermore, among them is the location of the mudrās;
indeed, it is the mandala for all mantras, containing the secret of all mantras.
All of this was previously proclaimed by all the Buddhas of great supernatural power;
the majesty of the destiny of mantras has been declared across all families as well.
In the past, by the primordial Buddhas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
the wheel of mantras was set in motion, as well as the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Following the wheel of peace, they have gone and taken refuge in the limit of reality;
all those Buddhas, possessing great supernatural power in the world, have attained peace.
All this was previously proclaimed by the Tathāgatas of the past;
I too, O Mañjuśrī of noble wisdom, shall teach it to you in this final age.
Having performed this, then [the following] should be addressed to the Buddha of great splendor:
"Mañjughoṣa, the Youth, indeed stands before you with palms joined in reverence."
He spoke to the Fully Awakened One, the best of speakers and the supreme among bipeds:
"O one of great wisdom, speak the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
"Thus, for the sake of brevity and without elaboration, [I have described] the arising of the fruit of the greatness of qualities.
Having been addressed in this way, Mañjuśrī remained silent.
Then the glorious Brahmeśvara, with a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird,
explained all of that concerning the arrangement of the mudrās and maṇḍalas.
At that time, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men, standing above the Pure Abodes, proclaimed the mantra and the tantra.
Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī, to the origin of the ritual procedures for the mudrās,
and to the detailed expansion of the qualities and majesty of the mantras and their tantric applications.
First, one should consider all the signs of the Tathāgatas, as well as the sentient and non-sentient,
their forms, conduct, gestures, and all their bodily movements and speech.
With both hands and feet, the head, and the joining of the fingers of one hand—
all that was declared to be a *mudrā* by the ancient primordial Buddhas.
A water-pot, an umbrella, as well as a lotus, a banner, and likewise a flag;
a fish, a thunderbolt, as well as a conch, a jar, and likewise a wheel.
Whatever various weapons are renowned in the world,
they are all included within the mandala of mudrās, including the mudrā in the form of a blue lotus.
They are situated here in successive order and are thus described according to the prescribed rule;
one should always draw all of them with forms and essential natures that are identical.
Having stated that the mudrā is within the maṇḍala, those mudrās are proclaimed to be properly arranged in their respective places throughout all the common [maṇḍalas].
In all mandalas, one should likewise apply one's own form;
and the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) should be placed upon the wheel, while the white [deity] arises in the uṣṇīṣa.
One should draw the white parasol as the primary [symbol] in the mandala;
likewise, the Wheel of Dharma for the Buddhas and the lotus for the Lotus family.
The vajra is prescribed for the Vajra family, the elephant for one born of the Gaja family;
likewise, one should employ the pitcher in the Maṇi family throughout the entire mandala.
One should draw the two preeminent divine and noble families, Śrīvatsa and Svastika;
and in the most excellent Yakṣa family, one should draw the fruit arising from the fruit-bearing tree.
Having drawn a swan for Mahābrahmā, one should also draw Śakra with his vajra;
for Maheśvara, one should draw a trident and also depict a bull.
One should also draw the trident and the sharp-edged spear, as well as the spear of Skanda,
and having drawn the discus and maces of Viṣṇu, together with the Dānavas.
One should always depict in their midst gods with various weapons, seated upon diverse thrones, and possessing various vehicles as well.
One should draw one or another of these [deities] exactly as they appear, with their forms correctly transferred as reflections, in every mandala.
The mandalas taught by the supreme Victors consist of one, two, or three, and so on up to an incalculable number; they are equal to the rows of their altars.
One should place in the center that person for whose sake the maṇḍala was proclaimed;
or else, one should draw a Buddha in the womb of the Jina family at the very center.
Then one should also paint the image of the Teacher situated within;
the second should be placed in the Lotus family, and the third one should paint in the Vajra family.
Having thus drawn all those gods and asuras in successive order,
one should thereafter draw all the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans upon the entire ground.

Then, having written the names of the heretics in their proper sequence as they are situated, one should likewise write the guardians of the directions and all those who have come from various origins. (Mmk 38.31)
In brief, one should draw the maṇḍala starting from a single dot, increasing from two onwards until it becomes innumerable, extending as far as the very limits of the directions above.
At that time, the surface of the earth within his mandala is indeed said to be immeasurable,
extending from a single point throughout the boundless expanse of the terrestrial realm.
The ritual procedure for the mandala has been proclaimed; indeed, three types have been specified:
the superior, the middling, and the inferior are thus celebrated.
In the highest [level], the highest accomplishment is attained; in the middling, the middling is declared;
and in the lowest, the minor accomplishment—so it was taught of old by the supreme Victors.
The supreme Victors have declared that success is threefold according to the mental dispositions:
great success for beings of great capacity, and middling success for those of middling capacity. Mmk_38.36 //
The third is for small creatures; it is taught as a minor rite.
When the mind is serene, Buddhahood arises as the supreme and fruitful result.
A being certainly attains [the result] simply by seeing the maṇḍala;
at that time, one with a middling mind shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
The others are said to be fixed in the state of a śrāvaka due to their lack of respect;
however, the greatness of the fruit is declared to be unfailing, resulting in a peaceful rebirth.
He will certainly attain heaven even without seeing the mandala;
likewise, he shall obtain all the supreme mudrās and the mantras in their full detail.
The mudrās and maṇḍalas are said to be of three kinds and three types, bringing happiness; now the benefit of mantras is being told.
Beginning with a single syllable and extending as far as the numerical limit,
however many words are spoken in a mantra, that many are proclaimed.
Idle chatter, weeping, laughter, and likewise crying,
as well as all talk and prattle, shall become beneficial for all mantras.
Those mantras are also threefold and proclaimed to be of three types;
just as they are described in the mandala, so indeed are they among the mudrās and mantras.
This ritual procedure, as prescribed by the leaders of the world, is thus joined;
in that very way, it proceeds in three ways, in many ways, and even in a thousand ways.
It is threefold, of three types, and likewise thrice-innumerable;
for a mantra indeed depends upon the mind, and there is no mantra devoid of the mind.
One who is joined with the mind-mantra and properly united will accomplish [the goal]:
those mantras which belong to the Tathāgata family, as well as those in the Lotus family. (Mmk 38.47)
And those songs which are sung in the Lotus family and in other families by others,
all worldly mantras indeed— all of them have emerged here.
The mantra which was spoken by the Jina and the sons of the Jina for the sake of sentient beings— whosoever, being diligent, recites it, shall certainly become a Buddha.
Those mantras which are indeed neutral, he who recites them is declared to be a Pratyekabuddha by virtue of his lineage; this is certain.
Those who are indeed engaged in other mantras spoken by Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, as well as those worldly beings intent upon the recitation of mantras; Mmk_38.51.
He will certainly be established in the lineage of the Śrāvakas of great supernatural power;
even there, one should apply the ritual action to the superior, the inferior, or the middling [levels].

In rites of pacification (śāntika), there shall be the enlightenment of a Buddha; likewise in rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika), that of those possessing the sword [the pratyekabuddhas]. By other minor mantras, however, the enlightenment of a śrāvaka is declared.
Therein, the mind is to be observed; it is divided into three types, and it is further divided manifoldly, even into incalculable divisions.

Thus concludes the thirty-sixth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for all activities concerning the mudrās and maṇḍala tantras, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 336) Now follows the thirty-ninth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, and having surveyed all world-systems and all sentient beings with his Buddha-eye, once more [addressed] Mañjuśrī—
He addressed the Youthful Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, within the detailed exposition of your mantra-tantra and mudrā sections, there exists an entry into all mundane and supramundane samaya-maṇḍalas;
it is the accomplishment of the common ritual conduct, the basis for beings who enter [the path], and the inconceivable activity of all mantras."
Listen as they explain, in brief, the practice that is the instruction on the treasury for all mudrās, all maṇḍalas, all sentient beings, and all those who have entered into mantras.
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and made this request:
"May the Sugata grant me his favor for our sake and for the benefit of the world;
that will be for the purpose, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of people, and out of compassion for the world."

Therefore, O Sugata, please explain to me the procedure for entering the commitments (*samaya*), the subsequent instructions, and the methods conducive to accomplishment regarding the recitation, fire-offerings, invocations, worship, and observances of all mantras, as well as all tantric mudrās; and the detailed chapters concerning the specific methods, both mundane and supramundane, applicable to all mandalas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One Mañjubhāṇī remained silent for that interval; the Omniscient One likewise remained silent during that interval.
The wise Mañjurava, pleased and knowing the Sugata, accepted this;
and all the Buddhas, gathered everywhere from all realms, were present.
Indeed, all Bodhisattvas, as well as all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and all beings of the three kinds within the beginningless wheel of existence— Mmk_39.2.
Those born of the womb who are bound and joined to the five states of existence—
the presiding lords over all hosts of beings, including rākṣasas, uragas, and humans— [are here].
Daityas, dānavas, and yakṣas; kūṣmāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, chief deities, leaders of the gaṇas, and the highly powerful mātṛs.
All the hosts of planets in the world, as well as the moon, the sun, and others;
Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, the Rudras, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Virūḍhaka.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Kubera, all the Vasus as well,
and all beings everywhere who are supported by the realm of sentient beings.

Bound by the threads of their destinies through actions that yield auspicious and inauspicious fruits, they are both liberated and unliberated everywhere; having arrived at the proper time, they remain steadfast.

Through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment, those born from auspicious wombs and those born from inauspicious ones, established here in three ways, hear [the teaching] by means of supernatural power.
Then all the Buddhas indeed heard that noble Dharma of the Sugata in the city of Śuddhāvāsa, which brings about the arising of the supreme and auspicious Dharma.
It is proclaimed as being invariably endowed with the three— mantra, mudrā, and samādhi—
and it is the secure, most auspicious path, namely the Noble Eightfold Path.
The threefold path of action, supreme and leading to the city of Nirvāṇa— namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration— is thus taught as the threefold path. (Mmk 39.11)
The Blessed One, the All-Knowing, spoke: "O steadfast one, initiate the practice of the limbs of the mantra path; with a slight smile upon your face, gaze upon Mañjughoṣa."
And then all the hosts of beings, standing there gentle and confident, heard this speech endowed with auspiciousness, which was like the sound of Brahmā.
"May there be no falling away from your commitment, lest it become useless; for by not understanding the words of the Buddha, it will be harmful to you for a long time."
"O child, you will fall into blinding darkness and become far removed [from the goal].
Therefore, these mantras and mudrās have been proclaimed for your ultimate welfare."
O worlds, you shall always perform favor and restraint;
you should consider that which is joined with my activity as indeed the wrath of Yamāntaka.
He will undoubtedly always exercise restraint during the age;
first indeed in a secluded, solitary place strewn with flowers.
Having mentally and through meditation drawn in [the deities] from all directions within the mandala to be constructed,
the wise one should first meditate upon a lotus for all the Buddhas.
The second lotus is like the rising sun, possessing great brilliance;
situated there is the glorious Mañjuvara, characterized by the form of a youth.
With five tufts of hair on his head, knees, ears, and elbows protruding,
his body covered in hair, and with palms joined in reverence, the boy questioned the Sugata, the Knower.
And speaking auspicious words in the abode of the Sugata,
one indeed [should visualize] the great lotus of all the Buddhas, arisen from crystal.
A lotus made of lapis lazuli with filaments arising from gold,
having a stalk of great emerald and a pericarp together with gold.
It has a great mass of branches, adorned with great jewels,
and is beautifully decorated in many ways with buds made of rubies.
Having visualized a very large lotus resting in the sky, adorned with divine sprouts made of emerald, upon that best of sages; Mmk_39.24.

Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas by concentrating the mind on a lotus that is smaller than that, possessing equal marks and being very beautiful. Mmk_39.25.
Therefore, one who possesses an intellect focused on effort should visualize the third lotus as smaller than that;
they know the fourth lotus, which is the *āvarta*, to be even shorter than that.
One should always meditate upon the fifth lotus, which is both short and shortest of all, equal in form and radiance, and pervading the entire sky. (Vaidya 338) Mmk_39.27 //
One who knows this should visualize a lotus situated upon the seven [syllables] by means of the mind;
likewise, for Vajrapāṇi, a lotus that rises like the sun.
To the right of Vighnāntaka is Mañjughoṣa, always upon a lotus;
beyond that is a smaller lotus belonging to the great-souled Lokīśa.
The third is indeed "the lotus" for one who has attained universal illumination;
the fourth is indeed "the lotus" for one who possesses inexhaustible eloquence.
O you of slightly pure course, the lotus is short in that which consists of the fifth principle;
from that, the sixth is the lotus known as the Noble One beyond phenomena (adharmasaṃjñita).
One should likewise visualize the ocean below and all around;
and from the great nāga Ananta, emerging halfway, [arise] Nanda and Upanandaka.
All-white great elephants, adorned with every ornament,
born from the waters, with smiling faces and gazes fixed upon the sky.
Possessing seven heads and great coils, adorned with jeweled earrings,
they are divine in form as human beings, while others likewise have the coils of half-serpents.
The seven [deities] with gentle countenances have half-eyes directed upward;
to the left, on a lotus, are the excellent sages, with five [of them] situated upon the uṣṇīṣa.
The wheel-turning [mantra] is thus both beginning and end; it is sharpened by the son of Śakra’s weapon. The single-syllable wheel-turner is a mass of splendor, white and lofty.
One should clearly visualize above Jayoṣṇīṣa, the King of Vidyās of great supernatural power,
and below him, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the yakṣas.
The wise one, skilled in mantras and the king of mantras, should always and at all times fix his mind upon these embodied beings and upon his own intellect while reciting the mantra.
One should meditate upon the Self as being situated there, established in restraint, seated indeed upon a lotus leaf, and seated cross-legged below.
One should always confess all misdeeds in the presence of the sages;
remaining there, born of discipline, the sage should supplicate the most excellent of the best of sages.
May those sons of the Sugata turn the wheel of Dharma and remain steadfast;

the nāga Maṇi-Śaṅkhapāla is slightly white in color;
and there are the great nāgas Sāgara and the renowned Mucilinda.
Furthermore, the Kṛṣṇanāga is proclaimed to be entirely black in color;
all of them are equal in size, and Nanda and Upananda are likewise well-elevated.
Then there is Elapatra, the lord of nāgas, possessed of great coils and world-renowned;
he is Sāgara, the sovereign of uragas, whose deeds are inconceivable and marvelous.
One performs various rites; listen now to those that are pure:
one must never perform them with a corpse or one who is unconscious from poison in the ocean.
Having indeed enveloped it with a thread and performed meditative yoga with a wise mind,
one who has died will quickly rise up, having been placed within the ocean.
One should always step upon a snake that is asleep from poison with one's foot and move it;
by placing it in the ocean, it becomes free of poison at that very moment.
In this same way, [one subdues] fevers, piśācas, flesh-eaters, and auspicious vyantaras.
[He destroys] the *rakṣasas*, *pretas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *piśācas*, serpents, and *mātṛs*, as well as the *grahas* in the world that always seize the life-force of others. Mmk_40.149.
Resorting to various forms of exertion,
they remain upon the earth as humans, having assumed human bodies.

One should contemplate with this meditation those beings who have seized the foolish; one should meditate on the mother-being as standing before the Naga kings of the ocean, arisen from thought— she quickly releases the foolish being.
In this way, for people bitten by insects or spiders,
or those afflicted by ringworm, skin spots, leprosy, scabies, itching, and eczema;
And likewise, one who has another [disease] arisen, and one who constantly suffers from fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara).
Plīhameda and Udara, as well as Padma and Supadmaka;
for the Yakṣas, there is Sapadmaka, as well as Padmottara and Kṛśa.
One should place all those afflicted by the disease of fever, including the human and monkey tribes,
within the ocean at the abode of the supreme serpent.
One should cast away all various miseries and sufferings, and the afflictions of every disease and ailment,
into the ocean-like abode by means of the power of meditation and contemplation;
for the Naga, who receives the command of the Sugata, will swiftly liberate one.
And thus, at that time, the entire aquatic realm was pervaded by all the auspicious serpents, who perform every task, along with the lords of the snakes.

They are supreme in every respect and in all directions, lords of serpents possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*). Knowing the *samaya*, they are intent on the initiation commanded by Mañjughoṣa;
always resorting to divine *yakṣas*, they bring about the arising of auspiciousness for human beings.
But by those whose actions are mixed, the arising of mixed results occurs;
they always bring rain at the proper time, having resorted to a righteous way of life.
When the crops, medicinal herbs, and grains have been brought to fruition by streams of water flowing from all sides, it bears fruit according to its cause.

Embraced in the form of clouds, they wander upon the surface of the earth; possessing great supernatural power and great majesty, they endure for an eon and experience great prosperity. Their city, named Bhogavatī, is situated within the clouds.
When mortals everywhere in Jambudvīpa are devoted to the Dharma,
then the great nāgas and their retinues indeed abide within them.
Then, having experienced the war between the gods and asuras, those desiring victory remained situated upon the Jambu tree in the center of Jambudvīpa.
They visited men again and again, being beyond the range of perception everywhere;
they should apply all virtuous deeds toward those nāgas.

Those nāgas who have fallen from their commitment and dwell in the waters cause all harm; taking refuge in the faction of the asuras, those nāgas release poison— both stationary and mobile— from every direction, like swarms of insects.
Pramāthin, Jhalujhala, Kapardin, Mahodadhi,
Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Durmukha, and likewise Bahumukha.
These and other great nāgas are exceedingly arrogant and conceited;
they are constantly established in black karma, or others in mixed karma.
When the mortals dwelling in Jambūdvīpa become most unrighteous, they will be of great power and terrifying form, yet filled with poison and malice toward others.
Then they will cause great fear, most terrible poison-induced fainting,
vomiting, and dizziness, as well as many afflictions of a great pestilence.
In this world, they release wicked serpents that bring about misfortune;
likewise, those great nāgas cause many kinds of calamities and inauspiciousness.
"Those who delight in what is harmful, bringing about drought after drought—[one] should undertake this meditation for the destruction of their pride. Mmk 40.170.
Mañjughoṣa, the greatly wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power,
holds a blue lotus in his left hand and bestows boons with his right;
he has the luster of split gorocanā and rivals gold and saffron in brilliance.
One should meditate upon the Son of the Sugata mounted upon Garuḍa, the king of birds,
at the heads of those fanged creatures, [neutralizing] all their fierce poisons.
Then, with their hearts broken and their minds terrified and agitated,
they turn back again and go, entering the abode of wrath in anger.
Having seen various kinds of portents, as well as inauspicious ones accompanied by sounds,
the knower of mantras, being composed, should thus meditate upon Mañjughoṣa.
O knower of mantras, one should fashion snake-fangs of many kinds;
indeed, those of the egg-born biters take on various forms and appearances.
I shall explain correctly, according to the vision of the scriptures and through ritual action,
how those born of that lineage— namely the serpents— bite humans upon the earth.
O Garuḍa, one should perform all the rites for embodied beings by means of that very scripture prescribed by the rules of the King of Birds.
The nāgas such as Kṛṣṇa, Śukla, and others— those nāgas who roam throughout the entire earth within the mandala on the ground— move through the bodies of embodied beings in the form of the sun.
Then, having understood what is curable and incurable, as well as the four beneficial [remedies] for poison— whether it has entered the bile, the phlegm, or is mixed with the wind— Mmk_40.179.
They say that due to phlegm it is "of Varuṇa," being white in color and circular;
while that which arises from ignorance is called "pitta," appearing triangular in shape.
Always fire-colored and slightly reddish, with arms somewhat tawny; like one established in a lineage until the end of bondage, it is four-cornered and variegated. (Mmk 40.181)
That which is dark-colored and very lofty should be known as belonging to Mahendra;
they say that among elephants, the one born of phlegm (kapha) is characterized by hatred and arises from bile (pitta).
Delusion should be known as born of wind, variegated and black in color; that very same [delusion], when characterized by phlegm, should be understood as sattvic and white in color.
That which appears silver-like should be known as pertaining to bile (paittika), shining with yellow and red hues;
that which is dark should be known as pertaining to wind (vātika), characterized by a variegated and uneven luster.
One should observe that the gender is mixed everywhere, even among all the *vyantara* spirits, among insects, boils, and the like, and among all reptiles.
One should clearly contemplate Mañjughoṣa arising there, possessing a dark-blue luster,
seated comfortably upon Garuḍa, appearing as a youth, and the source of happiness;
one should contemplate him amidst the Vyantara spirits who are wicked among humans at the joints of the body.
Then one should contemplate the divine youth in the form of a child,
the great-souled one of universal form, seated upon Garuḍa.
Then the wise one should meditate upon that illustrious being, who resembles a stalk of autumn rice, seated with his two thighs [crossed], neither touching the navel nor reaching the sky.

The meditator should visualize Mañjughoṣa, who possesses great heroism, has a golden luster, resides in the region of the chest during deep sleep, and is mounted upon the foremost of birds, the king of birds.
Likewise, one should meditate on the inconceivable Garuḍa-bannered one in the place of the head;
one should then contemplate him as white-hued, seated upon Vainateya, and situated outside.
In the case of a *sāttvika* [victim], there is fainting from poison, yet they vomit phlegm in all directions;
saliva flows incessantly, and they sink down again and again.
One should know that such a person has been bitten by a *sāttvika* [serpent]; it will be beneficial during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
When the Lord of All is in a state of paralysis or agitation, he wanders and trembles;
furthermore, when there is poison born of bile, fainting occurs and a terrible burning sensation arises.
In the rājasa [nature], there is fang-bearingness and biting; such is its activity.
In the tāmasa [nature], there arises delusion, fainting, and sleep.
When mixed, however, the activity becomes mixed and dreadful;
when the *sattva* is present, it appears white, and in the fangs, it is human.
The passionate (rājasī) should be known as yellowish, and the complexion of the skin is somewhat [yellow];
furthermore, the deluded one (mohātmā) has a black complexion, and the complexion of the skin arises accordingly.
When mixed, it is smoke-colored, and sometimes likewise pale-white;
those born from the white fortnight arise from the *sattva* and *rajas* qualities. (Mmk 40.196)
Those born of snakes who are dark-complexioned are of a *tāmasa* or mixed nature;
for these belong to that family-lineage, O Lord of the Chiefs of Serpents,
and they roam the surface of the earth embracing the demonic faction.
Among these humans in the world, there are species of nāgas who are most unrighteous;
they are cruel and even more cruel in the world, always intent upon the pursuit of food.
Some are for the purpose of causing harm, others are fanged and life-destroying; [others] are for the purpose of destroying poison for those who subsist on all kinds of venomous creatures.
This supreme and primary meditation, which follows the characteristics [of the object], should be applied to sentient beings; when contemplated, it quickly releases them from that poison.
One should employ it at all times and in all circumstances for all diseases;
established in meditative absorptions, it destroys all calamities.
Just as with the *nāgas*, so it is with sentient beings, *rākṣasas*, *grahas*, and *mātṛs*,
as well as humans of malicious intent who take the lives of others;
one should apply these [rites] specifically to the symptoms of all those afflicted by diseases in the world.
One should always place the meditation, the object of meditation, as well as liberation and action;
[this] youthful form is auspicious, pure, and the destroyer of evil.
Mañjughoṣa, the great hero, the son of the Jina endowed with great supernatural power,
is seated comfortably upon Garuḍa as the solar disc rises.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord of the Lords of Mantras, who faces every direction;
when visualized everywhere, he destroys all diseases through meditation.
One should perform all rites at all times toward all sentient beings;
for this [mantra] paralyzes everything and beautifies everything auspicious.
And all the mantras of the worlds, when understood within this meditation,
quickly attain accomplishment even in another kalpa, as declared here.
And those mantras belonging to the Tathāgatas, as well as those of the Vajra and Lotus families,
and those of Śakra, Indra, Brahmā, and Rudra.

For one who meditates upon this ritual manual (kalpa), all mantras pertaining to the Ādityas, Vasus, Indras, the lunar mansions, planets, and luminaries, as well as those of Garuḍas, Uragas, Yakṣas, and the foremost Ṛṣis together with the Pūtanas, shall be accomplished.

Even when performing rites according to the dependent method, one should accomplish the success of the ritual quickly, whether by means of an independent rite or an internal one, while truly absorbed in meditative concentration.
Having meditated upon the solar disc, they arise in their universal form.
Then [he saw] the Youth, appearing as a child, adorned with the ornaments of a babe,
blazing upon the orb of Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
Having seen such an unmanifest form, even when well-visualized for the sake of strength, the desired result arises as a paralysis of the enemy's forces.
And all those who have been bitten become paralyzed and dance with one another; all embodied beings, possessed by the *grahas*, laugh while being afflicted.
Those afflicted by fever and those who have fainted rise up from there quickly;
crying out in various ways of distress, they indeed let forth a terrifying roar.
A practitioner of mantra, being composed, should then recognize those humans on earth who have been seized by the *graha-mātṛs* and *kūṣmāṇḍas* through these signs.
By his mere will, he can swiftly effect the transference of poison;
then, with a desire to sport, the yogin causes the spirits to play.
In one who has fainted from poison, the solar channel (nāḍī) should be employed;
by the application of the solar channel, one shall cause all living beings to move.
While asleep, one becomes free from all poisons, both stationary and mobile;
thereafter, one who has been poisoned and fallen asleep will undoubtedly rise up quickly.
And another person on this earthly plane quickly grows ill from poison;
yet another again, and yet another as well, or even someone else besides them.
In this manner, by means of hundreds and thousands of such applications everywhere,
one should cause the elements to ripen through the practice of the channels until [the goal] is reached.
Likewise, upon clothing, a wall, a jar, our water, or fire, one may in an instant move the channel; therein resides the poison within the venom.
Indeed, all those who were afflicted shall become healthy at that very moment upon the earth. By means of this initial application, one should perform eight hundred rites,
or one may perform an incalculable number of rituals using the blood of the supreme mantra.
This application for practitioners of recitation has been taught in brief;
indeed, this entire ritual procedure of Garuḍa, which is dependent on others, must be employed.

It is taught that the Śaiva [mantras] are born of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), especially so; and all worldly mantras (*laukikamantra*) should be employed within the detailed visualization (*dhyānavistara*). (Mmk 40.224)
In this Mañjurava Kalpa, which is especially distinguished by meditation and well-honored by the applications of all tantras as well as by mantras,
those mentalities that serve the purpose of the Kalpa should always be employed here.
In this divine yoga, proclaimed here as the King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja),
all [beings] should be engaged through meditation within the stainless state characterized by the causes and methods of application.

For one who constantly recites and meditates upon this subtle, pure [mantra] concerning the object of the mind, which is the basis for the accomplishment of mantras, proclaimed by the Son of the Sage and rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, there shall be the abundant fulfillment of all accomplishments.

Thus ends the chapter, the instruction on the section concerning the meditations for all rites and the methods for accomplishing the play of Tārā according to the reality of all worlds, from the thirty-eighth great king of kalpas within the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
(Vaidya 357) Now follows the forty-first chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni—
Once again, having surveyed the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa deities,
he addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there exists..."

In this great expansion of your Great King of Kalpas, which is rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, which follows the practice of the Great Mantras, which has entered into all samayas, and which serves as the foundation for entering the Great Root Kalpa— this Garuḍa, the king of birds, possesses the superknowledge of the knowledge of the cries of all beings and the inconceivable domain of the knowledge of the cries of all beings; he is the master of the superknowledge of the knowledge of the cries and the practice of his own mantras among all mantras.
He alone shall explain to you the self-vow of all mantras and all ritual manuals belonging to all mundane beings who have entered into it,
as well as the knowledge of the sounds and the conduct of all those in the animal realm and all the Garuḍas, kings of birds, who range within the domain of mantra rituals.

Then, indeed, from that circle of the assembly, Vainateya Garuḍa— surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of garuḍas through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva— rose from his seat, circumambulated the circle of the assembly,
and approached where Mañjuśrī was.

With palms joined in reverence at the feet of the Mahābodhisattva, he addressed Mañjuśrī: "O Mahābodhisattva, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings, I shall proclaim one hundred varieties of ritual actions, together with their secret instructions, within this Great King of Kalpas.
Therefore, it would be well if the Mahābodhisattva would grant his approval."
Then Mañjuśrī said this to Vainateya: "Speak, speak, O Great Being, out of compassion for sentient beings!
Then Vainateya, through the empowerment of the Buddha, sat upon his own seat and, with a joyful mind, spoke the hundred supreme rites along with their secret mysteries.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, Śakuna, Great Śakuna, you of outspread wings, destroyer of all serpents! Kha kha, khāhi khāhi! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ! Stay! The Bodhisattva commands: Svāhā!
He spoke one hundred and eight rites:
the summoning of nāgas and the subduing of nāgas.
The subduing of nagas, the causing of possession by snakes whether bitten or unbitten, the summoning of a snake by means of speech,
the performance of the subjugation of snakes, and the playing with poison;
It dispels all poisons—
whether by speech, mind, or intellect—
for one who observes the poṣadha and has fasted for three nights.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, on the bank of a river in a pure location, having constructed an eight-cubit mandala with five-colored thread established upon eight lotuses, one should depict the Blessed One in its center teaching the Dharma.
To his right, one should depict the noble Mañjuśrī with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of the Blessed One.
To the left of the Blessed Buddha, one should depict Nārāyaṇa with four arms, holding all manner of weapons in his hands. Near him, one should depict Garuḍa of deformed appearance.
Immediately after that, one should draw Vinatābharaṇa. Behind Āryamañjuśrī, one should draw Āryākṣayamati, Sudhana, and Subhūti, with their palms joined in reverence.
Thus should the inner maṇḍala be drawn.
Outside at the eastern gate, one should draw a vajra with white ashes; to the south, a sword with black pigment; to the north, a mace with yellow pigment;
and to the west, a noose of red color.
Thus, having summoned all the deities from the outer maṇḍalas with the root mantra,
and having worshipped them with all kinds of flowers and all kinds of perfumes,
[one should offer] incense of *guggulu*.
Having offered a bali-oblation with the three sweets,
and having kindled a fire before them with fuel-sticks of khadira wood,
one should maintain a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Seated upon a serpent-throne, one should offer eight thousand oblations of snake-venom thorns smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
Then, as a sign of success, serpents will arrive;
an offering of honor (arghya) should be presented to them.
In this way, success is achieved.
Having recited one's own mantra, one should say: "Having granted me success, depart.
Then they depart.
Then, having performed the dismissal with the root mantra itself, one should sprinkle [the area] thoroughly.
Thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
And all the offering substances for the bali should be cast into the water.
Afterwards, by mere speech alone, one performs all rites involving poisons.
One who desires to create enmity should offer twenty-one oblations of serpent bones smeared with poison;
enmity will ensue.
Desiring to destroy [an enemy], one should offer twenty-one oblations of fragments of a snake’s slough; he is destroyed.
One should offer twenty-one oblations of crow feathers; immediately he wanders about like a crow.
For the subjugation of women and men, one should offer twenty-one oblations of mustard seeds anointed with ghee; they become submissive.
To subjugate a king or a high official, one should offer twenty-one oblations of excellent food smeared with ghee; he becomes submissive.
Having consecrated a clod of earth with mantras, one should throw it into the fire; it does not burn.
Liberation is achieved by means of grass.
Fish are not caught by what has been spoken. One attracts a being, whether sentient or insentient, with a snap of the fingers.
By sprinkling water over one suffering from all diseases, one becomes healthy. Having empowered a staff with mantras, one should strike the door; it shall be opened.
Taking that very staff wrapped in blue cloth, one should go into battle; the enemy army will break apart upon merely seeing it.
By tying a knot in one's own garment, all mantras become paralyzed.
When [the victim] is released, there is liberation.
One should fill the mouth of a snake with ashes. By uttering the name of whomever one performs this rite, [that person is liberated].
He becomes mute.
One should strike a tumor with water over which the mantra has been recited once;
the tumor shrivels up.
And the knowledge of others falls away;
with this one binds,
and likewise one liberates.
Having consecrated a brick and turned it around, one should recite the mantra;
this causes the knots tied by others to tremble.
Likewise, if one desires to cause rain, one should draw the previously mentioned mandala.
Having performed the worship and kindled the fire,
one should offer eight thousand oblations of *varuṇa*-fuel sticks.
It rains an *āḍhaka*;
likewise, it rains up to ten *āḍhakas*.
Having consecrated a *pippalā* fruit and grasped it with the hand, [one should recite the mantra].
In whichever direction one casts it,
there the food is transferred. This same procedure applies even in the case of a fire conflagration.
The descent into the water should be performed in this manner:
it drives away the nāgas;
having fashioned a snake out of clay, one causes whichever [nāga] one desires to bite.
This same procedure applies to the charcoal-snake;
it releases [the victim] once again.
One should scatter mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited seven times in the four directions.
Snakes are coming;
a ritual boundary (maṇḍala-bandha) should be established.
Having sprinkled them with water, one should dismiss them.
Liberation [from poison] is achieved by water; for the summoning of a *nāga*, one should take a clod of earth, recite the mantra over it, and throw it into water;
they become free of poison.
Taking a bow, four arrows made of non-metal should be shot in the four directions.
Taking a snake that has moved during the autumn, they approach;
and that nāga should be told:
"Drink the poison!"
The one bitten drinks and rises;
then, when one sprinkles water upon the waters to strike down the snakes, their arrows fall one after another,
yet the snake remains unhurt.
One should fashion four mongooses out of earth from an anthill. Having consecrated water with a mantra, one should sprinkle it [upon them];
then, having gone [to the site], the snakes will abandon it and depart.
Those who have arrived should be told: "Drink the poison!
If they drink it, the dead person rises up.
Having empowered charcoal with mantras, [one should act].
Having drawn a line,
one should strike it with the *arkalatā* plant;
then a snake, being dragged along by those to be slain, comes forth.
One should say, "Drink the poison," and he drinks it;
the one who has been bitten becomes free from poison.
One should consecrate either a banner or a parasol with mantras.
As many as there may be who are dead or have drunk poison, upon seeing [the practitioner], they all become free from poison. Having consecrated a musical instrument, one should play it;
upon hearing it, they become free from poison.
Having drawn a mandala with five-colored dust, the sound of a palm-clap should be given.
Then the nāgas and sarpas will come from the four directions;
they enter the maṇḍala.
One must not be afraid.
One should perform the binding of the topknot and the protection of oneself. Having consecrated the eyes with mantras and looked at the two angry ones, one should press the left thumb;
at that very moment, [the eye] falls out.
Like a snake, it acts through form;
in liberation, there is liberation.
In this way, by means of speech, one causes [the venom] to enter or release, whether it has been bitten or not.
Having consecrated the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings with mantras, wherever one throws them— whether on a street or in a house—
at that very moment a serpent bites a human being.

If sprinkled with water, they become free from poison. By raising one's hand [in this manner], one gains immunity for six months. Having consecrated oneself with mantras, one may allow oneself to be bitten by snakes at will.
Poison does not affect him.
He adorns himself with bracelets, armlets, and earrings.
Having empowered dust with mantras, he should mutter them into his ear.
By means of water, or a fan, or even by mind, having recited the mantra, one should cast dust upon the ground;
the deceased then rises.
Incense made of human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*) together with ghee brings about nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Incense made from powdered human bone and the feathers of crows and owls causes death;
incense made from *madana* seeds and husks causes emaciation;
and incense made from mustard seeds and *rājikā* causes fever.
The excrement of a *kodrava*-eating cat causes enmity;
furthermore, by mixing the powder of a skull with the powder of *madhūka* and applying it as incense with honey, one effects eradication.
*Moraṅgī* and castor stalks used as incense also effect eradication.
Cow bile and human bone, with clarified butter, serve as an incense for the killing of an enemy.
Fish roe, *prasannā* liquor, combined with cotton seeds,
is an incense that quickly brings back a man who has gone to another land.
Split lentils and the flesh of a hen’s egg—this incense should be offered to one who is entering; beyond this is the summoning.
One should combine the seeds of *bhallātaka* with sesame oil;
this is the summoning incense, which one should offer for the purpose of summoning.
One should offer ghee and guggulu;
this incense destroys disease.
Having offered incense made of sesame and mustard seeds, one should offer those very same substances as oblations.

For seven nights, at the three junctions of the day, one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt and black mustard seeds under the name of whomever one desires to bring under control; this should be done at the three junctions for seven nights. This is the method for subjugating a great man.
Having consecrated powdered skull with a thousand recitations, one brings whoever one desires under control by touching them with that powder.
By mixing it with cremation-ground ashes, one causes whomever one pulverizes to be seized by fever; likewise, one releases them.
If one burns an incense of mongoose hair, mustard seeds, and a snake’s slough while reciting someone’s name, that person becomes hated by the whole world.
One performs subjugation with sesame seeds and brings about the production of wealth;
with sesame and rice grains smeared with ghee, one brings a woman under one's control.
If one offers frog fat as an oblation at the site of a *nāga* for three nights,
one causes the gods to send rain.
Having fashioned a clay image of Garuḍa, holding it with cupped hands and descending into water reaching up to the shoulders, one should recite the mantra at midnight.
By whose name he becomes subject to one's control:
having scattered rice grains in a cremation ground and established the *devahṛdaya*, one should recite the *praharaṇa*;
this provides a livelihood for [the deity] together with his retinue.
Incense made from the hair of a mongoose and a rat, along with cotton seeds and bone, brings all beings under one's control.
Incense made from poison (*viṣa*) and *bhallātaka* mixed with honey is a means of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Incense made from the shells of hen’s eggs together with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) is also a means of subjugation.
Palāśa, seeds of *surasā*, and *madana* flowers constitute an incense for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
An incense made of *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, the excrement of a frog, and that of a sparrow is for the purpose of subjugation.
Barley, sesame, and *dūrvā* grass mixed with cow urine form an incense for subjugation.

Haritāla and kākajihvā, burned as incense with blood, cause muteness. Human hair combined with cow-flesh and oil makes an incense that causes disease. Crow feathers and owl feathers, together with nimba oil, are used for eradication (uccāṭana).
This incense, consisting of guggulu resin and clarified butter mixed with sidhu liquor, brings joy to all sentient beings.
Incense made from patra, tvak, and turuska causes all sentient beings to follow one;
they become obedient to one's command.
Turuṣka, sandalwood, camphor, and collyrium constitute the means for subjugating a king.
Having performed the ritual of worship and offerings, one should offer eight oblations of *mahāmāṃsa* before an image of Viṣṇu, and then recite the mantra eight thousand times for three nights.
Whatever object one desires,

With pure bodily conduct, possessing pure mantras and knowing the mantras,
one should then employ the supreme mudrā, having bathed, sipped water, and purified one's mind through recitation.
Both hands should always be washed with clay, cow dung, and fragrant substances, using pure water that is clean and free from worms and small creatures.
When both hands have been purified by washing with fresh water and are thus made clean,
they should be joined together in a hollowed, cup-like gesture while held in the fists.
Slightly hollow on all sides, six finger-breadths in height,
situated between both thumbs, and bent at the little fingers.
Then, having placed it upon the region of the heart covered with a white cloth,
one should display it in all ritual actions for the accomplishment of the goal.
Indeed, for all beings, whatever is desired is quickly accomplished merely by drawing [this seal];
this is the Mañjurava mudrā, the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites. // Mmk_43.34 //

Thus concludes the second chapter from the *Ekacatvāriṃśattama-paṭalavisara*, the "Great Seal Chapter," which serves as the means for accomplishing all supreme rites, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 372) Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [uttered] that which is sealed with the seal of the countless Victors, reaching the limit of reality, and consisting of the inconceivable array of qualities of the supreme dharma of all Tathāgatas.

This chapter on mudrās is the sign of all sentient beings, the most supreme secret of all; it is conceived through the ritual procedures (*kalpa*) of the mantras and tantras for all mundane and supramundane excellence;

it serves as the path for all sentient beings to enter the way of seeing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); it is common to all mantras and all designations; and in this very life, it fulfills all the hopes of all sentient beings and is the cause for the supreme bliss of propitiating all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, serving as the means for the complete fulfillment of the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).

It is the summoning and dismissal [of deities], the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, all garlands, and ritual gifts; the entry of the vidyās and the manifestation of their forms; the accomplishment of all purposes and aims; the subduing and mastery over all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and kūṣmāṇḍas—both those of fierce and gentle nature—as well as the lords of bhūtas and the sovereigns of all activities; the manifestation of all deeds, the blazing [of fire], traveling through the sky, invisibility, the power of subjugation, and the wondrous, marvelous signs that constitute the equipment for awakening.
It is guided by the meaning of all mantras and tantras, honored by all the kings of vidyās, the accomplisher of all vidyās, invoked by all the Buddhas and Mothers,

fulfilling the desires and wishes of sentient beings according to their aspirations, producing the causes for the visible results of all mantras, and, in brief, it is effective in whatever way it is applied.
In whatever way it is accomplished, in that very way it is realized.
Mañjuśrī, I shall speak this supreme chapter on the ultimate truth of all Buddhas, which is the most profound secret of the ultimate truth;
it was spoken by all Buddhas of the past, and the Blessed Buddhas of the future shall speak it as well.
Now I shall speak;
listen to that, O Mahāsattva, I shall speak;
listen to that, O Mahāsattva, I shall speak.
Pay close and careful attention, Mañjurava; I shall speak, I shall speak—possessed as you are of delightful eloquence.
The Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men, the perfectly awakened one, the supreme among sages,
having realized the welfare of beings, perceives the ultimate reality.
O bull among sages, you indeed speak of the secret mudrās for the sake of the mothers,
in the delightful city of Śuddhāvāsa, which is inhabited by pure beings.
Then, when that king of manuals (kalparāja), which reveals the reality of Mañjughoṣa, was being spoken in the supreme assembly of sages, the abode of those free from passion.
Then the sons of the Buddha, the ministers who were wise and knew the supreme truth, said to the assembly: "Listen, O assembly, to this discourse! (Mmk 44.4)
"The eldest son of the Buddha, who abides in the supreme dharma of the Mahāyāna,
indeed named Samantabhadra," he spoke these excellent words.
"You are described by the Jinas as a youth, possessing both the form of a child and a great form;
born of the Śākya clan, skillful and glorious, you are beheld as a Buddha."
For you, O one of universal great wisdom, out of a desire to favor the world,
have [revealed] this extensive collection of your own ritual manuals (kalpavisara) sealed with mudrās.
O son of the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural power, entreat the Great Hero,
the essence of this eon, who possesses great supernatural power.
Thus addressed by the heroic and wise son of the Buddha,
Mañjuśrī quickly became intent upon performing the play of a child.
Having bowed to the Sugata, the Protector, the sole eye of the world,
he spoke sweet words with a voice resonant and moistened by compassion.
May the Blessed One, the Buddha, who knows the reality of the power of wisdom,
explain how all mantras indeed certainly succeed for those who recite them.
How indeed do they proceed unfailingly for living beings without conceptualization? How could they achieve success when merely cast or muttered, even if not applied to all purposes? Mmk_44.12.
From the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell,
and all those living beings who dwell within these three-and-a-half realms of existence.
They are summoned, restrained, and possessed while all look on,
by means of causes for satisfaction and nourishment, joined with every rite and purpose.
Those who abide on the ten stages and stand upon the path of the Sugata— the Bodhisattvas, as well as those awakened ones who rely on the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha— Mmk_44.15.
The great-souled ones who have transcended passion are summoned when they are well-honored;
they are joined by mantras and sealed with these mudrās.
The yogins speak according to reality— whether independent or seeing— the past events that have occurred or not, as well as those in the present.
Discourses on the heavenly realms are inconceivable, whether they concern one's own body or another;
likewise, the future is described as it truly is, and illustrative examples are also set forth.
When impelled by mantras and mudrās, they speak according to the rule;
likewise, when worshipped with mudrās, they swiftly bestow accomplishment as well.
Accompanied by ministers who are experts in mantras, and being well-honored with offerings and oblations,
the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas likewise bring about accomplishment most swiftly.
Even the great-souled Arhats, the Khaḍgins, are always bestowers of accomplishment;
so too are the worldly mantras and those others which are supramundane.
And those who are perfected ones, as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
asuras, suras, and always the beings—all sentient beings are established in three ways.
In these infinite directions and in other world-systems, among the beings in the five destinies who are always engaged in what is appropriate and inappropriate; Mmk_44.23.
They shall swiftly attain accomplishment when well-sealed with these mudrās;
this is known as the Vimala [mantra], proclaimed by the Sugatas, the knowers of mantras, and the sages.
The *viṭaka* is to be known according to the rule, and the *visara* is the supreme chapter; these have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas in the world for the sake of the highest welfare. (Mmk 44.25)
The wise Mañjughoṣa proclaimed this mudrā called Pañcaśikhā by all the Buddhas for the sake of the welfare of living beings. Mmk 44.26.
It should be known that those born from all sides are for the [ordinary] heads, while those born from the crown belong to the Tathāgatas;
that [crown-born hair] should be known as the bestower of all aims and the fulfiller of the treasury of Dharma.

For the purpose of completing the mantras and mudrās, there is that which possesses great supernatural power, which is always the most excellent among all mundane and supramundane [practices]. (Mmk 44.28)
In the tantra of Mañjughoṣa, however, this [practice] is considered the foremost and most excellent;
by its power, one shall swiftly accomplish all activities according to their intended purpose.
Having become pure, one should bind the supreme mudrā of the Lord in a pure place;
first, indeed, having made the two hands hollow and joined like a casket.
With the thumbs slightly separated from the palms and the thumbs placed [on top], it is indicated by "tha";
with the five fingers arranged like five needles, this becomes the *pañcaśikhā* mudrā.
Always placed at the location of the head with a single finger’s breadth,
the Evacīrā mudrā is applied to the positions on the crown of the head.
The little fingers are placed together and the two middle fingers are likewise closely joined;
both thumbs are pointed like needles.
From the union of the three needle-like forms, the triple-crested (triśikhā) mudrā is proclaimed.
With all the fingers joined together, hollowed out by the formation of a cavity,
and always placed at the position of the head, this mudrā becomes the supreme crest (śira-varā).
That same [mudrā], with the two fingers raised and their tips slightly bent,
is to be known as Mahāvīrā, the great mudrā of great supernatural power.
"These five great mudrās were previously taught by the supreme Victors; O wise ones, they declare [the essence] of all mudrās."
Jyeṣṭhā is the foremost among the mudrās;
she is sealed by all those that are supramundane and by all those that are mundane in every respect.
These five great mudrās are the applications that cause success;
they are well-accomplished and most excellent, declared to be supreme and foremost.
They are the power emerging from the crown of Mañjughoṣa’s head, possessing wondrous and marvelous activity.

As many as there are seals (mudrās) of the Sugatas, which are the causes for the accomplishment of all [attainments], they are renowned as "seals" (mudrā); [this is] the glorious one arising from the sprout.
The hair from the crown of Mañjughoṣa’s head is supremely meritorious and auspicious;
by binding it on, great beings will certainly attain enlightenment. (Mmk 44.40)

One should always perform the ritual action according to the rules for that faithful person, who is adorned with the great chief [of mantras], whose faculties are unimpaired, and who is joined with wisdom through sacrifice.
When properly joined with such a being,
this mudrā indeed accomplishes all desired objectives in abundance.
However, through instruction, those who are wise, discerning, and effective in accomplishing their goals—the disciples approved by the teacher—should always be accepted in the world. Mmk 44.43.
In this world, by a person who has observed the ritual actions and who is devoted,
this mudrā is always employed by those who have entered the Mahāyāna.
When applied to mantras in three ways,
all these mudrās are indeed the foremost and most excellent in the world by virtue of their power.
For the sake of accomplishment for those desiring success, these [mantras], when well-applied with mantras,
quickly bring about their purpose and bestow the fruit of all happiness.
Mañjughoṣa himself abides in meditative concentration through these mudrās;
in whatever place one performs these, Mañjurava himself is always present.
For the Son of the Conqueror, possessed of great supernatural power, should arrange this supreme protection;
he is indeed a Great Being in the form of a child, appearing in various forms and endowed with great supernatural power.
He appears in many forms for beings, and in the form of mudrās for embodied ones;
yet for foolish beings wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra, he appears as such.
Acting for their benefit, he quickly remains in the form of a seal (mudrā),
born from the head of Mañjughoṣa and established upon the crown of every head.
For by merely reciting these, joined with the root mantra or that which follows the heart-mantra, they are endowed with the accomplishment of all goals.
All those mantras belonging to the Lotus family,
as well as those of the Vajra-holder and the one with matted hair, are well-joined with the Sugata-mantras.
When joined with all worldly mudrās as well, they bestow the fruit of the intended purpose;
these five great mudrās, when joined with mantras, bestow the fruit of the intended purpose.
Having abandoned that which is conceptualized as residing in mantras, it yields fruit through mudrās;
it is a great protection and a source of great merit for embodied beings by its mere binding.
By merely recollecting these great mudrās, great protection is established;
how much more so when they are employed through the mere recitation of mantras supported by mudrās?
Or rather, all those who perform the recitation will certainly attain awakening;
others, however, are the great mudrās arising from the trident and the spear.
Now, the Great Sūla among mudrās is said to be terrible and fierce;
it is employed here by the preeminent King of Wrath, Yamāntaka.
He performs various kinds of dreadful deeds that deprive beings of life and bestow great terror, even upon a high-souled person such as Vipaśyin.
Created for the destruction of wicked beings within the three realms of existence,
various mantras have been joined with them, relying upon diverse mudrās.
They were always created by the supreme Victors for their very destruction;
they were devised for the purpose of the teaching, endowed with the meaning of mantra practice.
The mudrās, which reveal the meaning of the tantras, have been prescribed by the Lords of the World as a remedy for the poison,
sin, and diseases employed by wicked beings.
It was taught for the very purpose of destroying them, performing all rites;
for the destruction of Yama’s command and for liberation from the noose of death.

This mudrā, when employed constantly in conjunction with the mantra, is known as the merit-bestowing destroyer of Yama’s messengers and the annihilator of death. It takes away life [from enemies] and is ever-present.
She is known as the giver of life, who brings back those led by the command of Yama;
she grants fear even to Yama himself for the sake of destroying all diseases.
Likewise, this life-sustaining [practice], joined with the foremost sages, is beneficial;
for those who have faith in this teaching, protection is ordained for their welfare.
The Gītā of Mañjurava is fruitful, destructive of the wicked, beneficial, and the bestower of all aims; it is proclaimed as the Goddess Mahāmudrā.
Regarding the great weapon, they say there is another, the supreme among mudrās:
likewise, having placed the hands together, the two index fingers are formed into a noose.
The two little fingers should always be joined by the application of the fist;
the hands are always joined in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭita*), with both thumbs raised.
This mudrā is of great merit; it is joined with the Great Spear (Mahāśūla) and arises from various weapons produced by the Lords of the World.
If a practitioner of recitation should think of the weapons of an enemy, by that very thought he shall cut the body [of the foe]; it shall come to pass through the mere arising of that thought.
When applied together, mudrās and mantras will certainly destroy the enemy;
they shall strike down all hosts of enemies, even those possessing great supernatural power.
The hosts of Yama’s messengers, obstacles, and planetary spirits, as well as the mothers, Pūtanās, Skandas, Rudras, and pretas of great supernatural power. (Mmk 44.72)
Having recited [this], one may traverse all the worlds of Vaivasvata along with Indra;
one should employ no other mantra than that of the wrathful king Yamāntaka.
One should employ these mudrās, which are equal to great thunderbolts;
they would instantly destroy even Vaivasvata—how much more so mere humans on earth?
This is the seal (mudrā) that strikes down all [enemies] and destroys all who are wicked;
it was established by the World-Leaders, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds.
In the same way, one should form the hands by joining them at the middle fingers;
likewise, having positioned the hands here, one should form them through the application of the fist.
The tips of the two thumbs are pressed together;
the fingers are joined with hollows formed between them, while the middle fingers are raised up.
Likewise, with the two needle-tips always resting upon the index fingers—
this excellent and formidable mudrā, the best of sages call "the Trident" (Śūlā).
When both index fingers are slightly bent, it is the Mahāśūla;
when they are extended, it should be known as the Paṭṭiśa—the supreme and excellent Great Mudrā.
When those same fingers have their tips contracted and are raised by three finger-breadths,
the wise declare this to be the *triśūla-mudrā*.
These should be known as various weapons when both thumbs are raised;
for they are like great spears, possessing great power and being terrifying.
In this supreme Mañjurava Tantra, for the sake of destroying evil beings,
these Great Mudrās of wondrous activity have been taught as the tamers of those who are difficult to subdue.
Fierce, life-taking, and arising from a distorted form,
they are most exceedingly terrible, wrathful, and established in extreme cruelty.
The most formidable and excellent Jyeṣṭhā goddesses, possessing many forms, have been revealed;
everywhere the Buddhas who recite [their mantras] are freed from old age and disease.
These perfected practitioners of recitation always traverse these worlds;
they were ordained by the Fully Awakened Ones, the preeminent sages, for the destruction of death.
One should employ these [mantras], which destroy old age and disease, for the sake of destroying death;
when applied by practitioners, they quickly become terrifying even to Death himself.
The glorious and supreme Lord would manifest this seal in the excellent city of Śuddhāvāsa for the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men and the most eminent of sages. (Mmk 44.87)

The Buddhas do not speak mantras, nor do they [teach] mudrās for those who perform cruel deeds; rather, out of affection for the sake of sentient beings and for the purpose of fulfilling the goals of the Omniscient One, [they teach them].

Whether for the purpose of sporting with supernatural powers, as a cause for accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, for the sake of training beings through skillful means, or for establishing them in the supreme Mahāyāna; Mmk_44.89 //
Filling the great saṃsāra...
[it is] for the sake of beings who have the power of resolute conviction that the mantra and mudrā have been proclaimed.

Even that which is called "space" is neither a Buddha nor conceived by speech; for those who are endowed with the reality free from conceptual proliferation, how could it be within the sphere of discursive thought?
The ultimate limit is equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and equal to the pinnacle of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
for those joined with mantras, the ultimate limit is sealed by the mudrā.
They declare that it is always the cause for the liberation of the factors of existence;
it is called the seal of the Omniscient One, which fulfills the purpose of all-knowledge.

For the sake of honoring the meaning endowed with logic, the mudrās and their sealings have been proclaimed by the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas, whose sphere of activity is the inconceivable within the inconceivable.
The mudrās of the All-Knowing Seers, such as the Uṣṇīṣa and others, have been manifested;
then there is the Avalokita-mudrā of Vajrapāṇi, and those that are worldly.
For the sake of the welfare of embodied beings, they have been spoken and will be spoken,
as long as the mudrās have been taught by the sons of the Buddha and the most excellent sages.
The seal that fulfills all aims is conceived through inconceivable power;
indeed, mantras have been taught in three ways for the sake of the conceptualization of beings.
There is but one mantra that has been spoken by the Buddhas;
for the sake of the Sugatas' purpose, indeed, this single mantra is proclaimed among all mantras.
The glorious Lord of the Uṣṇīṣa is always of a single color;
he shall eternally become a universal monarch (cakravartin) when the letter *ta* is joined with the letter *ra*.
Always joined with the letter *ū*, it is then chanted;
he shall become the glorious Cakrin, the supreme one born from the crest of the Buddhas.
They call this the supreme mantra of the wise Son of the Buddha;
by its power it should be known as equal [to the others], for the letter *ma* is proclaimed as the ultimate meaning.
This celebrated heart-mantra of Mañjughoṣa, born from the crest of the Buddha, should be known for its extraordinary power, great merit, and vast supernatural efficacy. (Mmk 44.102)
The mantra fulfills all purposes;
when accompanied by the five-crested mudrā, they fulfill the purpose of both [self and others].

The five-crested mudrā, or even when joined with the syllable *makāra*, brings about the realization of the ultimate meaning; it grants both the goal in this very life and the attainment of enjoyments.
They say there is another mantra: ...
the letter *ja* joined with the letter *ra*, honored for its meaning as a voiced sibilant (*avoṣman*). (Mmk 44.105)
This indeed is the supreme and foremost of mantras, born from the head of Abjaketu;
when joined with the excellent lotus mudrā, it is for the noble ones who seek the purpose of nourishment.
It shall bring about the accomplishment of the rites for those who recite [the mantra], fulfilling all goals and purposes.
Furthermore, there is the mantra of the Vajrī, the syllable *Hraṃ*, which is born from the arm and the head.
This supreme and foremost mantra is indeed proclaimed as Caṇḍa;
when employed with the Vajrālaya mudrā, it shall accomplish the purposeful rites for those who seek their goals.
This mantra is a formidable tamer of the difficult-to-subdue and a cause of destruction;
one should perform the ritual as prescribed for the sake of what has been taught and for the purpose of instruction.
One should not perform evil deeds out of a zeal for the suppression of sentient beings;
one should never employ the supreme mantra against gentle beings at any time.
One should not abandon a being who has committed an offense due to a minor fault;
one should not, out of delusion, treat living beings with such disregard for even slight transgressions.
For those with malicious minds toward the teaching, for the sake of inspiring faith in the faithless,
for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, and for the sake of subduing the flesh-eaters.
However, for the purpose of subduing the wicked and pacifying those of gentle nature, this most excellent and supreme mantra has been taught; yet one should never employ it to take life.
This supreme and excellent mantra is declared to be the foremost among all worldly mantras, for the Vajra-holder of great supernatural power, and for all worldly deities.
This other supreme mantra is indeed known as the crown of all worldly deities; therefore, Śiva is the single-syllabled [mantra].
The Lord of all worlds is the master of worldly mantras;
the wise know him as Parameśvara, and the experts understand him as Svakāra.
All mantras whatsoever that are known as worldly are sung;
they are all indeed bound within this mantra and are honored everywhere. (Mmk 44.117)
These mudrās have indeed been prescribed by the best of sages and are to be employed everywhere;
they are considered most auspicious, supreme, the foremost among worldly things, and conducive to meditative concentration.
Indeed, they include Īśvara and others, as well as the mothers of the planets such as Vipaśyin,
and the flesh-eating Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Kaṭapūtanas, Yakṣas, and so forth.
These mudrās have been proclaimed for Viṣṇu, whose banner is Garuḍa, and also for Brahmā; they are prescribed as beneficial for subduing those who are difficult to tame.
For these mudrās have been declared by the wise to be praiseworthy and auspicious;
they are the causes for subduing, bewitching, and attracting spirits and beings.
But in a secluded place, always well-adorned with white flowers, thoroughly cleansed with the perfumes of the Siddhas, and with white sandalwood and saffron; Mmk_44.122 //
Having worshipped the Lord Sugata, the Lion of the Śākyas, the one of great merit, the sovereign lord of all mantras, with garlands of jasmine flowers; Mmk_44.123.
Having prostrated with devotion at all times before the Tathāgata, the Omniscient One,
as well as the Lord of Mantras, Lokeśa, and the Vajrī, according to one's ability;
With a concentrated mind, one should [worship] the great-souled Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the Dharmadhātu, the Guru, all the sons of the Buddhas, and the Buddhas themselves, in due order.
Seated upon a beautiful, moist bundle of *kuśa* grass or a sprout accompanied by milk,
one should be pure and facing the east.
In rites for pacification, one should face north; however, in the subsequent invocation, one should not face that direction.
One should not perform any rituals facing the temple of the deity.
Engaged in compassionate action toward all beings, one who is compassionate in the performance of mudrās should apply the mudrās everywhere; thus one shall accomplish every siddhi.
Facing east, one should certainly perform rites for prosperity and the summoning of mantras;
however, facing west, one should perform all rites pertaining to spirits for the purpose of subjugation.
One should know that when facing north, it is for pacifying rites that destroy all diseases;
however, one should never perform sinful acts or those that end in death while facing south.
Above, there is the destruction of obstacles; arise, O Lord of Pātāla, you who grant the supreme siddhi! At that time, perform the rite in the city of the asuras.
And she should turn her face downwards, being unopposed everywhere;
and in all intermediate directions, wherever she has taken her resort.
One should perform [these rites] in each of those [places], for they bring success to all embodied beings;
one who recites the mantra should perform the ritual of the mudrās and the fire-oblation (homa) everywhere.
Those situated therein attain accomplishment, as do those who are sealed by its mouth;
let the supreme rite be told—listen to it!
Having become pure in body and pure in clothing, composed in the purity of happiness,
one should employ this mudrā, which accomplishes all aims and is perfectly concentrated.
Raising both hands, one should [anoint them] with fragrances such as white sandalwood and saffron,
and with excellent incense free from animal products, including camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One who knows [the ritual] should prepare an excellent incense using saffron and other primary ingredients;
having offered various oblations, one should always perform the rites according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform the rite previously specified, as described in every ritual manual;
then, facing eastward, one should place both hands together in the gesture of a hollowed cup.
Then, having joined them together, they remain interlaced like a bamboo stalk with the fingers;
the two middle, the two little, and the two ring fingers are joined at their tips.
The two thumbs should be known as motionless, equal, and firmly established;
then, one should place them with devotion at the forehead, in the position of the head.
The salutation and likewise the mantra joined with six syllables:
the word *oṃ* followed by the word *namaḥ*, devoid of the utterance *svāhā*.
One should always recite the heart-mantra, which is free from the sound "huṃ," free from the sound "phaṭ," and is supreme, pure, auspicious, and foremost. Mmk_44.142 //
O Mañjuvara, this most excellent [mantra] for the one of beautiful form in the guise of a child is proclaimed as my heart-mantra, which subsequently assumes all forms.
These six should be known as the six-syllable mantras, the most excellent and supreme among heart-mantras; for this one is the foremost of them all, effective in all ritual actions.
One should employ this supreme seal-mantra in all ritual activities,
having applied it with proper method to the crown of the head and the region of the forehead.
One should move the middle fingers for the sake of subjugating all spirits;
and for the sake of attracting a deity, both tips of the thumbs should be bent.
One should constantly discharge the mantra-deities by means of those very [mantras];
likewise, one should dismiss the middle and the eldest [deities], as well as the Śrāvakas and the Supreme Sage.
With the two index fingers perpetually bent, one summons the Bodhisattvas born from the vajra and those who are lords of the ten stages; of this there is no doubt.
When the little fingers are joined and bent at the joints, it is called the *sarahva* [mudrā];
with this, one subdues yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas.
When this mudrā is fully worshipped, it treats the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, as well as the Yakṣiṇīs beloved by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), like a mother.
It bestows gain and loss, as well as constant desirable and undesirable fruits;
renowned as Mahāmudrā, it is sung of throughout the abode of the three worlds.
The wise one who has bound this seal and the great seal upon his head becomes invincible to all spirits; of this there is no doubt.
All obstacles and impediments pay homage from afar;
possessing merit equal to that of Great Brahmā, one will certainly attain awakening.
Thus concludes the forty-second chapter, the extensive section on the Great Mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
(Vaidya 383) Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
