Then those sisters, together with their brother, trembling and oppressed, overcome by a shudder and seized by fear, approached from the four directions through the power of the Bodhisattva and uttered these words: "Save us, O Blessed One Vajrapāṇi! Save us!"
We are afflicted, O Blessed One; we are deeply afflicted.
No other refuge exists. You alone, O Blessed One, are our refuge.
"You alone are our refuge."
In the meantime, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who were well-governed by the King of Vidyās within the Teaching,

as well as all sentient beings included within all states of existence, having been thoroughly disciplined and well-governed by the Great King of Vidyās through the power of the Lord of Vajras, remained there— those sisters together with their brother— terrified, thoroughly subdued, and wailing with piteous cries.
Then Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, addressed those goddesses together with their brothers:
"Do not fear, sisters; do not be afraid!
Go for refuge to the Buddha!"
Go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost among the two-legged; go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost among those free from passion;
the foremost among assemblies.
Then those sisters, with their brother as the fifth, went for refuge to the Buddha;
they went for refuge in this way,
and they went for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Then they became possessed of happiness and gladness, endowed with the highest happiness and gladness.

Perceiving themselves as released from their tight bonds, they were suffused with the joy and bliss of rapture; having attained serene faith, with the hairs on their bodies standing on end from supreme delight, they uttered this inspired exclamation:
"Oh, what a marvel has been attained here at the source of the Three Jewels!
Having gained this moment, we are made happy and forever freed from all miserable rebirths; our minds are now ever fixed upon the higher realms, heaven, and liberation."
Then, with a contented mind, look upon Mañjughoṣa;
having prostrated with your head at his feet, utter these words:
"O Protector from all sufferings, you are the refuge, O one of great splendor!"
O Protector, you who teach the profound, syllable-less state of all phenomena, you who have become a kinsman—to you, we pay homage. Mmk_47.30.
"Command me, O Great Hero, Lord of Mantras, Son of the Victors!
Why have we been brought here by Your Majesty? What command shall I carry out?"
Thus addressed, the heroic and all-pervading Lord, the son of all Buddhas,
being exhorted by the deities, spoke these sweet words.
Go once more for refuge, O son of the Conqueror, to Vajrapāṇi;
for the irreversible Saṅgha indeed arises from the foremost of Bodhisattvas.
Having first established the Three Jewels, the lineage-born son of the Supreme Victor,
and having aroused the mind toward awakening, be full of loving-kindness and eager for liberation;
then, having performed this everywhere, they struck at the state of self-abiding.
Then all those deities, having prostrated before the Son of the Jina and having fulfilled his command, turned toward where the Vajra-holder was.
Having quickly paid homage to that Vajrapāṇi of great splendor and having praised him, they all then stood with their faces turned toward him.
Then the maiden, together with her four brothers as a fifth,
having gazed upon him, stood looking at Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the yakṣas;
they became eternal refuges for the sake of the impermanent, goddesses adorned by the purpose of the impermanent.
He uttered sweet words, beautiful with his own mantras and their meaning:
"Homage to you, [the essence] of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power! (Mmk 47.38)
O one of great splendor, we shall explain the Pratyekabuddha-saṅgha, the assembly of non-existent yogins, and the extensive meaning of the mantras of the self.
For the sake of the people on earth to realize reality as it truly is,
and for the purpose of protecting the secret mantras that have issued from your mouth along with their esoteric secrets,
[compose] this ornament which serves as the foundation for the meaning of the mantras.
When this had been said, the Lord of Mantras, Vajrapāṇi of great splendor,
with a slight smile upon his face, looked out with a blossoming countenance.
He honored that maiden along with her brothers and circle of friends, saying:
"With my permission, you shall be free from all doubt."
Having proclaimed the extensive ritual manual together with its secrets and mandalas,
you shall always grant boons at all times to those beings who constantly worship you.
You are worshipped by the ṛṣis, by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras,
by the garuḍas, devas, and gandharvas, and also by the asuras of great supernatural power.
Together with the Kūṣmāṇḍas and all the Mothers, with Soma and Bhāskara, with the World-Protectors, the Lord of Wealth, and likewise the Vasus as they descend; Mmk_47.45.
By those lords of the gods, by the piśācas, uragas, and humans;
by the lords of spirits, the lords of the night, the flesh-eating vyantaras,
and by the chief lords of the rākṣasas who are fierce-minded and harmful— by these [this earth] is likewise [protected].
And by hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, by Yamas, and by Pretas of great supernatural power;
and also by humans and non-humans, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
"You shall be worshipped by the foremost of gods, the great elders, the siddhas, cāraṇas, and pūtanas, as well as by yogins and the sons of the Victors."
There is no doubt regarding the powers and the excellent sequence;

There are ninety million mantras with their extensive tantras and ritual manuals;

If the caravan leader Tumburu were to sing for nine koṭis [of years],

"All this is known as Śaiva by all the inhabitants of the earth;

Afterwards, other people spoke of the various ritual manuals (kalpa) and mantras individually:

The vastness of the eons for this Śarva, the one with matted hair, is infinite;

"Then you are indeed authorized before the King of Kali; therefore,

always speak at length regarding the mantras and tantras, together with their secrets, their mysteries, and even their most profound esoterica, which bring about the arising of happiness for all sentient beings."

remained silent for a while upon the raised jewel-lotus.
Then those maidens, together with their brothers as the fifth, quickly prostrated before the Lord of Mantras, the Lord of Yakṣas, the son of the Supreme Victor.
He addressed the great hero Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign lord of the masters of mantra and the all-pervading one,
with sweet words, one by one in due order.
I shall now describe the mandala briefly, which possesses two arms;
they call it the "Supreme Mandala," for Jayā sang the supreme [mantra].
In a solitary, secluded place, when the great crowd has departed,
in a hidden spot free from congestion, on a riverbank or a mountain peak.
In a secluded and delightful forest, in a dwelling occupied by the Buddha,
in an empty temple, or in a purified empty house.
On a single, auspicious, and beautiful tree situated by the great ocean;
in a cremation ground with a solitary linga, free from smoke and dust;
and at the most meritorious Vajrāsana or the magnificent Dharmacakra.
Where the Buddha attained peace, where the Great Sage was born—
these places are preeminent and auspicious for drawing a mandala;
likewise, everywhere along the banks of the Gaṅgā, as well as on islands and sandy shores.
And on all the banks of those foremost rivers which have been celebrated and are renowned throughout the world, one should constantly draw the maṇḍala.
On all sides, extending to the ends of every waterway and submerged within the great ocean—
the rivers flowing from the Himavat and Vindhya mountains reach the edge of the waters at the sea—
one should, on the banks of the most excellent of rivers, prepare and draw the mandala.
Or else, in a secluded spot on the earth, or in a beautifully adorned dwelling, or in delightful temples of the gods, or even at a very lofty stūpa.
Likewise, in a reliquary containing relics, in a shrine, or in ponds, wells, and pathways.
On all those banks and also in their centers, they are beautifully adorned with cow-pens,
lotus ponds, various water-reservoirs,
or other excellent sites, constantly beautified by monasteries and groves.
On the earth frequented by sages, there is satisfaction for one whose mind is as desired;
it is marked by mountain peaks, planets, and caves along with their surrounding slopes.
With divine dwellings that are peaceful, devoid of living beings even among the planets, conducive to meditation, praiseworthy, and frequented by the foremost of sages; Mmk_47.70.
Or rather, one should draw the mandala wherever the mind finds satisfaction;
for in these places, when properly honored according to the instructions, [the practice] is always effective.
The deities will swiftly descend and establish their presence;
in that place, the ritual procedure consists of the constant performance of recitation and fire offerings.
Those mantras to be accomplished— whether they be of the highest, lowest, or middling grade—
all these mantras indeed attain accomplishment here in the fields of accomplishment that have been proclaimed.
All mantras—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are indeed accomplished;
for there are various accomplishments in this world, and the ritual procedures are likewise of three kinds.
Mantras are of three types according to the threefold division of time;
at the three junctions of the day, all mantras are oriented toward the results of their threefold activities.
Peaceful rites are prescribed in the auspicious mandala called Jaya;
those for the sake of nourishment in the one called Vijaya; and malevolent rites in the one called Ajita.
Likewise, for minor rites, that which is designated as "Aparājita" should always be used;
however, for all rites, the knower of mantras should draw the one called "Tumburu."
Five mandalas are to be known for those dwelling in the ocean;
one should dig into the earth a square shape on all sides, as merely prescribed.
Having again purified an area of four or eight cubits by hand, one should remove gravel,
charcoal, husks, hair, and refuse.
Then, having personally cleansed with his hand that ground defiled by skulls, bones, and excrement,
he should recite the mantra over all the refuse there while others do the same.
The practitioner, having diligently cleansed [the vessel] which is infested with worms and insects,
should fill it with pure and fragrant earth from the forest.
With [clay] produced on a riverbank, which is pure, or from the top of an anthill,
or from between the ground of a cow-pen, or with other earth-born substances.
Having covered it on all sides with sand, or else with earth mixed with cow dung, one whose mind is serene [should do so] on every side.
One should quickly smear [the image] all over with various unctuous substances mixed with fragrances, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and smeared with saffron.
Having carefully smeared the ground all around with clay, the knower of mantras and the knower of the mantra-tantras should indeed prepare the mandala on every side.
With various powders of the five ingredients, scented with incense,
one should draw the divine maṇḍala, measuring four cubits on all sides.
A mandala measuring eight cubits is called the largest;
four cubits is the smallest, while that which is in between is proclaimed as the medium.
The renowned [mandala] is five cubits, and that which is released by the left hand is six cubits;
this is declared to be the measurement of the mandala for all the goddesses together with their brothers, being square on all four sides.
One should draw the divine maṇḍala, which has four gates, four corners, and is adorned with four archways; it is praiseworthy and beautiful in form.
In the center, one should draw the Youthful One (Kumāra), beautifully adorned with the ornaments of a child,
possessing a complexion like the color of saffron, standing in the middle of the left side,
and graced by a blue lotus held in his hand on all sides.
The great lord Mañjughoṣa, the deity who bestows boons, holds in his right hand a long, auspicious *śrīmāla* fruit.
With eyes slightly opened, one should indeed draw the deity of the slight glance all around with the right hand, as well as the great ocean.
Standing there, one should draw the Goddess seated upon a boat with her five brothers,
all well-attired and of beautiful form, for those who possess the mantras and vidyās.
Adorned with various ornaments, brandishing various weapons,
possessing the appearance and gestures of maidens, yet exhibiting the prowess of young princes accompanied by their brothers.
Tumburu [protects] the female caravan leader who has embarked upon a ship with her brother as the fifth member, accompanied by a helmsman.
The great ocean stands all around within the mandala,
filled with creatures such as fish and others, abounding in bubbles and honored by the waters.
The wise one should draw the maṇḍala in a secret, secluded place on all sides,
exactly as prescribed by the ritual rules and as the reality has been proclaimed. (Mmk 47.97)
One should cause all that to be performed quickly and employ it among worldly people;
whatever [rites] exist in this Śaiva Tantra and also in the Gāruḍa Tantra—Mmk_47.98.
By Brahmā and the other foremost sages, by Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Kāśyapa, and also by the excellent sages Mārkaṇḍeya, Pulastya, and Agasti; Mmk_47.99 //
By the Vasus and the Śakra-devas, by Rudra, Indra, and the Sun,
by various preeminent beings, and by Yama and others who possess great supernatural power among the pretas.
Together with the planetary mothers and kūṣmāṇḍas, who are worshipped by yakṣas and rākṣasas,
they are masters of mind and possess great supernatural powers in the world of humans and non-humans.
Honored by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra throughout the expanse of the eons,
the entire majesty of the eons has been proclaimed upon the earth.
In that maṇḍala, they should be applied; they will achieve success here, without a doubt, through various primary wombs and various forms of activities.
They have spoken and will speak at length on the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the goddesses;
at that time, one should employ it in the mandala called Jaya.

Thus concludes the first chapter from the forty-fifth section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, entitled "The Most Secret Chapter on the Entry into the Maṇḍala of the Four Sisters and its Samaya."
(Vaidya 413) Now follows the forty-eighth chapter. Then, indeed, the goddess named Vijayā, having gathered there in that very assembly, sat down.

He spoke this procedure for accomplishing the ritual service of his own maṇḍala: "First of all, in a secluded place, hidden and private, one should draw the maṇḍala with five-colored powders— namely white, black, yellow, red, and green— on the fifth day of either the bright or dark fortnight, or on the fourth day."
One should draw a great ocean in the center of the mandala, measuring four cubits on all sides, square with four corners, adorned with four archways, and embellished with four mudrās.

In the center is the Sārthavāha, having the form of a mudrā-mandala and the luster of the moon; in the northeast corner is the mudrā of Jayā, white and shaped like a half-moon; in the southeast corner is the mudrā of Vijayā, triangular in shape.

In the southwest corner, one should form the seal of Ajitā in the shape of a noose, with a reddish glow; in the northwest corner, the seal of Aparājitā in the shape of a vajra, appearing black; and all the seals should be depicted as being garlanded with flames.
Having first become pure in conduct, one should place four full jars at the four corners, their mouths covered with mango sprouts and their interiors filled with all kinds of grains and jewels.
In the center, however, the fifth jar for the caravan leader Tumburu should likewise have its mouth covered with mango sprouts and be wrapped in fresh cloth.
And just as it was for the mudrās, so too should the offerings of bali, food, flowers, and so forth be prepared.
The colors, flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth—all of these should be prepared in that same manner.

An offering (bali) should be cast in the four directions. For malevolent rites (abhicāruka), it should be performed at midnight or midday; for nourishing rites (pauṣṭika), at dawn; for pacifying rites (śāntika), in the afternoon or when the sun has set. Furthermore, these three types of rites should be performed according to the prescribed times during the construction of the maṇḍala, the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation (japa), and the accomplishment (sādhana).
It should be applied.

Pure men and women of skillful character, who are free from distress, should be admitted; likewise, female attendants who maintain the secret mantras should be admitted first. Having positioned them facing east, one should consecrate water with the root mantra of Vijayā, reciting it seven times, and sprinkle it over everyone.
This applies to those who have fasted for one day and night, are dressed in clean garments, and number from eight down to one, entering through the rear door while facing east.
Having covered each one with a fresh cloth, having bound the mudrā of Vijayā upon each, and having formed the añjali gesture and offered yellow flowers, he should cause them to enter.
Having recited the mantra of Vijayā and wiped their faces, he should cause them to behold the maṇḍala.
One should cause them to perform circumambulations and show all the mudrās;
then, they should be admitted one after another in sequence until eight have entered.
First, one should invoke the deities together with their brothers using the invocation mantra and the root mantra, respectively, with appropriate flowers.
Having first and then offered incense and performed the appropriate salutation, wherever the disciple— whether a woman, a man, a boy, or a girl— is capable,
he should be consecrated outside that maṇḍala like a king, with all necessary implements or according to his preference.

One should consecrate [the disciple] with that mantra of the maṇḍala-ācārya by which he might be pleased, or with that by which [the deity] might be pleased. Having been consecrated, one or three should be consecrated by means of the noble consecration (āryābhiṣeka).
And one thing must be said:

"Listen, noble son or daughter of good family! Others than those should be consecrated with the consecration of knowledge;

As for the rest, having instructed them in the practice of their own mantras, they should be dismissed.
Then, the mandala master, having sprinkled [the deity] with sandalwood water and offered the *argha*, should dismiss the deity with his own mantra using incense, flowers, and so forth.
All the ritual implements should be taken by himself.
Having taken one's own portion, a third part must be given to all those who are destitute;
the remainder should be cast into the water.
Having thoroughly smeared that spot of earth, making it very beautiful and free from dust, one may depart as one pleases.

They should be instructed in their own mantra practices accordingly. All disciples should be made to bind the mudrās of their respective deities in a secluded, private place, free from the movement of people.
By means of those very mantras previously specified, all mantras will attain accomplishment with particular excellence.
Especially regarding the mantras for rites that bring swift accomplishment,

Prescribed by the ritual rules for that [deity], in the auspicious mandala named Vijaya,

In the second mandala, called Vijaya, which accomplishes all aims, there is the overcoming of obstacles and the commencement of undertakings that are destined for fruition.
Through seeing [the deity], the knower of mantras releases a person from all long-standing sins; through recitation and yoga, purification from evil arises.
And there shall be the defeat of other mantras on this earth—

In this world, that which arises from karma is fruitful, accomplishing nourishment, peace, and all goals;
for this one, born from the ocean of the maṇḍala, is indeed the accomplisher of all aims.

This is the fifth great mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all activities.
"O Blessed One, it is precisely this that the five great mudrās become, bestowing the fruit of all desires."

Vijayā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, there are five great mudrās of mine. Having placed the left hand inside so that the nails are not visible, one should form a firm fist; then, by means of the yoga of striking and wiping away, one should look downward.
This is the first great mudrā."
The second is for looking upward;
the third for looking toward the southern direction; the fourth for grasping all directions;
and the fifth is placed upon the head.
These very five great mudrās are the bestowers of the fruits of all desires.

Ajitā spoke thus: "Having joined both hands together and inserted both thumbs into the middle, forming the shape of a hollowed *añjali*; having made the middle fingers like needles and the little fingers raised in the shape of a noose; and likewise pressing down the index fingers and the ring fingers—this is the Great Mudrā named Ajitā."
The meritorious one who subdues the difficult to tame and accomplishes the purpose of all actions—
precisely that mudrā one should direct toward the southern direction;
the second great mudrā is named Vijayā.
In this way, one should not cause [the deity] to descend from the western direction;
this is the great mudrā named Jayā.
In this way, one should not cause [the deity] to descend from the northern direction.
There is a great mudrā named Aparājitā;
in this manner, one should cause her to appear in the eastern direction.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Mahāsārthavāha exists;
these very five Great Seals are the fulfillers of all hopes.
Aparājitā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, there are exactly five great mudrās for me.
Having washed the hands as before, they should be bound during the dark fortnight.
They are to be applied according to that same procedure as in this sādhana."

Standing facing south in front of the goddesses, one should join both hands together; forming a trident with the middle, ring, and index fingers and so forth in the shape of three prongs, and inserting the little fingers, the middle [palms], and the thumbs into the center, one should then place them upon the surface of the hand at the position of the head.

First, there is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Aparājitā; in this manner, all [seals] should be employed, just as with Ajitā. Whatever be the names of the sisters together with their brothers, the Great Seals for all of them shall bear those same names.
That which is this palm of the hand is the ocean;
that which is this thumb is the brother Tumburu; and these fingers are all the sisters known by their successive names:
the index finger is Jayā, the middle finger is Vijayā, the ring finger is Ajitā, and the little finger is Aparājitā.
Following this sequence, one should apply [the practice] with the feet alone.
When meditated upon and saluted, they manifest their presence; when visualized, the mudrās become effective, whether intentionally or unintentionally.
The great mudrās, which perform all actions and fulfill all hopes, should be meditated upon when one is in a state of distress;
then no fear will arise.
Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke thus: "Now, there is a general designation for these remedies. And there is the power of our medicinal herbs by which all spirits are brought under control.
What, then, is that?"

Having likewise formed the mudrā, one should have her drink it while facing east; thus the woman will conceive a child.
One gives birth to a long-lived son; one should sleep with a good husband.
Taking the root of those very [plants] under the constellation Mūla, when the moon is in the northern direction, one should have fine powder prepared on a Sunday.

One should act in such a way that [the essence] enters the bodies;
one touches with speech and attends upon it with being. That very [essence] is the sprout; by that same procedure, one should drink it from the woman as well as from oneself.
Even if one approaches a hundred women, his semen remains uninterrupted;
likewise, it produces a large penis even in a woman.
A *gorjaruka* or a centipede, along with human semen, should be ground into a powder and drunk with milk by one who has a hundred women in his household.
In this manner, having excluded one's own primary mudrā accompanied by its mantra, everything else—including poison and secondary poisons—should be employed.
And in all rites, the supreme subjugation of all beings is to be accomplished.
Jayā said: "Taking the root of Jayantī, one should perform it in such a way that it accomplishes all the rites of Tumburu.
Now, if one should desire to travel through the sky:

having wrapped the root of Jayantī with the three metals (triloha), on a Monday joined with the Puṣya asterism, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, on the full moon, or on the fourteenth or eighth day, one who has fasted for three nights and is pure [should take] it mixed with saffron."
Having prepared it, they should be cast into one's mouth.
When the lunar eclipse has ended, [the pill] becomes invisible.

Having recited one hundred thousand syllables of one's own mantra and cast in the pill when the lunar eclipse has ended, one becomes a *vidyādhara*, able to assume any form at will, moving wherever one desires, and lives for twenty thousand years.
When it is vomited out again, it is seen once more;
thus, in a human being, it performs all its functions once again.
Vijayā spoke thus: "However, there is this distinction:

having taken *agasti-vandāka* and ground it with *jyeṣṭha*-water or divine water, one should consecrate it with one's own mantra and smear it on the feet; thus one performs the going and coming for a hundred *yojanas*."
One should act in the same manner until one abandons it without weariness;
having grasped the root of *vijayā*, one should proceed likewise,
for in this way one accomplishes everything through *jayā*.
Ajitā spoke thus: "Having taken the root of Ajita, one should proceed exactly as described;
it accomplishes everything.
Aparājitā spoke thus: "Having taken the root of Aparājitā, together with its white and black leaves, fruits, and roots, one should proceed in every respect exactly as the caravan leader did."
However, this is the distinction:
it acts swiftly and is accomplished quickly. Putrajīvarī, Kṛtāñjali, Sahā, Sahadevā, and Mahauṣadhī.
Likewise, the goddess Chatrādhicchatrā, the renowned Mahākāla,
Nākulī, Gandhanākulī, and Saṅkucitakarṇikā.
Having taken the roots of these [plants], one should have powders of *śūrpa* prepared;
by this, as soon as they are sprinkled upon them, embodied beings come under one's control.
The husks of red śāli rice, saffron together with sandalwood,
combined with musk, and immersed in divine water— Mmk_49.3.
The knower of mantras should fashion a pill from the three metals as prescribed;
having made it the size of a seed of the *akṣa* tree, he should then place that pill in his mouth.
During a lunar eclipse or at night, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind;
at dawn, having accomplished the mantra, the embodied being proceeds wherever he desires.
The pill always remains in his mouth as he performs the recitation;
or, assuming the form of any animal at will, he wanders everywhere across the earth.
Likewise, when it has been recited, the practitioner becomes one whose mind is fixed on the recitation;
otherwise, if it remains in the mouth, it would always take on a universal form.
One who has performed the recitation is distinguished by protecting oneself with one's own mantra;
otherwise, the pill is stolen if the reciter does not provide protection.
All mantras, including the king of mantras belonging to all worldly realms,
are accomplished through the worship of all ritual manuals (kalpas) spoken by all [the Buddhas].
They attain success in this [tantra] as taught in the mantra-tantras.
They roam the entire earth, assuming various guises;
dwelling in different states of existence and wombs, they take the forms of dogs,
crows, cats, owls, mice, frogs, and scorpions.
Crowded with all types of origins, bodiless yet residing within bodies,
they wander the entire earth, uttering the cries of all living beings.
When all beings are under control, when they are intent on the arising of what is dear to all creatures,
and when mortals always act accordingly— at that time, one should employ them. (Mmk 49.12)
It is not spoken of to others in the world, for it is honored by the deities;
it is to be known as all-encompassing in every respect, and the accomplisher of all mantras.
Whatever has been spoken, and whatever other men on earth shall speak— all that [is contained] in this extensive collection of ritual manuals (kalpavisara) as taught here by the Mothers of the World.
Thus addressed, the gods, together with Sūtrāntasaha as the fifth,
remained silent and stood there, having bowed to the Bull among Conquerors.
He sat within that most excellent assembly to hear the Dharma,
[receiving] the empowerments of all the Buddhas and the sons of the Jinas without exception.
Having requested the Great Hero, they remained silent thereafter;
then the glorious Vajradhṛk worshipped the deities.
Out of a desire to benefit those beings, he gave them his approval, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Therefore, O maidens, remain diligently within the pledge."

Thus concludes the third chapter from the forty-seventh detailed section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, entitled "The Detailed Section on All Rites, Mantras, Tantras, Herbs, Mudrās, and Rules for Recitation as a Means for the Four Maidens."

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, the general of the yakṣas, was present, having assembled in that assembly.
Having sat down, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, regarding that wrathful king named Yamāntaka who was spoken of by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, [please explain] its ritual manual (*kalpa*) in detail."
It was not revealed by the Blessed One, nor by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
O Blessed One, it is I who, having regard for future generations at the time when the Blessed One has passed into parinirvāṇa and the teaching is on the verge of disappearing, [shall reveal it].
In this present time of great terror, in this lowest of ages, in a buddha-field devoid of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,

for the sake of protecting the teaching of the Tathāgata, for the sake of the long endurance of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), for the sake of warding off all wicked kings, for the sake of subduing those who harm the Three Jewels, and for the sake of fulfilling the inconceivable bodhisattva conduct through skill in training sentient beings—
And, O Blessed One, for the sake of bringing about the inconceivable maturation of sentient beings, in the final age, in the final time of the Sugata,
when the destruction of the teaching is occurring, whoever shall employ this King of Wrath named Yamāntaka according to the ritual prescribed in the manual, for him there will be success.

This King of Wrath must certainly be employed against wicked kings and those beings who harm the teachings, as well as against great yakṣas who are highly energetic, engaged in both subduing and favoring others, and devoid of great compassion;
it is not for others.
Then the Blessed One entered the samādhi called "The Empowerment of the Buddha’s Miraculous Transformation" through silence.
Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, also remained in silence.
And the entire circle of the assembly experienced a sixfold earthquake.
The hosts of gods were terrified, and all the lords of the children were struck with fear;
so too were all the gods, the nāgas, the lords of the dānavas, and the mātṛs.
All the hosts of deities, headed by the chief grahas, trembled;
humans trembled with broken minds, and the pūtanas were filled with evil intent.
Then those kings, distressed and terrified, with fierce minds,
sought refuge in the teaching of the King of Dharma.
Terrified of the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great splendor, and of Mañjughoṣa the Youth himself, that king of mantras then made a covenant in the presence of Mañjughoṣa.
"O Child, you who have compassion for all beings, save us!
Today we shall consume you with extremely terrible and cruel mantras.
For today, overcome by wrath, we stand upon the surface of the earth."
Then the Bodhisattva, of great splendor, appearing in the form of a youth, said:
"Do not fear, O all you gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and dānavas!"
I have indeed declared this commitment to you, which is not to be transgressed by any deities,
nor by humans or non-humans, nor by any beings whatsoever.

Always maintaining a mind of loving-kindness, one should constantly recollect that mantra— the Perfectly Awakened One, the foremost among bipeds, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men. (Vaidya 428) Mmk_50.8 //
By him alone was the mantra spoken, beginning with Uṣṇīṣa and including Locanā;
it is the teacher of the three worlds, the wheel-bearer, the mass of splendor, born of victory.
Vijayōṣṇīṣa and the other mantras, Padmapāṇi together with Lokita, the Lord Avalokiteśvara, Bhṛkuṭī, Tārā, and Yaśasvinī.
And the goddesses Sitavāsinī, Mahāśvetā, Yaśovatī, and Vidyā Bhogavatī, as well as Hayagrīva, the king of mantras. Mmk_50.11 //
For these mantras, issued from the Victor, are preeminent within the Lotus family;
the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch is the sovereign lord of all mantras.
Having recollected the God of gods, the Lord of Mantras of great splendor,
there arose from him a wrathful manifestation known by the name Yamāntaka.
The thoughts of Avalokiteśvara, arising from compassion,
were revealed by former Buddhas whose minds were drawn forth by great compassion.
That Tārā, spoken by Avalokita, delivers sentient beings;
she is a noble vidyā born of samādhi, designated as "woman," and possessing a conceptual form.
Then the Bodhisattva practices the supreme conduct of awakening throughout thousands of world-systems, indeed many times over in incalculable numbers.
Then the Goddess, wandering for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings,
assumed the form of a woman through the nature of mantra for embodied beings.
One should establish those beings who are to be disciplined by means of ritual rules in the vehicle of awakening;
thus has the inconceivable conduct of the bodhisattvas been revealed.
One should likewise recollect the heroic Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign lord of mantras,
and the goddess Māmakī, the lady of the family, who is honored throughout the three worlds.
Śaṅkulā, Mekhalā, the illustrious Vajramuṣṭi,
Krodhendratilaka, Śatru, Nīladaṇḍa, and Bhairava.
These hosts of female messengers, the wrathful ones, are proclaimed as the presiding deities of the Vidyās;
they are all preeminent in the Vajra family, for they are indeed protected by us.
Likewise, Gajagandha, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power in the world;
and Mahāsthānagata, the wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
But whoever at that time should remember Samantabhadra, the most beautiful and foremost of sons, for them no fear shall exist.
As well as Maṇibhadra, and the supreme Yakṣa Jambhala, who are ever-present— how could there be any fear from any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas? (Mmk 50.24)
Through recollection and worship of them, great protection is proclaimed;
then, O gods, there is the vast fruit and the merit of those who are beyond conceptualization.

To the goddess who assumes a female form, who is free from passion and possesses great supernatural power, who indeed performs worship to the Three Jewels and is devoted to the teaching of the Jina; Mmk_50.26.
When they no longer experience any fear regarding friends or enemies,
that is said to be the "pledge" (samaya) there, which must not be transgressed by any practitioners of mantra.
This is proclaimed as the supreme wrathful [mantra] of Yamāntaka;
when beings abide in this commitment (samaya), all humans shall not devour them.
Then all those gods and non-human beings, with joyful minds, stood together in agreement with the son of the Jina, Anubuddhi.
Then the Yakṣa general, enraged at the words of defeat,
caused all the innumerable world-systems to tremble.
Why was this King of Wrath revealed by the Sons of the Conquerors in the past? It was for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings, yet it appears to be useless.
"The power of the King of Wrath has been proclaimed as it was in the past.
Having spoken thus, the Vajra-holder then cast down his vajra and stood still.
Then, having laughed, the wise youth Mañjughoṣa, possessing great supernatural power and appearing in the form of a boy, uttered these words: Mmk_50.33 //
Do not be corrupted, O great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power;
for this King of Wrath of great supernatural power has been revealed by me.
I shall grant you the mantra; reveal it as you wish, for it is not possible for you to fully describe the power of Krodha.
For this one, established in that very state, is seen here dwelling within the body;
indeed, by him you have been drawn [to me], if you ask about your heart.
For it is not possible to turn back one who is possessed by anger here, O Lord;
therefore, having granted permission, reveal as you wish, setting aside the [usual] rule.
When [the practitioner] has not bathed, is fast asleep, is engaged in vulgar conduct, has anointed himself with oil, is unprotected, or is always possessed by a wicked mind; Mmk_50.38.
Abandoned by all the best of mantras among those who are not serene toward the teaching,
such a mortal is full of doubt and lacks faith among those who are ill-situated.
They should be rejected by those established in the jewel-like Saṅgha of the True Dharma,
as well as by those who are naked, always impure with leftovers, and whose conduct and sphere of activity are unclean. (Mmk 50.40)
For in a place that is unprotected, devoid of mantras, constantly defiled by food remnants, and merciless;
or in the dwellings of the gods, at sacred shrines, or within the courtyards and mandalas of monasteries— Mmk_50.41.
There, those who delight in sexual intercourse will be destroyed by anger;
they have fallen from their commitments, yet they remain complacent, being ignorant of the application of mantras.
Their gait and conduct are faltering; anger shall strike them down.
Among all humans in the world, heedfulness is not found.

Those who are addicted to negligence and do not guard against the violation of their commitments are slain by the King of Wrath, even though they are practitioners of mantra who have failed to apply themselves properly.
In every way, all fools are subject to negligence,
with the exception of those who have transcended passion— the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas.
"All indeed are to be slain and punished in every way by the King of Wrath.
Thus was it said, O Mañjuśrī, by one whose mind was permeated with compassion.
"The conduct of the Buddhas and the great supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
Having spoken thus, they all then remained silent.
Then the glorious Vajradhara, having once again grasped the vajra, was delighted; and having received permission, he spoke thus.

Thus concludes the forty-eighth chapter, the detailed section on the description of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, the mantras, their greatness, and the rules of discipline, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas, having surveyed the entire great assembly circle, addressed all those hosts of beings seated above the Pure Abodes:

Listen, worthy sirs, to the procedure for the cloth-painting of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, as spoken by the Great Bodhisattva himself— of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, possessed of immeasurable strength and prowess, the tamer of the unsubdued, the ender of Vaivasvata’s life, and intent upon the subjugation of wicked beings;
first of all, there is the ritual for the painting.
Neither a specific lunar day nor a constellation is prescribed, nor is fasting required;
when fear of enemies has arisen, one should have this painting executed.
Having taken a corpse on the fourteenth or eighth lunar day during the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa, one should obtain the garment of a Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having taken it at night, one should dye it with blood;
thereafter, one should again perform purification with water and cause it to be thoroughly dried.
One should have a fierce, wrathful, and terrifying painter execute [the image] in a cremation ground during the dark fortnight; one should complete it in just three nights.
On the nights of the eighth and fourteenth days, the painter, stationed there, should always remain facing south, illuminated by a lamp fed with human fat.

Having performed the protection ritual and being composed, the mantra-practitioner— whether afflicted by the suffering and fear of enemies or not— should himself draw [the mandala] upon a human skull while seated.
When the first night has begun, even the enemy experiences great fear;
on the second, he is seized by a high fever and the enemy falls into a swoon.
If he releases his life-breaths on the third [day], he will have gone to the next world;
how could there be peace for him when the mantra-practitioner is displeased? (Mmk 51.8)
The body of the enemy indeed withers away and the destruction of his house occurs from thus painting the cloth of Yamāntaka during a great danger. *Mmk* 51.9.
One should draw [the deity] with six faces and six legs, black in color, with a large belly,
wrathful, and clothed in a tiger skin.
He wields various terrible weapons, holds a staff in his hand, and is fearsome;
he has blood-red eyes, is full of wrath, and is marked by the movement of the three-eyed one.
With hair standing erect and matted, smoke-colored in some places and resembling black collyrium in others, he is formidable, with a radiance like a monsoon cloud.
One should depict him resembling the form of Kṛtānta, mounted upon a buffalo,
performing cruel deeds, most terrifying, fierce, and the slayer of Rudra.
It truly brings about the destruction of twin lives, rises up as a slayer of beings, is cruel,
exceedingly fierce in all its actions, and is terrifying, calamitous, and dreadful. (Vaidya 432) Mmk_51.14 //
Having drawn this supreme wrathful one, the terrifier of all embodied beings who strikes fear even into fear itself, using one's own blood as pigment.
One should write with mixed substances, brilliant and blended with great animal fat and cow's ghee,
using vessels made of skulls and well-prepared from human bone.
Having fashioned tufts (*kūrca*) from the hair of a corpse,
he should draw [the image] himself or have it drawn by an artist, while remaining without food.

One should cause the excellent cloth [painting] to be adorned at the beginning, the end, and the middle with abundant offerings of food and flowers, red garlands, choice sandalwood, incense of human flesh and fat, and lamps of fat; this is the worship. Mmk 51.18.
Having clearly performed the *phaṭ* [mantra] and having given wealth to the artisan,
one should indeed provide a generous price by which he is always satisfied;
one must never harm him, and one should also practice the Dharma together with fearlessness.
One should perform for him, in brief, whatever is desired as the hero’s fee;
the work for the artisan should be fruitful, and one should avoid that which is devoid of reward.
One should employ [the ritual] in such a way that he is thoroughly satisfied;
great protection must also be performed, for otherwise he will die.
The practitioner, along with his family, perishes; therefore, one should protect oneself.
The recitation of the vidyā must be performed by one who has mastered it; the ritual procedure is not prescribed for others.
Having made the cloth painting clearly manifest, or having seen it as desired by the mind,
one should perform all rites that are fierce and destructive to enemies.
Taking the excellent cloth, one should go wherever desired or wherever wished for,
[to encounter] great yakṣas, great kings, and those who are proud of their vast wealth.
[It is ineffective] for those with great pride and arrogance, the cruel and those who perform cruel deeds,
those who harm the Three Jewels, the nihilists, those devoid of mantra,
those who do not worship mantras, and those who revile the truth of its devotees.
And for those who revile the practitioners of recitation, as well as their defeat,
one should employ the ritual application according to the rite seen in the scripture.
Against those who are most unrighteous, ever-constant in their malice, and who cause suffering to all sentient beings,
one should employ a rite that immediately obstructs their life-force.
One should take the fruit, leaf, bark, and root of the *ariṣṭa* tree, along with sour gruel mixed with acidic substances and powdered human bone. (Mmk 51.28)
Pungent oil, poison, sour vetasa, fresh ginger, black mustard, and blood originating from human beings; Mmk_51.29.
Having taken all the required materials and placed the cloth in a secluded place,
one should face south while the cloth faces north.
Having prepared a fire-pit as desired with white wood produced from pungent trees,
and having kindled it with thorny branches, one should, being composed, offer into that pit all the sacrificial substances combined according to the prescribed ritual.
Furthermore, having summoned Agni with the mantras of the Wrathful King,
one should bind the trident mudrā in all rites here.
One should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire-pit with wrath;
when the first being has been reached, there shall be the death of a son.
In the second [dream], his wife indeed appears, along with his courtiers and leaders;
in the third, there is the death of that person for whose sake the rite was performed.
When the recitation is performed at midnight in the presence of the cloth-painting for the purpose of slaying enemies, it proceeds exactly according to that intent.
The destruction of his kingdom shall occur, and calamities shall arise within his army;
fire, great winds, and heavy rains shall break forth.
The entire wheel is struck from all sides by the wheel of others;
he shall be beset by various calamities and overwhelmed by great diseases.
The entire body of that king will surely wither away; there is no doubt about this.
His entire house will be crowded and agitated by non-human beings.
He finds no peace upon his bed and tosses about upon the ground;
his house is surrounded by *rākṣasas*, *pretas*, and flesh-eating demons.
Afflicted and deeply distressed by intense sufferings, he fears everywhere;
the gods on earth, such as Maheśvara and others, are powerless to protect him.
Brahmā and the other world-protectors, Śakra and the other lords of the thirty-three gods,
all mantras, all deities, and everything that arises in the mundane world.
For one who is wicked, arrogant, and angry, his life shall end there;
for at midnight or at midday, wherever the reciter speaks,
the enraged Vaiśravaṇa becomes manifest as Yama, the King of Death himself.
Having placed the cloth-painting on the ground at will during the dark fortnight,
and having performed a great worship and offering of oblations produced in a cremation ground or a forest, [one should proceed]. (Mmk 51.43)
Likewise, under a single tree, at a linga, on a mountain, on the edge of a forest, or in caves,
one should always undertake the ritual practice alone and without a companion.
In the great forest, in a secluded place, in empty temples,
in an empty mansion, by a river, or on the shore of the ocean.
In that place, or nearby, or while staying there as desired,
one should always cause the rites to be performed within a range of up to a hundred *yojanas*.
One should always have these rites of measurement performed by a pure person;
or else, one who abides in the immeasurable, having gone to the immeasurable realm, being pure [may perform them].
In the realm of inconceivable mantras, the scope of mantra is inconceivable;
the miraculous power of mantras is inconceivable, and the success of those who recite them is inconceivable. Their activity appears as inconceivable, and their fruit is likewise inconceivable.
The great-souled Yamāntaka, King of Wrath,
possesses a field of miraculous power and a transformative activity of great success;
the inconceivable accomplishment of those who possess form is indeed seen upon the surface of the earth.
All Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are unable to protect [one];
how much less so can worldly mantras, along with the grahas and those mātṛs?
Īśāna together with Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Purandara— even they,
along with the Victors and the sons of the Victors, have been bound by you under oath.
Even the great-souled Bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages,
as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who are free from passion and possess great supernatural powers,
were unable to protect the pledge formerly made by them.
I shall speak in brief; listen, you who desire the welfare of beings!
No one else is capable of turning back a reciter who is displeased; how then could there be peace for him here while the supreme mantra remains unsatisfied?

"Listen, O hosts of gods, and all you multitudes of spirits who have issued from the realm of sentient beings! Having smeared that *liṅga* with human blood, mustard seeds, and sour gruel, and having worshipped it with *picumarda* leaves;

They become powerless in all their activities.

In brief, however it is employed—even according to the ritual procedures of all worldly and transcendental mantras—he accomplishes all of that.
It accomplishes everything;

Having prepared a mandala in the place of one's head and burning guggulu incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times while remaining silent, alone, pure, and having closed the door. Within a month, she will certainly arrive at night.

If she enters his abode, he lives for five thousand years;
otherwise, she wanders right here in Jambūdvīpa.
She lives for five hundred years;
he sports with her and carries out all her commands.

Revatī is the most excellent of yakṣiṇīs; she is playful and fond of sexual union.

The Yakṣī, beautiful in all her limbs, who is always devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, bestows desires and enjoyments eternally; one should designate her as the giver of boons.

The mantra of Mekhalā is: *oṃ mekhale mahāyakṣiṇi mama kāryaṃ sampādaya svāhā*.
The mantra of Sumekhalā: Oṃ mekhale sumekhale mahāyakṣiṇi sarvārthasādhani oṃ samayamanusmara svāhā.

It causes even an enemy situated a hundred *yojanas* away to be slain;

surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of yakṣīs;

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand *priyaṅgu* flowers smeared with ghee at the three junctions of the day for one month;

On a wooden board, a cloth, or a wall, using non-adhesive pigments and brushes made from new vessels,

Clad in silk garments with a silken upper robe, golden-hued, and possessing a wonderfully beautiful form— one having painted such a cloth-painting in a clean place, while remaining pure and subsisting on a milk diet, should recite the vidyā ten thousand times.
Having performed a great worship according to one's ability, at the conclusion of the recitation, the yakṣiṇī, assuming a divine form, will herself appear, emitting a great radiance.

One should say, "Become my mother."
Having done so, he disappears;
yet one should not corrupt one's mind regarding that,
nor should one pray for anything connected with sensual desire.
That noble lady possessed great supernatural power, yet her desire was not fulfilled;
from that time forward, she performed all tasks for him like a mother,
providing food and clothing for him and his retinue of eight hundred.
It protects one who is in a precarious situation;

and it provides whatever food is desired.
He bestows all things, such as juices and elixirs;
he complies with whatever is desired;
and he conjures up dwellings, huts, and so forth.
He bestows a thousand pieces of gold day after day;
all of it must be spent on that very same day.
If he does not do so, his [merit] is severed.
It becomes entirely effective in every respect.
Furthermore, there is another rite for this [deity]:
having kindled a fire before this very cloth [painting] with *khadira* wood, using embers from which the flames and smoke have departed;
Having drawn an image with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) on the palm of the right hand and the name of a man or a woman on the palm of the left hand,
one should heat them upon that very heap of charcoal while reciting the mantra;
thus, one brings the woman even from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*.
Whatever is spoken, he causes all that to be done;
this rite is for the night, not by day.
The mantra of Naravīrā is: *oṃ naravīre svāhā*.
In the same manner, having had her image painted on a cloth, one should have it depicted as residing in an *aśoka* tree, excluding the cave-dwelling.
This is its specific distinction: the entire ritual procedure is exactly the same as that for Guhavāsinī.
And she should be addressed as "sister."
It has another ritual application:
during a lunar eclipse, one should wrap gold-colored ochre in birch bark, place it in the mouth, and recite the mantra until the moon is released.
Then, by writing the name of a man or a woman with that gold-colored ochre, one brings them forth even if they are situated a hundred *yojanas* away.
At dawn, she leads [the practitioner] to that very place;
she performs her duties like a sister;
and in times of calamity, she provides great protection.
By merely reciting [the mantra], one brings all women under control;
this is the ritual procedure for Naravīrā.
The mantra of the Yakṣakumārikā is: *oṃ yakṣakumārike svāhā*.
This is its ritual procedure (*upacāra*): it should be caused to be written on birch bark with bovine gallstone (*gorocana*).

A young girl (*kumārī*) with half-curly hair, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a single garment, holding a citron fruit in her right hand, and grasping a branch of an *aśoka* tree with her left hand, [should be depicted].
Such a birch-bark leaf should be placed above the location of the head.

One should sleep alone in a secret place. Having made a mandala with white sandalwood and having scattered jasmine flowers at the three junctions of the day while burning guggulu incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times for the duration of one month.

Then, on the full moon day, having performed a great worship with *jātī* flowers and having offered lamps of ghee and sacrificial foods, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra throughout the night until the daughter of Vaiśravaṇa herself arrives, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred maidens.
Having surveyed every quarter of the horizon, she remained in the sky in her own form and spoke thus:
"What should I do?"
Then the practitioner should say: "One of these three boons—one of motherhood, sisterhood, or wifehood—should be requested. If she becomes a mother...
One must not corrupt the mind;
for one who corrupts it, destruction arises.
One should behave toward them as toward a mother.
And that mother provides food, clothing, and various excellent ornaments for her retinue of five hundred merely by thinking of them;
she gives a thousand dīnāras every day,
providing everything for those wandering right here in Jambūdvīpa.
When she becomes a sister, then she brings a woman even from a hundred yojanas away;
she leads her right there and accomplishes all tasks just like a sister.
Then she becomes his wife and her own abode;
she lives for a thousand divine years.
When she dies, she is reborn into a wealthy family.
She carries out every command like a wife.
The mantra of Vadhuyakṣiṇī is: Oṃ niḥ.

This is Vadhuyakṣiṇī. Her ritual service (*upacāra*) is as follows: having smeared the right arm with white sandalwood paste, [one should apply] saffron empowered by a thousand recitations of the mantra.
Having acted alone and in silence at night in a secluded place, having closed the door, one should cast five or eight *vibhītaka* fruits into sesame oil and recite [the mantra].
Taking that oil and discarding the *vibhītaka* fruits, [one should place it] in a new vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay.

Or, having placed [the substance] at the foot of the bed and consecrated it one thousand times with this very mantra of the One-Syllable Yakṣiṇī, one should sleep in a secluded place in the darkness upon a bed strewn with flowers;
then the non-human female will arrive and anoint one's feet.
Her face was divine and the palms of her hands were soft to the touch;
by the mere touch of them, a divine sleep of pleasant contact would arise,
such that even at sunrise, at the end of the night, one would awaken with difficulty.
Even when awakened, one should contemplate that very same thing;
she must neither be desired nor spoken to with mantras.
Within six months, she becomes accomplished.

Then she, possessing a divine form, resembling a young bride in age, surrounded by female attendants, holding a lamp in her hand, illuminating the surroundings with her own radiance, carrying a bed and seat, and resplendent with various ornaments, arrives and speaks. Carrying the requisites for sensual enjoyment, she comes and embraces the practitioner around the neck.
From that time forward, she followed him like a beloved wife;
having arrived, she was to be desired, and after attending to him at night, she would vanish at dawn.
Leaving a pearl necklace worth a thousand gold pieces upon the bed, she would depart day after day.
Everything must be spent without remainder;
if one sets aside anything, it will not suffice again.
It must not be told to anyone.
If he says that [the practitioner] will not come again or will cause harm,
then these supreme Guhyakas— which are the ultimate secrets— will bring about death; for they do not tolerate revealing [the mantra] to a second being.
It must not be disclosed even to one's mother, father, friends, masters, or kinsmen;
it must not be entrusted even to animals or beings of the animal realm.
This is the supreme secret.
This very same procedure applies to all Guhyakas and all Yakṣiṇīs;
even those who have attained accomplishment become unaccomplished if they disclose [the secret].
And one should always avoid sexual intercourse with the wives of others, as well as with one's own wife during her menstrual period.
The mantra of Manojñā is: *oṃ manohare madonmādakari vicitrarūpiṇi maithunāpreye svāhā*.

Regarding her ritual service (*upacāra*): having caused a well-proportioned hut to be built beneath an *aśoka* tree in a garden grove—one that is most secret, with constructed doors, bolts, and high walls—a pure person should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Then one should begin the ritual action:
having collected human fat and made a wick with cemetery rags, one should close the door and light a lamp;
furthermore, one should place a clean cloth, free of hair, outside the door.
Freshly at night, she comes naked, puts on that garment, and enters having assumed the form of a human woman.
Then the practitioner enjoys himself with her as long as the lamp burns;
when the lamp goes out, she vanishes.
Having tied a single gold coin to that garment and discarded the garment, she departs from the bed;
then the practitioner seizes it by the hand.
Taking off a single finger-ring, he steps forward;

then from his neck a divine pearl necklace, then from his arm a bracelet, from his waist a girdle, from his feet an anklet, and from his head a jewel— thus, whichever various divine ornament is taken,
he gives it away wherever it is seized.
He goes and comes without being hindered.
In this manner, it must be spent entirely every day.
When he consults [the king] after such a number of months, then he should be consulted.
She becomes his wife;
remaining constantly present, she bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*) which, when drunk, enables one to live for a long time.
Having meditated with the mind, one should drive a stake of *khadira* wood into the ground.

once it has been raised, it vanishes.
This second mantra belongs to her.
"Oṃ mahānagni nagnije svāhā. Having lit the lamp with that very [mantra] and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with this mantra, one should employ it;
[the deity] will certainly come.
Furthermore, having consecrated a ritual stake (kīlaka) with the mantra, one should drive it into the ground.

When the lamp has been lifted and extinguished, there is disappearance. A human *kīlaka* (stake) and a *vasākīla* (fat-stake) should be carried on a horn—either a cow-horn or a buffalo-horn—to the cremation ground with a cloth-wick;
it bestows [the desired result] in another land, wherever one wishes.
Either he performs it himself,
or the mantras must not be given;

Whatever one gives to another, that very thing accrues to that person.

this accomplishment does not depart once it has been turned back.

Or he may cause another woman to take pleasure [with him], yet he does not converse with them. The mantra of Surasundarī is: *oṃ surasundari svāhā*.
Regarding the ritual service for this: having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter.

At the three junctions of the day for one month, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, sitting upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass in a clean place, the practitioner, being pure, should recite the mantra in secret until, at midnight, she certainly arrives.
Then the mother, sister, and wife act exactly as before; all of that should be performed, and everything should be explained in detail.
Thus, these seven yakṣiṇīs, by the command of Vajrapāṇi,

Some yakṣīs wander among the compassionate, fond of sexual union with mortals; others are noble, while still others are childish and deluded. Mmk_52.5.2.
Likewise, at night, she wanders about, intent on her desire for lions;
greedy for meat-eating, she seeks the destruction of the lives of children.
Likewise, drawn by the scent of blood, the yakṣī who takes life has come indeed to Jambūdvīpa; she is constantly fond of blood.
They roam through all houses, whether they contain a corpse or a birth;

Just as attachment and bondage are [described] here for the foolish,
so has all this been taught for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
Just as a practitioner seeking sexual union, blinded by passion and deluded in mind,
might summon and enjoy a yakṣī or a rākṣasī through mantras; so too [is this].
And likewise a nāgī, a gandharvī, a female daitya, and a kinnarī.

The wise practitioner of mantras should enter the delightful abode of Pātāla, the supreme city of the asuras, where there are countless women; having gone there, the knower of mantras who recites the mantra may dwell for an eon.
When the Perfectly Awakened One named Maitreya becomes a Buddha,

Having summoned a daughter of the asuras, a goddess, or a noble woman of the vidyādharas by means of mantras, he should then enjoy the delight of divine happiness.

For the foolish, supreme accomplishment may sometimes arise through that;

One should not touch a human woman, who is a vessel of suffering— of the pain of disease, as well as grief, ending in death, and the separation from those with whom one has shared delight.
Impermanent, suffering, likewise empty, void, insignificant, and non-eternal; it is a deception of the foolish, arising from conceptual construction.
The mantra practitioner should not pursue any desires born of beginningless craving;
the cessation of these is called liberation, and within them lies the attainment of accomplishment.
The mantras of one who is indeed detached from desire will truly succeed,
even when [the deity] is worshipped as being smeared with feces, urine, and blood.
One should not touch a human body afflicted by old age, death, and great sorrow;
therein, those whose minds are blinded by delusion and possessed of passion do not practice sexual union.
Success is not obtained by those who are always impure and devoted to mantras;
