Padmoccā, Samodā, and also Ajitā and Jayā always;
Śyāmāvarta and likewise the Yakṣī—these are the Yakṣīs of great supernatural power.
The mantra of Padmoccā is: oṃ padmocce svāhā.

The ritual procedure for this is as follows: on the bank of the Gaṅgā or at the shore of the ocean, having constructed a pavilion in the midst of a garden or flower grove, and having become exceedingly pure oneself, one should fashion a stone-slab-like form out of clay right there. Then, closing the door during that very night and bringing all necessary articles of enjoyment and pleasure, one should place them there near oneself for the Yakṣiṇī.
One should prepare a bed;
then one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times. In this way, within the span of a month, she will certainly arrive.
And having arrived, she becomes a wife who may be enjoyed for sensual pleasures;
casting off her divine pearl necklace and her bed, she departs at dawn.
In this manner, day after day, she becomes permanently established there within six months.

That pearl necklace must not be accepted; if one accepts it, one is reborn in that very state. After six months have passed, that necklace, worth a hundred thousand *dīnāras* and adorned with precious gems, becomes a permanent wife who grants all desires.
Having assumed whatever form is desired, she appears;
she manifests herself according to her own inclination.
This is the procedure for all yakṣīs according to the wish of the practitioner, as has been described here and elsewhere.
The mantra for victory: Oṃ jaye sujaye jāpayati sarvakāryāṇi kuru me svāhā!
The goddess Kanakābhā has variegated limbs and dark, curly hair; she is beautiful in every limb, auspicious, fortunate, and sublime. Mmk_52.6.1.

One should point out Jayā as having a pleasing voice, being the best among women, beautiful in form and lovely to behold, with praised limbs and a bright complexion, highly honored by all the world, and wearing slightly reddish garments. Mmk_52.6.2.
The ritual procedure for this is as follows: first, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.
Then, having entered a great forest and subsisting on fruits, one should continue the recitation until she appears in her own form.
And when she has arrived, she asks, "What shall I do?
If she is one's mother,
she fulfills all hopes like a mother.
It bestows sovereignty;
it makes one a master of great wealth;
and it grants the blessing of long life.
Then the sister brings whatever woman is desired, even one residing a thousand *yojanas* away; she gives a hundred thousand *dīnāras* day after day,
and that [wealth] must be spent.
Then she becomes his wife; he leads her to his own abode, mounts a divine celestial chariot with her, and enjoys himself with her.
For a long time—thirty thousand years—he wanders as he pleases.
He becomes like a great yakṣa.
The mantra of Pramodā is: Oṃ ṣṭhrīḥ hrīṃḥ mahānagni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Regarding its ritual procedure: at midnight, an immeasurable recitation (jāpa) should be performed.
One should go to sleep again;
within a month,
she will certainly come and become one's wife, granting all desires.
Day after day he gives him twenty-five dinars, and he himself provides him with clothing and keeps him alive for a long time.
In this way, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs;
likewise, there are piśācas, piśācas of great supernatural power, nāga maidens, asura maidens, apsarases, celestial women, and daitya maidens.
In the same manner, there are mantras for all the vidyādharīs, from every quarter, and for both human and non-human women.

Likewise, there are innumerable mantras of the yakṣas, gods, nāgas, ṛṣis, gandharvas, asuras, pretas, and rākṣasas, as well as those of Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, Mahāviṣṇu, the Mothers, and the goddesses headed by Aindrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Vārāhī; all these exist individually, and they have all been summoned here by the Wrathful King Yamāntaka according to the samaya.
She was brought, seized, established at the proper time, and offered to Mañjughoṣa; she followed as a retinue, standing in succession as a servant.

In brief, for all [these rites], wherever there is an image, one should either make a likeness oneself or recite the mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, until the reflection trembles, shakes, or perspires.
These come in their own essential form;
they accomplish everything that is commanded.

(Vaidya 448) Likewise, this same procedure applies even to those four maidens who are great yakṣiṇīs, accompanied by their brother Tumburu, possessing divine forms, dwelling upon the ocean, mounted upon a boat, highly honored by all the world, and acting for the benefit of sentient beings; namely:
Whether depicted on a cloth, a wall, or a wooden panel,
she is shown mounted upon a boat, yielding to her elder brother.
Having placed the maiden, who is like a clever woman, within the ocean and keeping her hidden from them,
one should begin the recitation while suppressing one's anger.
Trembling, shaking, and perspiration arise everywhere;
then, knowing that [the mantra] has been mastered, the reciter of mantras should cease the recitation.
At the end of the night, they declare the auspicious and inauspicious by their very nature;
indeed, those practitioners who perform the recitation become successful in every way.
When commanded by the excellent planets beginning with Soma, as well as by sages and likewise by rākṣasas, they all perform [the task], drawn forth by wrath and overcome by it.
Those of great supernatural power are well-honored by the Piśācas and the Garuḍas;
those of great supernatural power are likewise honored by Maheśvara and other such beings.
And by these [Buddhas], the rituals (kalpa) for the mantras and tantras have been taught in detail;
all of them, along with their ritual manuals and extensive procedures, should be put into practice.
All those [beings], as many as there may be— whether they be mantras, withered ones, or those arising from dejection— remain effortlessly under the power of the King of Wrath.
All those noble mantras that are indeed distinguished and all-pervading have been appointed and revealed by the King of Wrath.
For these mantras have been spoken by the supreme Victors as excellent, preeminent, and foremost;
likewise, O mantra-holder, they have been proclaimed by me as well.
Furthermore, there are other principal mantras belonging specifically to the five families,
which were spoken by the sons of the Conquerors, as well as worldly ones possessed of great supernatural power.
Having drawn them all forth, the King of Wrath, possessed of great supernatural power,
binds them all here within this teaching by means of the mantras, tantras, and weapons.
Whichever procedure has been prescribed for those [deities], by that very one this Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, is enjoined; he is supreme and effective for all rites.
And Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, as well as Pāṇḍaravāsinī,
Mahāśvetā, the Vidyā, Māmakī, and she who is born from the vajra.
Uṣṇīṣaprabhā, the deity Sarvalocanā,
all the Tathāgata-vidyās, and the wise Mañjughoṣa.
Mahāsthāman, Samanta, and likewise the Lord Padmavara,
as well as the Bodhisattva Yakṣeśa of great supernatural power in the world.
As it was said: "The Son of the Conqueror, renowned throughout the world in all his limbs, Vajrasena, Suṣeṇa, and also my wise daughter."
The reciter should not treat with contempt those mantras spoken by me;
he should always honor them all, for they were spoken as inviolable.
The reciter should not employ the well-worshipped King of Wrath there;
one should never effect the severance of the vidyās within those mantras.
And likewise all worldly mantra-deities according to their respective rites,
including Umā, Śaṅkara, Brahmā and the others, as well as Hari who is well-worshipped.
Just as it has been done for all mantras in the tantras,
so too should one undertake every mantra from every source;
indeed, the manifestation of all mantras is seen to arise from the Wrathful One.
This mantra is the Great Wrathful One, known by the name Yamāntaka;
having summoned [the victim], it shall swiftly cause even the great-souled Yama himself to be slain.
Indeed, even Śakra [is subdued] by that high-souled one; he is Vaivasvata, the Ender (Kṛtānta), the attractor, the wearer [of the garland], the wise one, the master who tames the untamable.
This mantra, a great mantra, has been taught by Mañjubhāṣin;
it performs all rites, is fierce, and accomplishes all mantras.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Vajrapāṇi, possessed of great supernatural power,
bowed down to the Buddha, the Great Hero, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men; and relying upon the mantra, the Vajra-holder uttered the mantra of great supernatural power.
"Let all sentient beings indeed listen, as well as all the auspicious hosts of spirits;
I, the presiding lord of the host of universal loving-kindness, shall speak this supreme mantra."
This was spoken by the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa:
a formidable subduer of the difficult-to-tame, which wards off all that is evil.
However, for the sake of training sentient beings, it was spoken by the Bodhisattva;
and I too speak here, in the midst of this assembly, that which is most formidable.

Homage to all Buddhas, who have arisen from the nature of non-existence. Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas. Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the lords established on the ten stages, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
It is as follows: Oṃ kha kha.

Eat, eat, O tamer of wicked beings! You who hold a sword, mace, noose, and axe in your hands; four-armed, four-faced, six-legged! Go, go, O destroyer of great obstacles! You of deformed countenance, who strikes terror into all spirits! You who utter a loud laugh! You who are clothed in a tiger skin! Act, act! Perform all rites! Cut, cut all mantras! Attract, attract all spirits! Crush them!

Churn all the wicked! Enter, enter into the center of the maṇḍala! O ender of the life of Vaivasvata, accomplish, accomplish my task! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Shatter, shatter! O fulfiller of all hopes! O Blessed One, why do you tarry? Accomplish all my aims! Svāhā!
O worthy ones, O hosts of all the gods, this is he, the wrathful king named Yamāntaka, who brings even King Yama himself, slays him, withers him, cooks him, and subdues him.
In this way, he [subdues] all mantras and all gods; how much more so a miserable human being?
He brings even those bodhisattvas established on the ten stages.
How much more so, then, worldly mantras?
Thus, this King of Wrath possesses immeasurable strength and prowess;
likewise, he accomplishes all rites even among those spoken in all mantra-tantras.
Just as it is employed among all mantras, so does it act;
this King of Wrath named Yamāntaka is accomplished through mere recitation and is thus complete.

Thus concludes the third detailed chapter, the "Universal Rule for All Procedures" concerning the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Homage to the Buddha!
This concludes the ritual manual (kalpa) of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.
(Vaidya 451) Now begins the fifty-third chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having arisen from that samādhi, [addressed] the assembly-circle which was like the great ocean.
While teaching the Dharma, seated before all sentient beings and the entire assembly of spirits, he was surrounded by many thousands of incalculable bodhisattvas headed by Vajrapāṇi;
many thousands of incalculable arhats headed by Śāriputra; incalculable sons of the gods of the Four Great Kings headed by Vaiśravaṇa;

incalculable sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven headed by Śakra; and [the gods] from the Suyāma, Santuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, as well as those of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara realms, up to...
The Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, and Tṛṣṭātapākaniṣṭha gods addressed the assembly of deities:
"Listen, O hosts of gods, all Bodhisattvas, and noble Śrāvakas!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to the nature of arising and passing away."
For having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss.
All things arise through the power of ignorance, accompanied by their causes;
indeed, the aggregates, arising together with their cause, have been declared to be the root of suffering.
The knowledge that brings about their cessation— the performance of happiness which is the cause of happiness—
is called, in brief, the abandonment of suffering and its prevention.
That very threefold vehicle has been taught by me here:
that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and momentary.
It is taught that all the bonds of existence are always and at all times empty;
those beings who have emerged from their spiritual lineage proceed in three ways through detachment from them.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas, the Buddhas, those established in Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment,
as well as others who are free from passion, possessors of great supernatural power, and destroyers of the afflictions [will appear] day after day.
Relying upon the awakening of the śrāvakas, they have indeed attained the threefold peace;
this dharma, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been taught by me in brief.
One should always avoid what is unwholesome and always practice what is wholesome;
one should practice non-violence toward all beings, as the Dharma has been revealed.
There is but one single path for all phenomena within the five destinies:
that which is the untainted dharma, resting upon the limit of reality.
This very path has been taught by the ancient primordial Buddhas;
I too have explained it all, leading to peaceful nirvāṇa.
By relying upon the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is attained;
the limit of all phenomena is declared to be the limit of reality, which is itself without limit.
This Dharma has been revealed in brief as being of two kinds; let all the gods and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power listen! Mmk_53.12.
My arhats and śrāvakas, when my nirvāṇa occurred upon the earth,
took place in the midst of a śāla grove in the Himalayan valleys.
On the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī river, in the vicinity of the Mallas,
amidst the Yamaka-śālaka grove, my parinirvāṇa shall take place.
As long as there is perception, so too shall my nirvāṇa be upon this earth in that city, at the Makuṭavardhana shrine, and always on the delightful riverbank.
Indeed, all the bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas of great supernatural power,
as well as the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and the world-protectors of great supernatural power, [are present].
Śakra, Brahmā, Suyāma, and others such as those of Akaniṣṭha—
indeed, the assemblies of all of them will gather in that place.
There, in the Yamakaśālaka grove,
the funeral rites for the Mallas were performed on the northern bank of the Ganges, that great river.
On the southern side of the Himalayas, in the Sāla forest,
my final resting place shall be in that very spot.

Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

one then becomes a Vidyādhara-banner-holder.
Unimpeded everywhere,

on the auspicious day of the full moon during the fortnight of miracles, one should perform a great worship before the cloth painting. Having prepared a maiden who is graceful, well-bathed, and adorned, and having performed worship before the cloth painting according to one's means, one should stand holding her with the left hand and recite the mantra until it blazes together with her; by that very act, one becomes a *vidyādhara*.
Placing one's hand upon a solitary linga, one should recite the mantra until one's companions do not see [the manifestation].
One becomes invisible to all accomplished masters (*siddha*), unapproachable, and gains the power of disappearance (*antardhānika*).

On the thirteenth day, during a lunar or solar eclipse, one should place yellow orpiment behind a leaf of the Bodhi tree at a shrine (*caitya*) containing relics in a temple of Maheśvara; one should recite the mantra until it emits smoke.
Having applied this as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), one becomes invisible.
Subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times at the three junctions of the day for seven nights at the foot of a tree on the seashore;
one will see jewels in the ocean and may take them as desired.
Subsisting on mung beans, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for twenty nights;
then the gems and jewels situated upon the mountain will become visible.
Thereafter, having placed it upon the head of one’s hand, one should sit upon it and recite eight thousand times.
Thus for seven days; he becomes subject [to one's will].
Desiring to bring a king or a high official under one's control, one should fashion an image of him from beeswax and cast it into smokeless embers; after seven nights, he becomes submissive.
Desiring clothes, one should recite the mantra once over white flowers that have not been crushed and cast them into water for seven nights;
one obtains a pair of garments worth eight thousand [pieces].
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over cow's ghee, one should apply it to a woman;
she becomes free from pain.
If one is anointed with fresh butter over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, one may enter the fire.
And it is not given;
yet, anointed with that very [substance], one enters the water and becomes immobilized.
While reciting the mantra, one consumes almsfood according to one's capacity.

Having fashioned an iron sword the size of a span, having installed the cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics, and having performed a grand worship, one should place the sword upon *aśvattha* leaves that curl to the right and recite the mantra until it blazes. Once it has been grasped by him, he flies up together with his retinue.

Surrounded by a thousand *vidyādharas*, he becomes invincible to all *vidyādharas* and lives for ten million years. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a grand worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), feed the monks designated for the *saṅgha*, and then, having drawn a hundred-petaled lotus on the ground with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*), sit upon the pericarp of that lotus.
One should recite until, having split the earth, a lotus emerges;
and upon the petals of that lotus, twenty vidyādharas appear seated.
Surrounded by them, one flies up.
He goes together with as many beings as he sees and by whomsoever he is seen;
and that lotus is adorned with many jewels;
he lives for an eon equal to the duration of a world-system.
When the body has perished, she takes a lover of her own choosing.
If one sprinkles a withered tree with water consecrated eight thousand times,
it will flower and bear fruit.
Having descended into a dry riverbed, one should recite [the mantra]; it becomes water.
One should recite while crossing a river;
for one who is weary, it becomes dry land.
One who desires to bring a king or a high official under their control should, beginning on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
offer eight thousand flowers before the cloth painting and perform eight thousand oblations of salt.
The king will certainly become submissive.
Beginning from that very eighth day, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times over *gorocanā* at the three junctions of the day until the eleventh day.
Having made a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with it, whoever one looks upon becomes submissive.

If one desires to bring a boy or a girl under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds before the cloth painting. Taking the dust from their footprints and fashioning a small image, whoever’s name one utters becomes subject to one’s will. One who seeks rain should take cow’s ghee and, during a lunar or solar eclipse, place it in a copper vessel and recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment occurs.
When it becomes warm, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing; whatever one hears, that one grasps.
When it becomes smoky, there is the attainment of alchemy and elixirs.
By its blazing, one becomes a rememberer of past lives.
One should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers as an oblation;
this bestows one hundred thousand *dīnāras*. One should present eight thousand *arka* flowers before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).
One obtains one hundred dīnāras.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of śāli rice grains smeared with ghee;
one obtains five dīnāras.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with curd, honey, and ghee before the cloth painting;
one will obtain three hundred *dīnāras*.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds.
One obtains more than a hundred dīnāras.

Desiring to bring a patriarch (*kulapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) at the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
the patriarch will become submissive.

Desiring to bring a lord of the world (*lokapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
One who performs this attains the status of a Kaula leader for as long as they live.
One desiring to bring the noble Saṅgha under their control should offer eight thousand *arka* flowers before the cloth painting for seven nights.
Whatever purpose one undertakes, by constant recitation one obtains that object, seeking it out.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills before the cloth painting;
one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of kunduru incense before the cloth painting for seven nights.
One obtains a treasure.
Before the cloth painting, one should offer a thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day using fuel-sticks of *arka* wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one obtains a thousand *dīnāra*s.
For the subjugation of enemies, one who observes the *poṣadha* vows should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds before the painting at the three junctions of the day for seven days;
all enemies will become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of lac for seven days.
One becomes beloved by all people.
One should offer eight thousand grains of śāli rice three times a day for seven days;
one will obtain a hundred kārṣāpaṇas.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take a corpse with its limbs intact, bathe it, adorn it, and worship it with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, treading upon its chest with the left foot, one should strike it on the head;
thereupon, it rises.
He should strike a sword made of *puṣpaloha* iron;
he will obtain gold of native hue (*jātarūpa*).
If he does not wish for it, he should be told: "Vomit!"
Then the *cintāmaṇi* emerges.
Having placed it on one's head or neck, or having tied it elsewhere, whatever one thinks of appears before one.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should descend into a river flowing to the ocean with water reaching up to the shoulders and cast ten thousand *jāti* flowers into the current.
One obtains ten māṣakas,
or a thousand pieces of gold.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer ten thousand lotuses into a river flowing to the ocean for seven nights.
One obtains a collection of treasures.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should descend into that very river and cast ten thousand flowers into the current for seven days;
one then obtains ten villages.

Having made a pill the size of a chickpea from *aśoka* flowers, one should offer eight thousand oblations of them, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
Whatever one seeks, that one obtains;
this is the ritual procedure using *apāmārga* fuel-sticks as well.

One obtains a thousand gold pieces by offering ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* seeds mixed with *aśoka* pills before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), using clarified butter three times refined. By uttering the name [of the person], one obtains a princess within a single month. One who desires to bring under control a king together with his ministers should kindle a fire before the cloth painting with *aśoka* fuel-wood and offer ten thousand oblations of *aśoka* flowers alone, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
That minister will come under one's control.
Having kindled a fire before the cloth painting, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* wood and *śatapuṣpā* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One will see a treasure in one's own house.

Having descended into a river flowing to the ocean until the water reaches the waist, one should offer ten thousand oblations. Then, forming a fist with the left hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for those who smell it.
Then one becomes accomplished.
Having released [the visualization], one sees [the deity].
Having installed the cloth-painting at a shrine containing relics, or on a riverbank, or on a mountain, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses as an oblation.
One beholds prosperity.
By this very same procedure, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of blue lotuses;
one beholds all ritual procedures.
One should offer one hundred thousand pills of guggulu;
one obtains one hundred thousand dīnāras.
One should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers.
One obtains ten million garments.
By means of guggulu incense offered one hundred and eight times, one fulfills one's heart's desires.
One should offer sesame and mustard seeds before the cloth painting (paṭa) every day for three days, reciting the mantra eight thousand times each day.
One obtains twenty-five dīnāras.
By this very procedure, one should offer oblations for seven nights;
one obtains a hundred dīnāras.
Having repeatedly cut a figure made of salt, one should offer it into the fire eight thousand times;
whoever one desires, whether a woman or a man, becomes submissive.
One should offer mustard seeds, moist with both hands and smeared with ghee, eight thousand times for three days.
It pacifies all obstacles.
Having placed one foot in water and keeping the other on dry land, one should recite the mantra until the foot in the water becomes light;
then, one becomes liberated from evil.
Having kindled a fire with *arka* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *rājikā* seeds for seven days;
the karmic obscurations will be exhausted.

Having made equal portions of the powders of *brāhmī*, *guḍūcī*, and *pippalī*, one should recite the mantra over them twenty-one times in the presence of Mañjuśrī while offering arghya, and then lick them for seven days.
One becomes intelligent;
after fourteen nights at most, one becomes supremely intelligent;
through two months of practice, one becomes a possessor of the power of retention (*śrutidhara*).
Having performed eight thousand recitations before a cloth painting or an image, one should afterwards drink [the water].
Reciting thus day after day in silence,
one becomes possessed of great intelligence.
Whether bound or imprisoned, one is released by recitation alone.
Upon seeing thieves, one should recite;
one will not be robbed by the thieves.
Having consecrated oil eight thousand times with mantras, one should smear it on the head;
one will become beloved by all people.
Those who touch [the practitioner] in the presence of the Blessed Buddha will all become submissive.

With this very mantra, one should smear the wound of a person struck by a weapon with oil over which the mantra has been recited eight thousand times; the wound will vanish and no pain will arise. Having consecrated a clod of earth with this mantra seven times, one should throw it into water.
The binding of the mouths of sea-monsters, tortoises, and other such creatures is accomplished.
Having fasted for three nights on the full moon day, one should descend into water reaching up to the navel and offer one hundred and eight white flowers;
one will obtain a pair of garments worth five dīnāras.
During a lunar eclipse, one should prepare pills from finely ground *guñjā* seeds mixed with ghee and honey at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics.
Covering them with seven *aśvattha* leaves and shielding them with the hand, one should recite the mantra until they burst into flame.
One who consumes them becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*).
By this, one should perform rites for all the sick.
For those suffering from colic, burning sensations, dysentery, urinary distress, or jaundice, one should recite over oil and, having applied it, the patient becomes free from disease.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight and fasting for three nights, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of jasmine buds smeared with ghee, curd, and milk at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree.
One obtains one hundred coins.

If it is not successful, one should perform the ritual action; one obtains one hundred coins or sees [the result], as this destroys piśācas, fevers, bhūtas, and grahas, and releases [the victim] with a thread.
For a woman who is unable to give birth, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times over oil and smear it on her navel or the region of the hips.
It becomes free of arrows.

By reciting [the mantra] over a clod of earth one hundred times and holding it, while looking at the moon at a reliquary containing relics, and having combined *anantā*, *vetasī*, *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *bṛhatī*, and honey,
one should chant until one is released.
It swells;
having consumed it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
In battle, having consecrated a *pratisarā* cord eight hundred times and tied a knot upon the hand, one’s strength remains unassailable.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should perform the rite in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone down to a river that flows into the ocean and observed the fast for a fortnight while subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should offer blooming white lotuses into the water.
One will then see a treasure.

Having purified the body with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one who has performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, having fasted for three nights at the conclusion, takes a thread spun by a young girl; having bound it to the hand with ten thousand recitations in a shrine containing relics, in an image, or in a house, one becomes invisible.
Having installed a cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics, one should offer thirty thousand oblations of lotuses.
Having kindled a fire with charcoal from *khadira* wood, one sees [the deity] in his own form;
whatever one seeks, that one obtains.
Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the fifteenth,
having fasted for three nights and performed a grand worship at a shrine containing relics, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer oblations of clarified butter; thus,
one obtains a village.
On the bank of a river flowing to the ocean, one should cause a thousand stupas to be constructed.

Every day, having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth to each individual stupa, one should cause them to be consecrated with eight thousand recitations until the final stupa blazes with light.
Then it should be known that the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva, is approaching;
as he approaches, the earth trembles and fragrant scented winds blow.
One should recite [the mantra] until then.
As long as he remains in his own form,
whatever boon he requests, he obtains it.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of pieces of *khadira* wood leaves before the Blessed One.
He receives one dīnāra every day.
Having gone to the forest, subsisting on alms-food, he should offer twenty thousand oblations of wild cow-dung smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
When the tree deity arrives, having assumed the form of a lion—
And he offers a pretext,
saying, "You must not accept it;
come to me yourself."

One should give a kingdom, wealth, or other jewels; one must constantly provide enjoyments to be used for the Three Jewels. Having retired to a forest, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
again, one should recite it one hundred thousand times.
In front of an image made of agalloch wood, one should offer seven thousand oblations of cow dung mixed with honey and ghee into the fire for the Blessed One.
The tawny wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) arrives.
If she does not arrive, one should again offer twenty thousand oblations of calf-dung.
Once she has arrived, she becomes accomplished (siddhā).
One gives milk to a thousand men.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers smeared with ghee and honey;
for six months, one obtains a thousand *dīnāras* or a thousand *paṇas*.

One should offer a hundred thousand blossoming lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into a reliquary stupa (*caitya*) containing a relic; the deities who have faith in the Buddha will then grant boons.
Having performed worship to the noble Mañjuśrī, one should scatter white mustard seeds that have been consecrated seven times during a battle, and peace will prevail.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight during the *pratihāraka* period, having performed worship with perfumes and flowers, one should offer eight thousand oblations of blooming lotuses smeared with ghee.
Then, taking the ashes and applying a mark (*tilaka*) on one's forehead, one should enter a village or city;
all will become submissive.

Starting from the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight until the fifteenth, having fasted for one night, one should smear a mandala measuring four cubits beneath a tree, offer perfumes, flowers, and incense, perform worship to Noble Mañjuśrī, and present an offering to the yakṣas. Then, taking human bone, one should fashion a trident;
casting it with the left hand, one who has fasted for seven nights or three nights should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers as an oblation.
By that, the trident blazes;
from that, one becomes accomplished.
Whatever one creates by will, that one obtains.

In a divine house, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a shrine containing relics, or before an image, one should take a *pala* of cow’s ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, place it in a golden vessel, perform worship to the Blessed One, and while not looking at the moon, cover it with a cloth and recite the mantra until it becomes warm.
It froths,
it blazes;
by drinking it while it is steaming, one gains power over all sentient beings.
Having drunk it while it is foaming, one becomes invisible;
having drunk it while it is flaming, one travels through the sky.

By one who has performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for six months, subsisting on cow’s urine and barley, observing a vow of silence, and reciting the mantra constantly, one obtains a hundred gold pieces without asking.

Beginning from the day of the full moon, one should perform worship before the Blessed One, the Noble Mañjuśrī, for one year, offering perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while observing the eightfold poṣadha vows.
When the year is complete, one becomes successful;
the Blessed One performs the binding of the turban upon him.
Having performed worship to Noble Mañjuśrī, beginning from the first lunar day until the full moon day, one should perform increasingly greater worship day by day;
monks should also be fed.
Then the words "I have attained success" will issue forth.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of ghee;
peace will come to another.

Having performed worship of the Blessed Buddha during the fortnight of miracles (prātihārakapakṣa), and having offered sublime perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, and so forth to the noble Mañjuśrī, [one should offer] śaṅkhapuṣpī flowers soaked in iṅguda oil.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations;
then villages, cities, elephants, horses, chariots, cows, and buffaloes will come to be.

For seven nights, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel and observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should fill a vessel with clarified butter strained through a cloth, light a lamp with a white wick, and show it to young boys and girls.
Right there, one perceives the attainment of even limited knowledge;
there shall be no fear from any calamities.
One who constantly recites the mantra should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee-soaked fuel-sticks from the Bodhi tree.
In the same manner, one should sleep upon a bed of kuśa grass before the cloth painting;
in a dream, one will see twenty thousand pieces of wealth,
a portion of which is to be applied to the Three Jewels.
In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon,
one should recite the mantra eight thousand times every single day during this interval.

Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, at the conclusion, having fasted for three nights and observed a vow of silence while reciting the mantra, one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) into the hands of the attendants and go to a great highway.
One should announce that the spirit is cruel;
it should be told, "Accept [this offering].
Then, taking a *droṇa* measure of white mustard seeds, one should scatter them in the ten directions and below.

Having consecrated [the object] twenty-one times, one should manifest it to oneself. Likewise, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having entered the Gandhakuṭī and performed an offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth before the Blessed One, one should recite the mantra a thousand times. Then, in a dream, one sees the Blessed One, the Noble Mañjuśrī.

In the month of Vaiśākha, during the dark fortnight, one who observes the *poṣadha* vows, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and so forth at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*). Furthermore, monks should be fed day after day. One should place four jars filled with water and containing roots that grow out of season;
having cast all medicinal seeds into them, one should consecrate each jar eight thousand times by night and place it where there are no crows, near one's sons, wife, or daughters.
Regarding sovereignty:

having performed worship to the Blessed One and to the noble Mañjuśrī on the eighth day of both fortnights, one should kindle a fire from a cremation ground and offer eight thousand *śatapuṣpa* flowers;
food and drink will then become inexhaustible.

Taking that very ash and having made a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) on the forehead of oneself or another, one may enter into battle; all [enemies] will become submissive. It shall release one from bondage and fetters, and it destroys [the danger] arising from fire.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *mālatī* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee,
while subsisting on cow urine for six months;
one will obtain a thousand *dīnāras*.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer eight thousand blue lotuses;
he in whose name one offers them becomes submissive.
If one offers eight thousand *pañcakālaka* flowers at the three junctions of the day in the name of someone, that person becomes submissive.

During the fortnight of miracles, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley gruel, one should recite the mantra three times daily before the cloth painting on the fifteenth day, until the Blessed One arrives;
then the flame of the lamp increases in height and the earth trembles.
Either the cloth moves,
or the words "it is accomplished" issue forth,
and one obtains a thousand dīnāras.
One becomes a lord of a realm. Having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for six months,
one obtains five thousand *dīnāras* within six months before an image containing relics (*sadhātuka*) at a shrine (*caitya*) in the presence of the Blessed One, the noble Mañjuśrī.
Having performed worship at a reliquary containing relics, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
one will obtain a thousand gold coins.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at a reliquary containing relics.
He becomes a granter of all desires.
For one who wishes to effect the pacification of all diseases, having empowered a thread spun by a virgin with one hundred and eight thousand recitations, it should be tied [around the wrist].
One obtains good fortune,
and illness is pacified.
Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer eight thousand black sesame seeds.
One obtains wealth and grain.

At a reliquary containing relics, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight and fasting for three nights until the fifteenth day, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer one hundred thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains five villages. Having kindled a fire with the wood of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of white sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
If, having fasted for three nights on the fifteenth day, those sesame seeds go in every direction and intermediate direction, then one becomes accomplished;
one brings all sentient beings under one's control.
One should first recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in the presence of Noble Mañjuśrī.
Then, during a lunar eclipse, having offered eight *palas* of ghee, one should recite it until it begins to foam; by drinking it, one becomes a possessor of the power of retention (*śrutidhara*).
One should offer *kunduruka* incense one hundred thousand times.
One obtains a single ancient [object] that was not asked for.
If one offers eight hundred fragrant flowers daily before the noble Mañjuśrī,
one becomes glorious.
One should offer eight thousand oblations daily of Apāmārga wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one obtains a village.
Having kindled the fire with Bahuputrikā wood fuel-sticks, [one should proceed].
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *vacā* root.
With that ash, one should make a sectarian mark (*tilaka*); by this, one becomes invisible.
If it does not happen, one should perform the rite three times.
During a lunar eclipse, having gone to a riverbank and kindled a fire with *bilva* wood fuel, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *bilva* flowers smeared with clarified butter.
A *yakṣa* maiden will arrive.
At midnight, having again recited the mantra eight thousand times, then one [maiden] will come forth.
Whatever word is spoken, he does that.

At the site of a treasure, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times after performing worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth; then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed the offering of bali, one should recite it.
The piśācas will come.
Then one should dig;
a treasure-trove will arise. Having taken it, one should give it oneself to the Three Jewels.
The rite for binding the turban is likewise:
having kindled a fire with *vibhītaka* wood in front of the Blessed One, one should offer eight thousand sesame seeds and rice grains every day;
a widow becomes submissive.
To subjugate a minister, one should offer oblations of white mustard seeds; he becomes submissive.
To subjugate a king, one should offer oblations of resin of *sarja* wood;
he becomes submissive.
To subjugate men and women, one should perform oblations in this very same manner.
Having kindled a fire with *agasti* wood, one obtains a hundred *dīnāras* by offering lamp-wicks before the cloth painting.
One should offer oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks while subsisting on a diet of milk.
Three times every day,
one obtains a hundred gold pieces.
Having gone to a river that flows to the ocean, one should offer oblations hundreds of thousands of times.
One should take as many jewels as one obtains;
a portion to be used for the Three Jewels must be given.
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform recitation throughout the entire night.
One is liberated from the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).

Having performed worship of the Blessed One, the Noble Mañjuśrī, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, one should offer oblations of *apāmārga* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, dedicating it for oneself.
One becomes liberated from all sins.
Having consecrated seven grains of black pepper with mantras, one should consume them when there is no crowing of crows;
one then grasps five thousand verses.
One should maintain this for as long as one lives; having performed one hundred thousand recitations before the Blessed Buddha, one effects the binding of serpents.
Alternatively, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the noble Mañjuśrī.
At midnight, one obtains five hundred *dīnāras*, half of which is to be dedicated to the Three Jewels.
One should offer eight thousand white water lilies day by day;
one will then be liberated from the Vināyakas.

During the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, subsisting on milk and barley gruel or on vegetables, observing the *poṣadha* vows, and having fasted for three nights on the fifteenth day, one should offer one hundred thousand seeds of the *vaikaṅkata* tree smeared with ghee.
One obtains a thousand gold coins and becomes a village headman;
half of this is to be used for the Three Jewels.

Having smeared a mandala the size of a cow-hide on a clean spot of ground, having constructed an altar in the shape of a lotus in its center, and having prepared an offering of various perfumes, flowers, incense, and oblations, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, each measuring a span of the Sugata.
Blue-colored flames in the form of fire will then issue forth.
Having circumambulated the practitioner from left to right, they enter the fire-pit once again;
in this way, it becomes accomplished.
In all ritual practices, the fire must be invoked.
In this way, one becomes accomplished.
Having entered the waters of the Gaṅgā up to the armpits, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times until the solar disc is seen in the sky.
Then the Blessed One becomes accomplished.

If one does not see [the deity] and does not achieve success, one should go to a *ekavārāhī* and, having performed the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, and bali, recite the mantra for the entire night until dawn;
then one becomes successful.
And she should be told regarding all the ritual accomplishments:
"She gives me a hundred gold coins day after day;
they must all be spent."
Otherwise, he will not give.
Having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of forest cow-dung smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one obtains a hundred cows.
One should offer eight thousand *mātulaṅga* fruits into a fire of *palāśa* wood until Gaṇapati arrives. He should be addressed thus: "Give me one *dīnāra* every day."
One should give;
everything must be spent.
One should say, "Touch the feet of the Blessed One," and then it becomes accomplished.

Alternatively, if one does not give [the results], one should fast for one night before a painted image at a shrine containing relics, offer eight thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into a fire kindled with *vaikaṅkata* wood,
and by this rite one becomes glorious.
One becomes the sovereign of a realm. One should offer *kiṅkirāṭa* flowers eight thousand times every day for seven days.
One obtains eight paṇas.
One who desires to perform a rite for pacification (śāntika) should offer eight thousand oblations of parched grain;
peace will ensue.
One desiring nourishment should kindle a fire with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice at the three junctions of the day for three days; thus,
nourishment will come to pass.
Having kindled a fire with mango wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* sprouts;
in a dispute, one becomes the respondent.
At sunset, having uttered the name [of the opponent], one should offer oblations of rice husks with the left hand.
One becomes subject for seven nights.
Having kindled a fire with *rāja* fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand sesame seeds and rice grains at the three junctions of the day;
within three days, he grants wealth.
In a pure place on the banks of the Gaṅgā, free from the sound of pestles, one should take earth from both riverbanks and construct a square altar seven cubits in size.

Having fashioned a thousand-petaled lotus in its center, one should place upon it a wheel made of the five red metals, measuring one span of the Sugata’s hand. This should be accomplished in the middle of the maṇḍala before the cloth painting, having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and white sandalwood.

Having offered a garland of red mandāraka flowers and performed worship with perfumes and other offerings, one should present seven rows of ghee lamps; four jars of ghee should be lit in the four directions.
In the four directions, four vases filled with all kinds of seeds and containing precious gems should be placed.
Incense made from *kunduru*, *agaru*, *śrīpiṣṭaka*, and *guggulu* should be offered.
Having performed the ritual offering (*bali-vidhāna*), one should offer curd-rice and cakes in the four directions as previously described;
to the south, one should offer the "fierce" (*krūra*) offering for the spirits (*bhūta*), mixed with water.
In the western direction, one should offer a vessel filled with the milk of a female deer;
in the northern direction,
one should present an oblation consisting of a vessel filled with milk-rice.
Then, having kindled the fire with *palāśa* wood fuel, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter from *apāmārga* wood fuel that has been consecrated seven times,
while uttering the name [of the person].
That person becomes submissive.

Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *rājavṛkṣa* wood and having fashioned an image out of salt, one should offer eight thousand oblations— beginning from the head down to the feet— with each individual offering consecrated seven times while uttering the person's name;
thus the king becomes submissive.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or on the eighth, having observed the *poṣadha* vows and fasted for a full day and night, one should take unfallen cow dung and smear a sacrificial ground the size of a cow-hide. At a shrine containing relics, one should take fresh butter churned by a young maiden from the milk of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, using either a silver vessel or one dedicated to Noble Mañjuśrī. Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, holding the vessel with the left hand, one should [hold] the ring finger of the right hand.
One should recite while stirring it until it becomes warm;
that should be drunk.
One becomes wise.
If it catches fire at the first utterance, one becomes a master of subjugation; if it smokes, one gains the power of subjugation;
if it blazes, invisibility is attained.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bahuputrikā* wood.
With that ash, one should prepare four water-pitchers by mixing them together.
Having tied a mantra consecrated eight hundred times to one's right hand, one becomes a superior debater in every instance.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *aparājita* flowers;
one then remains undefeated in battle.
Knots should be made and tied with a thread spun by a maiden over which the mantra has been recited seven times;
by this, neither stationary nor moving poisons will have power here.
For one bitten by a fierce serpent, having grasped the victim's name, water mixed with powder over which the mantra has been recited seven times should be given for drinking.
Even one who is dead rises up;
likewise, having consecrated it with mantras in the four directions, it should be given for drinking,
and even one bitten by Takṣaka lives.
One should smear the breast-root with clay consecrated seven times;
[the person] is liberated,
and no pain occurs.

In the midst of a city during an outbreak of pestilence, having smeared a sacrificial ground at midnight and offered a white *bali* oblation, one should kindle a fire with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees and offer a thousand oblations of milk; this pacifies the pestilence.
If it is not pacified by this means—
Then, on a certain day at the time of midday, having kindled a fire with *śleṣmātaka* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*).
This immediately pacifies pestilence.
When this rite has been performed, all beings as many as there are within the area of the "poisonous bond" come under his control.

For the subjugation of a kūṣmāṇḍa spirit, one should offer eight thousand oblations of kūṣmāṇḍa wood; this pacifies an epidemic. For the subjugation of a preta, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame flour.
Pretas become submissive.
To subjugate piśācas, one should offer eight thousand oblations of rags from a cemetery;
the piśācas will then become submissive.
To subjugate yakṣas, one should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
the yakṣas will become submissive.
To subjugate those afflicted by epilepsy, possession, or madness, one should offer eight thousand oblations of wool.
They become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills smeared with clarified butter;
the planetary spirits who follow Mahādeva become submissive.
Having taken realgar purchased from a hero and kindling a fire with fuel-sticks of *arājavṛkṣa*, one should recite the mantra until it becomes the color of fire.
Then, having prepared fresh butter from the milk of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same age, one should quench it in that clarified butter;
likewise in a vessel full of curd and in one full of honey.

Then, having performed protection with this very [mantra] and placed it in a casket, one who has fasted for three nights during a lunar eclipse should perform worship before the noble Mañjuśrī at a shrine containing relics; having placed it upon four leaves of the *aśvattha* tree facing north,
he should recite the mantra until it emits heat.
It smokes and it blazes;
[it effects] subjugation, invisibility, and traveling through the sky.
Likewise, so too with collyrium, yellow orpiment, and gorocana.

This is the specific procedure for using *rocanā*: on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having placed [the substance] upon a lotus leaf and holding it with cupped hands before the noble Mañjuśrī, one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
These rites are to be performed before the principal image (*mūlapaṭa*).
Having fashioned a lotus out of the five metals for seven nights, and having ground saffron, *rocanā*, and camphor in water, one should smear the lotus with this.

Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having fasted, bathed at the three times of day, and dressed in clean garments, one should recite the mantra before an image of Noble Mañjuśrī containing relics, holding it with the right hand, until it blazes forth. Then, by holding it, one becomes a vidyādhara.
One lives for ten thousand years.
Likewise with bracelets, crowns, and chains.

In the same way, one should take mountain red sandalwood, guggulu, the root of nandyāvarta, the chaff of girikarṇikā, rice, kuṣṭha, tagara, honey, long pepper, and turuṣka, and having combined them, have them made in equal portions.
Then, having taken the milk from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, one should mix it with butter churned by a maiden and form it into pills.
A lamp should be offered with sesame oil.

Then, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one who observes the *upoṣadha* vows and has fasted for a full day and night should place the pill between *aśvattha* leaves and recite the mantra before the noble Mañjuśrī until it emits smoke.
Having given it to his companions, he should place it in his own mouth;
he becomes invisible.
Then, when it blazes, he becomes a traveler through the sky.
There is another procedure:

at a reliquary containing relics, having performed a magnificent worship before a painted image on the day of the *poṣadha*, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* wood sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Starting from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight until the fifteenth,
one becomes truly accomplished;
thus, one who observes the *poṣadha* vows should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Rites are accomplished through others;
one becomes successful by means of this prior service.

Now, if one desires to bring a king or a high official under one's control, one should perform worship of the Blessed One and offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, anointed with *iṅguda* oil.
Starting from the fourteenth day until the fifteenth day,
by this ritual even one of immoral conduct attains success.
One who desires to bring the four castes under control should bring milk-rice and sacrificial food, as well as drinks and curd-sugar, and offer them as oblations.
They become submissive.
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while pure at night,
it liberates one from all bonds.

For the pacification of anger, one should perform a homa with rice-husks. To bring a maiden under one's control, one should offer sesame seeds. For the sake of obtaining clothing, one should offer *karppaṇa* seeds.
Having consecrated a stalk of *vacā* root eight thousand times, and having bound it on the hand for seven nights, whatever one asks for, that one obtains.
By means of constant recitation, if one binds to someone's hand the *Pratyaṅgirā* mantra—consecrated eight thousand times with lotus fibers and so forth—a protection is established for that person.
One desiring wealth should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu pills.
For seven nights, one desiring to become a leader of a family (*kulapati*) should offer incense, and for seven nights, [offerings] smeared with clarified butter.
One obtains a village.
If one gives flowers over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times to someone, that person becomes submissive.
Saffron, tagara, tālīśapatra, lotus stalks, śatapuṣpa, and śrīveṣṭa, combined and consecrated according to the ritual procedure...

At the king’s gate, one should wear a garland of cloth; this brings subjugation through the employment of men and women and effects victory in battle. Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over a banner and having consecrated scents, flowers, and incense, one should offer the *arghya* oblation into seven vessels of curd.
By the mere sight of it, the enemy army perishes.
Having consecrated black sesame seeds eight thousand times in front of the cloth painting, whoever eats them while reciting the name of that person will become submissive.
Having recited [the mantra] eight thousand times over all seeds, all medicinal herbs, all perfumes, fragrant flowers, or lotuses, and having placed them all in a jar of unseasoned radish,
one should recite it eight thousand times at the Bodhi tree.
Whether one bathes oneself or causes another to bathe,
one becomes liberated from all calamities.
By offering either a lotus or a lotus petal into smokeless embers while reciting the name of someone, that person becomes submissive.
One should offer eight thousand *bilva* leaves mixed with honey;
this subjugates either the wife of a king or the queen consort.
To bring all beings under one's control, one should offer oblations of *priyaṅgu* flowers;
by offering red *śāli* rice while uttering the name of a specific person,
that person becomes submissive.
To subjugate a maiden, one should offer kesara flowers as oblations.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer milk-porridge eight thousand times;
by means of whose name [the rite is performed], that person becomes submissive.
Having installed the cloth painting facing east at a shrine containing relics,
and having spread a sacrificial altar with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the northeast starting from the first day of the bright fortnight,
one should kindle the fire with *bilva* wood fuel.

One should offer eight thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day using blossomed lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; incense made of agaru, turuṣka, kunduruka, and śrīpiṣṭaka should be offered,
and an offering of milk, curd, and cooked rice should be presented.
One should offer a *bali* of all elemental spirits to the obstacles.
Then, beginning from the eighth day, one should perform three thousand eight hundred oblations at the three junctions of the day using blooming white lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains a great treasure or a realm;
by offering eight thousand yellow flowers anointed with curd, honey, and ghee day after day,
one obtains a country.
Having fasted for three nights, or subsisting on a diet of barley meal, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*).

In this manner, even for one who has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), success is achieved through seventy hundred thousand offerings. Likewise, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains ten million gold pieces.
Having risen at dawn, being self-restrained and having bathed while observing celibacy, one should kindle a fire;
desiring to bring under one's control a Nāgakeśara tree, a Priyaṅgu plant, a king, or a high official, one should offer eight thousand oblations.
By performing this at the three junctions of the day,
one obtains distinguished results and abundant wealth within three months.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of cow-calf dung;
one obtains a hundred cows.
With fuel-sticks of *priyaṅgu* and *nāgakesara*, for whomsoever one offers [the oblation] while uttering that person's name;
He becomes submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day;
one will obtain a great treasure.
That which is given in this manner becomes inexhaustible.
Having descended into a river that flows toward the ocean,
one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away.
One sees a treasure equal to a heap of lotuses.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits before the painting at the three junctions of the day;
this produces enjoyments.
Having combined sesame seeds and rice grains, one should offer them eight thousand times before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
inexhaustible food will arise.
One should offer *nāgapuṣpa* flowers to the *nāgas*.
They become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand pellets of guggulu incense before a cloth painting of the Yakṣas,
three times a day for seven nights, using fuel-sticks of Aśoka wood.
The yakṣiṇīs become submissive.
One should offer śrīvāsaka incense before the cloth painting;
the kinnaras become submissive.

One who desires to bring the gods under one's control should offer eight thousand oblations of agalloch wood fuel sticks smeared with ghee before the original cloth painting (mūlapaṭa) at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one nights;
they will become submissive.
One should offer *kunduruka* resin before the cloth painting;
the *preta*s will become submissive.
One should offer *sarjarasa* resin.
The Vināyakas become submissive;
by means of an offering of oil-cakes (piṇyāka), one brings everyone under control.
One who desires to bring a king or a high official under control [should perform this].
Before the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with oil for seven nights;
they will become submissive.
Whatever one says, that he does.
To bring a princess under control, one should offer an oblation of black mustard seeds before the cloth painting.
Desiring to bring a royal priest under control, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter before the cloth painting.
For a Kṣatriya, [one should offer oblations] with armfuls of fuel;
for the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer milk;
for the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer kṛsarā.
For the subjugation of all women, one performs a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with salt; for a widow, with beans (*māṣa*);
and one brings all sentient beings under control by anointing them with sesame oil.

For all [these], there is a fire sacrifice (*homa*) of eight thousand [offerings] for seven nights. Having become pure and having fasted for four meals, one should kindle the fire with *bilva* fuel-sticks and offer *bilva* fruits into it.
One sees a treasure-trove of a hundred thousand [pieces].
Having subsisted on milk and barley gruel for twenty nights, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of white mustard seeds;
one obtains wealth.
Having performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should offer oblations of white mustard seeds smeared with ghee before the cloth painting for a full day during the night.
Within a month, there will be a bountiful rain wherever one desires.
Having fasted for four meals, one should offer ten thousand oblations of the same [mustard seeds].
One obtains wealth by installing a cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics,
having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood.
One should offer one hundred thousand blue lotuses (*utpala*) and obtain a village.
Before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), while subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should offer lotuses along with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One obtains a thousand pieces of gold. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations before a cloth painting of Kumuda; whatever one contemplates in the mind, that [is attained].
One obtains that:
one should offer a thousand *bilva* fruits before the cloth painting;
one beholds a treasure-trove.
Before the cloth painting, one who subsists on milk and barley gruel should offer one hundred thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
he shall obtain a thousand pieces of gold.
Having fasted for three nights, one should offer eight thousand pieces of agalloch wood as fuel.
Then, the recitation for the entire night should be performed;
the cloth painting will tremble,
or the garland of flowers will sway.
Then one becomes successful;
whatever one conceives in the mind, that he bestows.
For the subjugation of great persons, one should offer *jātī* flowers before the painting.
One should offer oblations of *karavīra* flowers for the sake of poison;
one should offer oblations of *karṇikāra* flowers;
one obtains a hundred *dīnāras*.
One who desires the position of general should offer *kundapuṣpa* flowers;
he will obtain the command of an army.
One should offer *tārāvartta* flowers.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations to Mucilinda;
one obtains a thousand pieces of gold.
By performing a fire oblation (*homa*) with white *karavīra* flowers, one becomes bound by a triple seal.
One also obtains a kingdom; furthermore, having kindled a fire before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), worship should be performed daily in increasing measure.
One should offer a thousand oblations of gold, each the size of a *tuṭi*, anointed with fragrant oil.
Until the Blessed One becomes the Giver of Boons,
one then becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas; whatever one prays for, that one obtains.
One should offer silver powder as an oblation;
it bestows a kingdom.
One should offer iron powder as an oblation.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of saffron mixed with scented oil;
for as much as one prays for, [that shall be attained].
One obtains that;
one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of all types of incense,
and one obtains whatever object is desired.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of camphor; one obtains a hundred thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks smeared with fragrant oil.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of gold and garments;
one obtains a thousand dīnāras.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *agaru* wood fuel-sticks;
one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*).
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *dhāsaka* wood fuel-sticks smeared with fragrant oil.
There is the pacification of great diseases.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of nimba fruits smeared with fragrant oil; this liberates one from all bonds.
Taking the ghee of a cow that has a calf of the same age, [one should proceed].
One should drink [the substance] consecrated one hundred thousand times;
one becomes intelligent.
One should offer one hundred thousand arka flowers as an oblation.
One becomes beloved by all beings.
Having consecrated flowers and fruit seven times with mantras, whoever they are given to becomes submissive.
Having observed the poṣadha on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should smear a mandala with fallen cow dung at a shrine containing relics,
perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and ghee lamps,
and kindle a fire with udumbara wood.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *brahmī* fuel sticks;
by subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one becomes wise.
For the subjugation of Brahmins, one should offer milk as an oblation.
He becomes submissive.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation belonging to a Kṣatriya;
he becomes submissive.
For the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer oblations by mixing barley with curd and sacrificial food (haviṣya) together;
he will become submissive.
Upon seeing an enemy, one should recite the mantra.
He becomes paralyzed.
By means of water consecrated seven times with the mantra, he fulfills all hopes.
In all diseases, it serves as a cleansing agent.
One should anoint the eyes with seven-times consecrated *loghragulikā*;
this removes eye disease.
For one who is ill, a thread consecrated seven times should be tied [around the wrist].
All planetary spirits (grahas) have no power over one.
With ashes consecrated seven times, there is the binding of a mandala; by tying it as a crest-lock (śikhābandha), self-protection is achieved.
With a clod of earth consecrated seven times, there is the binding of the directions.

For one experiencing difficult labor, oil should be given after reciting the mantra over it; she will give birth easily. For one with a retained fetus, at the time of her fertile period, after she has bathed following her menstrual flow, one should take cow's milk and consecrate it by reciting the mantra eight hundred times.
Having caused [the practitioner] to prostrate to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
one should give [the medicine] for him to drink;
furthermore, he should be fed with supreme milk-rice mixed with ghee.
Then she gives birth to a son who is pleasing to behold.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should install the cloth painting facing east and offer eight thousand pellets of guggulu incense every day.
At the three junctions of the day,
he grants whatever one desires.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should install the cloth painting in a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*).
Having offered an oblation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and food,
one should perform a fire sacrifice before the cloth painting for seven nights at the three junctions of the day, using *agaru* wood sticks the size of a thumb-joint, anointed with *turuṣka* oil;
this bestows a kingdom.
It bestows the state of a Vidyādhara, invisibility, the power to travel on foot through the air, or the faculty of retaining all that is heard.

Now, for one who wishes to accomplish the pill (*gulikā*): having combined the filaments of the *karṇikāra*, *nāgakesara*, white sandalwood, and elephant ichor, one should prepare a pill and dry it in the shade.
One should grind [the substance] from a girl wearing clean clothes;
this should be performed under the Puṣya constellation.
Having purified oneself, one should place seven pills, encased in three metals, inside a casket of black agallochum.
One should recite the mantra before the cloth painting until it makes a rattling sound. Having grasped that [sound], one should offer one portion to the Blessed One.
Having thrown it into his mouth, he becomes invisible.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of a hundred thousand grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one will obtain a treasure.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *kadamba* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
all sentient beings will be brought under one's control.
Having descended into a river that flows toward the ocean, [one should perform the rite].
Having observed the fast, one should offer eight thousand kesara flowers;
one will obtain ten pairs of garments.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand jasmine flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day.
For seven days,
one becomes beloved by all sentient beings;
one bestows and receives their realm.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of white water-lily flowers smeared with curd, honey,
and ghee for seven days; [the practitioner] will obtain the five sensory objects and achieve the subjugation of kings.
One should offer oblations of black mustard seeds for seven nights.
To bring a Brahmin under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *karaṇṭaka* flowers.
For seven nights;
for the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer eight thousand *saugandhika* flowers as oblations for seven nights;
for the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer eight thousand [oblations] into the fire for seven nights.
A widow should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood fuel for seven nights.
Then, having consecrated a piece of *rocanā* (bezoar) eight thousand times at a reliquary containing relics,
she should go to the royal court.
All become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* sprouts;
peace will be established for another.
One who desires to bring peace to oneself should offer milk as an oblation at the three junctions of the day;
peace will then ensue.
Having placed ghee in a copper vessel before the southern image of Mahādeva, one should proceed.
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand times and offer a bali-oblation consisting of all types of spirits;
then the clarified butter will move.
Then one becomes accomplished;
by applying a tilaka on the forehead,
one becomes beloved by all people.
Having performed worship to the Blessed One Amitābha and the noble Mañjuśrī for the purpose of increasing intelligence,
one should place ghee in either silver or copper and recite the mantra as many times as required.
Up to the threefold accomplishment:
having drunk that, one becomes wise;
when it smokes, there is invisibility.
By means of [the mantra] blazing, one attains the power of traveling through the sky.
One who desires to accomplish *manaḥśilā* should subsist on a diet of milk and barley gruel and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having fasted for three nights before Mahādeva, he should establish [the substance] upon seven *aśvattha* leaves.
Having covered [the area] with the three [mantras] and offered the *bali* consisting of all-enriching substances,
one should recite [the mantra] for as long as it takes to perform protection for oneself and one's companions without restraint.
Up to the threefold accomplishment:
by means of the blazing [mantra], one lives for ten thousand years;
having fashioned an iron wheel, [one achieves the same].
Or, having performed a magnificent worship and grasping a trident with the right hand,
Seated cross-legged before the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra until it makes a crackling sound or blazes up with light.
Having taken that, one becomes a Vidyādhara;
all gods and humans become subject to one's will.
One desiring to perform the ritual of the finger (*aṅgulīsādhana*) should take earth from both banks of a river.
One should have a finger made;
having placed that finger in front of the cloth painting, one should draw it forth.
When she says, "Come," she becomes accomplished;
by her, one causes whatever [action] to be performed.
He comes,

desiring to accomplish the *rocanā* [ointment], having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and having established it before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and offered perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One should recite it until it blazes;
by that accomplishment, one lives for five thousand years.
One who desires to accomplish the lotus should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood,
install the cloth-painting in a reliquary stūpa containing relics, and take hold of it before that [stūpa].
Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes;
having grasped it while it is thus blazing, one becomes the universal sovereign (cakravartin) of all vidyādharas,
and the gods who frequent Kailāsa become subject to one's will.

One becomes invincible to all vidyādharas. Poison is neutralized by water. One may prescribe cures for fever and other ailments. By reciting [the mantra] once over one who has been possessed by a spirit, that person is restored to health; it also provides protection for oneself.
Protection for one's companions is achieved with water over which the mantra has been recited once;
the binding of the directions with it recited three times;
and the binding of the mandala with it recited four times.
Having fasted for a day and night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should fashion an image of Noble Mañjuśrī from the fallen cow dung of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color;
having placed it facing east and performed a great worship, [one should proceed].
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times before him;
then the Blessed One will nod his head or display some other sign of accomplishment.
Then one becomes accomplished;
whatever one contemplates, all that one performs.
The Blessed One becomes a granter of boons; he fulfills all desires and reveals what is auspicious and inauspicious in dreams.
