One should employ [this] as desired.
In the forenoon, by reciting it one thousand times, a handful of food is produced.
Observing the *poṣadha* vows and subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it one hundred thousand times.
A vision occurs;
he accomplishes his desire.
Before the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *kunduruka* resin for seven nights.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*),
one becomes a king in a single region.
One should offer eight thousand grains of rice at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*).
Throughout the entire night,
one obtains a hundred dīnāras.
Having kindled a fire with *āṭaruṣaka* wood, one should offer eight thousand *āṭaruṣaka* flowers smeared with ghee.
One obtains gold.
Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer eight thousand mustard seeds smeared with ghee;
one obtains a thousand silver coins (rūpaka).
Alternatively, one may go to a village;
having kindled a fire with *śleṣmātaka* wood in front of the cloth painting,
one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots for three nights.
One obtains a thousand garments.
One should offer eight thousand *surasī* leaves;
one obtains a divine house.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times mentally, one obtains a thousand Purāṇas.
One should offer a thousand oblations of rice flour (*śrīpiṣṭaka*) three times a day for seven nights;
one then obtains a thousand *dīnāra*s.
It accomplishes everything according to one's desire;
one becomes glorious and fortunate.
One should offer red flowers into the fire at a river;
one will obtain red garments.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight or the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, in a secluded place on the earth, [one should perform the rite].
Having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes, as well as a garland, beneath a white *arka* tree to the noble Mañjuśrī, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Afterwards, one should have an image of the noble Mañjuśrī made, the size of a thumb-joint.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, in a secluded place at an anthill, one should offer white perfumes, oblations, garlands, and incense, and recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Then, having taken earth from an anthill,
one should knead it with scented water;
using that earth, one should make a counter-seal for the previously made seal of the image by means of the milk of the *arka* plant.
Then, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the eighth day, one should perform worship of the Blessed One three times a day and offer a bali-oblation; thereafter,
he should be struck with eight thousand *jātī* flowers.
One who observes the *poṣadha* vows, subsists on a diet of milk and barley, and sleeps upon a bed of *darbha* grass should accomplish this;
he obtains a thousand *dīnāras*.
By constant recitation, he attains success in his journey.
If one recites it seven or eight thousand times for seven days,
one obtains a village and becomes illustrious.
One who desires to produce wealth should go to a cow-pen on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and, subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
On the fourteenth day of the following dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, he should recite it another hundred thousand times in that very place;
he will obtain eight hundred *dīnāras*.
Whatever one desires—
whether gold or a village— one obtains it.
Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire before the cloth painting using wood from the Bodhi tree.
One should recite the *vacā* mantra eight thousand times to obtain one hundred *dīnāras*.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood,
one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *guggulu* pills smeared with curds, honey, and clarified butter before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).
One obtains one hundred dīnāras.
One should offer a hundred flowers a hundred thousand times;
one obtains one hundred dīnāras.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *bilva* fuel-sticks;
whatever one desires,
that one accomplishes.
On the bank of the Ganges river, or on a seashore, in a place that is uninhabited by humans and undisturbed.
Having fashioned a stūpa out of sand measuring one Sugata-span,
and having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense according to one's means, one should empower it with eight thousand recitations of the mantra.

In this manner, by offering perfumes and other substances day after day until one thousand and eight stupas are completed, one obtains the binding of the silk ribbon (*paṭṭabandha*). One should offer eight thousand sesame seeds;
whoever one desires shall come under one's control.
Having performed worship at a reliquary containing relics, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
it will declare what is auspicious and inauspicious.
One who wishes to perform a nourishing rite should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from a milk-tree, anointed with ghee, before the Blessed One.
Then that vidyā becomes nourished;
it should be employed during the seventh stage of practice.
Having gone to a place where a *brahmarākṣasa* or another being who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) resides,
one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
It bestows a great treasure.
Subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should recite the mantra for one year at a shrine containing relics.
Having installed the cloth-painting (paṭa) in that very place, [one should proceed].
Having fasted for three nights on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having performed a magnificent worship and presented an offering,
one should kindle a fire in front of the cloth painting.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
the yakṣas, headed by Kubera, will arrive.
One must not be afraid, and [the rite] should be maintained.
Having formed a firm ball of clay into a cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) upon it and grasped it with the hand, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes.
In the meantime, it pacifies the suffering of all those in the hells and the animal realm.
Assemblies of vidyādharas gather,
and then, having paid homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, it should be taken up.
Followed by the vidyādharas, he goes to the city of the vidyādharas;
he becomes a king of the vidyādharas,
and all the vidyādharas worship him.
One becomes a dweller for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
By this method, specific weapons such as the discus, sword, and mallet are to be accomplished.
If this vidyā, while being practiced, is not perfected;
Having performed worship of that [image] and of the Blessed Buddha in front of the cloth painting (paṭa) together with this mantra,
one should recite it eight thousand times;
there, one should sleep upon a bed of kuśa grass.
In whatever place one seeks that which is deficient or excessive, there, accompanied by a yakṣa and a yakṣiṇī, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).
Having smeared a mandala there, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds.
She comes;
she may be addressed as desired;
when requested, she bestows [the gift].
By eating that, one's lifespan becomes equal to a kalpa.
If, however, it does not come,
one should perform the rite for seven nights.
He approaches.
Then, if one desires to perform a rite of pacification, one should offer eight thousand oblations of milk or sprinkle with scented water before the Blessed One;
peace is attained.
One should wipe away a snakebite with a sprout or a peacock's eye;
one becomes free from poison.
Having ascended the peak of an anthill, fasting and standing on one leg, one should recite [the mantra] from the forenoon until the afternoon.
The karma to be experienced in this very life is exhausted;
at that place where one stands,
there is prior service.
Having gone there and smeared a mandala, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds;
the yakṣas will arrive.
One should then present an offering of water with fragrant scents using the flask previously prepared.
The yakṣas said, "What should be done? We have been summoned. [He] replied, "It should be said: 'O yakṣas, may you be obedient to my commands.'"
Having said, "So be it," the yakṣas disappear;
they become accomplished and grant whatever one seeks.
They provide divine elixirs of taste and medicinal preparations. Then, even for one surrounded by a thousand followers, they provide food endowed with the six flavors,
whatever he seeks.

He bestows all of that. Thus, for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), having fasted for three nights, performed the protection rites (*kṛtarakṣa*), and being well-restrained, one should offer eight thousand pellets of *guggulu* resin, soaked in ghee, into smokeless embers before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), using either of the two black [substances].
At midnight, a deity arrives;
one should say [to her],
"Give me the medicinal herb."
Or, for one who seeks something,
if one who desires clothing offers eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass stalks smeared with ghee,
one obtains garments.

Having consecrated *vacā* root eight thousand times with mantras and placed it in one's mouth, one becomes the winner in all legal disputes. Having recited [mantras] over fragrant oil, one should smear it on the face.
In royal courts, one becomes the superior disputant;
having consecrated collyrium eight thousand times with mantras, one should apply it to the eyes,
and one will become the superior disputant in legal proceedings.
Or during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
having placed *śrotāñjana* in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra for that long.
As for the phrase "until he is liberated":
having performed the nourishment and having established protection, one should empower the collyrium eight thousand times and then apply it to the eyes.
One becomes invisible.
If one offers a hundred thousand oblations before the cloth painting with all kinds of perfumes,
one beholds Śrī.
Whatever boon one seeks,
that one obtains;
as a silent one subsisting on alms, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
He becomes invisible.
Having smeared a mandala in front of the cloth painting and having scattered flowers upon it,
Seven mouthfuls of water, consecrated seven times, should be drunk for seven days;
one becomes wise,
and what was previously studied is not lost.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over a karṣa of *brahmī* juice and a karṣa of milk, it should be drunk;
day by day, one's intelligence increases.
For as long as twenty-one nights, he maintains and receives five hundred [mantras].
For protection, water consecrated by reciting [the mantra] seven times should be applied to the head.
The binding of the maṇḍala:
one effects possession by means of stakes of *khadira* wood over which the mantra has been recited twenty-one times, and by means of *guggulu* incense.
Medical treatment for poison is performed with a small knife, or the destruction of planetary influences (*graha*) is achieved with a sprout.
One should bathe those seized by planetary spirits with white flowers or guggulu incense over which the mantra has been recited seven times. A thread should be tied [around them].
One should offer oblations of white mustard seeds mixed with sesame and smeared with ghee.
One becomes eloquent.
At night, there is a fire offering (homa).

On the full moon day, at a reliquary (caitya) containing relics, having respectfully smeared a mandala, one should recite the mantra while offering eight full jars, eight flower garlands, and burning incense of agallochum, turuṣka, sandalwood, and kunduru. One should continue the recitation for that duration.
Then, it bestows the accomplishment of the body.
At a reliquary containing relics, one who subsists on milk and barley gruel should perform worship according to one's means and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one then becomes capable of performing rites such as paralyzing and deluding.
Subsisting on barley meal, one should descend into a river up to the depth of the shoulders and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One becomes highly proficient in the applications of subjugation, invisibility, and [the manipulation of] stones and other such objects.
One should offer cotton seeds as an oblation at the abode of the nāgas;
the nāgas will become submissive,
and whatever one seeks, that one obtains.
Having consecrated a finger from the right hand eight times with the mantra,
one should threaten an elephant;
it becomes submissive.

By this very procedure, one may paralyze elephants, tigers, buffaloes, and so forth. Through the oblation of sesame seeds, there is the subjugation of men and women; through the sale of [the empowered] rice, there is protection—namely, protection for oneself and protection for others;
and with [rice] consecrated seven times, there is the binding of the topknot.
In battle, in the royal court, or in dispute, victory comes to one who recites this mantra.

If one desires to perform an empowerment for oneself, one should take four jars filled with water from a river, a pond, or a spring that is not in its natural season, or otherwise, having cast all types of fragrant seeds into them and consecrated them eight thousand times with the mantra,
one should sprinkle oneself with that water.
One becomes completely freed from all obstacles, Vināyakas, and misfortune.
In the case of a Piśāca fever, one should sprinkle [the patient] with scented water over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times;
he will become healthy.
Having prepared a *vetāḍa* by means of well-consecrated stakes of *khadira* wood and *vālāśallaka* facing east,
and having stationed men with swords in their hands in great effort in the four directions, one should proceed.
Having sat upon the heart of the Vetāḍa,
one should offer iron filings with an iron *sruva* ladle;
from its mouth, the tongue emerges.
Having cut that [cord] with a sharp weapon,
there arises a sword resembling a blue lotus;
by grasping it, one flies up together with one's retinue.
He becomes a king of the Vidyādharas and lives for eleven hundred million years;
when his time has passed, he is reborn among the gods.
Having fashioned a *muṇḍi* made of *puṣpaloha* endowed with the proper characteristics,
and having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) before the cloth painting, one should consecrate it for seven nights; then,
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for three nights and performed a magnificent worship, one should offer a thousand oblations (*sahasrasampātāhuti*) before the Blessed One.
Having performed the ritual offerings, the protection rites, the binding of the maṇḍala, the binding of the boundary, and so forth, and having fed the noble Saṅgha according to one's ability,
one should prostrate at their feet.
Having obtained the permission of the noble Saṅgha, one dies.
Having placed a heap of white mustard seeds before the cloth painting,
one should recite the mantra over the heap and then offer it.
It effects the expulsion of all planetary influences (*graha*).
By means of *guggulu* incense, it pacifies all untimely deaths and arrests all winds and clouds.
By casting mustard seeds while reciting the mantra (*jāpa*), [these effects are achieved].
With firm resolve, one should cast [the mantra] into the sky;
this is the suppression of all clouds.
A stake of khadira wood, consecrated seven times with the mantra, should be driven in.
One becomes free from poison.
In all cases of strife, quarrels, disputes, and litigation, one should take a five-colored thread, empower it eight hundred times with the mantra,
and wear it on a hidden part of the body.
All strife, quarrels, conflicts, and disputes become paralyzed. For all types of poison, water consecrated seven times with mantras should be given;
one becomes free from poison.
One who desires wealth and pleasure,
being pure and dressed in clean garments, having fasted for a day and night, should offer kunduruka incense before the cloth painting;
it will speak of what is auspicious or inauspicious in a dream.
One obtains seven thousand *rūpakas*.

For the purpose of enjoyment, one who desires wealth should establish the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) at the confluence of rivers, in one of the ponds, or in some other pure location, and having used the ashes from the breaking of all mudrās, should commence the recitation (*jāpa*) and fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee,
or two hundred thousand;
thereupon, one attains all desires.
By performing three hundred thousand homas, one bestows a kingdom;
by performing twenty-one thousand homas, one becomes a great lord of wealth.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu pills smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
For twenty-one nights,
prosperity arises;
one obtains a thousand dīnāras.
It should be thrown against a wall;
all enemies will be paralyzed.
Having made a circle of cow dung, [it should be cast].
Having taken the thread and placed it in the center of the mandala, and having offered guggulu incense,
one should recite the mantra.
If he lives,
the thread moves;
if he does not live, it does not move.
Having smeared a mandala with cow dung,
measuring four cubits in size, and having offered flowers and incense, one should remain standing right there and recite the mantra to paralyze enemies.
Having recited the mantra over a weapon seven times, it should be buried in the earth;
all karkoṭakas will be severed.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times over a staff, it should be cast against the enemy army;
one becomes invulnerable,
and it destroys epilepsy.
Having kindled the fire with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks,
one should offer oblations of black sesame seeds mixed with white *karavīra* flowers;
the seizure-demon of epilepsy will perish.
In all fevers, a black thread should be tied [around the patient].
Against all *grahas* and *ḍākinīs*, a blue thread should be tied.
For the cutting away of portents, foul odors, pustules, sores, and iron-stains, white clay is used.
When there is an eclipse of the moon or sun for all sentient beings, having observed a fast, one should recite the mantra over oil;
with that oil, one should smear the face.
One should enter the enemy's camp;
a mind of loving-kindness will arise.
By this very procedure, having consecrated eight thousand recitations of the Pratisarā mantra, [one should act].
Having bound it on the hand,
one may enter into battle;
one becomes unconquered.
Having risen at dawn and prepared a cow-dung mandala before a shrine containing relics,
one should measure out two handfuls of water, reciting the mantra over each one seven times.
One should drink without speaking.
At the time of the morning meal, one should eat after first reciting the mantra three times over the food.
At the evening meal, one should sleep after reciting it one hundred and eight times.
All one's actions are purified;
there is purity of speech;
and day by day, one masters a hundred verses.
In this manner, having consecrated water seven times over seven days, one then achieves mastery over the finger;
thereafter, one can summon [beings] with the finger.
Whoever touches it becomes submissive.
Having consecrated clay with the mantra, it should be applied as a binding.
If one is bound, it shall be severed. For abdominal pain, one should recite [the mantra] seven times over the hand and wipe [the afflicted area];
one will become healthy.
Having recited [the mantra] three times over the corner of the robe, the corner of the robe should be tied;
thus the thieves become bound.
Having recited [the mantra] over oil, it should be applied to the body.
Whatever one gives, that one receives.
Having made a mandala of cow dung,
and having filled an iron vessel strewn with flowers with ashes, [one should proceed].
Having placed it in the center of the mandala and having recited the mantra over the brush one hundred and eight times,
one should stand upon it.
Having offered guggulu incense,
one should snap the fingers while reciting the mantra;
the thief goes wherever one draws a mandala with ashes.
He becomes submissive.

For the immobilization of all beings, one should, while focusing the mind on the rite, kindle a fire before the cloth-painting with wood from a Bodhi tree on the day of the full moon during the bright fortnight, and offer eight thousand sesame seeds as an oblation.
One becomes subject [to control].
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times over a stake made of khadira wood,
one should bury it in the four directions.
The binding of the boundary is accomplished; the binding of the mandala is accomplished;
and by water over which the mantra has been recited twenty-one times, there is the expulsion of sentient beings.
If one recites [the mantra] with mustard seeds before an angry person, that person becomes appeased. Furthermore, if one desires to bring a king under one's influence,
one should offer ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of *arka* wood, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, before the cloth painting.
One becomes submissive.
This is the ritual for subduing with the finger:
having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes before the cloth painting, [one performs the rite].
Having placed the ring finger of the right hand upon seven *aśvattha* leaves,
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
then, one gives gold coins and garments to a third party for oneself.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter;
one becomes possessed of great intelligence.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *nāgakeśara* flowers.
One becomes a maiden.
One should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers;
one obtains garments.
By one hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a rememberer of past lives;
seven hundred diseases are cured. By subsisting on milk and barley gruel for one hundred thousand recitations, one has completed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
Having fasted for three nights on the eighth day of the bright fortnight and having performed a grand worship of the cloth painting,
one should recite the mantra until a ray of light issues forth.
Then he becomes a perfected one (siddha);
whatever he contemplates in his mind— whether sovereignty or the state of a vidyādhara—
he obtains that.
Merely by reciting it, all evil friends are paralyzed;
all obstacles and Vināyakas are destroyed.
Having wrapped [the object] with a red thread and placed it within a pair of earthenware bowls, one should perform worship before a reliquary containing relics or before an image.
One should recite until the threefold accomplishment occurs:
when [the mantra] becomes warm, one travels five hundred yojanas by walking on foot.
All those who walk upon his feet become subject to him;
when smoke issues [from the fire], he becomes invisible;
and he should not touch the ground with his feet by more than four finger-breadths.
He lives for a thousand years,
travels a thousand yojanas,
and possesses the strength of ten men.
If it blazes, he lives for three kalpas;
he becomes a vidyādhara and becomes invincible.
On a full moon day of the fifteenth, one who observes the poṣadha vows should offer ten thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the cloth painting.
Then, a divine woman rises from the fire-pit and grants a boon.
One should take [the image] as one's mother or sister;
from that time forward, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley, one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion, having fasted for three nights, on the fifteenth day, one should perform worship before a reliquary containing relics or before an image.
One should recite the mantra before the Blessed One on a bed of aśvattha leaves until a woman of divine form appears;
having offered her the arghya water, one should request a boon.
She bestows food, ornaments, and clothing;
one lives for a thousand years during a lunar eclipse.
Having taken the fresh butter from a cow that has a calf of the same age,

and having fashioned a small image measuring six finger-breadths, one who has fasted for four meals, having prepared a bed of *aśvattha* leaves, should recite the mantra eight thousand times and then consume [the butter].
All kings become submissive.
Taking a piece of *kanakavīcikā* and *manaḥśilā*,
one who observes the *poṣadha* vow should perform a magnificent worship on the full moon day of the fifteenth.
One should strike the heart with eight thousand fragrant flowers;
for the remainder of the time, one should recite the mantra continuously.
One will obtain five hundred dīnāras.
Having performed worship while observing the *poṣadha* fast,
one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
it reveals auspicious and inauspicious matters in dreams.
One should offer oblations of items anointed with ghee three times a day for seven days;
one should recite the mantra eight thousand times. This brings even a king under one's control.
Having kindled a fire with wood from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one should pierce a doll made of *madana* wood adorned with all ornaments with a needle and heat it so that it does not melt.
By reciting the mantra eight hundred times at the three junctions of the day, one can summon [the target] even from the underworld (*pātāla*).
Having fashioned a six-finger-long wooden statue of a girl out of *aśoka* wood,
and having taken it,
he ascended a mountain peak.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains a village;
by reciting it two hundred thousand times, one performs whatever actions one desires.
By reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, one exhausts the obscurations of karma;
by reciting it four hundred thousand times, Noble Mañjuśrī grants a vision;
and by reciting it five hundred thousand times, the purification of a buddha-field occurs.
By reciting six hundred thousand times, one is reborn in whichever world-system one desires.
By reciting seven hundred thousand times, one attains a dhāraṇī.
One who wishes to arrest fire should recite [the mantra] over a strip of cloth seven times.
It should be thrown into the mouth;
in water, this same success is achieved.
In a dispute, one should take a thread and empower it by reciting the mantra eight hundred times.
Three knots should be made; the respondent becomes [successful]. Having placed a pala of cow's ghee in a vessel on the fifteenth day,
Having offered a maṇḍala made of cow dung and agarwood incense before the noble Mañjuśrī,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and drink [the water].
Having drunk it, one must not sleep.
One becomes intelligent.

For seven days, by means of recitation (*jāpa*), there is the dispatching of fevers, the dispatching of spirits, self-protection, the raising of *vetāḍas*, entry into caves, entry into forests, protection, the binding of boundaries, and the binding of the directions; thieves, tigers, and *ḍākinīs* are paralyzed.
One who desires to become invisible should empower the root of *śatāvarī* one thousand times with mantras and bind it [to oneself];
one becomes invisible.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before the painted cloth (*paṭa*).
Then, having purchased *śatapuṣpā* flowers at a heroic price, one should offer them as oblations smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Whatever the price for which they were purchased may be, the result becomes a hundredfold that amount.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed for seven days.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *sumana* wood for seven days;
one then obtains wealth.
One should recite [the mantra] for one month before a cloth painting;
one will obtain four dīnāras.
Having consecrated a marīca fruit seven times with the mantra and placed it in the mouth, one may converse with whomever one chooses.
One who considers himself to have a son should place [the substance] before a Buddha image in a reliquary containing relics and cast it into water;
for fishermen, there will be no fish.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *śephālikā* flowers.
One should apply incense made from horse dung over which the mantra has been recited seven times; thus, bedbugs will not appear.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times over a flower or a fruit, mosquitoes do not appear;
this is a method for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
It effects entry at the king’s gate, the chewing of a tooth-stick, the offering of fruit, the offering of perfume, the binding of the ground, and the binding of thieves.
It paralyzes all fangs, causes paralysis [of others], shatters fetters, paralyzes water, paralyzes fire,

cleanses poison, transmits poison, binds poison, subjugates spirits, and releases one from the grasp of *ḍākinīs* and seizing demons. Having written this with *gorocanā* on birch bark for one whose knowledge has been lost, one should recite it one hundred times before the Blessed One at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing sacred relics.
At dawn it becomes full.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times over white mustard seeds, one should scatter them in a village or a city;
those who dwell there [will be affected].
They sleep as if dead until sunrise. [This rite is for one] desiring to bring under control a woman or a man, in whichever direction or part of the house that person's home is situated.
Facing that direction at an improper time, one should recite it eight thousand times and then go to sleep;
she will grant a vision.
In this manner, for seven days, she becomes submissive.

By sprinkling water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, the mouths of all fanged creatures are bound. By binding the medicinal herbs with the mind, one achieves the binding of a treasure-store; one should bury stakes of *khadira* wood at twenty-one locations for treasures and in the four corners. Thus, one remains for an eon, honored by all accomplished adepts (*siddhas*). The same ritual procedure applies to obtaining alms-bowls, swords, water-pots, and so forth.

During a lunar eclipse, a monk should cause [the mantra] to be heard by all these [beings]. He becomes a dweller of the kalpa, a celibate practitioner whose course is unimpeded, and he wanders at will.
Subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel, he should recite it two hundred thousand times; he obtains eight villages.
Wherever he desires, there he remains.
Having installed the cloth painting on the seashore, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
the Sāgara Nāga King will then lead one into his own abode.
One seeks the wish-fulfilling gem;
once it is grasped, one becomes capable of performing all activities and even goes to the buddha-field of the Tathāgata.
Abiding for an eon,
he is unimpeded.
One should tie knots with a thread spun by a maiden that has been consecrated eight thousand times.
All obstacles and impediments will be destroyed.

Subsisting on alms, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times on a riverbank. Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite it one hundred thousand times at the confluence of rivers.
He becomes invisible;
he becomes the master of all means of invisibility.
Having taken a bowl that is in accordance with the Vinaya regulations, he—
Seated cross-legged before the cloth painting, holding a bowl with his right hand,
he should recite the mantra until it blazes;
then he becomes a vidyādhara.
Thus, wherever one shall abide, there growth occurs;
in this way, immeasurable qualities come to be.
Now, if one desires to perform a rite of pacification,
one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times over fragrant flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
supreme pacification will occur.
For the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*):
having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks from milk-trees, [one should offer] sesame, rice, mung beans, black gram, and so forth, along with women who have been anointed with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should offer eight thousand oblations;
supreme nourishment will ensue,
whether with or without the cloth-painting.
One who maintains the poṣadha vows, has taken refuge in the Three Jewels, and possesses the bodhicitta should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Then, on the full moon day or during a lunar eclipse, having offered a bali-oblation for all desired aims and having fasted for a day and night, one should recite it throughout the entire night.
Thereupon, he becomes capable of all rites;
he becomes unimpeded in all directions;
and by a mere summons, he brings the dead back to life.
One should send water over which the mantra has been recited seven times;
having drunk it, the afflicted person becomes healthy.
For the flight of seizing spirits (grahas), one should perform a thousandfold oblation of mustard seeds.
Having installed the cloth-painting at the entrance of an asura cave, one who remains under strict discipline should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then an asura maiden will emerge and lead one inside.
Having placed it in the mouth, one should recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment is attained;
when it becomes warm, there is subjugation.
When it emits smoke, one becomes invisible;
when it blazes, one travels through the sky.
Having installed the cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics, [one performs the rite].
Beginning on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses;
one becomes a king.
One should have a staff made of red sandalwood, sixteen or twelve finger-breadths in length, fashioned by a craftsman who observes the *poṣadha* vows.
Then, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times in front of the cloth painting.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should perform a magnificent worship on the full moon day.
Holding a wooden staff in the right hand,
one should recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
When it becomes warm, one becomes a superior debater among all disputants;
when it emits smoke, one becomes invisible;
and when it blazes, one travels through the sky.
Having wrapped oneself entirely in a white cloth,
one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth.
One flies up with a retinue of a thousand;
one should recite in front of the cloth painting until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
In front of a cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of apāmārga wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
a king or one of royal rank will become submissive.
Subsisting on milk or vegetables and observing the poṣadha vows, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times at a shrine containing relics.
Then, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds;
one obtains a thousand *kārṣāpaṇa* coins.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills before the painting.
Whichever one desires among men or women,
one brings them under control.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu pills.
Whatever one desires,
one becomes beloved by all people and becomes a superior debater in the royal court.
One should anoint oneself with [the substance] consecrated eight thousand times;
one will become fortunate.

In front of the cloth painting, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, bathing three times a day, and changing one's garments three times, [one should practice].
While burning agallochum, turuṣka, and sandalwood, one should present the *triśukla* offering; having presented an external *bali* for all spirits (*sarvabhūtika*),
one should offer fragrant flowers— whether aquatic or terrestrial— and fragrant food offerings, as well as three lamps of cow's ghee.
Having fasted for three nights, one should perform the recitation throughout the entire night;
whatever one prays for, that one obtains.
And a communal meal for the Saṅgha should be provided according to one's ability.
Having installed the painting in a shrine containing relics,
one who has fasted for three nights should offer thirty-two thousand oblations of *ariṣṭa* wood fuel smeared with curds, honey, and ghee.
Then, flames issue forth from the cloth, the earth trembles, and the flame of a lamp emerges.
A garland of flowers moves;
by these signs, one becomes successful.

Having placed *śrotāñjana* between the leaves of an *aśvattha* tree and having offered it into the fire a thousand times with the ritual oblations (*sampāta*), one is freed from great diseases by reciting [the mantra] once for six months.
One should recite [the mantra] for one month; thus, one becomes one who has fulfilled the vow.
By means of guggulu incense, one causes the victim of a bite to enter [into possession].

For the purpose of subjugating women, one should offer twenty-one oblations of lalāṭā smeared with honey before the cloth painting for seven nights, three times each day, during fevers that recur every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, and so forth;
they will become submissive.
In the same way, for a widow or a man,
one should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before a painted image.
She becomes submissive.
For kings, queens, and others, one should offer oblations of salt at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one nights;
they will become submissive.
Having empowered one's head seven times with three [recitations] at the king's gate, one should enter;
one will become a favorite of the king.
Having empowered a peacock's eye with a hundred [recitations], [one should apply it].
One should wipe away poison;
it is destroyed.
Having placed realgar between the leaves of an aśvattha tree, [one should apply it].
One should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
it removes sciatica. For one afflicted by fever, one should perform a cleansing with *kuśa* grass and tie on a thread spun by a virgin.
One becomes fortunate.
If one offers one hundred thousand *karṇikāra* flowers as an oblation,
one obtains twelve *koṭis* of garments.
Having fashioned a wheel made of *puṣpaloha* and having installed a cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics,
one should fast for a day and night and perform a magnificent worship.
Having taken up the wheel, one should recite the mantra until signs appear;
sparks of light issue forth from the wheel.
It continues until it blazes;
then, success is attained,
and all the hosts of vidyādharas assemble.
Accompanied by his retinue,
he flies up as a king of the Vidyādharas,
remaining for an eon.
With unimpeded movement,
having risen in the morning,
one should recite [the mantra] for one year.
He becomes a granter of boons.
One should recite [the mantra] twenty-one hundred thousand times before the painting;
a vidyādhara should recite it eleven hundred thousand times.
One beholds Noble Mañjuśrī;
having recited [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times before the cloth painting,
one becomes invisible.
One who is afflicted by disease should recite [the mantra] twenty-one hundred thousand times before the painting;
the disease will perish.
One who has completed the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) should recite it one million two hundred thousand times.
Or one obtains a medicinal elixir;
having consumed it, one becomes free from wrinkles and gray hair.
Having recited [the mantra] two hundred thousand times, [one attains this].
One should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds;
the queen becomes submissive,
and within seven nights, she becomes a provider of wealth for him.
Excluding anything associated with sensual desire,
one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel before the cloth painting;
one will obtain one hundred *pala* of gold.
One should offer eight thousand parched grains for seven nights; no obstacles will arise. One should offer eight thousand portions of oil-cake.
He becomes beloved by all people;
among three requests, he obtains whatever he desires.
Whether it be the state of a Vidyādhara or a kingdom, I shall become exactly as the Blessed One is.
This accomplishment is achieved by one who gives gifts with a compassionate mind, free from worldly desire, for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having fasted for a day and night and performed a grand worship of the cloth painting (paṭa),...
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* fuel-sticks;
whoever one desires will arrive in that very instant.
Having ground equal parts of agallochum, *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgakesara* into powder, [one should proceed].
Having placed it in a hollowed-out leaf-cup and having consecrated it eight thousand times before the southern image of Maheśvara,
Having smeared one's body with that [substance], one should offer eight thousand oblations in battle while reciting the mantra;
one becomes invincible and shall not suffer untimely death.
By offering eight thousand *nāgapuṣpa* flowers before the cloth painting, a king becomes submissive.
For all diseases, one should take earth from a malignant ulcer, empower it seven times with the mantra, and apply it;
[the disease] will be pacified.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and purified the body with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should bathe three times a day and subsist on milk. Then, before the original cloth painting (*mūlapaṭa*), one should perform eight hundred recitations (*japa*).

Afterwards, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having made offerings according to one's ability, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass before the painting and offer eight thousand oblations of *vilva* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
A ray of light issues from the head of Noble Mañjuśrī;
having circumambulated the practitioner, it disappears into the image of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, one beholds Noble Mañjuśrī.
If he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin),
then the practitioner’s hut blazes forth;
by the swaying of the garland of flowers, he becomes a regional king (māṇḍalika).
Having prepared a mandala with white sandalwood in front of the cloth painting, and having offered perfumes, incense, flowers,

sacrificial food (bali), and ointments, one should take three hundred kesara flowers, light three ghee lamps consecrated eight hundred times, kindle a fire with fuel-sticks of udumbara wood, and then offer the flowers— one by one— after each has been consecrated eight hundred times, anointed with ghee.
Whoever desires [this] comes under one's control within seven nights.
For one who recites it three times a day, the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya) become attenuated.
By reciting it one hundred and eight times every day, even the killing of a Brahmin becomes attenuated.
By constant recitation, one obtains whatever village one desires;
whoever is seen by one's eye comes under one's control;
and by reciting during a debate, one becomes the victor.
One should offer sesame and mung beans to produce wealth.
One should offer eight thousand tips of banyan shoots after performing prostrations to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; one should then recite [the mantra] ten times.
One obtains the power of divine hearing.
One should have the noble Mañjuśrī painted on a cloth or a leaf using colors that do not adhere [to the surface] according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed worship before him, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Sleeping on a bed of *kuśa* grass, subsisting on milk and barley gruel, bathing three times a day, and dressed in clean garments, one should perform the recitation while observing the eightfold *poṣadha* vow, beginning from the first lunar day until the fifteenth;
thereafter, it pacifies the disease.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), subsisting on milk and cow urine or on barley gruel (*yāvaka*), bathing three times a day, and observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should install the cloth painting (*paṭa*) in a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*). Every day, ghee lamps should be lit and worship should be performed with a thousand lotuses.
Recitation (*japa*) should be offered during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
The practice should be commenced on the first day of the bright fortnight.
Having fasted for three nights and performed a magnificent worship on the full moon day, the recitation should be carried out throughout the entire night.
As soon as it blazes, one flies up into the sky and becomes a Vidyādhara.
Surrounded by a retinue of a thousand Vidyādharas, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old with curled, ringlet-like hair, he is invincible to all Vidyādharas.

One may effect possession by means of incense, the destruction of calamities by means of a sprout, and self-protection by means of recitation (*japa*). Beginning on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and continuing until the fifteenth, one who is pure, dressed in clean garments, and observing the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-poṣadha*), shall obtain whatever he seeks before the painted cloth (*paṭa*).
Having consecrated clarified butter (*ghṛta*) one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should drink it.
For seven days one becomes intelligent.
One should offer eight thousand *mallikā* flowers before the painting for seven nights.
Wealth is produced.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for three nights, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of *udumbara* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains five hundred *dīnāras*.

A blind person, observing the poṣadha fast on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, should light eight thousand lamps and offer eight hundred lamp-wicks as a burnt offering. Thereafter, the recitation should be performed; through this, one regains one's sight.
A deaf person, having caused a book to enter a perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭī), should offer eight thousand oblations of lotuses consecrated eight thousand times with mantras;
peace will ensue.
Before the cloth painting (paṭa), one should offer eight thousand oblations of jasmine flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

Peace is attained. One who has completed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) should, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, install the cloth painting in a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), perform a great worship, present a magnificent offering (*bali*), and after presenting an outer offering for all spirits (*sarvabhautika-bali*), he should fashion a small image (*puttalikā*) with priyaṅgu powder and draw [the deity].
Having performed the binding of the mandala and the binding of the directions, seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass, one should recite [the mantra] until a meteor falls;
then one should recite again until the cloth [painting] trembles,
and other signs of accomplishment will also appear.
Then, having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he flies up;
he becomes a vidyādhara,
able to assume any form at will, and can hear from a distance of a thousand yojanas.

He becomes invincible to all vidyādharas. Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and having performed a grand worship, one should take all unbroken rice grains, adorn them with perfumes and flowers, fumigate them with incense, and taking them in the right hand,
recite the mantra until they burst into flames.
Having placed *rocanā* before the image of Noble Mañjuśrī on the cloth, one should recite the mantra until it blazes;
then it should be taken up.
By the mere act of taking it up, one becomes possessed of the strength of a *nāga*.
The weapons of others have no power over him;
whoever he directs with this mantra comes under his control,
and he lives for three hundred years.

Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire in front of the cloth painting with wood from the *bilva* tree and offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks smeared with pungent oil.
For seven days, whichever maiden one desires shall become submissive.

Having fasted for one night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should go to a cremation ground, smear a mandala with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, take an unbroken skull-cup, wash it with red sandalwood paste,
and worship it with red flowers and incense. Then, sitting there while reciting the mantra, one should summon [the desired object] using that skull-cup.

As long as the skull-cup moves, one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Whomever one draws toward oneself with a finger, that person comes and performs all those tasks. One who desires to effect pacification (*śānti*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before the cloth painting (*paṭa*);
thereafter, the painting will move.
Or, if a statue of the Tathāgata moves,
the accomplishment of the rite occurs within a kalpa.
One should consecrate a blue cloth with one hundred and eight recitations and tie it into a knot.
The wrestler will be victorious.
If ashes consecrated twenty-one times are placed upon the wrestler's head,
he will be victorious in battle.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should place [the medicine] together with ghee and milk in a copper vessel before the cloth painting, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and drink it for seven days;
one will become a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
This occurs if a ray of light issues forth from the mudrā of the noble Mañjuśrī.
Having circumambulated it clockwise along with its receptacle, one ascends;
one becomes a vidyādhara,
able to assume any form at will and unimpeded, and lives for three thousand years.

Having fasted for a day and night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and having become fearless, one should then strike a lion with a [mantra-empowered] weapon consecrated seven times by a Vidyādhara;
thereupon, the lion lets out a lion’s roar.
The practitioner becomes motionless;
he remains conscious for the duration of a nālikā.
Then the practitioner should recite the mantra seven times.
Then one should mount the lion;
all the vidyādharas assemble,
and the lion-vehicled [practitioner], together with his retinue, flies up into the air.
Moving with the speed of mind, surrounded by many vidyādharas, and remaining for an eon,
when he dies, he is reborn wherever he desires.
The Lion Sadhana:

Furthermore, one who desires to perform the Lion Sadhana should, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, observe absolute silence and subsist on a diet of milk and barley gruel until the next full moon, reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Remaining silent and observing the *poṣadha* vows, he should take wood struck by a thunderbolt and soak it in milk for seven days.
Then, having taken white clay mixed with sandalwood water, one should bathe the wood struck by the vajra.

Thereafter, the practitioner should have a lion fashioned by a goldsmith who observes the *poṣadha* vows. Then, under the Puṣya asterism, having performed a magnificent worship of the Three Jewels, one should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha.

Having performed a grand worship before the cloth painting and offered various sacrificial oblations (*bali*), the practitioner—pure and dressed in clean garments—should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. Grasping a lion with his right hand, he should recite the mantra until it moves like a lion. When it moves, various kinds of signs arise.
Then the *argha* offering should be presented;
furthermore, it should be recited one hundred and eight times.
The mustard seeds will come forth.
While reciting the mantra, one should touch a lion;
she becomes a woman,
and she speaks.
"What shall I do? she will ask. She should be told, "Enter into my body. Thereupon, she disappears into the palm of the practitioner's hand.

At that very moment, his hair becomes curled like a ringlet, he takes on the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, possesses a radiance equal to the rising sun, holds a spear in his hand, and gains unimpeded movement.
Upon seeing whomsoever he gazes upon, he flies up into the air together with them;
furthermore, all *vidyādharas* become subject to his power.
He remains for the duration of a kalpa;
when he dies, he is reborn among the gods.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), having consecrated the cloth painting (*paṭa*) at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), and subsequently placing it within the mouth of a casket, one becomes invisible.

One lives for a thousand years. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should install the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) on a mountain peak, worship it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times. Then, having taken ashes and earth from an anthill while observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should mix them with milk and knead them together. A peacock, measuring one span of the Sugata, should be painted by a painter observing the *poṣadha* vows using colors that do not require animal glue.
Having gone to a secluded place, having installed the cloth painting, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having offered a bali-oblation for all beings,
one who is pure and clad in clean garments should then place a peacock before the painting and recite the mantra as long as the peacock does not move.

Then, the vidyādhara, holding with his right hand a pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāvasampuṭa*) filled with *aparājita* flowers over which the root-mantra has been previously recited, should recite it until the sound of jackals is heard.
While reciting the mantra, he should place living beings from among his companions into his own mouth; thus he becomes invisible.
When all the *siddhas* come to him, he lives for two thousand years.
Having made equal parts of lotus filaments, *sauvīra* collyrium, and *śilājatu*, one should have them ground by the hand of a girl observing the *poṣadha* fast.

Having encased it in the three metals and performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should, under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense, including an offering (*bali*) consisting of all kinds of spirits before an image of Maheśvara, and then place it within a pair of earthenware bowls.
Holding [the vessel] with his right hand, he should recite the mantra until it makes a crackling sound (*khaṭakhaṭāyati*).

Having offered one portion to the Blessed One and distributed the rest among his companions, he himself should offer ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* wood-fuel smeared with curds, honey, and ghee.
He will obtain ten thousand pieces of gold.
Having taken bamboo resin and made pills encased in three metals, one should then go to a cremation ground wearing clean white garments.

Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having offered a bali-oblation to all spirits, one should place the pills within a hollowed skull-cup and recite the mantra until the sound of "kilakila" is heard.
One should not be afraid. Even having separated from one's companions, by placing [the mantra] in one's own mouth, one becomes invisible and lives for ten thousand years.
Taking an owl's eye along with collyrium, one should grind it in the hand of a maiden.
Having encased it in three metals and placed the pill within a pair of earthen saucers, one draws forth a yakṣiṇī for seven nights before a worshipful image of Maheśvara.
Observing the vow of silence like a piece of wood for six months, one should recite the mantra;
one will obtain the desired object.

Having fashioned an image of Arka made of wood six finger-breadths in length, having painted it with colors that do not stick, and having adorned it with all ornaments, one should recite the mantra before it for six months.
One obtains a regional kingdom or the state of a vidyādhara.
By remaining silent before the cloth painting for six months, consecrating the palm of the left hand, and reciting the mantra ten thousand times, one obtains a well-concealed treasure.
Having descended to a river flowing toward the ocean, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *arka* flowers smeared with curds, honey, and ghee into an *arka* leaf-cup;
the Sun-god then becomes a granter of boons.
Having likewise descended to that same river with water reaching only to the waist, one should cause sesame seeds and flowers to flow downstream.
The Grandfather becomes a granter of boons;
one should offer mandāra flowers,
and Śakra becomes a granter of boons.
In that very water, with *mandārava* flowers, the Giver of Wealth (*Dhanada*) becomes a granter of boons;
by reciting the mantra two hundred thousand times, one attracts a king;
by reciting it three hundred thousand times, one attracts all sentient beings.
Having descended to a river flowing toward the ocean, one should offer ten thousand *aśoka* flowers.

Having performed a grand worship before the original cloth painting (*mūlapaṭa*), one should place a wheel or a swastika upon a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and, seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), recite the mantra until it blazes.
By merely grasping that [wheel or swastika], one becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, with hair curled in locks and a complexion like the rising sun.
One flies up together with those by whom one is seen and those whom one sees.
Having taken the *sudarśana* root, grasping it with the hand and having recited the mantra over it a thousand times, one binds it to the hand; whoever one touches becomes submissive.
Having taken a wheel made of *kuśa* grass, having recited the mantra over it a thousand times, and having cast it into water, a *nāga* emerges.
If he asks, "What shall I do?", one should say, "Give me a hundred thousand. Then, subsisting on alms-food, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
The forms of the Tathāgatas appear before one;
having seen them, whatever one seeks to accomplish is accomplished,
and women appear adorned with every ornament.
And men who seek to propitiate the Buddha attend upon him simultaneously with laughter, dance, and other such performances;
whatever he thinks of, all that comes to pass.
At dawn, once [the offerings] have been removed, everything vanishes.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over a *karṣa* of *brahmī*, a *karṣa* of *sakarṣa*, a *karṣa* of cow’s ghee, and a *karṣa* of milk, and drink it for seven days;
one will become a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*).
Having placed a basket of various kinds of food and edibles before the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra until the food has disappeared.

Afterwards, food and varieties of rice are transferred [to the practitioner]. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should fashion a sixteen-spoked wheel made of the three metals and, having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [proceed with the rite].
Having performed worship at a crossroads and sat down, one should place a piece of realgar the size of a finger-joint in the mouth and recite the mantra until the mouth cracks open;
the realgar then becomes perfected.
Having applied the *tilaka*, one becomes invisible, able to assume any form at will, and lives for five hundred years.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should have a couch, a courtesan, and a trident fashioned.

On the following eighth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should go to a cremation ground and perform a great worship of the trident. Seated in the *paryaṅka* posture and holding the trident with the right hand, one should recite the mantra until—
A ray of light issues forth from the trident;
from that, one becomes accomplished.
If one buries it at night, a divine house is produced.

Having installed the cloth painting in a clean place and fasted for a day and night, one should fashion an image before the painting, worship it according to the ritual rules, and offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Then, a ray of light will issue forth from the forehead of the Blessed Mañjuśrī.
Then one becomes accomplished.
One obtains immeasurable gold and wealth.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should take a single *karavīra* flower before the cloth painting, go to a place where *nāgas* dwell, cast the flower into a *nāga* pool, and recite the mantra.
Nāgas and nāginīs become submissive, and whatever one desires, that one obtains.

Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and fasted for a day and night, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one desiring to destroy a fever should offer eight thousand oblations of *girikarṇikā* flowers.
Piśāca fevers are destroyed.
By performing one hundred and eight oblations with *khadira* wood fuel-sticks, one causes all seizing spirits (*graha*) to release their hold.
With ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times, the Lord of Mantras binds the mantras of others.
By sprinkling water over which the mantra has been recited once, liberation is attained.
Having written [the mantra] on cloth or birch bark, one should fasten it to the top of a banner;
the enemy army will be paralyzed.
Subsisting on water and barley-meal, having fasted for three nights on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should go to a solitary linga;
placing his right foot upon the top of the linga, he should bind it with *vālaśolaka* grass. Having clenched his fist, he should recite the mantra until the sound "I am dying" emerges.
On the third night, the fist becomes perfected;
having formed the fist, one lives for seven hundred years and becomes a member of Maheśvara’s retinue.
With a forehead mark made from *gorocanā* consecrated one thousand times,
all whom one sees become submissive.
Having risen in the morning, having consecrated water seven times and washed one's face, whoever one gives a look to becomes submissive.
Likewise, one who desires food should take a handful of water, empower it seven times with the mantra, and drink it;
he will obtain food without having asked for it.
When entering a royal court, one should take a corner of one's robe, recite the mantra over it twenty-one times, and tie a knot with the left hand; thus, one becomes one whose speech is unimpeded.
One should remember [this practice] in the midst of thieves;
it also liberates those who are bound.

For mantras that are broken, split, or deficient, one should fashion an image out of *śāli* rice, *vrīhi* rice, white *karavīra*, and white mustard seeds; then, having pressed down upon it with the left hand in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
The arousal of the mantras is accomplished;
one obtains a thousand cows.
By this very procedure, while burning ghee and resin (sarjarasa), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
One obtains twelve excellent villages.
By performing this very rite and constructing a stūpa, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses anointed with sandalwood;
one will obtain sovereignty over a country.
Having constructed a stūpa measuring one span of a Sugata and burning incense, one should offer one hundred thousand *campaka* flowers;
one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold.
Having constructed a stūpa measuring one span of a Sugata, or having drawn an image, one should stand upon it with the left foot and recite the mantra eight thousand times.
One comes under control by means of the lineage.
Having constructed a stūpa measuring one Sugata-span, one should offer eight thousand oblations of wedding parched grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into the fire.
Furthermore, a protection circle is formed with the ashes.

Having bathed at dawn, one should churn butter with this very mantra, take it, perform a grand worship, and while burning incense, consume eight thousand times consecrated [butter] without touching it with the teeth; by the name of whomever [it is done], that person becomes submissive—
provided it is not consumed for the sake of sensual desire.

Having fasted for three nights and performed a grand worship of the cloth painting with all kinds of perfumes purchased from a hero-seller, one should light a ghee lamp and personally recite the mantra.
Having fashioned a doll from that [powder] and placed it upon seven *aśvattha* leaves, one should recite the mantra until it becomes supple.
Having reduced it to powder, whoever is touched by it becomes submissive.

By this very same procedure, having fashioned an image from the powder of *nāgakeśara*, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations into incense-bowls; whoever one has in mind will be brought under control. By this very same procedure, one should offer oblations of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.

One who desires wealth should go to a cow-pen, fashion a stūpa one cubit high out of fallen cow dung before a painting, worship it according to the ritual rules, and while burning guggulu incense, recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
He will become invincible to all *vidyādharas* and shall travel through the paths of the seven winds.

Taking the index finger of one who has not yet reached the age of one year, and having fashioned a *caitya* the size of a hand, one should perform a ritual worship in the cremation ground according to the rules.
Seated facing east upon a bed of *kuśa* grass and having offered that finger as an oblation, one should press down with the [other] index finger and recite the mantra until a ray of light emerges.
The lamp-flame increases.

Having performed the protection-rite and taken possession of the kingdom, at dawn he draws [the desired person] with his finger; whoever he draws becomes subject to him. Having fasted for three nights, one should take the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same age and is full of milk, and [draw a] mandala before the cloth-painting.
Having prepared a ghee lamp and lit it, and having consecrated eight thousand times a portion placed upon a bed of *kuśa* grass, one should prepare milk in an earthen vessel.
Then, a *vināyaka*-oblation should be performed with curd, honey, and ghee.
After that, having prepared a mandala, [one should invoke] the guardians of the four directions.
Having stationed the instructor in the second mandala with mustard seeds in his hand, and a good assistant in the third mandala,
one who has performed protection and offered a great worship should sit facing east; grasping [the object] with the hand, he should recite the mantra until it emits heat,
smoke, and bursts into flames.
With the first [ointment], one whose eyes are anointed—whomever he looks upon and whoever looks upon him—all of them become subject to his will.
With the second, having attained accomplishment, he possesses the strength of nine thousand elephants, has the speed of the wind, and lives for five thousand years;
he becomes a master of all vidyādharas, never to be disregarded.

If one consecrates eight thousand invisibility-grants (*antardhānikā*), they will blaze with the color of the rising sun; with a body adorned with jewels and remaining for the duration of an eon, having performed the consecration eight thousand times, one may enter into the midst of enemies and no fear shall arise,
being invulnerable to all foes.

One brings about possession with a white flower; one causes dancing with water over which the mantra has been recited three times; one effects summoning with a *karavīra* flower over which the mantra has been recited three times.
It tells of the past and the future.
Binding is released by a snap of the fingers.

Desiring to accomplish the ointment (*añjana*), one should take *sauvīrāñjana* purchased at a "hero's sale," remove any insects from it, and grind it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using a pestle with an upward-facing bowl.
Having formed four pills with the ring finger and covered them with a lotus leaf, one should dry them.

In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), having kindled a fire according to the ritual rules and performed a thousand oblations (*sahasrasampātāhuti*), and having made a grand offering at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), one should kindle the fire with *palāśa* wood from the eight directions.
One should place it on the hip region;
thus the retention of semen is accomplished.
By tying a knot with the corner of a robe-cloth over which the mantra has been recited seven times, the binding of poison is achieved.
The treatment for poison:
by means of a sprout and through the differentiation of mudrās, possession [of the patient] is effected with water;
or, by means of guggulu incense or water, the binding of seizing spirits (graha) is accomplished.
Having recited [the mantra] over a finger, whomever one threatens becomes submissive.
One should recite it one hundred and eight times before the cloth painting;
it will show things as they truly are in a dream.

Having installed a painted cloth [mandala] before a reliquary containing relics, and having performed extensive worship before it, one should kindle a fire with *bilva* wood and offer one hundred thousand oblations of white lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one will obtain a kingdom. If this is not accomplished, one obtains a village consisting of a thousand households.
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand times before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) while holding either *gorocanā* or realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
Having applied a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made with that substance, whatever one seeks, one obtains it.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for one night, one should offer eight thousand oblations at night into a fire made from the wood of the root of the cloth painting.
One obtains a thousand gold coins.
Having fasted for a day and night on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should descend into a river that flows to the ocean and offer ten thousand lotuses;
one will obtain a kingdom.

To subjugate a man, having fasted for one night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire with wood from the Bodhi tree and offer eight thousand *kumuda* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
he becomes subjugated.
To subjugate a woman, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one should strike the noble Mañjuśrī with *saugandhika* flowers.
With the intention of binding medicinal herbs, she was to drive away bipeds and quadrupeds;
she gave five dīnāras every day,
which were to be spent without remainder.
For the purpose of providing offerings to the Three Jewels,
one should recite the mantra for one month before the painted image;
one will obtain twelve thousand dīnāras.
Beginning from the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] for six months at a reliquary containing relics;
it bestows sovereignty.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should take a bud of the *śleṣmātaka* tree before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and wrap it with a red thread.

Then, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood and consecrated a ritual stake (*kīlaka*) eight thousand times, one should recite the mantra over each individual fragment twenty-one times and cast it into the fire; at dawn, one obtains hundreds of *dīnāra* coins.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for one night, one should offer eight thousand *atimuktaka* flowers for seven days.
One obtains one hundred dīnāras.
By anointing the eyes with [a substance] consecrated seven times,
one becomes beloved by all people.

Having consecrated common collyrium with mantras, whoever one first sees becomes submissive. Reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times before a painted image (paṭa) while focusing on a specific person [brings them under control].
One should recite it one hundred thousand times at the entrance of a cave.

Just as prescribed, having installed a reliquary stūpa containing the *pratītyasamutpāda* formula on a mountain peak or in a cow-pen, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; one will obtain one hundred thousand *dīnāras*.

Having installed the cloth painting (*paṭa*) at a site of the *nāgas* and performed the protective rites well, one should kindle a fire with *jambuka* wood, offer a *bali* oblation of the "three sweets," and perform eight thousand burnt offerings (*homa*) of *nāgapuṣpa* flowers.
Then a king of the nāgas, appearing in the form of a brahmin, arrives. He says:
"And you must say, 'Give seven dīnāras every day.'"
Saying "So be it," he becomes invisible.
To subjugate a general, one should smear a large mandala, take the dust from his footprints, and offer a thousand oblations with the left hand;
he will become subjugated.
For the subjugation of an ordinary woman, one should fashion an image out of salt, cut it into pieces, and offer them as oblations with the left hand;
she will become submissive.
Furthermore, for the subjugation of a female servant, one should combine *punnāga* stamens, barley, and wheat, and offer eight thousand oblations.
He becomes submissive.
Having made an image out of rice flour, one should offer it into the fire after cutting it into pieces;
he becomes submissive.
To subjugate a widow, one should offer oblations of *māṣa* beans and *jambū* fruits;
she will become submissive.

If one takes *śrotāñjana* and places it between the leaves of an *aśvattha* tree at a single sacred shrine (*caitya*), having consecrated it eight thousand times, and practices this again, one's lifespan becomes doubled.
Having entered a granary and installed the cloth-painting in a clean place, one should recite the mantra silently for one fortnight while subsisting on milk and barley-gruel.

Then, having performed a magnificent worship of the painting and presented an even more magnificent *bali* offering, one should sit in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) and recite until rays of light issue forth.
Upon seeing them, even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) come to an end.
Then one becomes accomplished;
one obtains a great kingdom and becomes without rival.
Having consecrated yellow orpiment (*rocanā*) eight thousand times with mantras and fumigated it with incense, one should place it between the teeth;
one will become a superior debater,
and all people will come under one's influence.
Having fasted for three nights on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times before the cloth painting;
one will obtain one *dīnāra*.

Having fasted for three nights before the cloth painting, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, while burning *guggulu* incense and kindling a strong fire, one should offer eight thousand *karavīra* flowers smeared with curds, honey, and clarified butter as an oblation.
Then, one should take [the substance] from the fire-pit—which is the size of a lotus—from what resembles a *karavīra* flower, appearing as realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
While reciting the mantra, it should be grasped.
By taking it, one becomes a *vidyādhara*, possessing the color of the rising sun and having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
By means of the state of equilibrium with the wind, most desirable foods arise;
one lives for eighty thousand years,
becomes inaccessible to all beings, and brings about death.
One should perform the rite before a cloth painting; by casting [the image] into one's mouth, one becomes invisible.
First, the release from bondage must be performed:

having fashioned an effigy out of honey and beeswax—whether of a woman or a man—one should kindle a fire in a secluded place and, having consecrated it with mantras, cause it to be offered into the flames.
Having pierced [the target] one hundred and eight times with a *madanakaṇṭaka* thorn, one should cause it to be given;
they become submissive,
and whatever one prays for, that one obtains.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should offer eight hundred fragrant flowers;
one will obtain five *kārsāpaṇa* coins.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should kindle a fire before the cloth painting with *priyaṅgu* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fuel sticks.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times over it, all piercing pains are pacified.
For a woman experiencing difficult labor, water should be consecrated by reciting [the mantra] eight hundred times and given to her;
she will give birth with ease.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] with an increase of one thousand repetitions each day until the fifteenth day.
At the conclusion, having fasted for three nights, one should prepare a pill by means of the *guḍikā*-formula; having consecrated it and placed it in the mouth, one becomes invisible.

One should take blue *aśoka* flowers, the bile of a black antelope, and the heart of a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), together with the essence of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*); these, in equal parts, should be wrapped in *puṣpaloha*.

Having further encased it in the three metals (*triloha*), one who desires to accomplish [the rite] should place it before a statue containing relics, having installed a cloth painting (*paṭa*) in that very spot;
then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having performed worship and placed [the substance] upon seven *aśvattha* leaves, one should prepare a mandala.

Having placed a person with uninjured limbs in its center and having stepped upon his chest with his left foot, one who has performed the protection rite should recite the mantra until [the person] rises as before. Then,
one should feed him honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having formed a fist over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one should strike it upon the head;
then one vomits,
and by drinking that [vomit], one becomes invisible.
Having fasted for three nights, one should descend into water reaching up to the navel during a lunar eclipse and recite [the mantra] until it is released;
one obtains a hundred dīnāras.
If one repeats [the practice], one obtains auspicious results.

Having bathed with water mixed with salt one hundred and eight times, having applied an unguent, and having honored [the deity] with perfumes and garlands, one should feed [the person] previously prepared milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should form a handful and strike the head;
then, [the person] vomits.
Having consumed that, one becomes a vidyādhara who remains for a great eon (mahākalpa).
Having consecrated a weapon with one hundred and eight recitations, having cut it and pulverized it, one should strike [the target];
